News.title: 'Misleading' student loans information left out examples of higher-salary repayments
News.content:
Several universities in England have only been using below-average salaries in examples of student loan repayments on their websites, the BBC has found.

Treasury Committee chair Dame Meg Hillier, who led a recent inquiry into student loans, said some information about repayments was "misleading", including one instance where they were compared to the "cost of a daily coffee".

She also said the Department for Education (DfE) must include higher-salary examples on its own website, too.

The DfE said it would review the information it provides, while universities said their websites referred to government information and would be reviewed where necessary.

Student loan repayments are tied to earnings, so the more you earn, the more you repay every month - and graduates generally go on to earn more than non-graduates.

Current and prospective students in England take out Plan 5 loans to pay for their tuition fees and living costs. They repay 9% of anything they earn over Â£25,000 for 40 years, or until the loan is paid off.

The BBC looked at publicly available information on more than 110 university websites in England and found cases of inaccurate information about the salary at which they start repaying and the length of time they repay for.

It also found that 12 universities only gave students worked examples of repayments based on earnings that are less than the UK average, which is Â£39,039.

News.title: Firms should publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law, says PM
News.content:
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.

Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".

"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.

The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.

He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.

A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary., external

Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."

News.title: Two Gloucester schools in lockdown after boy hurt in incident
News.content:
Two schools are in lockdown as armed police search for a group of people involved in an altercation that left a boy injured.

One male was seen with a "long-bladed item" during the incident outside St Peter's High School in Gloucester earlier, police said.

Armed officers are now searching for a group involved who fled the area. The force said one boy had been taken to hospital with minor injuries.

The Tuffley school and nearby Willow Primary Academy are locked down and officers asked parents not to attend. A police spokesperson said there was "no ongoing threat at the school" and pupils were safe within the school grounds.

Adam, whose daughter attends St Peter's, said he felt frightened even though he had texted her and knew she was OK.

"I don't think this should happen at school. Thank God she is safe," he said.

The school had messaged parents to say everything was under control, he added.

News.title: How unprecedented changes to the polar vortex may impact the UK's weather
News.content:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

News.title: Tube drivers to stage strikes in Christmas run-up
News.content:
About half of the drivers on the network are members of the RMT union. Many others are represented by the Aslef union.

Finn Brennan, Aslef's full-time organiser on London Underground, said: "We are surprised that the RMT has, once again, decided to take strike action to try to prevent Underground drivers moving to a four-day week on a voluntary basis.

"The voluntary four-day week gives Tube train drivers an extra 35 days off every year with rosters based on a 34-hour week in return for some changes to working conditions and moving to electronic, rather than paper-based, systems for booking on for duty.

"Management have agreed that anyone who wants to keep working a five-day week will be able to do so without suffering any detriment, and we will be holding them to that.

"A strike designed to stop people having the choice of a shorter working week and more time off is a strange choice to make."

Under the proposals, most drivers would see their working week reduced from 36 hours to 35 hours, according to TfL. Their contractual hours would remain the same because paid meal breaks would be introduced.

This effectively means drivers would work longer days, but fewer days each week and fewer overall hours each week.

The RMT instead wants a 32-hour week over four days, meaning drivers would work three fewer hours each week for the same salary.

News.title: Train worker recalls repelling attacker with frying pan
News.content:
A train staff member who used a frying pan against a man accused of trying to kill 10 people on board said he did not want to "give up until the train stopped", a court has heard.

Samir Zitouni was working on the York to London King's Cross LNER service on 1 November last year when Anthony Williams attacked, leading to an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire.

Cambridge Crown Court heard Zitouni said he was trying to hit the knife Williams was holding and "not let him pass".

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder, and four other alleged attempted murders in earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

Jurors were played a video interview with Zitouni, who watched on from the public gallery.

The court has previously heard about the injuries suffered by Zitouni during the attack.

Both his lungs were punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.

News.title: MTV Dirty Sanchez star Michael 'Pancho' Locke dies aged 47
News.content:
Tributes have been paid to Michael Locke, star of MTV stunt and prank series Dirty Sanchez, who has died aged 47.

Locke, from Port Talbot, known as 'Pancho', starred in the show, and later went on to launch the Welsh clothing brand San Portablo.

His Dirty Sanchez co-star Mathew Pritchard posted a tribute on social media, saying he "was the best" and he would "never forget him".

San Portablo, co-owned by Locke, said the TV star was an "absolute Welsh treasure" who "lived an incredible life".

News.title: Bonfire Night violence condemned as six arrested
News.content:
Six people, including three teenage boys, have been arrested after a night of violence saw fireworks and bricks launched at emergency services on Bonfire Night.

Northumbria Police said its crews had been attacked after responding to reports of anti-social behaviour in the Waterville Road area of Meadow Well in North Tyneside at about 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

A number of officers were injured, the force said, and five police cars and three fire engines were damaged.

Ch Supt Daniel Whyte said anyone else involved in the disorder should expect a "knock on the door". Ian Miller, who runs the local community centre The Meadows, said people had a right to feel safe where they live.

So far two men, aged 25 and 27, a woman aged 27 and three teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder. They all remain in custody.

Whyte said there would be an increased police presence in the area to "offer reassurance".

The force said the disorder had been linked to misinformation about a building's future as a House in Multiple Occupation (HMO).

News.title: Childminder who left more than 20 children alone in her home jailed
News.content:
A childminder who admitted leaving children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home has been jailed for two years.

More than 20 unattended children, two under the age of one, were in Amanda Mathewson's house in Dunfermline, Fife, when she was arrested in August 2024.

Her offending only came to light after concerned parents spied on her leaving for a school run without their children.

An internal Care Inspectorate probe found Mathewson, who was been licensed to look after eight children under the age of 16 at any one time, had been tipped off about inspections by an unknown staff member.

Mathewson previously pled guilty to wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health.

Sheriff John MacRitchie said Mathewson had committed a "gross abuse of a position of trust" during sentencing at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court.

He read victim impact statements from affected children who described suffering from "nightmares, anxiety and a distrust of childcare providers".

News.title: Home Office investigating after BBC catches lawyer offering to make fines go away
News.content:
The Home Office has launched an investigation after a solicitor was secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Solicitors Regulation Authority has said it will also examine the BBC's findings to see whether there has been misconduct by solicitors or law firms.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine if he was able to find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Yousaf has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

The BBC's wider investigation also revealed at least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures exclusively obtained by the BBC.

In response, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

Mahmood said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

"Illegal working undermines honest employers, undercuts local wages, and fuels organised immigration crime," she added.

The Home Office said it would be investigating the allegations to see whether there had been a breach of immigration rules.

Senior politicians have since called UK immigration enforcement "weak" and a "laughing stock".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp has called for Yousaf to be "struck off as a solicitor", while shadow justice minister Nick Timothy has written to the head of the regulator for solicitors to take "urgent action, and stop Mr Yousaf practising as a solicitor".

Philp said: "Shabana Mahmood likes to boast about how many fines are issued, but now it turns out most just get ignored. No wonder we have a borders crisis with enforcement turning into a laughing stock."

A spokesman for the Solicitors Regulation Authority said: "We will be considering this information to see if there are any issues arising which we need to look into further."

The BBC also heard from a law enforcement whistleblower who, speaking anonymously, revealed it was a struggle to identify the real owners of businesses caught with illegal workers.

She said she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

"I've said to owners 'I see you've got a fine, are you going to pay it?' And they just laugh in my face, throw the fine back in a box and say 'it's got nothing to do with me'."

News.title: Policing needs reform to cope with modern criminals, Met Police chief warns
News.content:
In his speech, Sir Mark said organised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.

"The victim remains local but increasingly the threat does not," he said citing the example of children who are "groomed by predators on another continent".

He argued that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."

Merging forces would reduce duplication and could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing, he believes.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast prior to his speech, Sir Mark said crime had changed a lot over the years but the police was largely organised how it was 60 years ago.

"Obviously the world's moved on a long way in that time."

His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.

However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".

Dorset Police and Crime Commissioner David Sidwick reiterated his strong opposition to proposals to merge the forces.

"My concern is simple. If funding is diverted away from frontline services in Dorset to establish new national structures, local communities could end up receiving less rather than more."

In addition, Kent's Conservative police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said: "[Sir Mark believes] policing should suffer a decade of disruption, that local policing services should be cut back and made more remote, and that this can all be done without ever asking the public what they want from their local police force."

The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.

It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."

Asked on Breakfast what would happen if the reforms were not put in place, Sir Mark said: "the risk is failure".

"Failure means solving fewer crimes, less local presence, when you get exceptional incidents like a certain outbreak of disorder like we saw in Hampshire."

In September police clashed with anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth when 120 migrants arrived in a single dinghy.

"Standing still looks like a degradation of policing day by day, struggling even more as criminals outpace policing because we're not organised to meet it," Sir Mark added.

A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."

Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, saying that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010, which he said was as "a big hit".

"We do need investment as well, but if you threw loads of money at the current system it's still not going to fix the fundamental problem, it's not designed to meet today's challenges," he told the BBC.

"Throwing money at the current system isn't going to work."

Sir Mark said in his speech that years of underinvestment has left forces relying on ageing technology, and officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.

He also pointed to falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.

Additional reporting by Olivia Ireland

News.title: Two boys charged over Halloween party stabbings
News.content:
Two teenage boys have been charged after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party in Hampshire.

Police were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to a home in Park Road in Chandler's Ford where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event over a garden fence.

A 16-year-old from Southampton has been charged with attempted murder. A second 16-year-old, also from Southampton, has been charged with wounding with intent.

The pair, who cannot be named due to their ages, have been remanded in custody to appear at Southampton Magistrates' Court on Friday.

News.title: Andrew received up to £2,000 per month from sub-letting, watchdog reports
News.content:
But it emerged that as a tenant he had been intermittently sub-letting three cottages that were part of the property, which was thought to be for staff and at a below market rate, with Mountbatten-Windsor keeping the income.

The Crown Estate had told MPs that it did not have any oversight over how much Mountbatten-Windsor charged - and sub-letting was allowed as part of his lease.

But the MPs have recommended that in future the default position for such Crown Estate properties should be that such sub-letting should be banned, unless there was a specific exemption.

The Public Accounts Committee report also confirms what has happened since Mountbatten-Windsor's departure from Royal Lodge.

There was a payment of about Â£300,000 due to him for his early surrender of his lease, but because of "dilapidations" in the state of the building, there was a repair bill of Â£1.8m.

That meant the Crown Estate was owed Â£1.5m, which King Charles paid on his brother's behalf.

The watchdog's report also highlighted concerns about the level of rent being charged to non-working royals who had been given accommodation in three royal properties.

That was believed to be Mountbatten-Windsor's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and Prince and Princess Michael of Kent.

A National Audit Office report had revealed earlier this year that Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie do not pay anything themselves for their accommodation in St James's Palace and Kensington Palace respectively.

The King pays their rent to the Royal Household from his own private income.

But the group of MPs were concerned about whether the level of rent on such properties for non-working royals was based on up-to-date valuations and recommended a more consistent approach to ensure value for money.

There was criticism too for the Crown Estate concentrating too much of its urban property portfolio in London and the south east of England, with MPs calling for more of a regional spread.

There were also warnings about how the Crown Estate's administration costs had increased significantly, at a time when MPs noted government budgets were under pressure.

The report said administration costs had risen by 129% since 2020-21 and that the chief executive, Dan Labbad's salary had risen by 106% over that time. In 2025-26 his pay package was worth Â£2.3m.

In response, a Crown Estate spokeswoman said: "The Public Accounts Committee report is an important part of our accountability to Parliament. We are considering its findings and recommendations and will respond to the Committee in due course."

News.title: Huntingdon train worker used frying pan in attempt to stop knifeman’s frenzied attack
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A staff member on board a train on which a knifeman stabbed 10 people picked up a frying pan in an attempt to stop the attacker, a court has heard.

Anthony Williams, 33, has denied 10 counts of attempted murder in relation to the attack, on a London-bound LNER service, which made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon on 1 November 2025.

He has also denied four other counts of attempted murder relating to earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

Samir Zitouni, who was working in a kitchen area on the train, said “my thinking was try to hit the knife, to drop his knife”.

In a video-recorded police interview played at Cambridge Crown Court on Friday, Mr Zitouni, who was stabbed during the incident, said he was “in the kitchen doing my job” when the door to the galley opened and there was a crowd of people.

open image in gallery Samir Zitouni armed himself with a frying pan to try to stop Anthony Williams’s rampage ( British Transport Police )

“They were terrified and shouting ‘there’s a guy with a knife’,” he said.

“It was difficult to believe. I remember telling them ‘a guy with a knife, are you sure?’.”

He said he recalled “thinking I can’t go without anything – I was thinking about the frying pan”, and he grabbed it.

He said when Williams arrived, “the first thing I saw was the blade”.

Mr Zitouni said he “tried to hit the knife” but he was stabbed, and he said he did not remember parts of the incident.

He said he “was terrorised” and “it was hard to believe… my thinking was try to hit the knife, to drop his knife”.

He tried to defend “first myself as I was next to him and not to let him pass until the train stopped”.

Mr Zitouni said: “I didn’t want to give up until the train stopped.”

The witness, whose left arm was in a sling during the 16 December 2025 interview, said he had scars on his chest from the knife and that his diaphragm and spleen were injured.

open image in gallery Anthony Williams is charged with 14 counts of attempted murder ( PA )

He said he had told a colleague on the train “I think I’m going to die”.

Mr Zitouni sat in the public gallery of the court as his video interview was played to jurors on Friday.

Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, but they must consider whether he intended to kill.

Train passenger Michael Gawthorpe, who witnessed what happened and was not stabbed by Williams, said in a video interview that “someone passed [me] a fairly large toaster”.

He said: “I was holding it not really knowing what to do with it.

“I think instinctively my brain said throw it, so I threw it and it hit him [Williams], I’m pretty sure it hit him.

“I remember him looking at me and thinking ‘that’s pretty much it for me’ at that point.

“I think the train then started to slow down. That may have distracted him.”

open image in gallery Anthony Williams is seen in CCTV footage brandishing a knife ( British Transport Police )

He said a man he described as the “train guard” appeared to be “stabbed multiple times” by Williams, with the injured man stumbling back and moving behind him and another man.

“I don’t remember ever really looking backwards from this point on, I was fully focused on him [Williams] and what he was doing,” Mr Gawthorpe said.

He said there was a man who “just seemed to freeze stood next to him [Williams]” and the knifeman “slashed the guy’s face”.

Mr Gawthorpe said: “We shouted at him to run away.”

He said he could not remember when, but at some point a woman threw a drink at Williams.

He said Williams was shouting “they’re trying to kill me” or “something along those lines”.

“We were just shouting ‘calm down, calm down, put the knife down, put the knife down, we’ve got kids’,” he said.

He said earlier “people were putting things forward to barricade” the aisle, such as a catering trolley.

The trial continues.

News.title: Burnham praises victims who spoke out on Russell Brand’s ‘horrific’ crimes
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Burnham has described Russell Brand’s actions as “horrifying” and praised the bravery of the women who had the “courage to speak out” against the rapist comedian.

Brand faces a lengthy jail term after being convicted of raping one of his fans and sexually assaulting three women at the height of his fame.

Mr Burnham told Times Radio: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done. And I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out.

open image in gallery Russell Brand is facing a long custodial sentence (James Manning/PA) ( PA Wire )

“But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand and worse. So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to stand forward.”

Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley has said he would not be surprised if “many more” alleged victims of Mr Brand now came forward.

High -profile cases did often lead to an “upsurge” in reporting because it gave victims confidence to speak up about attackers in their cases, he said.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham praised ‘the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out’ ( PA )

He told BBC Breakfast: “It does make a difference because people see it is possible, and you will be believed.”

On Brand, he added: “There’s two more cases we’re investigating at the moment. I clearly wouldn’t be surprised if many more came forward.”

Mr Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a high-profile trial at Southwark Crown Court.

The comedian, 51, who denied all charges against him, was acquitted of two rape charges and a further accusation of attempted indecent assault.

A jury of eight men and four women took around nine hours to deliver their verdicts for each of the seven allegations against him.

After the verdicts were delivered, Mr Justice Bennathan told Brand that he faced a “significant custodial term”.

He is expected to be sentenced on Monday.

The PM is the most senior Labour figure to comment since the jury delivered their verdict.

Before any of the allegations came to light Mr Burnham was one of a number of politicians, including the foreign secretary Ed Miliband, who praised Brand. In 2014, Mr Burnham said he has used his celebrity status “to help others”, while then Labour leader Mr Miliband was interviewed by Brand as he courted his supporters in the run up to the 2015 general election.

More follows...

News.title: Meta U-turns on incredibly controversial change to how Instagram and Facebook would work
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Meta has U-turned on a controversial change to the way that Instagram and Facebook would work.

The company, which also owns Messenger, WhatsApp and Threads, has faced sustained criticism since it announced new terms for people with business accounts on its platforms. Those rules initially gave Instagram and Facebook the ability to scrape a users’ website and use it to train their models.

The updated terms led to global outcry after they were first reported in mid-October. Critics including politicians in both the US and UK voiced their opposition to the rules, arguing that they were not respecting publishers and other business owners by forcing them to give up control of their own websites if they wanted to keep using Meta’s platforms.

Over the weeks that followed, Meta continue to try and limit the outcry with a range of public statements and changes to the terms. The company removed the word “train” from the new rules, for instance, in the hope of stopping users’ worries that their work would be fed into AI systems.

Now, however, Meta says that it has “paused” the updates and that they would not go into effect on 20 November, as planned. That deadline was initially set for 30 October, but has already been pushed back repeatedly in the time since it was first announced.

“We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share,” an updated page on Meta’s Business Help Centre reads. “In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.””

News.title: Imane Khelif to box for first time since 2024 Olympics gender row
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Imane Khelif has announced her professional boxing debut as she prepares to fight for the first time since a gender row around her 2024 Olympics campaign.

Khelif, 27, will face Clarida Sarabia in Paris on 15 December, returning to the scene of her Olympic triumph.

The Algerian won welterweight gold at the 2024 Games, but her summer was overshadowed by debates around her participation due to her disqualification from the previous year’s amateur World Championships.

Imane Khelif won gold in the women's 66kg boxing event at the Paris Olympics ( AFP/Getty )

Khelif, who is not transgender, was disqualified from that 2023 tournament for allegedly failing to meet gender eligibility criteria. However, the World Championships’ organiser, the International Boxing Association (IBA), had previously been expelled by the Olympics movement due to concerns over its governance.

Khelif has long insisted she had the right to compete at the Olympics, and on 15 December, she will turn over to the professional ranks.

Khelif, who will face Sarabia at super-welterweight. said at a press conference per Yahoo: “It’s been over two years since I last boxed, and I've really missed being in the ring.

"The last couple of years have been quite difficult. The time has come to turn professional, and I’m going to give it my all.”

Although Khelif is beginning her pro career, she said earlier this year that she is not done as an amateur, with an intention to defend her Olympic title at LA 2028.

To do so, she would have to comply with genetic testing rules, which she said she would do. Khelif told CNN in February: “Of course, I would accept doing anything I’m required to do to participate in competitions. They should protect women, but they need to pay attention that while protecting women, they shouldn’t hurt other women. I’m not transgender, I’m a woman. I want to live my life. Please do not exploit me in your political agendas.”

However, one of Khelif’s coaches, Kamel Abdesselam, said: “She has ‌no interest in competing in the ​Games again. She’s already an Olympic champion.”

News.title: Rory McIlroy makes 11 birdies in Abu Dhabi second round after controversial penalty
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rory McIlroy put first-round controversy behind him to soar into contention at the Abu Dhabi Championship.

McIlroy took a two-stroke penalty for improving his lie at the 12th hole on Thursday despite insisting that had not been his intention, leaving him eight shots off the lead at Yas Link.

But an 11-birdie round of 63 on Friday moved him up to 11 under par, one shot behind three-way leaders Tyrrell Hatton, Jon Rahm and Francesco Laporta.

McIlroy said on Sky Sports: “I’d much rather be two shots worse off than be called a cheat. I made peace with it and at least I went out today and I had a clear conscience and I could just go and play.

“I had to take an unplayable at the first and made a bogey, it wasn’t like I got off to the greatest of starts today, but then obviously I got it going.

“I played well enough (on Thursday) to feel like I could play my way back into the tournament and I went out today and played a good round of golf and did get myself back into it. I’ve given myself a great chance and that’s all I can ask for.”

Overnight leader Laporta of Italy and Rahm both birdied the final hole to join Hatton on 12 under.

The Englishman had the best round of the trio with a seven-under 65, heralding a timely return to form after a difficult few weeks.

“Really happy how I played,” said Hatton. “Obviously there’s been a couple of mistakes but overall, compared to where I’ve been at over the last month and a half, it’s nice to put a couple of decent scores together again.”

Rahm narrowly missed an eagle putt on 18 and signed for a 67 while Laporta recovered from a double bogey at the 14th to post a two-under-par 70.

McIlroy is one of four players on 11 under along with English duo Matthew Jordan and Sam Bairstow and Pole Adrian Meronk.

Tommy Fleetwood birdied five holes in a row on the front nine but only one on the back nine in a 66 that moved him up to a tie for 12th place, four shots off the lead.

PA

News.title: Two children dead as school bus crashes in France
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Two children have died in a bus crash transporting school pupils in eastern France, according to French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu.

Several others are injured, according to education minister Edouard Geffray, who said that the students were “on their way to class”.

Three people are currently in a critical condition and 13 others have sustained minor injuries, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor’s office told BFMTV.

Images taken at the scene show a bus tilted over on the side of a road in what appears to be a ditch by a cluster of trees. Several people are seen surrounding the vehicle.

According to the Ain prefecture, the incident involved an intercity bus route in the Lent area, around 34 miles from the French border with Switzerland. The accident is reported to have taken place at 7am local time on Friday morning.

“A tragic accident this morning in Lent, in the Ain department,” Mr Lecornu wrote in a post on X on Friday.

open image in gallery French gendarmes and rescue workers at the site of a school bus crash in Lent ( Reuters )

“Two children lost their lives and several people were injured in a bus crash. Thoughts to their families and loved ones, as well as to all those affected by this tragedy.

“Thank you to the firefighters, medical teams, and law enforcement mobilised on site to provide aid to the victims. The minister of transport is heading to the scene.”

Lent mayor Yves Cristin said that the bus “left the road and hit a tree in the ditch”.

“I arrived minutes after the accident, and people were in shock,” he told BFM TV. “The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured.”

Transport minister Philippe Tabarot said that he was on his way to the scene following the “serious” crash.

open image in gallery Three people have been left in a critical condition while several others sustained minor injuries ( BFMTV )

He added that 70 people had been involved in the crash and that a community hall has been opened to provide care and shelter to crash victims.

Geffray expressed his sympathy with those affected, saying: “I cannot begin without first expressing my thoughts for these students and their families. For us, it is always a difficult experience when our students, when our children, are victims of accidents of this nature.”

He later added that he had been “deeply shaken” by the incident.

“On board this interurban bus were notably students who were on their way to class. All my thoughts go out to the victims and their families. I also think of the classmates and teachers of the students who were on board,” he wrote.

“On behalf of the entire educational community, I extend my support to them in this ordeal. I thank the firefighters, the medical teams, and the law enforcement forces who are intervening on site.

The Ain prefecture said it had “activated the departmental operations centre (COD) to coordinate the response of the various crisis management agencies. Emergency services and law enforcement are on the scene. Local mayors are also assisting with the rescue operation.”

The public has been asked to avoid the area and traffic diversions are in place.

Two helicopters have been deployed, according to BFMTV.

The French broadcaster initially reported two fatalities but a spokesperson for the civil protection agency told the broadcaster he could not confirm the deaths. The prefecture also said it could not confirm any deaths.

Cristin said that two people were reported to be in cardiac arrest and the civil security spokesperson said that their condition was “very serious”, according to the outlet. It was also earlier reported that one young adult and one child had died, before the prime minister confirmed both victims were children.

News.title: Tuchel snubs Palmer but calls up Jobe Bellingham and Josh King to England squad
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel has dropped Cole Palmer from the England squad but has called up Jobe Bellingham to play alongside his brother, Jude.

Palmer was picked to play in the first four matches last month but pulled out because of “load management” and has now been completely overlooked for next week’s Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain, despite his recent good form for Chelsea.

Jobe, 21, plays for Borussia Dortmund and has been handed his first senior call-up, raising the prospect of two brothers playing for England together for the first time since Gary and Phil Neville.

“Lee Carsley [England U21 coach] has been talking highly about Jobe for weeks and months, that he deserves it if there is a spot and a possibility to join and to make an impression in the first team,” said Tuchel.

“He had good matches and is on a good run of form with Dortmund so he deserves to be with us. We have 21 outfield players for the first match and then possibly 22 for the second match [because Myles Lewis-Skelly is suspended for the Croatia game].”

News.title: Cheap version of game-changing HIV preventive drug granted approval by US authorities
News.content:
Millions of people in low and middle income countries are set to get access to a game-changing HIV prevention drug within weeks, after US health authorities green lit a cheap form of the product.

Earlier this week the US Food and Drug Administration granted tentative approval to a generic form of the drug lenacapavir, made by Indian manufacturer Dr Reddy’s Laboratories.

Under an agreement hammered out between drug manufacturers and philanthropic donors in 2025 120 low and middle income countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East and the Caribbean, will get access to the generic drug, at just $40 per patient per year – compared to the US list price of $28,000.

Lenacapavir, a long-acting injection administered twice a year, was hailed as the scientific breakthrough of 2024 and a potential turning point in the fight against HIV. Clinical trials have shown it provides almost 100 per cent protection against catching the HIV virus for six months and it is more effective and convenient than taking daily pre-exposure prophylactic (PrEP) pills.

Last year, Gilead Sciences, which developed lenacapavir, signed royalty-free, non-exclusive voluntary licencing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable the production and supply of a generic. Dr. Reddy’s is the first to get FDA approval and it is hoped the first batches will be ready by the end of the year.

Jessica Burry, HIV technical officer at Unitaid, which in conjunction with the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI supported Dr Reddy’s in its bid to manufacture the generic, said it normally takes 10 years for a generic form of a drug to be launched.

“So we’re celebrating this milestone,” she said. “There’s a lot of demand in the countries where we’re working and we think having an affordable generic could make a real difference.”

Standard PrEP involves daily pills which some people find difficult to stick to.

“You can overcome the stigma, you can overcome the potential adherence difficulties so it’s really a game changer in terms of things to have in the toolbox,” she said.

News.title: The perilous road to parenthood: Mongolia’s fight to make childbirth safer
News.content:
As the 4x4 raced south, bouncing across Mongolia’s rocky valley roads and dusty forest steppes, an obstetrician was doing her best to ease Otgonbayar Odbayar’s pain and panic.

Hours earlier, the reindeer herder’s waters had broken. But Otgonbayar was six weeks early – and almost 250 miles away from the doctors who could provide the caesarean she knew she needed.

She contacted the nearest clinic, kicking off a relay of calls that spanned the length of Khuvsgul, a region bordering Russia. Soon, a plan came back through the chain: one health team would collect the 26-year-old and sprint south, while doctors from the provincial hospital in Murun would hurtle north. They’d meet in the middle.

Otgonbayar Odbayar with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But Otgonbayar’s three-hour journey was touch and go. “Halfway through, her contractions got very intense and very close together,” said Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh, the obstetrician who collected her. “She was in a lot of pain. We put her on an IV and were driving so fast.”

They made it to the small clinic in Tugul a little after 11pm, but then faced an excruciating 90 minute wait for the team from Murun, who had further to travel on Mongolia’s rutted roads. Dr Tsogbadrakh didn’t have a Plan B: the baby was in breech position, and the scar from Otgonbayar’s previous c-section still hadn’t fully healed.

Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“When [the doctors] arrived, I felt relief,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh. “If we had waited only 30 more minutes to start surgery, no one could tell what would have happened.”

Yet Otgonbayar’s ordeal is now the exception in Mongolia, underscoring just how far the vast country has come in its three-decade drive to tackle the childbirth risks posed by geography.

In 1990, 200 women died for every 100,000 births, but that ratio plunged to 47 by 2015 – making Mongolia one of only nine countries to hit global targets to reduce maternal mortality by 75 per cent over the 25-year period, according to analysis in the Lancet.

Strides have slowed but continued, and the rate now hovers at around 37. By contrast, other countries with a similar maternal mortality ratio in 1990, including Algeria, Brazil, the Philippines and Kiribati, still see more than 70 deaths per 100,000 births, according to Our World in Data.

In a country as vast and sparse as Mongolia – which is more than six times the size of the UK, but home to just 3.5 million people – health gains have been reliant “on overcoming the distance between women and the care they need”, said the health minister Batshugar Enkhbayar.

That has meant introducing telemedicine initiatives to bring specialist advice to remote clinics, waiting homes where pregnant women can stay in the final weeks before delivery, and better trained staff to spot risks before they become acute. In the last year, the country has also started to trial portable ultrasounds.

Northern Mongolia near the Russian border Credit : Simon Townsley

“We cannot always eliminate that distance,” said Mr Enkhbayar, “so we have to plan around it.”

The Telegraph spent a week in Mongolia to find out what this looks like in practice, driving hundreds of miles to meet pregnant women and new mothers in provincial hospitals, village clinics and remote herder communities.

There are also lessons for other countries: the latest data shows that globally, 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023 – one death every two minutes. In the UK, around 250 women died in childbirth between 2022 and 2024, equal to more than one expectant mother a week.

Obstetrician Otgongerel Uvgii with Otgonbayar Odbayar following her recent birth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But in low and middle income countries, the vast majority of fatalities are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as preeclampsia, which are all entirely preventable. Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives.

And, when a mother survives childbirth – like Otgonbayar eventually did – her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At 2:10am on October 4, the doctors safely delivered Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy weighing 2.3kg. The family hadn’t yet decided on a name when we visited the stuffy maternity room a day later – but they were already thinking about his future.

“It was very scary and painful, everything was going wrong,” said Otgonbayar, swaddling her newborn in a pink Peppa Pig blanket. “But I feel lucky now. I’m just so glad I’ve been able to meet my baby.

“He doesn’t look like me, [he looks] exactly like his father,” she added, smiling. “I hope in the future he grows to be a good person, and to be healthy.”

Almost 150 miles south in Murun, two expectant mothers are staying in the waiting home that Otgonbayar had planned to use. It’s a simple space: six single beds line the walls of the light and airy room, and there’s a basic kitchen next door.

More than 300 of these facilities are dotted across the country, attached to village clinics and provincial hospitals. Women can stay for free, for as long as they need – in Murun, 147 expectant mothers used the waiting home between January and September, for an average of eight days.

Dr Nyam-Ulzii Odkhuu, one of eight gynaecologists at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Giving birth is actually very difficult here – just imagine the road they have to take and the distances they have to travel, just to give birth to their babies,” said Dr Nyam-Ulzii Odkhuu, one of eight gynaecologists at Murun provincial hospital. “So it’s important to have maternity waiting homes, especially in Khuvsgul, as we have so many remote villages. It’s a necessity.”

The idea is not a new one. In the 1970s and 1980s, an ad-hoc system saw some towns and villages set up specific gers – Mongolia’s traditional, circular tents – so pregnant women from remote herder families could be close to a clinic before their due date.

But then the Soviet Union fell. Although not officially part of the USSR, Mongolia was considered almost a “satellite state” – a socialist nation that was heavily dependent on Russia. When the bloc broke apart, Mongolia faced a “violent economic crisis” and social turmoil that researchers have called the “lost decade”.

Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh and midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal making house calls on horseback Credit : Simon Townsley

In this climate the pregnancy gers almost disappeared, fertility rates dropped and the maternal mortality ratio rose, said Dr Buyanjargal Yadamsuren, a former director of medical services at the ministry of health. Until 2001, when the government – which was keen to boost its population size – decided to prioritise maternal health.

“[Waiting homes] were an approach that made sense,” said Dr Yadamsuren. “But when we reintroduced them nationwide, we really focused on strategy – the referral system, the criteria for who should use them, the funding mechanisms, and so on.”

This formalised approach included sending all women with high-risk pregnancies to give birth in provincial hospitals, which are better equipped and able to perform caesareans.

Khaliun Lkhamsuren in the maternal waiting room at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Khaliun Lkhamsuren is one of those expectant mothers. From a village roughly 90 miles west of Murun, the 34-year-old came to the hospital’s waiting home after a prenatal checkup found her baby was not only big, but in an awkward position. Midwives were concerned it might be a difficult delivery.

“I have no fear, because if things do go wrong I’m already in the hospital and the doctors are nearby,” Khaliun said, perched on the edge of a metal-framed bed. “It’s a very useful and convenient place for someone like me, who doesn’t have relatives to stay with in the provincial centre.”

Gansukh Dorj with his first daughter Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

She jokes that coming here is even “a bit of a break” – her husband has been left at home, in charge of their two young daughters.

At the other end of the province, Gansukh Dorj is doting on his third child, gently rocking her buggy back and forth to curb her tears. It’s his first daughter, and he can barely stop beaming.

“All I wanted was to have a girl,” the 40-year-old told the Telegraph, offering his visitors dried curd, milk tea and wrapped sweets before turning back to baby Gansuvd. “I think it will be different to raising boys, so at first I felt nervous, but now I’m getting used to it.”

Three months ago, his wife Narmanmdakh Battur gave birth in the nearest village health clinic, a four-hour drive on tough, unpaved roads from the picture-postcard valley where the nomadic family spend summer and autumn. The herders only have a motorbike, so a driver from the health centre picked them up in a 4x4 a week before Narmanmdakh’s due date.

The health team en route to house-calls in Khuvsgul Province, northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

From there, everything went smoothly until Dr Tsogbadrakh – the tireless obstetrician who also collected Otgonbayar – noticed the newborn had signs of jaundice. She asked them to stay at the waiting home for 10 days post-delivery, just in case.

“We wanted to monitor the baby there, because this is a very long way from the health centre in Renchinlkhumbe,” she said. “The waiting rooms are convenient before and also after delivery.”

But providing a space for women to stay close to doctors is only one pillar of Mongolia’s strategy to overcome distance. Health teams also reverse the journey to visit patients in their homes.

Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh and midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal, with the portable ultrasound device Credit : Simon Townsley

The Telegraph joined Dr Tsogbadrakh and her colleague, midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal, on one of these trips, a 14-hour day driving across northern Khuvsgul to meet three families.

“In the winter it’s even harder,” said Ms Ulziijargal, as the 4x4 paused to inflate a slow puncture. “Many times we’ve been stuck in the snow, which in some places can be as deep as 120cm. And if it really doesn’t work, we would ride a horse or use a sleigh to get to the patients.”

Sometimes the healthcare workers, both mothers themselves, are on the road for two or three days, relying on their patients’ hospitality as they travel hundreds of miles to deliver vaccinations, health checks – and now, even baby scans.

Munkhzul Tseveedendev has her six-month scan inside her own home Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Renchinlkhumbe is one of 20 remote village clinics trialling portable ultrasounds, in a pilot scheme launched last year and funded by the Ministry of Health, UNFPA and the Luxembourg government. The devices, which cost around $8,800 (£6,500) per machine, look deceptively simple – just like a large laptop.

They’ve already had an impact, said Dr Tsogbadrakh, as she set up the ultrasound at the first stop of the day, an isolated log cabin on the banks of a small lake.

The health team check Munkhzul’s eight-month-old baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

It feels slightly surreal, a clash of domestic and medical: beside a vibrant orange chest full of trinkets and family photos, the ultrasound machine’s screen is filled with a moving black and white image, as Munkhzul Tseveedendev has her six-month scan inside her own home.

“It’s been great,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, gently moving the imaging wand across Munkhzul’s belly. “Before the portable ultrasound, we used to ask pregnant women to travel to the [village], but now we can take it out to them.

“It’s helping because one of our biggest challenges is when women delay coming to the clinic for checkups, and suddenly arrive when there’s already a problem,” she added later.

Midwife Byambasuren Ulziijarga checks baby Gansuvd in the family ger Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

While the health team is there, they also give Munkhzul’s eight-month-old baby a once over. She won’t stop blowing raspberries – an ominous sign in Mongolian culture.

“It means bad weather is coming,” said the midwife Ms Ulziijargal. She laughs, but the clouds soon turned grey, threatening snow but instead spitting rain as we arrived at Gansukh and Narmanmdakh’s ger hours later – their daughter is due a three-month health check.

“It’s very impactful to have them coming here, as it’s very difficult for us to reach Renchinlkhumbe,” said Gansukh, watching closely as Ms Ulziijargal notes down his daughter’s weight, heartbeat and breathing. She had a slight cold, so vaccinations were postponed, but little Gansuvd is otherwise growing well.

Baasgaa Badamdorj, 31, sits outside his home in Renchinlkhumbe while his wife is visited by the maternal health team Credit : Simon Townsley

“The medical services have got much better [since my second sons were born],” added Gansukh, referring to his teenage boys. “I think the quality of check ups has got much better.”

For Dr Tsedmaa Baatar, a gynaecologist and programme analyst at UN Population Fund (UNFPA) Mongolia, this is a fundamental point: while waiting homes offer critical infrastructure, and portable ultrasounds an innovative new tool to boost access, much of Mongolia’s success rests on improved expertise.

“We’ve really worked on the maternal complications, on how to deal with haemorrhage, eclampsia, sepsis etc,” said Dr Baatar, in the UN agency’s office in central Ulaanbaatar, the country’s gridlocked capital.

Otgontuya Nasanbayar, left, and Byambajargal Naidan, right, with their one-month-old baby in their family's ger following a visit from the maternal health team Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I used to work in the National Center for Maternal and Child Health here, and 25 years ago all complicated cases from all over Mongolia would be transferred to Ulaanbaatar,” she said. “But now the local hospitals in rural settings have the capacity to provide high quality services, which is a huge change… and maternal complications have decreased dramatically.”

This is not just down to better training. Mongolia has also set up a telemedicine network which connects specialists with healthcare workers across the country.

“A classic telemedicine scheme is between the doctor and patient, but ours is to improve expert knowledge at local hospitals,” said Dr Baatar. “Our aim was not to introduce this fancy telemedicine department. We are simply using the internet… to allow for joint decision making for complicated cases.

Dorjkhand Nyamdorj, 27, with her three day old baby at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Mongolia is a huge, sparsely populated country and sometimes delivering a quality healthcare service is a real challenge, so the government is trying to use technology as much as possible,” she added. “But we also know that technology alone is not a solution, we need well-trained, committed healthcare workers.”

Here, Mongolia is still falling short.

As it stands, the country is not on track to meet ambitious targets to reduce maternal mortality to around 15 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. Part of this is because of new risks – rising rates of noncommunicable diseases, as well as social issues including domestic violence and substance abuse, are increasingly affecting maternal health.

Seven day old Yaruu-Egshig is treated for jaundice at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But staffing is also a stumbling block, said Dr Baatar. While World Health Organization data shows the number of midwives rose from 612 in 2002 to 1,169 in 2024, this is still well below international standards.

According to analysis in the European Journal of Midwifery, the average midwife’s workload in Mongolia is roughly three times higher than the global average. The strain is even more acute in remote regions: research published in the Journal of Global Health found Ulaanbaatar has 3.96 physicians per 1,000 residents, compared to just 1.39 in Khuvsgul.

The issue is on the agenda. Supported by UNFPA, the government launched a strategy in July 2025 to boost the number of people training as midwives, improve their training, and give them greater autonomy so they can ease the burden on obstetricians and gynaecologists. There are roughly 600 in the country, said Dr Baatar – also not enough.

“We’ve made substantial progress over the past two decades,” said Mr Enkhbayar, the health minister. “However, recent maternal mortality figures are a reminder that these gains cannot be taken for granted.”

A traditional ger in northern Mongolia Credit : Simon Townsley

Back in Khuvsgul, the sun is just rising above the snow-capped mountains as Dr Tsogbadrakh and Ms Ulziijargal make yet another house call – to a ger roughly half an hour outside the village, where Ariunbolor Ganbayar is in the final trimester of her pregnancy.

It’s a rapid turnaround for the healthcare workers: the pair got home from their 14-hour day at around 10pm the night before, only to be called in the middle of the night when another woman from the village went into labour. They delivered the baby without complications at around 4am – and neither of them complain that they’ve only had two hours’ sleep.

Renchinlkhumbe, Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It is a lifestyle, not only a job,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, carefully sipping strong coffee from a flask as the 4x4 bounced the dusty steppe. “For example, in the last 14 days I’ve been all the time on the road – I was in the city for training, then I collected [Otgonbayar] for the emergency c-section, then I was on the road to treat people. My kids complain I’m sometimes very absent at home.

“Sometimes it is hard,” added Dr Tsogbadrakh, who’s been Renchinlkhumbe clinic’s obstetrician for eight years. “But the thing I love about my work is that moment when you safely deliver the baby, and you get to see the mother and the baby meet for the first time.

“It’s the beginning of a new human life.”

Renchinlkhumbe is one of 20 remote village clinics trialling portable ultrasounds, in a pilot scheme launched last year and funded by the Ministry of Health, UNFPA and the Luxembourg government. The devices, which cost around $8,800 (£6,500) per machine, look deceptively simple – just like a large laptop.

They’ve already had an impact, said Dr Tsogbadrakh, as she set up the ultrasound at the first stop of the day, an isolated log cabin on the banks of a small lake.

The health team check Munkhzul’s eight-month-old baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

It feels slightly surreal, a clash of domestic and medical: beside a vibrant orange chest full of trinkets and family photos, the ultrasound machine’s screen is filled with a moving black and white image, as Munkhzul Tseveedendev has her six-month scan inside her own home.

“It’s been great,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, gently moving the imaging wand across Munkhzul’s belly. “Before the portable ultrasound, we used to ask pregnant women to travel to the [village], but now we can take it out to them.

“It’s helping because one of our biggest challenges is when women delay coming to the clinic for checkups, and suddenly arrive when there’s already a problem,” she added later.

Midwife Byambasuren Ulziijarga checks baby Gansuvd in the family ger Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

While the health team is there, they also give Munkhzul’s eight-month-old baby a once over. She won’t stop blowing raspberries – an ominous sign in Mongolian culture.

“It means bad weather is coming,” said the midwife Ms Ulziijargal. She laughs, but the clouds soon turned grey, threatening snow but instead spitting rain as we arrived at Gansukh and Narmanmdakh’s ger hours later – their daughter is due a three-month health check.

“It’s very impactful to have them coming here, as it’s very difficult for us to reach Renchinlkhumbe,” said Gansukh, watching closely as Ms Ulziijargal notes down his daughter’s weight, heartbeat and breathing. She had a slight cold, so vaccinations were postponed, but little Gansuvd is otherwise growing well.

Baasgaa Badamdorj, 31, sits outside his home in Renchinlkhumbe while his wife is visited by the maternal health team Credit : Simon Townsley

“The medical services have got much better [since my second sons were born],” added Gansukh, referring to his teenage boys. “I think the quality of check ups has got much better.”

For Dr Tsedmaa Baatar, a gynaecologist and programme analyst at UN Population Fund (UNFPA) Mongolia, this is a fundamental point: while waiting homes offer critical infrastructure, and portable ultrasounds an innovative new tool to boost access, much of Mongolia’s success rests on improved expertise.

“We’ve really worked on the maternal complications, on how to deal with haemorrhage, eclampsia, sepsis etc,” said Dr Baatar, in the UN agency’s office in central Ulaanbaatar, the country’s gridlocked capital.

Otgontuya Nasanbayar, left, and Byambajargal Naidan, right, with their one-month-old baby in their family's ger following a visit from the maternal health team Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I used to work in the National Center for Maternal and Child Health here, and 25 years ago all complicated cases from all over Mongolia would be transferred to Ulaanbaatar,” she said. “But now the local hospitals in rural settings have the capacity to provide high quality services, which is a huge change… and maternal complications have decreased dramatically.”

This is not just down to better training. Mongolia has also set up a telemedicine network which connects specialists with healthcare workers across the country.

“A classic telemedicine scheme is between the doctor and patient, but ours is to improve expert knowledge at local hospitals,” said Dr Baatar. “Our aim was not to introduce this fancy telemedicine department. We are simply using the internet… to allow for joint decision making for complicated cases.

Dorjkhand Nyamdorj, 27, with her three day old baby at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Mongolia is a huge, sparsely populated country and sometimes delivering a quality healthcare service is a real challenge, so the government is trying to use technology as much as possible,” she added. “But we also know that technology alone is not a solution, we need well-trained, committed healthcare workers.”

Here, Mongolia is still falling short.

As it stands, the country is not on track to meet ambitious targets to reduce maternal mortality to around 15 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. Part of this is because of new risks – rising rates of noncommunicable diseases, as well as social issues including domestic violence and substance abuse, are increasingly affecting maternal health.

Seven day old Yaruu-Egshig is treated for jaundice at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But staffing is also a stumbling block, said Dr Baatar. While World Health Organization data shows the number of midwives rose from 612 in 2002 to 1,169 in 2024, this is still well below international standards.

According to analysis in the European Journal of Midwifery, the average midwife’s workload in Mongolia is roughly three times higher than the global average. The strain is even more acute in remote regions: research published in the Journal of Global Health found Ulaanbaatar has 3.96 physicians per 1,000 residents, compared to just 1.39 in Khuvsgul.

The issue is on the agenda. Supported by UNFPA, the government launched a strategy in July 2025 to boost the number of people training as midwives, improve their training, and give them greater autonomy so they can ease the burden on obstetricians and gynaecologists. There are roughly 600 in the country, said Dr Baatar – also not enough.

“We’ve made substantial progress over the past two decades,” said Mr Enkhbayar, the health minister. “However, recent maternal mortality figures are a reminder that these gains cannot be taken for granted.”

A traditional ger in northern Mongolia Credit : Simon Townsley

Back in Khuvsgul, the sun is just rising above the snow-capped mountains as Dr Tsogbadrakh and Ms Ulziijargal make yet another house call – to a ger roughly half an hour outside the village, where Ariunbolor Ganbayar is in the final trimester of her pregnancy.

It’s a rapid turnaround for the healthcare workers: the pair got home from their 14-hour day at around 10pm the night before, only to be called in the middle of the night when another woman from the village went into labour. They delivered the baby without complications at around 4am – and neither of them complain that they’ve only had two hours’ sleep.

Renchinlkhumbe, Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It is a lifestyle, not only a job,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, carefully sipping strong coffee from a flask as the 4x4 bounced the dusty steppe. “For example, in the last 14 days I’ve been all the time on the road – I was in the city for training, then I collected [Otgonbayar] for the emergency c-section, then I was on the road to treat people. My kids complain I’m sometimes very absent at home.

“Sometimes it is hard,” added Dr Tsogbadrakh, who’s been Renchinlkhumbe clinic’s obstetrician for eight years. “But the thing I love about my work is that moment when you safely deliver the baby, and you get to see the mother and the baby meet for the first time.

“It’s the beginning of a new human life.”

News.title: US stocks plummet as Democrat victory sparks investor panic
News.content:
Wall Street suffered its worst sell-off since Donald Trump’s tariff rollout amid fears the Democrats will derail the AI boom.

The Nasdaq 100 plunged more than 6pc on Thursday - the biggest fall since April 2025 - with shares in semiconductor makers the hardest hit.

The downturn was the worst since Mr Trump’s so-called “liberation day”, when he rolled out tariffs to countries around the world.

Investors fear the Democrats’ midterm election victory will usher in tighter restrictions on AI companies, whose valuations have grown rapidly under Mr Trump.

Nvidia, which is the world’s most valuable listed company, fell by more than 6pc while rivals including AMD and Micron plummeted 13pc and 11pc, respectively.

News.title: Can the UK handle an Ebola infection?
News.content:
A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being flown back to the UK for treatment.

The patient, whose identity has not been revealed, but is believed to be a healthcare worker, is said to be in a stable condition.

They will be transferred to a specialist ambulance and then on to the Royal Free hospital, a rare diseases specialist hospital in north London, which houses the UK’s primary high level isolation unit.

Yesterday, a UK government spokesperson said there were “well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this” and that the risk to the public “remains low”.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DRC. The first cases of the Bundibugyo strain of the disease were reported in May, and there have so far been more than 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths, making it the second largest outbreak in history.

How will the British patient be treated?

The immediate priority will be to assess their condition.

On average, symptoms appear between eight to 10 days after exposure, but they can arise as soon as two days and as many as three weeks after infection. Doctors will have to determine how far the virus has progressed and identify any complications that require treatment.

Ebola can cause severe fluid loss, through profuse vomiting and diarrhoea, electrolyte imbalances and in serious cases organ failure. Experts will closely monitor his vital signs and fluid balance, bloods and organ function, providing intravenous fluids and other supportive treatment.

News.title: Bank of England raises interest rates for first time in three years
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The value of the pound has risen to its highest level in two months as the Bank of England prepares to raise interest rates.

Sterling climbed 0.2pc against the dollar to nearly $1.35 on Thursday, its highest level since September.

It came as traders responded to the likelihood that the Bank of England will increase rates for the first time in three years on Thursday.

This reflects the Bank’s attempt to keep inflation under control after the Iran war energy shock pushed price rises to an 11-month high.

Typically, higher borrowing costs strengthen the pound by boosting demand for UK interest-bearing assets among foreign investors.

The pound was also buoyed by a weaker dollar after the Democrats swept to victory in the US midterms on Wednesday.

Political upheaval hit the dollar as traders bet that deadlock in Washington will lead to curbs on Donald Trump’s runaway spending.

This brought down the cost of US government borrowing, which in turn brought down the dollar.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The prospect of a divided government eased concerns about the fiscal trajectory, given it’ll now be more difficult to pass tax cuts or spending packages.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Burnham makes new North Sea drilling illegal | Energy independence bill would prevent future ministers from easily reversing exploration ban

2) Blue wave threatens to derail America’s AI boom | Democratic candidates swept to power amid voters’ growing resentment toward data centres

3) Majority of London’s bridges are falling down | Advisers warn 24 Thames crossings are in poor condition and require urgent repairs

4) Silicon Valley investor shuts London office as US dominates AI | Firm known for early backing of Apple and Google doesn’t ‘see the need’ for presence in Britain

5) Trump rages at Fox News as Republican voters switch off | Once a powerful force in US politics, the Murdoch TV channel’s influence is fading

What happened overnight

Oil, chip stocks and the dollar were under pressure in Asia ​after ‌the Democrats swept to a series of stunning midterm election wins.

Brent crude dived nearly 9pc overnight, falling below $100 a barrel, and has dropped by about 20pc so far this week.

If sustained through to Friday’s close, it would make for the largest weekly drop in oil prices since April 2020 when US crude briefly fell into negative territory.

Tumbling energy prices encouraged a rally in bonds, which lowered yields, pulled the dollar to a one-month low of $1.1273 per euro, and helped stocks. The yield on the benchmark 10-year note fell to a two-month low and was last at 4.85pc.

Broad stock indexes climbed on the clear outcome, with the S&P 500 closing 1.6pc higher and European shares notching a two-month high, although tech stocks struggled as investors fear greater scrutiny over AI infrastructure build-out.

European stocks were on track to open 0.2pc higher, while the Nasdaq in the US fell 1pc in premarket trading, indicating investor angst over chip and data centre stocks.

Democratic data-centre ⁠opponents who campaigned, in part, on moratoriums on data centre construction won stunning victories in Texas and Georgia in a sign public opinion is shifting on AI.

South Korea’s chipmaker-heavy Kospi sank nearly 6pc and remained within a whisker of a new seven-month low. Taiwan’s benchmark index fell over 3pc, poised for an 8pc weekly decline, its worst weekly performance since April 2025.

Tech equipment suppliers dragged on the Nikkei, which ​fell 2pc, although the broader Topix was 0.8pc higher, underscoring the divergent ‌market reaction to the decisive election results.

Sports.title: How Alexia Putellas shaking up WSL by bringing Ballon d’Or to Bromley and boasting SIX TIMES more followers than league
Sports.content:
Next

ALEXIA PUTELLAS brought the Ballon d’Or to Bromley last week.

The 32-year-old won her third golden football on Monday at the London Palladium, just over 14 miles from Hayes Lane – where she now plays her club football.



Putellas joined London City Lionesses in July after ending a 14-year, trophy-laden spell with European champions Barcelona.

For some, it was a shock move – especially considering London City only earned promotion to the WSL last year.





But in reality, it was a huge statement of intent from owner Michele Kang.

The billionaire businesswoman hopes to build the Bromley-based side into a European powerhouse.

And with the help of Alexia, she is well on her way.

Putellas came to England with star power unlike the WSL had ever seen before.



The Lionesses became household names in the UK when they won the European Championship in 2022 and again last year, but Alexia is a name that is recognised worldwide.

The World Cup winner boasts 3.7million Instagram followers – over six times more than the official WSL account.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Her impact has already been felt at London City, with the club’s average attendance having increased by over 1,000 fans compared to last season.

Hundreds arrived at Hayes Lane early on Sunday to catch a glimpse of the Ballon d’Or trophy.



Ahead of the club’s WSL match against reigning champions Manchester City, the golden football was put on display to celebrate Putellas’ win.

Fans were even encouraged to queue up for pictures with it, with some people arriving over three hours before the midday kick-off.

The Spaniard’s arrival has brought a huge wave of new fans to Bromley, with one person even moving countries to be able to watch her play live.

The fan, who moved from Scotland recently, told The Cutback at the weekend: “As soon as I heard Alexia might be coming here, I moved to London.

“She’s just the best in the world. I’ve been to Barcelona to see her play, I was at her last game for Barcelona.



“She’s such an inspiration, not just for fans, but for young players as well. What she does is just amazing.

“I came for Alexia but I stayed for the other players, like Danielle van de Donk and Kadidiatou Diani.”

The presence of Putellas is also being felt on the pitch.

London City find themselves in a great position to potentially qualify for the Champions League at the end of the campaign.

They currently sit third in the WSL table after eight games, above the likes of Arsenal, Manchester United and Tottenham.
