Sports.title: Ocon's F1 story is one of success, even if this is the end
Sports.content:
There's really not much reason to think otherwise: it looks increasingly likely that this could be the end of Esteban Ocon's active Formula 1 career. A career blessed with plenty of highlights, a handful of podiums and a victory scored behind the wheel of a car that wasn't capable of winning on merit.

He made a lot of the opportunities that came his way - not just on the track, but throughout his career. And even if it ends now, that career has already become far more than anyone could reasonably have expected, given where he started.

There aren't many stories like his in modern F1, with kids from modest backgrounds - without wealthy families or rich sponsors behind them from an early age - reaching the pinnacle of motorsport, let alone achieving what Ocon has managed.

But his abrupt departure from Haas could well mark the end of that chapter of his racing career. Things could change. He could still return, because he's still one of the best drivers in the world. It's just very difficult to see how right now.

It's almost impossible to imagine Ocon on the grid when the 2027 season begins in Bahrain - if it begins in Bahrain - with most seats already taken and those potentially still available having plenty of candidates queuing up for them. And there's little reason to believe he'd suddenly jump ahead of the others.

There's still a question mark over Cadillac's second seat. But there's Colton Herta, with his American passport, and Yuki Tsunoda as another possible option. Liam Lawson's future hasn't been confirmed either, but Red Bull isn't suddenly going to add a 30-year-old Frenchman to the pool of candidates for its junior team. That's essentially a fight between Lawson and 19-year-old Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov.

What's more likely is that Ocon would once again have to find a place on the substitutes' bench, waiting for an opportunity until somebody slips in the shower.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

And there are plenty of examples of drivers who have eventually made it back after choosing that route. Even on the current grid, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Nico Hulkenberg are examples. Ocon himself belongs in that group: he returned to racing with Renault in 2020 after spending a year on the sidelines as Mercedes' reserve driver.

But, as uncomfortable as the truth may be, the way Ocon's 2026 season ended so suddenly makes the prospect of a comeback even less likely than it would have been had he simply finished the year with Haas.

There's no point speculating about what actually happened between him and the team. And it would be wrong to give more visibility to the rumours flying around.

What we do know is that something happened during the Mexico Grand Prix weekend. And whatever it was, it was enough for Haas to take Ocon out of the car and hand it to Ryo Hirakawa, a driver with no previous F1 starts, who made his grand prix debut at the age of 32 - something we hadn't seen since Andre Lotterer jumped into a Caterham at Spa in 2014.

Whatever happened, it was serious enough not only for Haas to sideline him for the weekend, but also to decide that he wouldn't race for the team again this season.

Yes, perhaps the situation was also convenient for Haas. It now has an opportunity to give Rafael Camara, its future driver, some actual race experience. That will certainly be useful for the Brazilian, but also for the team, which can identify areas to work on, get to know him better and benefit from all the other things that come with running a young driver in a grand prix.

But Haas wouldn't have shown Ocon the door just for that.

When a driver disagrees with his team, it's certainly not ideal. When it gets to the point where the team takes him out of the car, it's worse. And when the driver in question is Esteban Ocon, it's difficult not to talk about his reputation and see Mexico 2026 as another stain on it.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Reputation is a tricky thing.

It's often formed according to its own rules, through freak circumstances and, nowadays, through the mystery of social media algorithms. When there's something to hate, the modern world provides more than enough tools to multiply the effect, exaggerate it beyond recognition and turn the whole thing into a farce.

But reputation exists. And Ocon has a reputation for being a somewhat difficult character to work with.

After all, his previous spell with a team ended in a remarkably similar way, with Alpine asking him to vacate his cockpit before the end of the 2024 season.

And then there's the whole outcry over his collisions with team-mates.

It's not actually as bad as the social media hate suggests, and many of those incidents weren't even his fault. If you go back and look at the incidents themselves, the picture isn't nearly as clear as the usual social media reaction would have you believe.

But it is what it is. And it's also true that anyone considering Ocon as a future driver will inevitably have that preconception about him - however fair or unfair it may be.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team, Laura Mueller, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

There's a puzzling disconnect between that image and the person we see in interviews.

Believe it or not, Esteban Ocon is one of the nicest people in the F1 paddock to talk to. Friendly, chatty, very polite. Yet there are enough people who would tell you that he can be difficult to deal with at times.

We talked about it when I interviewed him for GP Racing magazine a couple of years ago. We'd visited him at his training centre in the south of France and then had a long conversation in the car on his way home to Geneva.

I told him that a sporting director from an F1 team had once described Ocon to me as one of the most brutal guys when it came to discussions in the stewards' room.

I asked whether he thought that was part of his character. And he agreed that he understood what people might be talking about.

"But yeah, when there's something that has to be said, especially in Formula 1, it has to be said," he told me back then. "We have no time to waste here. So, it's important to be straightforward. Maybe I'm too straightforward at times, but well… I'm not going to let anything go after I've worked so hard to get where I am. You see how many hours I put in every day here - and I don't want to get, you know, eaten alive by doesn't matter who it is, be it some team manager, team principal, or a world champion.”

And we talked about how that part of his character was perhaps formed in the early days of his career, when his future depended not only on results but also on his ability to stand his ground and be as pushy as necessary to secure support.

Esteban Ocon, Alpine F1, celebrates on the podium Photo by: Jerry Andre / Motorsport Images

His family had sold their house to fund his karting career, but they simply couldn't provide enough money for him to progress through the junior formulas.

He needed to be a fighter, because nothing was handed to him.

And you've got to admire that - just as you've got to admire his whole journey.

“That's probably the right way to put it: I had the weight of my family on my shoulders, from a very young age,” he said. “And I’m not saying it to seek pity: it was worth trying and we succeeded to end up where we wanted to be - and now everything is good. But it's clear that I had to deal with these sorts of pressures, I had to be tough when it mattered, and I had to be heard when people were not necessarily listening, or weren’t convinced. And, you know, to make these businessmen, investors listen to you, when you're 13 or 14, and really pay attention, is not easy.”

It's probably not right to look at this as though it has now become a problem for him in Formula 1. Because he made it this far thanks to being who he is. And a decade-long career at the pinnacle of motorsport, with a grand prix victory to his name, is something nobody will ever take away from him.

As sad as it may be, perhaps that's simply all there was for Ocon in Formula 1.

There's a certain irony in the fact that what could turn out to have been Ocon's final F1 weekend as a race driver was also the weekend Kimi Antonelli won the world championship with Mercedes.

Because Ocon was once Toto Wolff's favourite kid, too. Wolff even said it was only a matter of time before Esteban would drive for the Silver Arrows.

It was never meant to be. And perhaps there was a reason for that, too.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

Ocon is undeniably fast. You don't have a 10-year career in F1 without being fast, let alone win a grand prix. But Formula 1 is also Formula 1. And only the absolute best, with the complete package required to reach championship level, actually get there.

There's no denying that, in terms of pure speed, there are far more drivers capable of winning a world championship than there are actual world champions. There's luck. There are circumstances, which play a huge role in how careers develop. And some of those things simply didn't fall into place for Ocon. Or perhaps his complete package wasn't convincing enough at the right moments - for Wolff, for example, to put him in a Mercedes when the opportunity arose.

After all, Ocon was available when Lewis Hamilton decided to leave for Ferrari. But by then, Toto already had a new favourite kid.

And he was ultimately proven right.

Whatever happens next, even if Ocon never finds his way back onto the grid, there's no reason to look back at his career with pity or regret. Because the career he's had is one that thousands of drivers would give almost anything to have. It's a bit sad - and even silly - that it could end like this. But it's certainly not what he deserves to be judged on.

And also...

As difficult as it looks now, even if it seems impossible, we're talking about someone who's already made an impossible dream come true: a kid from a small French town, whose dad was a mechanic, making it all the way to F1.

Don't count him out just yet.

And whatever happens next, he deserves to be praised for what he's already achieved.

Sports.title: Lawson unsure if Racing Bulls will keep him: “I don’t know what else they want me to do” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Liam Lawson admitted he faces an uncertain future despite his strong performance for Racing Bulls this year.

He lies ninth in the championship with 83 points – eight of which he scored in his three-race stint at Red Bull – which is more than twice as many as any other midfield driver, bar Alpine’s Pierre Gasly

However Racing Bulls is yet to confirm whether Lawson or current team mate Arvid Lindblad will keep their seats. The team is also believed to be considering whether to promote Red Bull junior driver Nikola Tsolov.

Lawson, who finished seventh in Mexico despite starting from the pit lane due to a penalty for a technical infringement in qualifying, is pleased with his performance so far this year.

“If I look a year ago we were in a different position and I probably thought about it [my future] a lot more. I think I learned from that as well and this year I haven’t really thought about it so much.

“But also the racing has been a lot stronger this year. I think Mexico is more of a specific situation that obviously happened on Friday that made the whole weekend a bit more tough but in terms of the performance I was in the sort of same place I’ve been all year.”

The team is on course to finish fifth in the constructors’ championship. This would be the best result it has scored under any identity since it first entered the world championship as Minardi in 1985.

“Every weekend I’ve been trying to do my best and I feel like we’ve had a really strong year and we’re in a good position,” said Lawson. “We’re fighting Alpine, we pull away from Alpine every weekend and with a few races left we’re trying to stay on top of them.

“I don’t know what else they want me to do but it’s just one of those things at the moment.”

He admitted that the team’s late decision on its driver line-up could leave him with no alternatives in 2027. “It’s tough, isn’t it? It’s the end of the season.

“When something like this is pushed all the way to the end, you’re left with not really any options. It’s not the easiest situation.

“Obviously, I want to be racing Formula 1 and I’m trying to show my best every weekend. I feel like we’ve had a good year.”

Sports.title: Herta’s latest practice run does not mean he’ll replace me in 2027 – Bottas | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Valtteri Bottas remains convinced he will drive for Cadillac next season despite the team’s ongoing efforts to ensure their test driver Colton Herta gains a Formula 1 superlicence.

Herta will drive Sergio Perez’s car in today’s first practice session. His latest appearance will ensure the Formula 2 driver and IndyCar race-winner reaches the 40 point threshold required for him to gain a superlicence.

However Bottas told the official F1 channel he expects to continue racing for the team next year. “That’s what I think, yes,” he said. “If I would do betting – I’m not allowed to do betting by the way – but if I [did], I would bet for that.”

Cadillac has already confirmed Perez will return to drive for them again next year. Perez said the team faces a “difficult choice” between Bottas and Herta for a 2027 seat.

But Bottas expects to return for another season. “In my head, it should be okay,” he said. “That’s what I signed up for, long-term. I haven’t heard anything else than that. So in my head it should be all good.”

While all teams must run inexperienced drivers in practice sessions on at least four occasions during the year, this will be Herta’s fifth such appearance for Cadillac. Bottas believes this is because he will be unlikely to qualify for a superlicence if he fails to this year, as the points he scored for his second-place finish in the 2024 IndyCar season will expire.

“It kind of makes sense for him because I understood that if he misses the superlicence this year, then it’s going to be almost impossible to get it,” said Bottas. “And as long as he gets it now, it’s going to be valid for a few years.

“So I’m pretty sure the team wants to have that just in case, not necessarily for next year. So that’s at least what I hope.

“But from my side, nothing has changed. The team has told me they don’t want to change anything. So that is where we are.”

Sports.title: Ferrari must not throw away another ‘easy one-two’ again – Hamilton | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton is maintaining the pressure on his team mate over Ferrari’s Mexican Grand Prix defeat.

The two Ferrari drivers went off the track while disputing the lead on the first lap in Mexico, handing Max Verstappen a route to victory. Team principal Frederic Vasseur admitted they should not have lost the race after the two cars led into turn one.

Hamilton says Charles Leclerc raced him too hard at the start. “We should have easily had a one-two last race,” he said yesterday, “and we’ve got to work to make sure that that never happens again.”

He said the team is yet to discuss the incident. Vasseur returned to Maranello in between the two races while Leclerc travelled home to be present for the birth of his first child.

“We will have a sit-down,” said Hamilton. “I don’t think everything’s going to get squashed and sorted out in one meeting but it is important. What we build now will put us in the right position for next year.

“In some ways I’m glad we’ve had that experience – of course I would rather we had won and had a one-two – but from that you can learn and you can only really get stronger from that, I think.”

He said the team must find a way to prevent the situation happening again to maximise their chances of winning the world championship.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“We’ve got these incredible people that are working so hard in the background,” said Hamilton, “of course we’ve been a little bit on the back foot on power this year but the natural car has been phenomenal all year. Great reliability.

“Every day I go out on track I’m always thinking of getting the absolute maximum for them. I don’t always achieve it, and from that you learn.

But I think with years and experience, you understand the bigger picture when you’re getting to work with such a large group of people, and I would say that’s the privilege where the years that I’ve spent here and the teams that I got to work in.

“I really do believe that next year we could be fighting for the world championship. That is the sole goal. So right now, in the background, my focus is on continuing to hold on to the performance we’ve picked up in the last few races in terms of execution and then working on next year’s car.

“I obviously can’t do anything about the engine except for just push them and they’ll continue to push in the background, I believe they are. With the car, it’s steering it, making sure we’re steering it in the right direction and making sure we arrive next year on the right foot.

“And then Fred’s job is to make sure that we are all running in the same direction. Of course we’re all going to race hard, but fair, and make sure that we get the maximum and the best result for the team.”

Sports.title: “I’ve never had a season where there’s been so many blows” – Russell | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell said he did not speak to media after the Mexican Grand Prix because he was “extremely disappointed” by his latest technical problem.

The Mercedes driver qualified on the front row of the grid in Mexico but lost several places on the first lap due to a drop in energy deployment from his power unit. Mercedes’ deputy team principal Bradley Lord described it as “a de-rate out of nowhere because of one of the complex bits of the energy rules”

While Andrea Kimi Antonelli clinched the world championship on Sunday, Russell said he was more disappointed by his latest setback in the race.

“I was extremely disappointed on Sunday night, more from the fact of missing out on a great result from something, again, outside of my control,” he said. “That was just a real tough pill to swallow.

“This season has been: tough moment, pick yourself back up, tough moment, pick yourself up. I think as an individual I’ve continued to have that resilience of being able to always pick myself back up and it kind of just got to the point in Mexico where I was like, I need to just get out of here because it’s just been relentless of what’s happened this year.”

Having led the world championship at the beginning of the season, Russell has now fallen to fourth place behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton. He is determined not to let his disappointing campaign prevent him from coming back stronger next year.

“It has been very exhausting,” he said. “I think just the mental challenge of having setbacks and having to pick yourself back up, and then things [happening] outside of your control, and then when you arrive at the next race and the performance isn’t where you want, it’s been mentally very, very exhausting.

“I go into every weekend believing that we can win, and I love racing, but this season just clearly was not meant to be in every single regard. I’m not saying I want this season to finish today, I’ll always fight to the end, but as I said before I’ve never had a season where there’s just been so many blows.

“You get to a point and you sort of think how do you keep picking yourself up when it’s like every other weekend you’re getting knocked down again? So it is tough, but I believe in myself.

“I’ve had a lot more good years than bad years and I think every single athlete and person in the world, they don’t have every single year of their life that goes the way they want. We all deal with issues, we’ll have things going on in our life and we will have years of failure and this has been one of those years for me.

“It’s not going to define me, it’s not going to define my career, I just got to come back stronger.”

Sports.title: Verstappen says his sudden rise to second in the championship is a “big surprise” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen said he is surprised to find himself second in the world championship with four rounds to go.

The Red Bull driver was sixth in the standings three rounds ago when he scored his first victory of the season. He moved into the runner-up spot with his third victory of the season in Mexico last weekend.

“It’s a big surprise to be second, to be honest, in the championship, but we take it,” he said.

Red Bull had a difficult start to their first season in which they have designed and built their own power unit, in conjunction with Ford. Verstappen only reached the podium once in the first seven rounds.

“We had a lot of difficulties as a team in the beginning,” he said. “The car was not where we wanted it to be. Probably also we still had to learn quite a bit [about] the power units and I think we really learned a lot throughout the season.”

Red Bull has made significant strides in the second half of the season. But Verstappen said even when it was less competitive he was focused on extracting the best from it.

“The car has naturally been a lot more competitive, lately,” he said. “From my side, it’s just you never really give up or, in terms of, you just never really settle for P6 or P7, right?

“Even when I was in that position or fighting the midfield, I was still trying to do the best that I could get out of the situation. Sometimes that is a P6 when the car is not able to perform better.

“But then once the car is in a better window, then you can fight further up front and eventually, of course, [win] races. And of course, when you win, you take points out of everyone else.

Sports.title: Hamilton admits he’s “really struggled” with F1’s tyres since 2022 size change | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton said he has struggled to get the most out of Formula 1’s tyres since the series ditched the 13-inch wheel size in 2022.

The Mercedes driver holds the record for most pole positions and scored his 105th last weekend. However only two of those have come in the five seasons since then – and both came by a margin of less than a hundredth of a second.

Hamilton said “I knew all weekend that I had the pace to be on pole” in Mexico but “the key is getting the tyres working.”

“You see us all go out and it looks like we’re doing okay, but the tyres operate in a very small window where they’re good, and then they overheat. I’m really perfecting that.

“That’s been something I’ve really struggled with, I would say, probably the last few years, particularly as we went to the 18-inch tyre, just learning to drive differently. It’s a bit of a different skill set, or just a different way you have to drive and approach these corners and it requires a different type of balance usage.”

Hamilton drove on 13-inch tyres for 15 seasons before the current format with narrower sidewalls was introduced. He said he rediscovered some of his past techniques last weekend.

“I was able to utilise a couple more tools that I’ve not used for like 13 years,” he said. “I just got the tyres in the perfect window on that out-lap.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Once I was through turns one, two and three, it was kind of smooth from there, and I just don’t think I lost any time anywhere, to be honest.”

The thinner sidewalls make getting the tyre temperatures into the optimum window more hit-and-miss, says Hamilton.

“We have guidance of the tyre temperatures we need to reach. All of us are pushing very hard on out-laps to try and get the tyres to work and in the window.

“As you go down the straights, the tyres lose temperature, obviously, and it is quite a hard tyre. I remember back in the day we used to crawl around super-slow, and then you start pushing and the tyres are ready.

“I think the 13-inch period for me was a nicer, softer tyre. It took the bumps better. I liked the movement of the tyre. You could feel it more.

“This one’s just solid. It’s like a rock-solid wall. It doesn’t really move much because it’s such a short sidewall. It performs well when you get it working.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Qualifying in Mexico was one of the times Hamilton felt he was “able to extract the most from the tyre, and it stayed through the lap.”

“More often than not, you’re like, ‘The front tyre is not in for turn one, but the rears are,” and the fronts start coming in and the rears start going off. It’s this constant seesaw you’re having.

“Then sometimes the rears aren’t ready as you come out of the last corner to start the lap, but then at the end they’re better. Sometimes they’re too ready.

“Trying to find that balance, I’m telling you, it’s like finding a needle in a haystack. And honestly, it’s been very, very, very tricky to find. But where there’s a will, there’s a way. You just continue to work at it.”

Sports.title: Social Media: Williams show off 40-year-old Jacarepagua Brazilian GP trophy | Brief
Sports.content:
Williams marked this weekend’s upcoming Brazilian Grand Prix by sharing a close-up video of the trophy they won in the race 40 years ago, when it was held at Jacarepagua in Rio de Janeiro.

It was an important win for the team, coming just 15 days after its founder Frank Williams suffered near-fatal injuries in a road car crash, which left him with paralysis.

Anyone unfamiliar with the story might find it peculiar the team make no mention of the driver who scored the victory. Nelson Piquet not only won on his debut for the team, but did it on home ground, leading a Brazilian one-two with Lotus’s Ayrton Senna. The Jacarepagua circuit was named after Piquet before it was demolished.

Piquet did not last long at Williams. Unhappy at the team’s refusal to grant him ‘number one’ status, he left to join Lotus after winning the drivers’ championship with the team in 1987.

In 2022 the three-times world champion brought disgrace upon himself by making racist comments about Lewis Hamilton, prompting criticism from drivers, the FIA and Formula One Management.

Sports.title: Alan Jones, 1946-2026 | F1 history
Sports.content:
Alan Jones, who has died at the age of 80, was renowned as a tough competitor and won the world championship when Formula 1 cars were beasts to drive.

After making the long journey to Britain with wife Beverley to forge a racing career in the late sixties, Jones got his break when Harry Stiller gave him the chance to compete first in Formula Atlantic, then a privateer F1 operation. Jones made his F1 debut the following year in a Hesketh, then took over from the injured Rolf Stommelen at Graham Hill’s team.

Another world champion, John Surtees, hired Jones for a full season the following year. Jones showed potential with second place in the non-championship Race of Champions but got on poorly with Surtees and left at the end of the season.

Tragedy handed Jones a precious chance in 1977. Shadow’s rising star Tom Pryce was killed in a crash at Kyalami and Jones took his place. Following points finishes in Monaco and Belgium, Jones grabbed a breakthrough victory in Austria.

Memorably, the event organisers believed they did not have a copy of the Australian national anthem – having failed to realise it was ‘God Save the Queen’, the same as the British anthem – and for years afterwards Jones enjoyed telling the tale of how his first grand prix victory was marked by a solo trumpet rendition of ‘Happy Birthday’.

Frank Williams hired Jones for 1978, and though he often threatened the front runners, no further wins came. That changed the following year when Williams designer Patrick Head penned the neat, arrow-like, ground effect FW07 chassis. Reliability problems blunted their early competitiveness – notably at Silverstone, costing Jones the chance to score Williams’ first victory – but by the second half of the season he was flying, reeling off three wins in a row.

That laid the foundations for a championship bid in 1980 and Jones delivered. He clinched the championship in a controversial collision with Nelson Piquet in the penultimate race at the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

However the following year the new world champion fell out spectacularly with team mate Carlos Reutemann, who refused an order to let Jones win in the second race at Rio de Janeiro. While the atmosphere soured at Williams, Piquet took advantage, snatching the title from Reutemann at the final race.

Jones announced his retirement at the end of 1981. He may have come to regret the decision as Reutemann also quit the team in the off-season and Keke Rosberg, plucked from obscurity to fill Jones’ seat, took the 1982 title.

He clearly still had an appetite for racing. Arrows tempted him back for a one-off start in the 1983 Long Beach Grand Prix but could not agree terms for a full-time return. He made a one-off start in the CART IndyCar series substituting for Mario Andretti at Road America in 1985, taking a fine third place behind Jacques Villeneuve Snr and Michael Andretti.

The prospect of leading a new team with bespoke Ford engines and backing from US retail giant Beatrice tempted him back to F1 again with Haas (no relation of the current Haas team) the same year.

The Ford engines weren’t ready in time for the end of the season so Jones entered the final rounds in a single-car entry powered by a Hart motor. However the project faltered: Beatrice pulled out its funds and by the time the Ford engine came good, Haas had pulled the plug. Jones made his final start in his home race in 1986.

He went on to compete successfully in Australia’s popular touring car series, where he ran his own team. He was tempted back to race single-seaters in the short-lived Grand Prix Masters series, but pulled out mid-weekend citing neck pain after lapping off the pace. Jones also ran Australia’s A1 Grand Prix team, helping to promote the likes of future IndyCar champion Will Power.

Jones remarried and is survived by his partner Amanda and his six children Christian, Amber, Zara, Jack, Camilla and Emma.

Sports.title: Groves Expects Fury vs Joshua Despite Fury Injury Rumor
Sports.content:
George Groves fully expects Tyson Fury to step into the ring against Anthony Joshua, brushing off chatter that an injury could derail the December 11 date. His view is simple. Both men are battle-worn veterans, so expecting either to show up at one hundred percent is unrealistic.

The conversation kicked off after Frank Bruno claimed an insider from Fury’s gym told him an injury could stop the clash from happening. Groves did not have insider details on Fury’s body, yet he cast heavy doubt on the idea that the event is actually in jeopardy.

“I don’t know about any rumors, but there might be a lot of kidology, a lot of rumors floating about. Could have been leaked by anyone,” Groves told talkSPORT Boxing. “I genuinely don’t know, but I’ll be very shocked if that fight don’t happen. I think both guys will fight no matter what.”

Groves offered an unfiltered take on where both boxers stand right now. He views them as past their physical primes, meaning a completely smooth camp is out of the question for either side.

“I don’t think at this stage either one of these two guys who are veterans, way past their best, are going to be in perfect condition going into this fight. That doesn’t matter. They’re going to fight,” Groves said.

It is a harsh reality check for an all-British heavyweight meeting years in the making. Fans are getting the spectacle, but Groves points out that the clock has been ticking the whole time.

Looking back on his own ring days, Groves pointed out that modern training camps are never completely clean. Wear and tear, missed sessions, or personal distractions always creep in, no matter how sharp someone looks at the podium.

Whether Fury carries a genuine knock remains unconfirmed. Bruno’s story is secondhand talk, and Groves made it clear he has no direct intel. Still, Groves remains convinced that both heavyweights will walk through fire to make the bell.

When a guaranteed nine-figure bag is sitting on the table, standard training camp knocks take a back seat.

Walking away from a projected 100 million dollars each over an elbow tweak, sore shoulder, or bruised rib would be professional madness. At this stage of their careers, neither Tyson Fury nor Anthony Joshua has another payday of this magnitude waiting in reserve.

If one pulls out now with a minor complaint, there is zero guarantee the momentum, public appetite, or financial backing survives to reschedule it cleanly.

Both fighters have operated under fire while compromised before. Fury fought through severe cuts and facial trauma, while Joshua has spent years managing the mileage on his body. Every veteran north of thirty-five carries something into the ring; reaching fight night at one hundred percent physical perfection is a myth in modern heavyweight boxing.

Unless one of them suffers a catastrophic structural tear or a medical commission flat-out denies a license, they are walking to the ring on December 11 in Cardiff. At 100 million dollars apiece, you fight through the aches, take your shot, and settle whatever needs healing after the final bell.

Sports.title: Fury: Ryan Garcia Has The Star Power Haney And Shakur Lack
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury believes Ryan Garcia is primed to take over as the premier attraction in American boxing once Canelo Alvarez steps away. Fury points directly to Garcia’s charisma and gift for commanding headlines, putting pure drawing power ahead of pure technical mastery.

While Fury listed talents like Devin Haney, Shakur Stevenson, Abdullah Mason, and Richardson Hitchins, Garcia earned his clear vote. The challenge facing everyone else is something victories in the ring cannot automatically fix: reaching beyond the hardcore boxing bubble.

“Other than Canelo, which Canelo’s obviously on his way out too, then it’s Ryan Garcia in America,” Fury said on Behind the Mic. “He’s got a personality. He talks. He’s entertaining. He’s charismatic.”

Asked if he sees reflections of himself in Garcia, Fury agreed completely, admitting others might possess sharper fundamentals but insisting they cannot generate the same revenue.

It is a crucial division when assessing Canelo’s commercial heir. Observers can debate Garcia’s ring craft against elite competition, yet Fury focuses strictly on ticket sales and viewer attention. Boxing culture often conflates technical brilliance with stardom, even though they demand completely different skill sets.

Garcia keeps the public talking during long layoffs. His unpredictable persona draws viewers who would never bother watching sparring footage or checking divisional rankings. People tune in hoping to see him win or desperate to watch him get knocked out, but either motivation sells pay-per-views.

Fury sounded far more skeptical about the mainstream presence of other top contenders.

“Inside of boxing people know who they are,” Fury said. “Outside of boxing, you go and ask 50 people … they don’t know who they are.”

Haney, Stevenson, Mason, and Hitchins have built formidable resumes. Yet Fury argues that respect from devoted boxing circles will only carry an athlete to a certain ceiling. Becoming the marquee figure who causes general sports fans to clear their weekend calendars demands a bigger presence.

Fury also took aim at modern streaming setups, questioning whether current platforms actually build true mainstream excitement. He recalled previous eras where extensive profile features introduced contenders long before fight night, whereas modern streaming formats often show the event without making casual viewers care in advance.

Because of that shift, self-promotion falls squarely on the fighter. Fury stressed that young talent must chase interviews, drop consistent content, and hustle for their own spotlight instead of waiting for a promoter to do the heavy lifting.

Garcia naturally excels at that playbook. Pure spectacle does not guarantee long-term dominance, since keeping the public invested still requires memorable bouts and dependable results. Even so, Fury’s view holds firm: Garcia knows how to hook an audience before the first bell sounds, while his peers face a much steeper climb proving they can match that commercial reach.

Sports.title: Conor Benn Says Pacquiao Fight Offered For December
Sports.content:
Conor Benn has confirmed he received an offer to square off against Manny Pacquiao this December, but opted against the date to focus on family time and physical recovery. While Benn remains open to meeting the boxing legend in early 2027, major questions remain about which weight class could accommodate both men.

Benn pointed to the brutal toll of his recent cut to 147 pounds, alongside the arrival of his newborn son, as key reasons for passing on the end-of-year window.

“The fight got presented to me for December, and it was just too soon making weight. Got a newborn son,” Benn said to Sky Sports Boxing. “So for me it was really about spending time with my family and just enjoying this period, the festive period, with my family. But if Q1 he wants to get on again, I’m interested.”

While Pacquiao represents a lucrative, marquee target for a return bout, Benn’s physical transformation presents a major hurdle. Having bulked back up to around 185 pounds, Benn insists his days at welterweight are completely finished. He even dismissed campaigning at junior middleweight.

“My future’s at middleweight,” Benn stated. “I thought about light middle. There’s nothing in me at light middle even. That’s how bad the weight cut was.”

Without a designated catchweight, matching an eight-division champion who spent his career far lighter against a fighter settling into middleweight remains an unresolved riddle.

Reflecting on his recent loss to Ryan, Benn admitted that outside noise fueled his miscalculated attempt to hit the welterweight limit.

“I don’t know what I was thinking making 147,” Benn said. “There’s one thing making the weight, and then there’s one thing performing at your best at the weight, and it showed. I paid the price for, say, chasing greatness.”

Still, Benn gave Ryan full credit for landing the decisive blows and finding victory on the night. Though he wanted the chance to battle on after rising from the canvas, Benn refused to fault the referee for waving off the bout, taking full accountability for the outcome.

Facing Pacquiao offers Benn an appealing path forward in 2027, but bridging the massive weight gap will require serious negotiations before anyone can sign a contract.

Pacquiao is a novelty payday trap. Even if Benn wins, nobody gives him real credit for beating a faded icon. If he looks bad winning, he gets ridiculed. If he loses, he is finished at the elite level.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Needs to Stop Living in the Past to Sell Liam Paro Clash
Sports.content:
Devin Haney is digging into his past, using his victories over George Kambosos to hype his December 19 unification clash with Liam Paro at Chase Center. Dominating Kambosos secured undisputed status at lightweight, but rehashing those nights won’t fire up crowds to see him chase another belt.

“My resume speaks for itself,” Haney stated. “I’ve never been afraid to go into a champion’s backyard and put my record on the line. I went to Australia, took George Kambosos’ belts, and became undisputed lightweight champion of the world. Now I’m bringing another Australian world champion, Liam Paro, into my backyard. This time, I plan to take his belt and become a unified welterweight world champion right here at home.”

Rehashing those wins now doesn’t elevate Liam Paro; it just reminds everyone how limited Kambosos actually was. The problem is that nationality is not a fighting style. Paro earned his IBF junior welterweight belt by traveling to Puerto Rico and physically outworking Subriel Matias, a dangerous puncher who was supposed to run through him.

If Haney truly understood how to build a fight, he would talk about Paro traveling to Puerto Rico to derail Subriel Matias or how Paro will actually bring a fight to him. Instead, he defaults to his old comfort blanket because self-promotion has never been his strong suit.

Paro is a tougher, more durable, and fundamentally different stylistic threat than Kambosos ever was. By presenting Paro through the Kambosos lens, Haney actually diminishes his own opponent while making the matchup sound like an easy rerun.

Devin needs to stop pretending the fans only care about belts. Haney should focus on the homecoming angle by promising a style change from his normal pure boxing approach. If he speaks openly about having to stand his ground against Paro’s physical, brawling style, he gives people a reason to watch for drama rather than just waiting on the judges’ scorecards.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury Says Usyk Discussed March Trilogy Fight
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury claims Oleksandr Usyk signaled he could be ready to step into the ring again in March. That float keeps the door ajar for a third encounter, even with the Ukrainian holding two clear victories over him. Fury must handle Anthony Joshua first, yet he is already floating Usyk’s name for his next move.

Fury says the conversation happened when the Joshua matchup still hung in the balance. No paperwork exists for a trilogy, and Fury leaves crucial blanks, starting with whether March remains realistic once he steps out against Joshua.

“I actually spoke with Alexander to say, like, if he doesn’t fight, then we’ll do it. And he said he’s busy. He’s going on holiday with his family, but he could do a fight in March. So, maybe we do that in March. I don’t know yet. One fight at a time,” Fury said to Fighthype.

Booking the pairing again guarantees immense global interest, yet justifying it on merit gets tricky after back-to-back Usyk wins. Fury commands massive crowds, but he cannot claim unsettled business in the ring, no matter how vigorously he disputes the scorecards.

He still speaks as if the two losses solved nothing. When asked about those bouts, he doubled down on his claim that the judges got them wrong.

“I thought I won both fights,” Fury insisted. “I’m not bitter towards Alexander. He’s a good man. Like, he’s a God-fearing family man. I wish him all the luck in the world. But when he looks in that mirror every day, he knows he didn’t beat GK.”

That stance gives him an obvious marketing angle. He can insist he got robbed twice, promising to finish the job inside the distance next time. Spectators who watched Usyk take both contests will need stronger proof to believe a third chapter goes any differently.

Joshua might shatter this entire timeline anyway. Fury must defeat AJ and emerge unscathed for March to stay viable. A grueling war would instantly derail such a tight turnaround.

Fury also brushed aside talk about Usyk dropping down to cruiserweight to face David Benavidez, arguing that a Usyk trilogy offers the premier commercial draw.

“He just wants a big payday, and I’m his man to give him that,” Fury stated.

However, Saudis almost certainly pass on financing a third meeting, and outside of Riyadh, nobody else has the appetite to write those checks. Turki Alalshikh cares about global prestige and spectacle rather than standard event profit and loss, but he avoids financing fights that feel settled or stale. When one man has already collected 24 rounds of undisputed evidence across two fights, the storyline vanishes.

Alalshikh wants legacy events that captivate the sporting world, not expensive reruns where the outcome feels foregone. Unless Tyson Fury delivers an explosive, career-altering win that makes fans demand it again, Alalshikh will look to put his budget behind fresh pairings.

If the Saudis say no, the fight essentially dies right there. Here is why neither traditional promoters nor major streaming platforms would step into that breach:

Traditional promoters like Frank Warren’s Queensberry or Bob Arum’s Top Rank operate strictly on commercial reality. To stage Fury vs. Usyk 3 without Saudi site fees, they would have to fund massive eight-figure guarantees entirely through ticket sales, sponsorships, and pay-per-view buys.

The first two fights showed that pay-per-view numbers alone struggle to justify astronomical purses without state subsidies. Putting together $80 million to $100 million in combined purses on a pay-per-view model for a 2-0 rivalry would be financial suicide for any standalone promoter.

Netflix has entered live combat sports, but its entire strategy relies on massive cultural events and spectacle that drive mainstream global viewership without pay-per-view barriers. A technical chess match between two pure boxers, where the Ukrainian has already dominated the series, does not fit the kind of mass-market spectacle Netflix targets.

If Netflix is going to spend tens of millions on a live boxing broadcast, they will chase crossover draws or a massive domestic clash like Fury against Anthony Joshua, not a redundant third bout between Fury and Usyk.

Sports.title: De La Hoya Says Huge Paydays Hurt Boxing
Sports.content:
Oscar De La Hoya makes a legitimate point about the fallout from boxing’s oversized paydays. The moment an elite fighter lands an exorbitant purse, putting together another significant fight becomes an uphill battle.

A wealthy champion can comfortably afford to stay on the sidelines, waiting around for another monster payday rather than risking a world title against an unheralded, high-risk challenger for standard money.

This dynamic leaves skilled contenders with smaller fanbases stranded. They climb the ranks and secure mandatory status, yet they still struggle to bait a titleholder into the squared circle. Defeating an unheralded contender offers minimal commercial value to an established champion, while an upset defeat destroys their future earnings.

“Fighters are ducking their mandatories and taking forever to fight the very best opponents. Why is that? Because Turki’s paying for this,” De La Hoya argued during his latest Clap Back Thursday broadcast.

De La Hoya aimed his remarks directly at Turki Alalshikh, alleging the Saudi investor overpays competitors who fail to deliver in the ring. While that view concentrates blame on a single financier, the broader problem reaches far beyond whoever signs the checks.

A massive purse quickly morphs into an athlete’s baseline demand. Normal market offers suddenly appear insulting, even when those figures match actual gate receipts and broadcast revenue. Flush with cash, the fighter holds all the leverage to decline fights and sit idle.

The sport simply lacks enough marquee rivals capable of producing record-setting revenues on demand. When several elite boxers freeze their careers chasing the same small pool of opponents, extended layoffs turn into the standard routine. Top contenders get told to stay busy, taking on all the danger while the biggest names bide their time for optimal terms.

The classic rationale of high danger and low reward makes fiscal sense to managers, but fans have grown exhausted hearing about it. Holding a world championship should demand more than cherry-picking matchups that deliver maximum profit with minimal physical jeopardy.

Canelo Alvarez facing the choice between Hamzah Sheeraz and Osleys Iglesias highlights this exact problem. Facing Hamzah Sheeraz guarantees strong ticket sales and broadcast numbers, while Osleys Iglesias poses a dangerous stylistic nightmare that only dedicated purists recognize. The avoided challenger gets passed over precisely because he possesses the skill set to score an upset.

Riyadh Season bankrolling could ideally bridge that gap. If conventional promotional companies cannot guarantee the money required to finalize tough bouts, an ultra-wealthy investor holds the power to make them happen. Throwing massive capital at famous names accomplishes little for the sport unless the matchmaking forces champions into genuine danger.

When fighters realize giant checks arrive regardless of opponent quality, they have zero incentive to accept severe stylistic challenges. Convincing them to take tough fights for less money later turns nearly impossible.

The sanctioning bodies share substantial blame for enabling this cycle. When titleholders receive continual exemptions, mandatory challengers pay the price in lost prime years. Owning a championship belt must carry an ironclad duty to defend it against legitimate contenders, regardless of how many pay-per-view buys those challengers command.

Boxers take immense physical punishment and deserve every dollar they generate. De La Hoya’s point reminds everyone that financial compensation must remain tied to competitive matchmaking. Whenever excessive wealth allows champions to freeze divisions and avoid elite threats, the entire sport suffers long after the money gets spent.

Boxing has reached a state where capital is subsidizing inactivity. In past eras, financial pressure kept fighters active. A fighter made a living by entering the ring three or four times a year. If a champion held a belt, sitting idle cost real money, which meant dangerous mandatory challengers actually got their shot.

Contenders could leverage their number one ranking because champions could not afford to take an eighteen-month vacation waiting for an imaginary windfall. Once an unbacked financial bubble enters the ecosystem, the entire risk calculation collapses. A fighter walks away from one evening with forty or fifty million dollars.

From that moment on, their market value in their own mind is anchored to that unnatural number. An honest domestic or network promoter offering four million dollars to defend against an undefeated, dangerous mandatory looks like an insult, even if four million is the maximum revenue that gate and television rights can actually support. Because the champion is already rich beyond imagination, they hold all the leverage to say no.

They pack their bags, hit the gym casually, post workout clips on social media, and wait by the phone for the next massive check from a sovereign wealth fund or a deep-pocketed financier. The consequences for everyone else in the sport are brutal. Entire divisions freeze due to this problem. When three or four top names in a weight class are all parked on their couches waiting on the same financial patron to call their number, nobody fights each other. The pipeline stalls.

You end up with prime athletes fighting once every twelve to sixteen months, burning away their athletic peaks in hotel lobbies and negotiation rooms instead of under the lights.

The fighters who actually take the hit are the avoided, high-skill contenders. A guy who worked his entire life to become a mandatory challenger suddenly finds himself in an impossible trap. The champion will not fight him for realistic money because the contender does not bring casual pay-per-view buys. At the same time, the champion demands absurd money from outside backers to take on the stylistic hazard. The contender is told to stay busy, fight other dangerous guys for modest purses, and hope the superstar eventually runs out of soft alternatives.

It rewards marketability and name recognition while actively punishing ring ability. The sanctioning bodies completely capitulate, allowing it to happen. Belts exist to mandate competitive fights. Yet because sanctioning bodies take a percentage fee off the total purse, their financial allegiance lies with the massive check, not the integrity of their own rankings.

They gladly grant continuous medical exemptions, voluntary defense allowances, and special championship designations to mega-earners while stringing along the real number one contenders with interim straps. If the four sanctioning bodies had the spine to strip a wealthy champion the second an ordered mandatory defense deadline passed, this holdout culture would vanish overnight.

Boxing used to be built on hungry fighters needing to prove their dominance to sustain their livelihoods. Today, mega-purses have allowed elite fighters to operate like part-time consultants who only show up when the payout is absurd, and the opponent poses minimal threat to their brand.

Until the belts lose their marketing power or the infinite money well dries up, the sport will stay stuck in this loop of extended layoffs, ducked contenders, and synthetic events.

Sports.title: Devin Haney vs Liam Paro Faces A Tough PPV Sell
Sports.content:
Devin Haney’s first fight in more than a year will cost viewers extra. His December 19 bout with Liam Paro at Chase Center in San Francisco is officially a DAZN PPV, with Haney’s WBO welterweight title and Paro’s IBF belt at stake.

The belts give the fight a sporting purpose. Selling it is a different matter. Paro has earned his place, but he has a limited profile among American viewers, and a win over him would leave Haney with two of the division’s four major titles.

“I’ve never taken the easy road. I went to Puerto Rico and took the title off Matias in front of his own people. Devin’s a great fighter, and I respect that. But I’ve been the underdog plenty of times, and I’ve made history before. December 19, I’m coming to unify the division and make more history,” said Paro.

Placing a pay-per-view sticker on this card is going to be a tough sell. The entire model depends on casual interest or high-octane stylistic matchups, and this lineup offers neither to American buyers.

Haney sitting on the shelf for an entire year completely killed whatever tiny ripple of momentum he had after beating Norman Jr. Everyone remembers that bout as a safety-first wrestling match where Haney got on his bicycle, jabbed, and initiated clinches the second they got close. Purists might appreciate the ring IQ, but paying audiences want fireworks, especially when asked to drop extra cash on top of an existing subscription.

Paro is practically an unknown quantity to mainstream U.S. fans. His victory over Subriel Matias showed real grit in Puerto Rico, but casual viewers never saw it. His split-decision loss to Hitchins six months later only reinforced the perception that he is vulnerable to movers who control range. Sticking him in front of a San Francisco crowd against another defensive-minded boxer smells like another distance fight decided by jabs and positioning.

Then you look at the co-feature. Norman Jr. is fighting for redemption after losing his belt to Haney, but matching him against Abel Ramos is pure standard cable fare. Ramos is tough as nails, yet he has six losses and three draws on his ledger. Putting a former champion against a proven gatekeeper over ten rounds belongs on a regular DAZN Friday night stream, not on a premium broadcast that expects people to pull out credit cards six days before Christmas.

Unless Top Rank and Devin Haney Promotions pull off a miracle PR blitz or load the remaining two unannounced fights with genuine killers, this looks destined to struggle mightily at the box office.

“Now I’m bringing another Australian world champion, Liam Paro, into my backyard. This time, I plan to take his belt and become a unified welterweight world champion right here at home,” said Haney.

Sports.title: Ben Whittaker Climbs Rankings After Barely Surviving Wallace
Sports.content:
Ben Whittaker holds the mandatory rankings to demand a world title shot right now, yet his shaky finish against Wallace shows he is nowhere near ready for that step up. Owning two top spots does not prove he can last twelve rounds with Dmitry Bivol. Wallace had him out on his feet and clinging for life in the closing seconds, exposing flaws that an elite operator would punish without mercy.

Whittaker is now ranked at #1 WBO, #1 IBF, and #3 WBC at light heavyweight. Promoter Eddie Hearn suddenly holds multiple paths to steer his fighter toward a strap. The problem is those gaudy rankings build up heavy expectations that Whittaker simply failed to justify against Wallace.

He won the October 3 IBF final eliminator by scores of 117-111, 116-112 and 115-113, building his lead behind the jab before Wallace hurt him late. The way Whittaker fell apart physically in the later rounds showed that he’s not ready for Bivol or Artur Beterbiev.

Hearn is targeting February or March for Whittaker’s return, with Anthony Yarde and the winner of Joshua Buatsi against Willy Hutchinson among the possibilities.

The problem is that the blueprint is out on how to beat Whittaker. In the 2020 Olympics in Tokyo, Arlen Lopez and Imam Khataev exposed the flaws by walking through the flash, cutting off the ring, and roughing Whittaker up on the inside. Conor Wallace didn’t invent anything new in the late rounds; he just dusted off the same heavy-pressure game plan.

Every solid light heavyweight contender watched Whittaker gas out and resort to clinging once his legs stiffened up. Marinating the Bivol matchup only works if Hearn can keep matching him against fighters who lack the punch or the engine to execute that exact strategy. One slip against a live underdog with a sturdy chin, and the entire cash-out plan evaporates before Bivol even enters the conversation.

Hearn has twelve to eighteen months at most to let the fight marinate. The calendar is working against him far quicker than Matchroom wants to admit.

Whittaker turns 30 next summer. He entered the pros with an Olympic pedigree, but his physical peak as an agile, reflex-reliant fighter is happening right now. Waiting three or four years completely destroys his own physical advantages. Once his hand speed drops half a step or his legs fade five minutes earlier, he will not have the inside game or the durability to fall back on.

Waiting also assumes Bivol falls off a cliff overnight. Bivol turns 36 in December, but his style is built on footwork, distance management, and textbook fundamentals. Those attributes age far better than reliance on raw athleticism. A 37-year-old Bivol who has lost half a step will still possess the discipline and the tight combinations to pick apart a gassing Whittaker.

The real danger in stalling is the contender pool. Keeping Whittaker busy with fringe contenders or domestic rivals to run out the clock carries massive risk. The light heavyweight division is full of heavy-handed pressure fighters who took copious notes during the Wallace bout. If Hearn matches him with someone who has the engine to walk him down and the power to test his chin in rounds eight through twelve, Whittaker gets clipped before he ever sees a world title purse.

Hearn’s realistic window is late 2027. He can afford two tune-ups to work on conditioning and ring generalship under heavy fire. After that, he has to cash in the ticket, win or lose, before an ambitious contender beats him to the punch and ruins the entire investment.

Ghana News.title: GES extends Obuasi SHTS sexual misconduct probe by seven days – Daniel Fenyi
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Education Service (GES) has granted its committee investigating allegations of sexual misconduct involving the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, a seven-day extension to complete its investigations.

GES Public Relations Officer, Daniel Fenyi, said the committee had already engaged several people connected to the incident, including some of the alleged victims, but required additional time to ensure their experiences were adequately captured in its report.

Speaking on Joy FM's Midday News, Mr Fenyi explained that the committee was initially given two weeks to complete its work, with the deadline expiring on Wednesday.

However, the committee subsequently requested an additional seven days to enable it to engage all the victims identified in the video at the centre of the controversy.

He said the investigators were keen to ensure that the final report reflected the actual experiences of the alleged victims rather than being completed without their full representation.

The GES PRO expressed the expectation that the committee would reach all the victims by November 11 and submit its report to the GES Council.

Mr Fenyi stressed that investigations were still ongoing and dismissed suggestions that the Service had cleared Mr Abdulai or any other individual implicated in the allegations.

He emphasised that the GES had not concluded its investigations and that no final determination had been made as of Friday, November 6.

Ghana News.title: Artificial Intelligence and its intended consequences for national security
Ghana News.content:
The age and era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has gradually crept up on us. This means there is nothing we can do about it but embrace it. AI has positive and negative effects for organizations, stakeholders, the state, and national security. AI has numerous benefits all over the globe; it has become a tool that is being used for various purposes.

AI is used in hospitals for diagnosis, used in classrooms to aid learners, and even used in warfare, predicting enemy lines for counterattack. Advanced countries and institutions have resorted to the use of AI for ease in modern warfare and productivity. Weapons have now been fitted with aspects of AI to ascertain the exact locations of targets. This critical dimension makes artificial intelligence a tool that we in the Global South need to take seriously.

When we look at the aspect of misinformation and disinformation, we need not overlook the fact that AI is being used in a negative way. With associated attacks in cyberspace, misinformation and disinformation are very worrying when AI is used. Happenings around the globe with regard to the use of AI have shown that the tool is being used to destroy cryptocurrency investments.

Recent narratives have established that financial crimes were committed in the cryptocurrency markets because a worker's laptop was infected with AI software. This is a very worrying spectacle.

We are hearing financial institutions also losing their security space to AI threats. Some banks in Asia have been hacked using AI software, and automated cyber-attacks via AI tools are occurring across the globe.

The question then is: what happens with us in the Global South? So, for a country like Ghana, have we fully embraced artificial intelligence? Looking at the threats and challenges in the fight against cyber-attacks, what this means is that criminal elements have become more sophisticated, trying to find loopholes in the security system to be able to outwit the security agencies and managers of the country using AI tools. Arrests have been made regarding Ghanaian citizens alleged to have used AI to create fake images to engage in cyber fraud and romance scams.

Our security architecture must embrace this tool as a matter of national security. This will go a long way to assist fight crime and predict crimes and identify the perpetuators. In the end, the tool can have a positive impact on our security landscape when applied efficiently. Africa as a whole needs to really invest in artificial intelligence to understand the intricacies for security purposes, protection, and prevention of crimes and conflict. Otherwise, we'll be taken by surprise when attacks are targeted against our financial institutions and our security apparatus. We need to learn to use AI.

Various institutions in the country need to embrace it for the purposes of protection and prevention of any attacks. We must be mindful of the fact that the impact of AI is too great to leave unmanaged. Strong governance policies and investment in people are what will keep its use safe and effective.

Here are some of the key benefits of the use of AI in Cybersecurity:

AI in cybersecurity enables real-time threat detection, automated response, and large-scale data analysis to mitigate risks faster than traditional approaches. AI-powered cybersecurity strengthens endpoints, networks, and cloud security through phishing detection, behavioral analytics, vulnerability management, and authentication. AI reduces manual effort and human error while improving efficiency, accelerating response times, and enhancing overall security posture. Effective adoption requires high-quality data, continuous model updates, human in the loop, and integration across the security stack. AI-driven security introduces risks like adversarial AI and data poisoning, requiring adaptive and continuously evolving defense strategies.

Over the past few months, we have seen a rise in adversarial AI attacks, data poisoning, AI tools hacking one another, and simulated attacks. Organizations looking to adopt AI should invest in training their people. AI adoption is valuable, but only if organizations invest in AI training, establish governance processes, and continuously evolve their defense strategies.

Authors

Kwame Asomaning: Technologist & Cybersecurity Professional

Victor Doke, PhD, is a Security Analyst and Lecturer, Ghana Armed Forces Command and Staff College (GAFCSC)

Ghana News.title: NDC sets November 9 deadline for national executive nominations
Ghana News.content:
The National Democratic Congress (NDC) will conclude the filing of nominations for its national executive positions on Monday, November 9, as the party advances its 2026 internal electoral process towards the election of new national officers in December.

The filing of nominations is scheduled to take place from Saturday, November 7, to Monday, November 9, following the 14-day period allocated to aspirants to complete their nomination forms.

According to the party's electoral timetable, the vetting of national executive aspirants will take place on Thursday, November 12, and Friday, November 13, at the National Secretariat.

An appeals process has also been scheduled for Sunday, November 15, and Monday, November 16.

The national electoral process will culminate in the party's National Congress on Saturday, December 19, 2026, where new national executives are expected to be elected.

Regional elections scheduled for November 14–15

Ahead of the national congress, the NDC will hold its Regional Youth and Women Conference on Friday, November 13, followed by regional executive elections on Saturday, November 14, and Sunday, November 15.

The regional elections form part of the party's broader internal reorganisation process, which is expected to produce new leadership at the various levels ahead of the 2028 General Elections.

National Youth and Women Conference

The party has also scheduled its National Youth and Women Conference for Saturday, December 12, although the venue is yet to be announced.

The conference will precede the National Congress on December 19, which will mark the culmination of the party's 2026 internal electoral exercise.

Party urges adherence to timetable

The NDC has urged all regional and constituency executives, aspirants and members to carefully study the electoral timetable and comply with the stipulated procedures, timelines and deadlines.

It said strict adherence to the roadmap was necessary to safeguard the credibility and integrity of the elections and ensure that all stages of the process were conducted fairly and transparently.

The party also expressed appreciation to its members, executives and stakeholders for their continued dedication, discipline and commitment to its ideals.

It said the unity and collective spirit demonstrated throughout the reorganisation process would strengthen the party as it prepares for the 2028 General Elections.

Ghana News.title: 4.8 tonnes of marijuana with over US$1m street value heading towards Nigeria seized by Ghana Navy
Ghana News.content:
Two large wooden boats carrying 117 sacks of substances suspected to be marijuana, with an estimated street value of more than US$1 million, have been intercepted by the Ghana Navy in an intelligence-led operation on the Volta Lake estuary at Ada in the Greater Accra Region.

The operation, conducted by the Riverine Command of the Ghana Navy at about 1 a.m. on Thursday, November 5, prevented the suspected consignment from being transported outside the country via the sea.

The boats were discovered concealed along the banks of the river near the estuary.

They were in the preparatory stages of transporting the narcotics to Nigeria. They fled the scene and abandoned the boat when they saw Navy personnel approaching.

Addressing a press conference on Thursday, the Director of Naval Operations at the Naval Headquarters, Naval Captain Festus Osei-Brobbey, said the suspects abandoned the boats and fled upon sighting the naval patrol team.

He said the boats were subsequently moved to Ada Foah, where they were searched at about 5 a.m. in the presence of officials of the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC).

The search revealed 117 sacks containing approximately 80 packs of suspected marijuana each, bringing the estimated total weight of the consignment to 4.8 tons.

Naval Captain Osei-Brobbey said the substances have been handed over to NACOC to conduct the necessary laboratory examination.

He described the seizure as potentially the biggest marijuana interception by the Navy in the recent past, recalling an earlier operation in July during which about 60 sacks of suspected marijuana were intercepted.

He said the operation formed part of the Navy's commitment to combating illicit activities within Ghana's maritime domain and supporting President John Dramani Mahama's zero-tolerance stance on drug trafficking.

He indicated that the operation also reinforced national efforts to strengthen border security, improve inter-agency cooperation and prevent the use of Ghana as a transit point for illicit substances.

Naval Captain Osei-Brobbey warned financiers, sponsors, organisers and other individuals involved in drug trafficking that the Navy would intensify surveillance and monitoring operations to identify, track and disrupt criminal networks operating within the country's maritime corridors.

He said the Navy would continue to work with other security agencies and stakeholders to protect Ghana's territorial waters against drug trafficking and other illicit activities.

He also appealed to the public to provide credible and actionable information to support the security agencies in their operations. He also appealed to the public to provide credible and actionable information to support the security agencies in their operations.

Assembly

The Municipal Chief Executive (MCE) for Ada East, Kenneth Kofi Kabu Kanor, who also addressed the press conference, expressed concern about the growing challenge of drug abuse and its impact on families and communities.

He said the geographical location of Ada, with its river and sea connections, made it important for authorities to strengthen surveillance and prevent the waterways from being exploited for illegal activities.

Mr Kanor called for stronger collaboration between the district assembly, security agencies and the central government to tackle drug trafficking and other illegal activities.

He further stressed the need to protect the area's waterways and promote responsible use of its natural resources, saying the fight against illicit trade required collective commitment.

Ghana News.title: Minority demands probe into Akamai shutdown of digital health systems over US$64m debt
Ghana News.content:
The Minority in Parliament has demanded an investigation into the suspension of critical electronic health information systems in Ghana following an outstanding payment of approximately US$64,511 to technology services provider Akamai.

The caucus says the disruption raises serious questions about the government’s financial planning, contract management and oversight of the country’s digital health infrastructure.

In a press statement dated November 6, 2026, the Ranking Member of Parliament’s Health Committee, Dr Nana Ayew Afriye, said the Ghana Health Service (GHS) had disclosed in a communication dated November 2 that critical electronic health information systems, including the District Health Information Management System (DHIMS2), had been inaccessible since October 29.

The shutdown reportedly followed the suspension of ten servers by Akamai over an outstanding payment of US$64,510.95.

The Minority described the development as troubling, particularly against the backdrop of government’s assurances that the introduction of the Ghana Health Information Management System (GHIMS) would strengthen national control over health data and reduce dependence on private service providers.

In October 2025, Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh announced the introduction of GHIMS to replace the Lightwave Health Information Management System (LHIMS).

Although GHIMS and DHIMS2 perform different functions, the Minority says both are part of Ghana’s wider digital health ecosystem, raising concerns about the sustainability of the government’s digital health strategy.

The caucus has also questioned the resources committed to the digital health transformation, noting that the Ministry of Health’s budget increased from approximately GH¢17.8 billion in 2025 to GH¢22.8 billion in 2026, representing a 28 per cent nominal increase.

It is, however, demanding a detailed account of the specific allocations and expenditure on GHIMS and related digital infrastructure, as well as the measurable outcomes achieved.

The Minority further criticised the Ministry of Health and the Ghana Health Service for allowing outstanding contractual obligations to result in the disruption of critical national health information systems.

It also questioned Akamai’s decision to suspend the services despite the potential public health consequences, although it acknowledged that contractual obligations must be respected.

The caucus has called on the Ministry to review its agreement with Akamai and consider terminating the contract where justified by the established facts and contractual provisions.

Among its demands, the Minority wants government to immediately restore the affected systems and provide a clear timeline for their full operational recovery.

It is also calling for a comprehensive account of GHIMS expenditure, including budgetary allocations, actual spending, implementation progress and integration with existing health information systems.

Additionally, the caucus wants an investigation into the Akamai suspension to establish institutional responsibility and determine appropriate corrective action.

It has proposed an independent audit of Ghana’s digital health infrastructure, covering hosting arrangements, interoperability, data security and business continuity.

The Minority says sustainable financing and infrastructure safeguards must also be established to prevent similar disruptions.

It maintains that Ghana’s digital health transformation must be measured by the reliability, accessibility and sustainability of systems serving the public, rather than simply the introduction of new platforms

Ghana News.title: Petrol prices set for possible November cut as crude oil drops sharply
Ghana News.content:
Motorists in Ghana could see lower petrol prices from November 16 as a recent decline in international crude oil prices raises expectations of relief at the pumps, the Chamber of Petroleum Consumers (COPEC) has said.

COPEC Executive Secretary Duncan Amoah says crude prices have fallen by more than 12 to 14 per cent over 48 hours, creating the possibility of a downward adjustment in the next fuel pricing cycle.

However, he cautioned that the decline in crude oil prices would not immediately translate into cheaper fuel, as refined petroleum product prices typically take between six and seven days to respond to movements in the global crude market.

The next pricing window opens on November 16, with the National Petroleum Authority’s guidelines requiring the use of average free-on-board prices recorded between October 27 and November 11 to determine the applicable prices.

Mr Amoah said if the downward trend on the international market persists and feeds through to refined products within the assessment period, petrol prices could fall in the second half of November.

“If all things are equal, and what we have observed since the mid-term elections in America happened is that you have seen prices consistently drop on the international market, our prediction or projection will be that for the second window of November, the cost of petrol, particularly, would have witnessed some reduction,” he said.

Speaking on Citi FM on Thursday, November 5, he explained that the timing of the adjustment in refined product prices would determine whether consumers benefit from the November review or have to wait until December.
