As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".

Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.

"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.

"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.

Additional reporting by Davide Ghiglione

World.title: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".

World.title: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
World.content:
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.

But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.

Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.

The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.

"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.

Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.

"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.

He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.

He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.

Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.

President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.

Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.

World.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
World.content:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

World.title: Fighting Somali piracy needs local leadership, foreign naval backing
World.content:
Piracy off Somalia’s coast has resurfaced, with nine hijackings so far this year attributed to local raiders. In the latest incident on 29 October, the Iranian fishing vessel Azini was attacked off the coast of Puntland. India’s navy rescued the crew and vessel, preventing the pirates from using it to board other commercial ships.

The increase in incidents has renewed concerns over maritime security and created more problems for global shipping, adding to the war in Iran and rising consumer prices.

Geography plays a key role in creating conditions conducive to recurring piracy off Somalia’s coast. Puntland, the current epicentre, has been central to waves of piracy since the early 2000s. Much of Somalia’s coastline – the longest in mainland Africa – lies in Puntland.

Puntland and Galmudug States, Somalia

Puntland State’s security and governance presence is concentrated along the inland Bosaso-Galkayo corridor, where the main urban centres are located. This leaves much of the rugged, isolated coastline beyond state control, allowing pirates to operate from remote fishing hamlets.

Nonetheless, government security forces – including the United Arab Emirates (UAE)-supported Puntland Maritime Police Force, established in 2013, have remained the first line of defence against piracy. They have pursued bandits in urban areas, disrupted supply lines and dismantled shore-based hideouts.

Both joint and independent foreign naval forces are also present. The European Union Naval Force Operation Atalanta and deployments from China, India, Japan, South Korea, and Russia are mandated to protect their vessels off Somalia.

These layers of deterrence previously helped contain piracy, but are no longer effective due to both internal and external factors.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Puntland’s capacity to counter piracy has been increasingly constrained by overlapping security and political factors. Since December 2024, its security forces – aided by external actors like the United States (US) – have degraded and dislodged Islamic State from large stretches of mountainous territory, while simultaneously confronting al-Shabaab. Fighting these terror groups has stretched the state’s security capacity.

At the same time, the Puntland Security Force (PSF), a US-trained counter-terrorism special force, fell out with the state government over its operational autonomy and command structure. In 2024, the PSF pledged allegiance to Somalia’s federal government, placing it at the centre of the Puntland-Mogadishu rift. After armed confrontations between Puntland’s other security forces and the PSF, the PSF was defeated.

Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni – expected to run for national president in May 2027 alongside current President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud – viewed the PSF as a threat to his position. Indeed, the federal government has recently used force to oust state-level leaders who oppose its political agenda, including in Jubaland and South West states. The PSF rebellion distracted Puntland’s leadership from rising piracy, allowing the threat to escalate unchecked.

Externally, the Iran war and Houthi attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea have created opportunities for pirates. Redeployment of foreign naval forces to that conflict has left Somalia’s coast less patrolled, while rerouted shipping has brought more commercial vessels closer to the coast. Many of these ships also lack armed security guards.

Piracy responses must address these gaps and coordinate across international, federal and state actors. Responses so far have been siloed, with external actors increasingly resorting to force.

On 29 August, the federal government announced that Türkiye’s navy freed the MV Lutuf cargo ship, leading to 14 pirates’ deaths and four small boats being destroyed. Puntland rejected this, alleging Mogadishu and Türkiye paid a US$2.5 million ransom.

Nevertheless, Türkiye’s intervention mirrored that of the US under President Donald Trump, signalling a shift towards a more kinetic approach by foreign navies. In early 2026, Mr Trump drew a parallel between Somali pirates and Latin American networks smuggling drugs into the US. He said the same missiles used against drug traffickers were being used by the US against Somali pirates.

However, Somalia’s coastline is too vast for the small number of foreign naval vessels to patrol effectively. The Iran war has also limited the appetite for a major international anti-piracy operation. Meanwhile, pirates’ growing access to drones, satellite internet and GPS enhances their ability to monitor maritime activity and identify potential targets.

The selective application of military responses by foreign countries is also problematic. In the MV Lutuf case, Türkiye intervened because the vessel was carrying military hardware, communication systems and satellite equipment for Turkish military training in Mogadishu.

Although foreign navies’ kinetic operations produce short-term gains, they can be counterproductive. For years, many Somalis have viewed foreign naval forces in Somali waters as complicit in illegal fishing and waste dumping – a view local leaders share.

By targeting young men who are often lured into piracy after losing their jobs to foreign illegal fishing, foreign navies risk reinforcing perceptions of impunity and indifference to Somali lives. This harms anti-piracy efforts, which require strong public support to succeed. It could also deepen the grievances that helped piracy take root, ultimately generating greater public sympathy for pirates.

The lack of anti-piracy coordination between Somalia’s federal and state authorities is also a challenge, as evidenced by the aftermath of the operation to free MV Lutuf. Another example is that after defeating the PSF, Puntland launched its own anti-piracy military operation. Although three captive vessels were freed and dozens of pirates captured, five crew members died, and four were wounded.

And the piracy threat has been extended to a second federal state after pirates moved the captured vessel Asana from Puntland’s coast to Galmudug.

Influential countries such as the US, Türkiye, and the UAE should strengthen Somalia’s maritime security capacity and help mend ties between federal authorities and Puntland. Both Puntland and Galmudug should lead kinetic anti-piracy operations and ensure a permanent police presence along their coastlines to deny pirates a foothold.

Willis Okumu is a Senior Researcher on East Africa peace and security governance, and Said Abdullahi is a Research Intern on conflict prevention, management, resolution and peacebuilding in the Great Lakes Region, at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) in Nairobi.

(This article was first published by ISS Today, a Premium Times syndication partner. We have their permission to republish).

World.title: 2027: Professor urges journalists to probe campaign promises, prioritise citizens’ needs
World.content:
The Director of UNIZIK FM at the Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka (NAU), Ifeoma Dunu, has urged Nigerian journalists to shift focus from routine coverage of political campaigns and embrace accountability journalism ahead of the 2027 general elections.

NAU is a federal university in Anambra State, popularly known as UNIZIK, and UNIZIK FM is the university’s radio station, mainly for journalism students.

Mrs Dunu, a professor, made the call on Thursday while presenting a paper at a two-day media workshop in Enugu.

The workshop was organised by the International Press Centre (IPC) and supported by the European Union.

The professor challenged media practitioners to make public accountability, citizens’ welfare and rigorous fact-checking central to their election coverage rather than focusing on politicians and their statements.

She stressed that the forthcoming 2027 general elections placed an important responsibility on the media to strengthen democratic participation, promote accountability and safeguard citizens’ access to credible electoral information.

Mrs Dunu warned journalists against focusing largely on political parties, defections, rallies, endorsements, and contests among candidates.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Effective election journalism must move beyond reporting what politicians say to investigating what they do, verifying what they claim, and establishing how their decisions affect citizens’ lives,” she said.

She contended that journalists must rigorously compare political promises against available evidence, budgets, and implementation rather than focusing on campaign rhetoric.

“The media remains agenda-setters. Therefore, there’s a need to focus on the priority concerns of the people rather than the promises of politicians at campaign rallies.

“So, what people identified as their needs should matter to journalists more than what politicians are promising them,” she added.

Fact-checking

In his presentation, a fact-checker with the IPC, Olusola Oludiran, took the journalists on fact-checking and the utilisation of digital tools in journalism.

Mr Oludiran stressed the importance of verification and responsible journalism, especially in the face of the growing challenge of misinformation, manipulated information and artificial intelligence-generated content.

Media responsibility

Earlier, in his address, Lanre Arogundade, executive director of IPC, said the media has a responsibility to ensure that citizens’ voices are heard in the democratic process in addition to scrutinising political promises and holding public officials accountable.

“However, the effectiveness of this responsibility depends significantly on the quality of electoral reporting.

“An election period characterised by sensationalism, unverified claims, inflammatory rhetoric, and the unchecked spread of misinformation and disinformation can undermine public confidence, deepen social divisions, and weaken democratic institutions,” Mr Arogundade said.

Continuing, the executive director said: “Conversely, a media environment that prioritises accuracy, fairness, verification, conflict-sensitive reporting, and accountability can strengthen public trust and contribute to peaceful, credible, and inclusive elections.”

He also warned that while digital platforms have expanded information sharing and public participation, they have accelerated the spread of misinformation, manipulated content, hate speech and divisive narratives.

“The media must, therefore, strengthen its verification skills, exercise caution before publishing politically sensitive information, and resist the pressure to prioritise speed over accuracy.

“In this regard, fact-checking and verification should not be treated as optional additions to journalism. They must be integral to responsible electoral reporting,” he stated.

World.title: Tinubu to commission multi-billion naira projects in Akwa Ibom
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu is scheduled to commission eight major projects in Akwa Ibom State on Friday, but questions surrounding billions of naira allocated to the projects and the government’s compliance with public procurement laws have cast a shadow over the inaugurations.

The projects include the Airport-Okopedi Road, Ring Road 3, AKWA-GIS Office Complex, Command and Control Centre, ARISE Palm Resort, the International Terminal Building, International Airport Hospital and Ibom Aviation Village.

The presidency announced on Thursday that Mr Tinubu would visit Uyo, the Akwa Ibom State capital, on Friday to commission the projects executed by the administration of Governor Umo Eno before attending an All Progressives Congress political rally in nearby Rivers State.

An examination of successive budget documents by PREMIUM TIMES shows that many of the projects attracted substantial allocations between 2023 and 2026, yet their original contract sums, contractors’ details and procurement records are not publicly accessible.

The absence of these records raises questions about compliance with the Akwa Ibom State Public Procurement Law, which requires the government to publish procurement information on its electronic portal.

Billions in successive budgets

A review of the state government’s budget documents shows that the Airport-Okopedi Road, a 14.5-kilometre road connecting communities in Nsit Atai and Okobo Local Government Areas, has attracted repeated budgetary provisions.

The project, which dates back to the administration of former Governor Godswill Akpabio and continued under his successor, Udom Emmanuel, has experienced implementation challenges, including the revocation of some contracts along the route.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Under the current administration, the first phase, captured in the budgets as the re-award of the contract for the dualisation of the 14.5-kilometre Airport-Okopedi Road, received N3 billion in the 2023 revised budget, N8.5 billion in 2024, N23 billion in 2025 and another N15 billion in the 2026 budget.

These provisions amount to N49.5 billion over the four budget cycles.

Another major road project scheduled for inauguration is the dualisation of the 7.868-kilometre Ring Road 3, which connects Idoro Road to Ikot Ekpene Road through Uyo and Ibiono Ibom.

The project, handled by Hensek Services, attracted N21 billion in the 2024 budget, N15 billion in 2025 and N13 billion in 2026, bringing its cumulative budgetary provisions to N49 billion.

Despite the scale of the allocations, PREMIUM TIMES could not find the original contract sum or obtain publicly accessible procurement records detailing the award and implementation of the project.

The ARISE Palm Resort, another major tourism project initiated by the administration and listed for inauguration, also received substantial allocations.

The state budgeted N29.99 billion for the construction of the resort in 2025 and another N10 billion in 2026.

An additional N5 billion was provided for erosion-control facilities around the resort and connected to Udo Inwang Street, near the resort.

The resort is part of Governor Eno’s tourism development agenda, which has involved major public investments in recreational and hospitality infrastructure.

PREMIUM TIMES had previously reported concerns about the absence of procurement records and contract details for the administration’s Ibom ARISE Park and Resort project.

The newspaper found that the government had not published the contract sum, procurement documentation or bidding records for the project on the state procurement portal.

The International Terminal Building at the Victor Attah International Airport has also attracted substantial allocations under the Eno administration.

The state provided N21.1 billion in the 2023 revised budget, N14.35 billion in 2024, N16.2 billion in 2025 and N8 billion in the 2026 budget for the project.

The allocations total N59.65 billion across the four budget cycles.

The terminal, however, presents a separate accountability question because it was already commissioned by former Senate President Bukola Saraki on 26 May 2023, shortly before Mr Emmanuel left office.

In May 2025, PREMIUM TIMES reported that Governor Eno said he inherited the terminal at almost 40 per cent completion, despite its commissioning under his predecessor.

The newspaper also found that the state continued to allocate money to the facility after its inauguration.

The latest decision to include the terminal in the list of projects scheduled for commissioning by Mr Tinubu raises further questions about the extent of work completed after its initial inauguration and the additional public funds committed to it.

Airport facilities, other projects

Other projects scheduled for inauguration at the Victor Attah International Airport include the International Airport Hospital and Ibom Aviation Village.

The hospital project is captured in the state budgets as the remodelling and upgrade of the Victor Attah International Airport Clinic, including the construction of call rooms.

The government allocated N2 billion for the remodelling and upgrade in 2025, alongside N700 million for the purchase of equipment.

The Ibom Aviation Village, captured in the budget as the Aviation Housing Estate, received N6.62 billion in 2025 and N5.98 billion in 2026.

The state also made provisions for the Command and Control Centre, including N500 million for equipping and furnishing the facility in 2025 and another N1 billion in 2026.

However, PREMIUM TIMES could not identify specific budgetary allocations for the AKWA-GIS Office Complex in the budgets reviewed under the Eno administration.

For these projects, the government has yet to make publicly accessible details showing their original contract sums, subsequent variations, contractors and procurement processes.

Procurement law questions

The absence of publicly available contract information is noteworthy because the Akwa Ibom State Public Procurement Law provides for transparency in the award and implementation of public contracts.

Section 61(5) of the law mandates the Public Procurement Regulatory Agency and other procuring entities to promptly and routinely publish procurement information on the state’s electronic portal.

The provision is intended to ensure that members of the public can access information about government procurement and examine how public resources are committed.

However, searches by PREMIUM TIMES on the state’s procurement portal did not reveal the contract details of the projects scheduled for inauguration.

The newspaper also found no publicly available evidence establishing that the contracts were subjected to open competitive bidding, as provided for under the state’s procurement framework, or that any applicable exceptions were properly invoked.

Without the disclosure of contract sums, bidding records and award details, it is difficult for the public to on their own determine whether the projects were awarded in accordance with the law, whether the costs show value for money and how much the government has actually spent on them.

The concerns come against the backdrop of previous PREMIUM TIMES investigations into procurement transparency and fiscal accountability under Mr Eno.

Four days ago, the newspaper reported that the state government had received at least N3.218trillion in public revenue within 41 months of the governor’s administration but had stopped publishing detailed capital expenditure records, making it difficult to track spending on major projects.

Other reports by the newspaper have documented the government’s failure to disclose procurement details for major public investments, including its N42 billion compressed natural gas bus project and the N15.47 billion rehabilitation of the State House of Assembly complex.

Government keeps mum

PREMIUM TIMES sent a media enquiry to the Akwa Ibom State Commissioner for Information, Aniekan Umanah, seeking clarification on the projects and the absence of their procurement records.

The newspaper asked the government to provide the total cost of each project, including the original contract sums and any subsequent variations or revised costs.

It also requested details of the procurement methods used in awarding the contracts and whether the processes complied with the procedures and approvals prescribed by the state’s public procurement law.

Additionally, the newspaper asked why the contract awards, sums, contractors and other relevant procurement records had not been published on the state’s procurement portal, as required by law.

Calls to Mr Umanah did not connect. He also did not respond to text messages, WhatsApp messages or a message sent through Facebook Messenger.

The commissioner had not responded to the enquiries as of the time of this report.

World.title: Paraguay’s President resigns but Congress rejects his resignation
World.content:
Paraguay President Santiago Peña announced on Thursday that he was resigning from office after a political and financial crisis that collapsed the country’s banking system.

But the state’s Congress has rejected his resignation and is pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings.

Al Jazeera reported that the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach Mr Peña. The Senate also opened impeachment proceedings and summoned him to appear on Friday.

Mr Peña announced his resignation in a video address shared on X on Thursday.

He said, “I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me.”

The president said he resigned to protect stability, social peace, and democratic institutions.

A joint congressional session was called to consider the resignation, and the votes failed, according to Al Jazeera.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

As a result, he remains president and will face impeachment proceedings.

Paraguay’s financial crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Ueno Bank is the country’s largest lender. It claims to serve about 60 per cent of the population.

Founded in the 1970s, Ueno Bank grew from an obscure finance company into a major institution after Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates, purchased it in 2021.

Mr Peña was a shareholder in Grupo Vázquez until last year.

Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers.

It held pensions and some other public funds, and collapsed earlier this week. Thousands of citizens could not access money for food and basic daily expenses.

Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.

READ ALSO: Huge loss for Trump as Democrats take control of Congress

Lawmakers and opposition groups have accused Mr Peña of misconduct, but he has vehemently rejected these allegations.

Had his resignation been accepted, he would have become a senator for life and enjoyed a degree of legal immunity from prosecution, as members of the legislature do. This is entitled to the Paraguayan president after leaving office.

However, this benefit does not apply to a president who is convicted in an impeachment trial.

But Mr Peña has said he would appear for Senate impeachment proceedings to exercise his “right to a defence”.

On X, he wrote, “I will provide the information requested of me. Citizens deserve to know the truth, without cover-ups and without anyone being above the law.”

World.title: Troops rescue 16 kidnapping victims, recover two rifles, three bombs, 33 bikes
World.content:
Troops of the Nigerian Army have rescued 16 abductees and recovered two AK-47 rifles, three rocket-propelled grenade (RPG) bombs and 33 motorcycles during an operation in Niger State.

The operation was conducted on 5 November by troops of the Army’s 18 Brigade following intelligence about the movement of suspected terrorists from Mashegu Local Government Area towards Rijiyan Nagwamatse in Kontagora LGA.

In a statement on Friday, the Acting Assistant Director of Army Public Relations, 18 Brigade, Adebayo Adewumi, said the troops mounted an ambush along suspected routes used by the armed men.

He said the troops engaged the suspected terrorists, who had earlier abducted residents, neutralising an unspecified number and rescuing 16 victims.

Items recovered included two AK-47 rifles, seven magazines, three RPG high-explosive anti-personnel bombs, assorted ammunition, 33 motorcycles and ₦4.1 million in cash.

Mr Adewumi said the rescued victims received first aid before authorities handed them over to be reunited with their families.

In a related operation on 3 November, troops intercepted suspected terrorists travelling from Makuku village in Sakaba LGA, Kebbi State, towards Tungan Kawo in Rijau LGA, Niger State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the army spokesperson, the troops engaged the armed men in a firefight, forcing them to retreat into a nearby forest with gunshot wounds.

A subsequent search led to the recovery of five motorcycles, a mobile phone and ₦644,300, among other items.

The army said it kept the recovered items in military custody for further action.

Mr Adewumi quoted the Commander of 18 Brigade as commending the troops for their conduct and urging them to sustain the operations against criminal groups in the brigade’s area of responsibility.

Growing insecurity in Niger

The operations come amid a series of kidnappings and attacks on communities in Niger State.

On 31 October, suspected bandits abducted 14 pupils of an Islamic school and their teacher while they were harvesting maize on a farm in Tungan-Bako village, Rafi LGA.

The Niger State Police Command confirmed the abduction, saying joint security teams had begun rescue efforts.

READ ALSO: Police arrest 36 suspects in Niger State

The incident followed the abduction of 47 farmers while harvesting groundnuts in Tugan-Rimi, Mariga LGA, on 27 September.

On 21 August, gunmen reportedly abducted more than 500 worshippers from Juma’at mosques in Dekara and four other communities in the state. Families told Daily Trust that the abductors had yet to contact them.

The state has also witnessed attacks on farming communities, forcing residents in parts of Borgu, Mariga, Mashegu and Rijau LGAs to flee their homes and abandon crops on their farms.

Earlier, on 21 November 2025, armed men abducted 230 pupils, students and staff members from St Mary’s Catholic Primary and Secondary School in Papiri, Agwara LGA. The victims were later rescued after spending several weeks in captivity.

World.title: ‘Reports such as yours could always put us on our toes,’ UNIJOS dean reacts to PREMIUM TIMES report
World.content:
The Dean of Student Affairs at the University of Jos (UNIJOS), Professor Chris Piwuna, has acknowledged maintenance challenges at the university’s Village Hostel, which accommodates students with disabilities, following a PREMIUM TIMES investigation into the inaccessible and deteriorating facilities.

Mr Piwuna, who spoke with PREMIUM TIMES after reading the investigation, admitted that the hostel required further improvements but said the university had made several interventions to improve conditions for students with disabilities.

“Hostel maintenance is a huge problem, and I can only say to you we will keep trying our best,” he said in a subsequent message to the reporter.

He added: “Reports such as yours could always put us on our toes.”

However, the dean did not provide a timeline for renovating the hostel or explain when the university would address the accessibility problems documented in the investigation.

In the investigation, titled “Inaccessible Hostels, Other Facilities: How UNIJOS fails Students with disabilities,” PREMIUM TIMES documented the difficulties students face accessing bathrooms, moving around the hostel compound and reaching lecture halls.

During a visit to the Village Hostel in September, the newspaper observed that the bathroom was old and poorly maintained, with no ramps, grab rails or other accessibility features to enable wheelchair users to enter and move around independently.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The toilet area was dirty and emitted a strong stench, with human excreta visible in parts of the facility.

The investigation also documented overgrown bushes, uneven surfaces, potholes and other barriers that make independent movement difficult for students with disabilities.

Monica Joseph*, a wheelchair user, told PREMIUM TIMES that she crawls into the bathroom on her hands and knees because there is no ramp or support device that allows her to enter with her wheelchair.

“I become even dirtier after coming out of the bathroom,” she said.

Another student, James Patrick*, who is visually impaired, recounted falling from a bridge while crossing to school because there was no guide to indicate the safe path.

Dean disputes claims of neglect

During a telephone conversation with PREMIUM TIMES after reading the report, Mr Piwuna described the suggestion that the university had abandoned students with disabilities as unfair.

He said that shortly after becoming dean, he visited the Village Hostel and identified several problems requiring attention.

According to him, some of the hostel’s doors had fallen off, while others were unsuitable for the students’ needs. He said the university replaced the doors and repaired other parts of the accommodation, including window fittings.

“When I became dean, I visited that hostel. I noticed that their doors had fallen, and I thought it was, you know, unfair to their disability, having them in bathrooms without doors. We fixed the doors. We even fixed their room doors,” he said.

He also said the university repaired a borehole near the hostel after discovering that students had to walk to other parts of the campus to fetch water because the facility was not working.

Mr Piwuna said the intervention was supported by Professor C.J. Dakas, whom he identified as someone who provided financial assistance for the repairs.

He said the university also employed two staff members in the Directorate of Student Affairs to attend to students with disabilities, including blind and deaf students and those requiring mobility assistance.

The dean further said he personally intervened to address areas around the hostel that became difficult to navigate during the rainy season.

According to him, some sections where water accumulated were worked on to provide flatter surfaces for students to move around.

He advised PREMIUM TIMES to verify the interventions with former Students’ Union Government leaders and presidents of associations representing blind and deaf students.

However, PREMIUM TIMES’ observations during the September visit showed that significant accessibility challenges remained around the hostel.

Overgrown bushes, uneven surfaces, stones and potholes still surrounded parts of the compound, making movement difficult for students with disabilities, particularly wheelchair users.

Some sections remained inaccessible, with no ramps or other features to support independent movement.

University acknowledges

While defending the university’s interventions, Mr Piwuna acknowledged that the conditions at the hostel remained unsatisfactory.

He said maintaining university facilities was a continuing challenge, particularly given the financial and administrative demands involved in managing infrastructure across a large institution.

“The issue of hostel maintenance is a big thing in any university in Nigeria, so it requires constant maintenance. That is what is lacking. Sometimes the government or the university administration is unable to do all of those things,” he said.

He also acknowledged the conditions shown in the photographs published by PREMIUM TIMES.

“From the pictures that you’ve shown, if anybody knows what it means to maintain these things, you know, when you talk to such individuals, they will tell you that it’s an ongoing thing,” he said.

The dean, however, rejected the impression that the university had neglected the welfare of students with disabilities.

“Nobody is arguing that the hostel is at the level that it should be. No, that’s not what I’m saying,” he said.

“We need to do more. I have no doubt about that. I agree with you 100 per cent, but to say or give the impression that they are being abandoned, nobody cares about their welfare and all of that, is not true. In fact, the grass around their hostel, I made sure that at any point in time, those places are properly mowed so that snakes and other reptiles would not be around.”

Mr Piwuna also said the university had previously written to the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD), seeking assistance with improving the hostel.

He said the commission sent a representative to Jos to assess the facility and obtain estimates for the proposed work, but the intervention did not materialise.

He maintained that the failure to carry out the proposed improvements did not mean the university had forgotten about the students.

Response to PREMIUM TIMES’ questions

Before publishing the investigation, PREMIUM TIMES contacted Mr Piwuna, Vice-Chancellor Tanko Ishaya and the university’s spokesperson, Emmanuel Madugu, seeking explanations about the accessibility problems and the university’s plans to address them.

The newspaper sent Mr Piwuna a WhatsApp message on 12 October, detailing its observations at the Village Hostel and asking four questions about measures taken to improve accessibility, the use of students’ facility improvement and utility fees, plans for accessible hostels and other campus facilities, and timelines for addressing the concerns.

Mr Piwuna initially declined a telephone conversation and did not respond to the questions before the report was published.

After reading the investigation, he contacted the reporter and said he had missed or overlooked the earlier message.

“I must have missed or bypassed your message. As you can see, I even thought they all came in today. Sorry about that,” he wrote.

He subsequently sent another message outlining his position and suggesting that the newspaper verify his claims with former student leaders and representatives of associations for blind and deaf students.

“Well, this is what I have to say about the situation. I hope it helps in your future report,” he wrote.

He added: “You can confirm whatever I have said with either past SUG leaders or the presidents of blind or deaf students.”

He also acknowledged that the newspaper’s findings could help draw attention to problems requiring action.

“Reports such as yours could always put us on our toes,” he said.

Fees and renovation remain

While Mr Piwuna outlined interventions by his office, his response did not address all the questions raised in the investigation.

In particular, he did not explain how the university spends the N5,000 facility improvement fee and N30,000 utility charge listed in a student’s fee breakdown, or identify the specific improvements funded by the collections.

The investigation presented illustrative calculations based on the university’s reported student intake, estimating that the N5,000 facility improvement charge could amount to about N138.23 million across three academic sessions, if every admitted student paid the fee.

The figure is an estimate, not confirmed university revenue. The facility improvement fee is also not exclusively allocated to hostel improvements.

The investigation questioned how the money was allocated and what improvements students had received in return, particularly those living in the Village Hostel.

Mr Piwuna did not provide an account of the collections or explain how the charges had translated into improvements for students with disabilities.

He also did not state when the university would renovate the Village Hostel or provide a specific timeline for installing ramps, grab rails and other accessibility features in the bathrooms and across the campus.

While the dean says the university will continue trying its best, students with disabilities are still waiting for improvements they can see and use.

Note: Names marked with an asterisk have been changed to protect the identity of the students featured in the investigation.

World.title: Reforms must not become punishment, ANA tells FG
World.content:
The Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA) has urged the federal government to put a human face on its economic reforms, warning that many Nigerians are struggling with rising hardship and declining living standards.

ANA’s National President, Usman Akanbi, made the call in his opening address at the association’s 45th International Convention, held on 30 October at the Mamman Jiya Vatsa Writers’ Village in Mpape, Abuja.

Mr Akanbi acknowledged what he described as the government’s bold structural reforms and efforts to improve infrastructure but said their success should be measured by their effect on citizens’ welfare.

“Today, many Nigerians are facing an acute economic crunch and a nose-diving standard of living,” he said.

“Reforms, however well-intentioned, must not be perceived as punishment.”

The ANA president said the government must prioritise policies that restore public confidence and give young Nigerians reasons to believe in a better future.

“No nation can grow when its young people have lost hope,” he said. “And without hope, no reform can succeed.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Drawing from Thomas Jefferson’s position that the pursuit of citizens’ happiness was the legitimate duty of government, Mr Akanbi said public welfare should remain central to policymaking.

Insecurity, poor roads

The ANA president also urged the federal government to intensify efforts to address insecurity, saying writers and other Nigerians who travelled by road remained exposed to kidnapping, armed robbery and other dangers.

He described journeys to Abuja through several hinterland roads as difficult and unsafe, citing collapsed bridges and deteriorating road networks.

Mr Akanbi argued that while proposed coastal and border roads might have long-term benefits, roads connecting farms, villages, markets and towns deserved greater attention.

“The ordinary Nigerian feels that the hinterland roads the roads that connect farms to markets, villages to towns, and our state chapters to the centre should have been given far greater consideration and priority,” he said.

“A nation is fed and held together by its hinterland.”

Warning ahead of 2027 elections

Mr Akanbi also cautioned politicians and their supporters against inflammatory conduct as preparations intensify for the 2027 general elections.

He urged political actors to exercise restraint and avoid turning electoral competition into hostility or violence.

“We must ensure that the 2027 elections are conducted in an environment devoid of rancour, bitterness and ill will,” he said. “Our politics must not become a war.”

The ANA president maintained that building a functional country required cooperation between citizens and those entrusted with public office.

“Nation-building is a collective task. Government cannot do it alone, and citizens cannot thrive without responsible government,” he added.

Insecurity ‘censoring imagination’

The convention was themed “Literature, Security and the Place of Nigeria in the World.”

Explaining the choice, Mr Akanbi said insecurity affected not only lives and livelihoods but also artistic expression and intellectual development.

He described insecurity as “the greatest censor of the Nigerian imagination,” noting that creativity and reading could not flourish where farmers could not access their farms, traders were afraid to travel, and children could not attend school safely.

Mr Akanbi said Nigerian writers also had a responsibility to tell the country’s story, especially when international narratives about Nigeria were often dominated by insecurity and fear.

He urged authors to reclaim that narrative through works that acknowledged the country’s challenges without losing sight of its possibilities.

ANA’s recovery from internal crisis

Reflecting on the association’s history, Mr Akanbi recalled that ANA was established in 1981 under the leadership of novelist Chinua Achebe to defend freedom of expression, promote literary excellence and foster unity through writing.

He said the association had since established literary prizes, publications and annual conventions while supporting generations of Nigerian writers.

However, he acknowledged that ANA had also endured significant challenges, including internal divisions following its 2019 convention in Enugu.

According to him, the crisis fractured the association, led to legal disputes, and threatened its continued existence as a professional body.

Mr Akanbi credited ANA’s trustees, elders, fellows and state chapters with helping the organisation overcome the dispute.

“You held the line. You are the true heroes of this renaissance,” he told them.

Plans

The ANA president said the association’s plans would focus on institutional development, writers’ empowerment and stronger engagement with the government.

He said ANA intended to complete and fully utilise the Mamman Jiya Vatsa Writers’ Village as an international creative resort and sanctuary for writers.

The association also plans to provide workshops and publishing support for established and emerging authors while reviving literary clubs in schools.

Mr Akanbi said ANA would also seek a more active role in national orientation, cultural diplomacy and the creative economy.

He thanked the federal government for allocating the land for the writers’ village in 1986. He acknowledged the Nigerian Copyright Commission’s role in helping authors benefit from the reproduction of their works.

The ANA president said the association would continue to defend writers’ interests while contributing to conversations about Nigeria’s development, security and international image.

World.title: Police arrest 36 suspects in Niger State
World.content:
The police have arrested several suspects in connection with alleged thuggery, ritual activities, transformer vandalism and attempted livestock theft in different parts of Niger State.

The arrests, according to the police state command, followed intelligence-led operations and intensified security patrols aimed at curbing criminal activities and restoring public safety.

In a crime bulletin issued on Thursday, the Police Public Relations Officer, Wasiu Abiodun, said seven suspects were arrested on 29 October during an operation by the Anti-Thuggery Unit in Albishir, Minna, following reports of incessant attacks around Gurara, Albishir and Gbeganu communities.

The suspects were identified as Abdullahi Hassan, 20; Shafiu Yahaya, 25; Mohammed Abdullahi, 26; Idris Bashir, 24; Idris Mohammed, 22; Alhassan Isyaku, 26; and Aliyu Isah, 27.

A search conducted at their residences reportedly led to the recovery of a sword, cutlasses, a knife, suspected cannabis and a cable.

Preliminary investigations linked the attacks to a reprisal arising from a violent confrontation at a party in Albishir in 2025, which reportedly resulted in the death of one Sani Mohammed of Gurara.

The police said youths from Gurara had allegedly planned retaliatory attacks, during which Alhassan Isyaku was attacked while undertaking furniture work in Gurara.

Aliyu Isah also reportedly sustained deep cuts on his right leg and injuries around his neck during the violence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The suspects have been charged to court over alleged conspiracy, thuggery and causing grievous hurt.

The command also reported the arrest of 11 suspects following a violent clash between hoodlums from Kafintela and residents of Samande, Tunga, on October 16.

The incident, which involved the alleged destruction of shops and fighting, reportedly resulted in the death of one person from Kafintela.

Those arrested, aged between 15 and 25, were identified as Maikailu Yakubu, Badamasi Abdullahi, Yusuf Shafiu, Musa Umar, Sanusi Dauda, Sani Abdullahi, Umar Suleiman, Ibrahim Isah, Abdulrazak Yunusa, Sani Sadiq and Shuaibu Salisu.

The suspects were transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID), Minna, for further investigation and subsequently charged to court.

Similarly, 13 suspects were arrested on October 18 during a joint operation by police operatives attached to Bosso Division and vigilante members following reported youth unrest between Angwan-Biri and Tudun-Fulani communities in Bosso.

Dangerous weapons were reportedly recovered, while the suspects were also charged to court.

In another development, the police arrested five persons over alleged criminal conspiracy, possession of criminal charms, ill-treatment of domestic animals and membership of an unlawful society.

Mr Abiodun said the suspects were arrested on 27 October at about 8:30 p.m. in Garima area of Minna following intelligence reports about suspicious activities in an isolated compound.

The suspects were identified as Mohammed Idris Dogara, 57; Aliyu Sule, 25; Abubakar Abdullahi, 40; Ibrahim Mohammed Hamisu, 43; and Shehu Abubakar, 40, a native doctor.

Items recovered at the scene included blood-stained red and white clothing, four calabashes, two live chickens, three slaughtered chickens, a blood-stained knife and a large mat.

According to the police, preliminary investigations indicated that four of the suspects had allegedly approached the native doctor to perform money rituals using a human skeleton reportedly discovered during mining activities.

The police alleged that the four men offered their biological children as sacrifices in exchange for money, but the native doctor initially declined the request.

He was, however, said to have directed them to purchase chickens and assemble at a designated location, where the ritual would take place.

The suspects were reportedly arrested during the alleged ritual exercise, with one of them allegedly found holding a blood-stained knife while the others had slaughtered their chickens.

The command said the suspects had confessed to the allegations and were undergoing further investigation before being charged to court.

On transformer vandalism, the police said seven suspects were arrested in separate operations in Minna and Lambata over alleged conspiracy, vandalism and theft of electricity cables.

One of the operations took place on 28 October, when operatives of ‘A’ Division, Minna, arrested Hussain Innocent, 26, and Abubakar Rabiu, both residents of Railway Quarters, Minna.

The suspects allegedly confessed to vandalising electricity transformers in the Three-Arms Zone and other locations within Minna.

They reportedly identified Isyaku Muazu of Tudun-Natsira and Musa Haruna as alleged receivers of the stolen cables. A bolt cutter was recovered as an exhibit.

In a related operation on 6 October, police operatives attached to Gawu-Babangida Division, working with vigilante members, arrested Haruna Musa, 26; Abdulsamad Abubakar, 25; and Salisu Aminu, 35, in Lambata.

The suspects were allegedly found with vandalised cables, a bolt cutter, a knife and a torchlight.

Police investigations reportedly revealed that the suspects used the tools to remove three armoured cables from a transformer in the Kokogbe area of Lambata. They were subsequently charged to court.

Meanwhile, the Command disclosed that one suspect had been arrested over alleged criminal conspiracy, membership of a gang of thieves, attempted goat theft and screening of offenders.

The suspect, identified as Adamu Abubakar, popularly known as Yellow, was arrested on 26 October following a report that two unidentified men travelling in a Mazda vehicle with registration number KNT 38 AG and tinted windows were allegedly scouting for goats to steal around Angwan-Kampani.

Community members reportedly pursued the vehicle to the suspect’s residence behind Tipper Garage, Maitumbi, where the occupants abandoned it and escaped.

Police investigations identified Adamu Abubakar as the owner of the vehicle. He allegedly told investigators that the driver, identified as Danlami and residing in Korokpan, had taken the vehicle on an errand but failed to produce him for questioning.

The police said the suspect was subsequently charged to court and remanded at a correctional centre.

The command assured residents that security operations, intelligence gathering and visibility patrols would continue across the state to prevent crime and apprehend perpetrators.

World.title: Hamzat promises 40% funding for youth apprenticeship
World.content:
Hamzat

By Henry Ojelu

The Lagos State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship flag bearer for the 2027 election, Dr Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, has promised that his administration will provide 40 per cent funding for stipends of apprentices as part of efforts to equip young people with practical skills and improve their employability.

Hamzat made the pledge during an interactive session organised by the Lagos State chapter of the Nigerian Society of Engineers (NSE), where he outlined his plans for youth development, skills acquisition and innovation.

He said the proposed funding would encourage businesses to take on apprentices and work with professional bodies to provide young people with relevant vocational and technical training.

According to him, emphasis would also be placed on practical skills in artificial intelligence, AI, robotics and other emerging technologies, as well as vocational training and professional certification.

Hamzat said the initiative would enable young people to acquire skills and qualifications that would improve their chances of securing jobs and accessing finance.

He also pledged to strengthen the capacity of the Lagos State Science, Research and Innovation Council to support young innovators through funding, investment opportunities and global exposure.

He said the plan was to create an enabling environment for entrepreneurs to develop, commercialise and scale their innovations, while contributing to the state’s economic growth.

World.title: Troops nab notorious terrorist in Kaduna
World.content:
By: Kingsley Omonobi

Troops of Operation Fansan Yamma, have arrested a suspected terrorist during an intelligence-led operation in Kagarko town, Kagarko Local Government Area of Kaduna State.

The troops have also intensified air and ground operations to neutralise terrorists and deny them freedom of action in Zamfara State.

Spokesman, Captain Tamuno Sinivie while making this known on Friday said, “On 5 November 2026, troops of Sector 1, in conjunction with operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS), apprehended a suspected terrorist identified as Auta Maikyala during an intelligence-led operation.

“The suspect was arrested at a hospital in Kagarko, where he had reportedly gone to seek medical attention for a gunshot wound sustained during an encounter with a rival faction.

“Preliminary investigations revealed that the suspect is an alleged notorious criminal who has been involved in several attacks on communities, kidnapping and cattle rustling operations.

“He is currently in custody for further investigation and prosecution.

“Similarly, troops of Operation Fansan Yamma have intensified clearance operations aimed at neutralising terrorists and dismantling their hideouts in Zamfara State.

“On 5 November 2026, troops conducted clearance operations at Aljummu Hausa, Aljummu Fulani and Tunga Magaji villages in Maradun Local Government Area of Zamfara State.

“The ongoing operations have resulted in the clearance of several terrorist hideouts, further restricting the activities of criminal elements and enhancing the security of residents in the affected communities.

“In a related development, on the same day, the Air Component of the Nigerian Air Force, conducted air interdiction operations against identified terrorist locations suspected to be associated with the wanted terrorist kingpin, Dogo Gide, in Babban Doka and Kuyumbana Forest, Maru Local Government Area of Zamfara State.

“The operation followed credible intelligence indicating that the terrorists were assembling in the area to plan and coordinate their criminal activities.

“Troops are currently maintaining dominance over the general area.

‘Operation Fansan Yamma will sustain its operational tempo and aggressive posture to fulfil its mandate of protecting lives and property across the Joint Operations Area.

“The general public is urged to continue supporting ongoing military operations by providing timely and credible information on suspected terrorists and their activities to assist security agencies in eliminating criminal threats from our communities.”

World.title: ‎2027 Poll: INEC uncovers plot to kidnap ad-hoc staff, warns officers against partisanship
World.content:
INEC Chairman, Joash Amupitan

By Boluwaji Obahopo, Lokoja

‎

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has uncovered an alleged plot to threaten, intimidate and kidnap ad-hoc electoral personnel, including members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), ahead of the 2027 general election.

INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, disclosed that intelligence-led operations had led to the arrest of suspected kingpins allegedly behind the plot, adding that the suspects had been charged to court through the Department of State Services (DSS).

Amupitan warned that anyone who threatened or harmed electoral personnel would face the full weight of the law.

He also cautioned electoral officers against partisanship and administrative negligence, insisting that personnel found wanting in the discharge of their duties would face appropriate sanctions.

The INEC chairman spoke in Lokoja during the commission’s North Central zonal operational readiness assessment and interactive staff engagement, where he stressed that the credibility of the 2027 elections would depend largely on the neutrality, professionalism and commitment of personnel at the grassroots.

He said the commission was strengthening collaboration with security agencies under the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES) framework to identify and address potential threats before the polls.

According to him, INEC is also deploying Election Risk Management tools to identify vulnerable areas across the North Central zone and share the findings with security agencies for early intervention.

Amupitan said the commission was intensifying preparations nationwide to ensure that the 2027 general election was better managed than previous electoral exercises, stressing that credible polls could not be achieved through last-minute preparations.

He said INEC must sustain its operational readiness through adequate logistics, technological investment, staff welfare and improved administrative processes long before election day.

The chairman said the commission was preparing for an election involving more than 103 million registered voters and 176,846 polling units across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

He disclosed that the North Central zone, comprising six states and the FCT, had a combined 15.44 million registered voters, with Kogi State accounting for 1,932,654.

Describing the zone as strategically important to the electoral process, Amupitan said Kogi’s geographical position and borders with several states made its logistics, security and operational readiness critical to election administration.

He charged electoral officers to ensure that no eligible voter was disenfranchised through administrative lapses or logistics failures, urging them to uphold neutrality, professionalism and accountability.

On the voters’ register, Amupitan said INEC was working to address irregularities identified during the display of the register for claims and objections ahead of the publication of the final register on December 15, 2026.

He assured that necessary corrections would be made before the final publication.

The chairman also warned that misinformation and disinformation, particularly fake news and manipulated videos circulating on social media, posed a serious threat to public confidence in the electoral process.

He urged the commission’s voter education and publicity departments to intensify public enlightenment and advised citizens to verify information before sharing it.

On staff welfare, Amupitan said INEC had introduced the Consolidated Election Management Body Salary Structure (CEMBSS), effective January 1, 2026, to move its workforce away from the conventional civil service salary structure.

He added that an enhanced salary, hazard and field allowance package had been approved by the President, with implementation awaiting cash backing.

Other measures, he said, included a 150 per cent increase in overhead allocation to state offices, improved duty tour allowances, plans for an owner-occupier housing scheme and the procurement of new vehicles, including 500 pickup trucks for logistics operations.

He urged staff to see themselves as custodians of electoral integrity, saying the success of the 2027 elections would depend on their ability to uphold the law and discharge their responsibilities without fear or favour.

World.title: Uzbekistan places temporary visa ban on Nigerians
World.content:
Uzbekistan has introduced temporary restrictions on visa issuance and entry for Nigerian citizens.

A notice on the website of the Green Energy Technologies Central Asia (GETCA) exhibition states that restrictions have been introduced on the issuance of visas and entry into Uzbekistan for Nigerian nationals.

The notice reads: “Temporary restrictions have currently been introduced on the issuance of visas and entry into the Republic of Uzbekistan for citizens of your country.”

It also advises Nigerians seeking entry under exceptional circumstances to contact the consular section of the Embassy of Uzbekistan for further information.

Nigeria is also not the only country listed under the temporary restrictions on the exhibition website. Other countries, including Ghana, Kenya, Egypt, Iraq and Bangladesh, also have similar notices.

As of Friday, no formal public statement explaining the restrictions had been identified on the website of Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The ministry’s general visa information page provides details of the country’s visa arrangements for foreign nationals but does not specifically explain the reported restrictions affecting Nigerians.

The development could affect Nigerians planning to visit the Central Asian country for tourism, business, education and other purposes.

Affected travellers have been advised to contact the Uzbek embassy’s consular section to establish whether they qualify for exceptional entry arrangements.

Vanguard News

World.title: NYSC members’ kidnap: Court fixes Dec 16 for judgment
World.content:
By Chidi Nkwopara, Owerri

An Imo State High Court, presided over by Justice Emeka Orafu, will deliver judgement in the suit, HOU/22C/2026, preferred against Usman Aliyu, Babangida Aliyu, and Mohamed Ali, for their alleged involvement in the kidnap of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members, who were traveling to their orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom States.

Justice Orafu disclosed this Friday, November 6, 2026, when the two defense lawyers announced closure of their case after the third witness, Mohammed Ali, DW3, finished testifying.

The judge commended counsel on both sides for “responding very well” as the matter progressed.

He gave the defense seven days, with effect from Saturday, November 7, 2026, to file their briefs, and the prosecution five days, with effect from Saturday, November 14, 2026, to file his response.

Before adjourning the matter to November 24, 2026, for the adoption of their addresses, Justice Orafu fixed December 16, 2026, for the delivery of judgement.

Testifying earlier, the DW3, who was led in evidence by his counsel, Mr. Paschal Oforma, told the court that he hails from Kogi State and tends his cow in Kara, Aba.

He also told the court that he knows nothing about the kidnap but was arrested while sitting at Kara by the DSS, brought to Owerri, and detained.

Asked by his counsel if he had any other thing to tell the court, DW3 denied knowing the other defendants.

Cross-examined by the Director of Public Prosecution, DPP, Mr. Martins Udolwu, the DW3 said he has lived in Aba for about two years, accepted being a herdsman, but does not enter any forest.

He told the court that he has two boys that take the cows out in the morning and bring them back in the evening.

Answering another question, DW3 confirmed that he knows the DW1, adding that he sees him in the mosque but doesn’t know the DW2.

The court erupted in laughter when DW3 quickly withdrew his submission that he was beaten before the audio-visual recording was done and said the DSS tried to beat him, but they didn’t, before the audio-visual confessional recording.

Responding to the question put to him by counsel to DW1 and DW2, he said that he wrote one statement, filled one form in the presence of his counsel.

World.title: Beyond the Final Score: The Data Signals That Move Sports Betting Markets
World.content:
Image source: Pexels

Everyone is always trying to beat sports betting markets but it isn’t always easy. That’s because behind every shift in a spread, moneyline or player prop is a constant stream of information being assessed by bookmakers, traders and bettors.

With the growing influence of real-time data available in 2026, this has made understanding those signals increasingly important for anyone following sports markets. Let’s go through a few key ones to get you up to speed.

The players

Player availability remains one of the most powerful market-moving factors. A late injury, unexpected scratch or change to a starting line-up at the last minute can dramatically alter odds before a game begins.

The effect is particularly noticeable in sports where one player has a large influence on team performance. Even before official confirmation, credible reports circulating on social media or reports from a trusted source about a player’s status can fluctuate odds as markets anticipate the potential impact.

If you’re looking to bet on sports at Spinoli it’s important to note that recent performance data also matters although context is definitely crucial. A team’s last five games may tell part of the story, but bettors and analysts increasingly look deeper.

Shot quality, possession, efficiency, yards per play, expected goals and other underlying metrics can reveal whether recent results are sustainable long term or whether they have been fortunate over a short period.

So, while the final score records what happened, advanced data can provide clues about why it turned out a particular way.



Another important signal is market movement itself. When prices shift across multiple sportsbooks or exchanges, that movement can indicate that new information has entered the market before it has reached the public domain.

A recent example from UFC betting showed just how dramatic those movements can become, with the odds for Sean Brady vs. Joaquin Buckley shifting sharply before the fight. Comparing prices across platforms can therefore provide a useful snapshot of how market expectations are changing – and help to explain why.

Consider the conditions

Weather and venue conditions can also influence certain markets. Wind, rain, temperature and playing-surface conditions may be particularly relevant when it comes to betting on football, baseball, golf alongside other outdoor sports.

Rather than ignoring the weather forecast, sophisticated models can incorporate it into projections for scoring, player performance and even the tempo of the match.

The growing role of live data has made these signals even more dynamic. During a game, markets can react to possession changes, shots, fouls, player substitutions, pitch position and other events within seconds.

Prediction markets have added another dimension to this process with contract prices providing a continuously updated indication of how traders assess an outcome.

Trust your gut

What is important to note is that no single data point should be treated as a guaranteed indicator.

Markets already incorporate enormous amounts of information and an apparently “obvious signal” may already be reflected in the price. The challenge is separating meaningful new information from what could just be noise.

That is ultimately what makes modern sports betting markets so data-driven. The final score tells the story of what happened on the pitch or court, but the numbers surrounding the game help explain what the market expected, what changed and why prices moved.

For fans interested in the analytical side of sport, following those signals can provide a deeper understanding of the contest long before the scoreboard delivers the final verdict.

World.title: FG seeks seven-year ban on establishing new federal universities, polytechnics
World.content:
Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa

…Alausa tells Senate to stop approving establishment bills, cites NN1.3trn ASUU revitalisation debt, infrastructure deficits

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The Federal Government has moved to halt the establishment of new federal universities, polytechnics and colleges of education for seven years, warning that Nigeria risks expanding its tertiary education system at the expense of academic quality and the survival of existing institutions.

The government said it could no longer afford to spread scarce resources across an increasing number of institutions while existing federal tertiary institutions grapple with severe funding shortages, decaying infrastructure, inadequate manpower and overcrowded classrooms.

Consequently, the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, has appealed to the Senate and other members of the National Assembly to stop considering and passing bills seeking to establish additional federal tertiary institutions during the seven-year moratorium.

The appeal was contained in a November 2, 2026, memo addressed to Senate President Godswill Akpabio and copied to Senate Majority Leader Senator Michael Opeyemi Bamidele.

In the memo, marked FME/DUE/NASS/153/Vol.1/147 and sighted in Abuja on Friday, Alausa disclosed that the Federal Executive Council had approved the seven-year moratorium at its August 13, 2025, meeting as part of efforts to address the proliferation of public tertiary institutions, duplication of academic programmes and under-utilisation of existing facilities.

The minister’s intervention comes amid persistent concerns over the government’s ability to adequately finance existing universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, with billions of naira in outstanding revitalisation commitments yet to be met.

Making a case for the policy, Alausa argued that Nigeria’s immediate challenge was no longer the multiplication of tertiary institutions but the strengthening of those already established to deliver quality education.

He warned that continuing to establish new institutions without guaranteed funding would deepen the crisis in the sector, potentially leaving more institutions struggling to provide basic academic facilities and services.

“The Federal Government’s position is that the immediate challenge confronting the tertiary education sector is not merely the expansion of access but the urgent need to strengthen existing institutions,” he stated.

According to him, the moratorium would allow the government to consolidate previous investments, address existing deficiencies and improve the carrying capacity of operational institutions before considering further expansion.

Alausa expressed concern that despite the government’s policy direction, bills seeking the establishment of additional federal tertiary institutions continued to receive legislative attention.

While acknowledging the constitutional powers of the National Assembly to initiate and enact laws establishing institutions, he urged lawmakers to consider the prevailing realities of the education sector, including demonstrable national needs and the long-term financial implications of such legislation.

He identified inadequate lecture halls, overcrowded classrooms, poorly equipped laboratories, shortages of qualified academic personnel, accommodation deficits and deteriorating infrastructure as some of the major challenges confronting existing federal institutions.

The minister warned that creating more institutions under such circumstances would amount to spreading already inadequate resources thinner, with potentially damaging consequences for academic standards.

Alausa also presented figures showing the extent of the Federal Government’s outstanding financial obligations to the university system, particularly its commitments to the revitalisation of public universities.

He disclosed that of the N1.3 trillion pledged under the 2013–2018 Federal Government-ASUU revitalisation agreement, only N250 billion was reportedly released between 2013 and 2021.

Similarly, he said that out of the additional N150 billion approved in 2025 for Needs Assessment Intervention, only N50 billion was initially released.

The minister argued that the outstanding commitments raised serious questions about the government’s capacity to assume additional financial responsibilities through the establishment of new institutions.

“These funding gaps demonstrate the difficulty of meeting existing obligations and raise legitimate concerns about the capacity to sustain additional institutions without corresponding and guaranteed budgetary provisions,” he stated.

To further strengthen his argument, Alausa cited the experiences of Ekiti and Imo states, where the establishment of multiple tertiary institutions reportedly created financial and administrative challenges.

He recalled that three state-owned universities in Ekiti were consolidated into one institution, Ekiti State University, Ado-Ekiti, in 2011.

He also noted that Imo State had undertaken institutional reviews and integration following the establishment of several tertiary institutions under previous administrations.

According to him, some state governments had also approached the Federal Government seeking takeovers of their universities because of difficulties sustaining their operations.

He warned that institutions established without credible and sustainable funding arrangements could eventually become liabilities, forcing subsequent administrations to embark on expensive mergers, restructuring or outright closures.

“The institutions established without sustainable funding arrangements may subsequently require costly restructuring, merger or integration by successor administrations,” he cautioned.

Drawing lessons from other countries, the minister said Australia, Finland, Japan, the United States and South Africa had adopted institutional mergers and consolidation to tackle funding constraints, duplication of programmes and administrative inefficiencies.

He said such reforms had helped improve institutional governance, achieve economies of scale, strengthen research capacity and ensure more efficient deployment of public resources.

Alausa maintained that Nigeria needed to embrace a similar approach by placing institutional viability, academic standards and efficient resource utilisation above the continuous creation of new tertiary institutions.

He further warned that the establishment of additional institutions could undermine other ongoing government interventions in the education sector, which also require substantial and sustained funding.

Among the programmes he identified were infrastructure interventions by the Tertiary Education Trust Fund, the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, vocational and skills acquisition initiatives, as well as the Consolidated Academic Tools Allowance (CATA) and the Consolidated Tertiary Institutions Tools Allowance (CONTTA) for academic and non-academic personnel.

The minister stressed that establishing a tertiary institution involved far more than enacting an enabling law, noting that such decisions imposed long-term financial obligations on successive administrations.

He listed land acquisition, take-off grants, construction of infrastructure, recruitment of academic and non-academic personnel, procurement of equipment, utilities and recurrent expenditure among the costs the government must shoulder.

He warned that passing establishment bills without comprehensive feasibility studies, clear evidence of national educational needs and credible long-term funding arrangements could produce institutions that exist only on paper but lack the capacity to function effectively.

“Such institutions may eventually become financial liabilities, compelling future administrations to undertake costly mergers, restructuring or outright closure, with attendant consequences for students, staff, public investments and the national education system,” he stated.

Rather, he said the government intended to use the period to strengthen existing institutions, improve infrastructure, address manpower shortages, raise academic standards and ensure that any future expansion was backed by adequate financial and administrative planning.

He therefore appealed to Akpabio and the leadership of the National Assembly to align legislative activities with the policy.

“In view of the foregoing, I respectfully appeal to Your Excellency and the distinguished leadership of the National Assembly to support the Federal Government’s seven-year moratorium by exercising restraint in the consideration and passage of Bills for the establishment of additional Federal Universities, Polytechnics and Colleges of Education during the period,” he stated.

The minister maintained that the country’s educational progress should not be determined by the number of universities, polytechnics and colleges established but by their ability to provide quality education, produce competent graduates and contribute meaningfully to national development.

“The success of our education system should be measured not merely by the number of institutions established but by the capacity of existing institutions to deliver high-quality education, produce competent graduates and contribute meaningfully to national development,” he added.

World.title: FIFA U-17 WWC Final: Nigeria vs Japan – date, time and where to watch
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos will face Japan in the final of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco on Saturday, November 7, as they seek to make history by winning their first title.

The final, which will be the 52nd and last match of the tournament, will kick off at 7:30 p.m. Nigerian time at the Mohammed VI Football Complex, Pitch 3, in Rabat.

The encounter will be the first meeting between Nigeria and Japan at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup and the first time the two countries face each other in a global final.

Where to watch Nigeria vs Japan

Football fans can watch the final live and for free through FIFA+, with streaming available via DAZN.
