The utility’s biggest deadbeat is its owner. Of US$34.0 million owed to LEC at end-2025, about 91 percent was owed by government ministries and agencies, most of it more than a year old. In December 2025, core government paid 0.3 percent of what it owed, against about 21 percent for customers overall. The government, the report notes, is at once LEC’s shareholder, regulator, least reliable customer and lender of last resort.

Businesses pay the price. More than 90 percent of Liberian firms now own a generator, up from 73 percent in 2017. Auditors also found LEC operated for at least five years without documented board minutes or adopted by-laws. The planned expansion of the Mount Coffee hydropower plant from 88 to about 130 megawatts by 2028 offers relief — if the utility can be run to use it.

What the Bank prescribes — and what to watch

The Bank is careful not to overclaim. It says it has not established that state firms cause Liberia’s jobs problem. Its argument is narrower and harder to dismiss: without accounts, audits and a register of who sits on which board, no one can say what the portfolio costs, what it delivers or what risk it poses to the treasury.

Its fix is deliberately unglamorous. By end-2027, it wants every entity classified as commercial, public-service or hybrid; a published register of entities and directors; a minimum annual reporting template for all 47 operating firms; and audit firepower focused on the five biggest exposures — LEC, NASSCORP, the National Port Authority, the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company and the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation — with private auditors brought in under the Auditor General’s oversight. By June 2028, it wants government’s tangled money flows with those firms reconciled, public-service obligations costed, the first public aggregate report on state enterprises, and a legal inventory of the 15 dormant companies.

The wider outlook is cautiously positive but exposed. The Bank projects growth averaging 5.3 percent a year over 2026–2028, inflation of 7.0 percent in 2026 and a VAT launch in early 2027. But global growth is forecast to slow to 2.5 percent in 2026 as the Middle East conflict lifts oil prices. A 15 percent fall in gold and a 20 percent fall in iron ore prices would wipe about US$295 million off export earnings, with reserves covering only about two months of imports.

For a country that has heard many reform plans, the test is simple. Growth figures can be announced. Whether the state can account for its own companies — and pay its own electricity bills — will show whether Liberia’s boom is starting to reach the people living through it.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai’s Anti-Corruption Credibility Tested as Indicted Gbarpolu Superintendent Gets Presidential Commissioning
World.content:
President Boakai commissioning indicted Gbarpolu County Superintendent Zinnah

MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s commitment to fighting corruption is facing renewed public scrutiny following his decision to commission Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah, who is among five individuals indicted in connection with the controversial US$425,000 Yellow Machines procurement scandal.

By Augustus D.R. Bortue

The controversy has intensified as the corruption case remains unresolved, with the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC) reporting that proceedings scheduled to commence on September 14, 2026, at the 16th Judicial Circuit Court in Bopolu were postponed after a member of the defense reportedly submitted an excuse for nonappearance.



The latest development has renewed concerns among citizens and political stakeholders about the pace of justice in a case involving public development funds intended to improve infrastructure in one of Liberia’s least-connected counties.

While an indictment does not constitute a conviction, critics argue that the President’s decision to commission an official facing unresolved corruption charges raises questions about the administration’s judgment, consistency and commitment to public accountability.

The controversy also revives an earlier demand by Gbarpolu Senator Botoe Kanneh for indicted county officials to be temporarily relieved of their duties while facing prosecution.

The US$425,000 Controversy

The case centers on US$425,000 allocated from Gbarpolu County’s Social Development Fund for the procurement of three heavy-duty machines: a bulldozer, an excavator and a motor grader.

The equipment was intended to support road construction, rehabilitation and other infrastructure projects across the county.

On September 8, 2025, the LACC announced that the Grand Jury of the 16th Judicial Circuit Court had returned a True Bill on all counts of the indictment against five individuals: Superintendent Zinnah, former Superintendent J. Keyah Saah, former Fiscal Superintendent Anthony Yorkor, former Project Management Committee Chairman Robert Benda and City Lion Inc. Chief Executive Officer Omaru Sheriff.

According to the Commission’s allegations, the procurement process involved irregularities, questions about the quality of the equipment supplied and possible violations of public procurement and financial management requirements.

The LACC also raised concerns about whether the machines delivered met the specifications and represented value for the public funds invested.

Reports that the equipment has remained largely non-operational, with concerns about oil leakages and other defects, have further intensified public demands for answers.

However, the allegations remain subject to judicial determination. All five defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty by a competent court.

Boakai’s Commissioning Decision Under Scrutiny

The decision to proceed with Zinnah’s commissioning has become a focal point in the broader debate about the credibility of the Boakai administration’s anti-corruption agenda.

Critics argue that although an indictment does not automatically disqualify an individual from holding public office, the circumstances demand careful consideration by the Presidency.

They question whether the President was fully briefed on the LACC indictment before commissioning the superintendent and what considerations informed the decision.

The controversy is particularly sensitive because the Boakai administration has repeatedly presented accountability and the fight against corruption as central pillars of its governance agenda.

However, the legal distinction between an indictment and a conviction remains important. Zinnah has not been convicted of the charges, and his constitutional rights must be protected throughout the judicial process.

The question confronting the administration, therefore, is not whether the President should pronounce judgment on an accused official, but whether the government has adequately addressed the public confidence concerns arising from the commissioning.

Critics have also drawn comparisons with the case of Abdullah Kamara, former Chairperson of the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, whom President Boakai suspended after his indictment by the LACC. Kamara was subsequently acquitted by the court.

They argue that the differing circumstances surrounding the two cases warrant an explanation of the standards guiding presidential decisions involving public officials facing corruption allegations.

Trial Postponement Fuels Public Frustration

The latest postponement has added another layer to the controversy.

According to the LACC, its prosecution team traveled to Gbarpolu County on September 14, 2026, expecting the trial to commence, but was informed by the Clerk of Court upon arrival that the matter had been postponed.

The Commission said it had been notified that a member of the defense had submitted an excuse for nonappearance before the prosecution team arrived in Bopolu.

The LACC described the development as one of the challenges affecting the timely prosecution of corruption-related cases but reaffirmed its readiness to proceed through the judicial process.

The postponement has raised questions about when substantive proceedings will begin and whether the five defendants will be available to face trial.

It also comes amid growing impatience among residents who believe the case should not be allowed to linger while the equipment purchased with county development funds remains largely unusable.

Youths Demand Speedy and Impartial Trial

On September 14, 2026, concerned citizens and youths in Gbarpolu staged a peaceful demonstration and issued a statement demanding a speedy, transparent and impartial trial.

In their statement, the youths expressed concern over what they described as continued delays in the proceedings, calling on judicial authorities to ensure that the case is handled without unnecessary postponements.

They emphasized that their demonstration was peaceful and lawful, adding that the people of Gbarpolu deserve accountability over public resources allocated for their development.

Their demands reflect growing concerns that prolonged judicial proceedings could further weaken public confidence in the institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting corruption.

Senators Had Earlier Called for Zinnah’s Recusal

The controversy surrounding the indicted county officials is not new.

In 2025, Gbarpolu Senator Botoe Kanneh called on the Senate to engage the Executive Branch to ensure that Superintendent Zinnah and other indicted officials were temporarily relieved of their duties pending the court’s determination.

In a communication to the Senate Plenary, Kanneh said the indictment and ongoing judicial proceedings had generated deep concern among citizens, local leaders and development stakeholders.

She warned that the situation could undermine public trust in the justice system and the integrity of public service.

Citing the Code of Conduct for public officials, Kanneh argued that the Senate should take cognizance of the LACC indictment and consider engaging the Executive Branch to temporarily relieve the indicted superintendent of his responsibilities while the case proceeded.

The communication was referred to the relevant Senate committees for investigation and appropriate action.

The Senate subsequently mandated its Committees on Judiciary and Internal Affairs to investigate concerns surrounding the indictment of Gbarpolu County’s local leadership, including Superintendent Zinnah.

However, the committees’ findings, recommendations and any subsequent decisions by Plenary have not been made public.

More recently, another Gbarpolu Senator, Amara Konneh, has also called for the speedy trial of the case, adding to pressure on the judicial authorities to ensure that the matter is resolved.

Zinnah Insists on Judicial Process

For his part, Superintendent Zinnah has maintained that he respects the rule of law and is prepared to respond to the allegations through the courts.

In a letter dated July 14, 2026, addressed to LACC Executive Chairperson Cllr. Alexandra K. Zoe, Zinnah declined an invitation to appear before the Commission for further discussions about the yellow machines.

The invitation, dated July 9, was for a meeting scheduled for July 16, during which the LACC intended to obtain additional information about the equipment, including its current condition and the circumstances surrounding its assembly.

The Commission had requested that Zinnah attend with his legal counsel and the individual or individuals who initially assembled the machines.

However, the superintendent argued that the matter was already before the Sixth Judicial Circuit Court and should therefore be addressed through the judicial process.

He maintained that participating in discussions outside the courtroom while the case was pending could compromise the integrity of the proceedings.

Zinnah subsequently reaffirmed his willingness to cooperate with the legal process and respond to the allegations in accordance with the law.

He has not publicly responded to the latest concerns raised by citizens over his commissioning or renewed calls for him to recuse himself while the case remains before the courts.

Gbarpolu Wants Value for Its Money

Beyond the political debate surrounding the President’s decision, the central concern for residents remains the condition of the three machines and whether the county received value for its US$425,000 investment.

The equipment was procured to address infrastructure challenges, particularly poor road connectivity that continues to affect communities across Gbarpolu.

Residents deserve an independent technical assessment establishing the machines’ current condition, compliance with contractual specifications, actual market value and the cost of restoring them to operational condition.

Such an assessment would help establish whether the county received what it paid for and identify the appropriate remedies if procurement violations or contractual breaches are proven.

The government must also ensure that the equipment’s condition is properly documented and that public resources are protected while the judicial process continues.

A Test of Institutional Consistency

Analysts say the controversy presents President Boakai with an opportunity to clarify his administration’s position on public officials facing corruption allegations and demonstrate that accountability standards apply consistently across government.

They called on the Presidency to explain the circumstances surrounding Zinnah’s commissioning and whether any consideration was given to the pending indictment.

For the people of Gbarpolu, the expectations are straightforward: public money must deliver public value, the courts must determine the truth, and every public official must remain accountable under the law.

The administration’s credibility will depend not only on what it says about fighting corruption, but also on how consistently its institutions and leadership act when accountability questions arise within its own ranks.

World.title: Liberia: Joint Chambers Reconstruction Estimated at Over US$10M as Speaker, Deputy Cite Lack of Funding
World.content:
MONROVIA – More than one year following the severe incident of destruction at the Joint Chambers of the Liberia Legislature, Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon and Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah jointly toured the destroyed segment and expressed disappointment over the condition.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

During the tour, Deputy Speaker Fallah, specifically, expressed profound sorrow over the state of the facility, noting that rebuilding the heavily damaged structure will demand significant financial resources and extensive construction work.



The tour comes ahead of a multi-stage damage assessment that will involve both government estimators led by the Ministry of Public Works and international experts.

While financing remains a concern, both leaders confirmed there is no plan of taking out loans to fund the necessary repairs.

Uncertainty Hangs Over Renovation Process

Addressing inquiry from Legislative reporters during the tour, Speaker Koon provided a response that somewhat dashes all hope and expectations that the renovation process is far from happening.

Speaker Koon tells the public that in the first place there is no money now neither had any money being budgeted towards this projected which is estimated around US$10M.

He pointed out that the shutdown of the Joint Chambers continues to undermine and impair the function of the Legislature, especially during the SONA [State of the Nation Address].

“It depends on how soon the estimate can be given to us, so we can commence. We don’t have money budgeted, but we are not going to take a loan for this place, because this place is undermining our work and impairing the function of the Legislature, especially during the SONA – the State of the Nation Address. We have to find other places and secure them to have the President’s address,” Speaker Koon intoned.

Sad Moment

In remarks, Deputy Speaker Fallah described the destruction as a “sad,” “embarrassing,” and “frustrating” and warning that the building will have to be rebuilt from scratch.

Deputy Speaker Fallah, who has been at the Capitol for the past 18 to 20 years, asserted that it was his first time entering the building since the incident.

“This is a sad moment, very sad. Today is my very first time honestly entering this place to see the level of destruction that took place. I feel so sad as a national leader, as a statesperson, to have known how this place was in the past and to see it like this today,” he stated.

US$10 Million to Rebuild

The Deputy Speaker estimated that restoring the building to the standard required would cost at least $10 million.

“I am not a technician, I am not an engineer, but I know I have been involved in construction. To see something like this tells me that to bring it to the standard we need will cost us nothing less than US$10 million. We are constructing from scratch, because it is not secure, so you have to do a lot of work,” he asserted.

Though the cause of the incident is yet to be established, but the Lofa County Electoral District #1 Representative stressed that destruction of public property must never happen, whatever the political disagreement.

“There should be no point in time when we destroy state property or facilities that belong to the state, even private property. That should not be the case.”

“The Legislature is the theatre of disagreement. We all come from different political persuasions, different political backgrounds, but we should never resort to destruction,” Deputy Speaker Fallah, among other things, indicated.

World.title: Liberia: Wife, Family of Convicted NSA Agent Peter Bon Jallah Appeal to U.S. Ambassador, Raise Questions Over Trial
World.content:
Monrovia-The family of former National Security Agency, NSA, Peter Bon Jallah has appealed to the United States Ambassador to Liberia, seeking international attention to what they described as serious concerns about the fairness of his trial and the handling of evidence that they believe deserved greater judicial scrutiny.

By Willie N. Tokpah

In separate communications dated October 26, Bon Jallah and his wife, Shirley Jallah, called on the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia to take note of the circumstances surrounding his conviction on charges of statutory rape and kidnapping and consider whether appropriate diplomatic or human-rights channels could help bring their concerns to the attention of relevant authorities.



The appeals came three days after Criminal Court ‘E’ at the Temple of Justice found Bon Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping involving a 16-year-old boy, while acquitting him of gang rape.

The conviction has triggered questions from the defendant’s family, which maintained that important aspects of the defense’s case, including medical findings, forensic evidence, witness testimonies, telephone records and observations relating to the alleged crime scene, were not adequately addressed in the court’s determination.

In an appeal addressed to the U.S. Ambassador, Bon Jallah described the verdict as raising serious questions about the impartial evaluation of evidence and requested that the Embassy consider whether the matter could receive attention through appropriate diplomatic or human-rights mechanisms.

His wife, Shirley Jallah, separately appealed for assistance, questioning the sufficiency of the prosecution’s evidence and whether the defense’s arguments and witnesses received adequate consideration.

Family Turns to Washington for Attention

In his October 26 communication, Bon Jallah specifically requested that the United States Embassy take note of the concerns surrounding his trial and consider whether appropriate channels were available to raise questions about due process and judicial accountability.

He acknowledged that the United States cannot interfere in Liberia’s judicial proceedings but argued that judicial independence should operate alongside transparency, accountability and respect for fundamental rights.

“My intention in raising these concerns is not to undermine the Liberian judicial system but to advocate for fairness, accountability, and public confidence in the administration of justice,” Bon Jallah wrote.

He urged the Embassy to consider directing the concerns to relevant organizations or authorities if direct diplomatic engagement was not possible.

His wife made a similar appeal, saying she was deeply troubled by the circumstances surrounding her husband’s conviction and believed that questions remained about the evidence presented during the trial.

She specifically raised concerns about forensic testing, the handling of evidence and what she described as insufficient consideration of the defense’s arguments.

The family’s appeal effectively seeks to bring the case to the attention of an international diplomatic mission, although the U.S. Embassy has no judicial authority to overturn a Liberian court’s verdict or direct the outcome of an ongoing legal process.

JFK Medical Center Report at the Center of Dispute

One of the principal issues raised by Bon Jallah concerns the medical examination conducted at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center following the alleged incident.

The family argued that the medical report contained findings that deserved closer consideration by the court, particularly regarding the reported absence of certain physical signs associated with the allegations.

Bon Jallah questions whether the court adequately explained how the medical findings were weighed against the complainant’s account and the other evidence presented during the trial.

The defense’s concerns also extended to the forensic evidence and the interpretation of findings presented by the prosecution. According to reporting on the court proceedings, the prosecution presented forensic evidence involving DNA profiles associated with biological material recovered from clothing exhibits.

However, the defense challenged the significance and interpretation of the findings, including their ability to establish when or how the biological material was deposited. The medical and forensic evidence, therefore, became an important part of the competing arguments presented during the trial.

The family maintained that these issues should receive particular attention in any review of the proceedings.

Defense Witnesses and Questions About Their Testimonies

Another important aspect of the family’s appeal concerns the testimonies presented by witnesses called by the defense. According to the court proceedings reported by FrontPage Africa, the prosecution presented 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses, while the defense presented eight regular witnesses and three subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Orange GSM and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

The involvement of witnesses from these institutions was significant because their testimonies formed part of the evidentiary record surrounding the medical examination, telephone records and other issues raised during the proceedings.

Bon Jallah’s family believed that the defense presented evidence that challenged important aspects of the prosecution’s allegations and deserved careful consideration.

The family is particularly concerned about whether the court adequately addressed the evidence and explanations offered by the defense witnesses before reaching its conclusions.

The exact substance of each witness’s testimony and how the judge evaluated it will be important in assessing these concerns against the official trial record.

Telephone Records Raise Questions About Defendant’s Whereabouts

Bon Jallah also raised concerns about telephone records that, according to his understanding, did not place him at the alleged crime scene at the relevant time. He believed the records were important to the defense’s effort to establish his whereabouts and should have received detailed consideration in the court’s evaluation of the evidence.

The issue is particularly relevant because telephone records and related technical evidence can assist in examining a person’s movements and communications, although such records do not automatically establish a person’s precise physical location.

The family argues that if the records were properly presented and admitted, their significance should have been clearly addressed in the court’s final reasoning.

Judge’s Visit to Alleged Crime Scene Also Questioned

The family has also questioned the circumstances surrounding a reported visit by the presiding judge to the residence where the alleged incident was said to have occurred.

Bon Jallah maintains that the physical conditions of the residence raised questions about certain descriptions provided during the complainant’s testimony.

He is concerned about whether observations made during the visit were properly documented and considered in the court’s final decision. The family argues that where a judge personally observes the location associated with disputed testimony, any relevant observations must be handled in accordance with applicable evidentiary and judicial procedures.

They are seeking clarification on whether the reported discrepancies were adequately addressed in the proceedings.

Wife Questions Sufficiency of Prosecution’s Case

In her separate appeal, Shirley Jallah questioned whether the prosecution sufficiently established her husband’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. She expressed concern that the defense’s arguments and evidence were not given adequate consideration and raised questions about the fairness and impartiality of the proceedings.

She also asked the U.S. Embassy to consider whether any appropriate assistance or guidance could be made available within the limits of its diplomatic mandate.

Her appeal emphasized that the family was not asking the United States to interfere in Liberia’s judicial system but wanted concerns about due process and fundamental human rights to receive appropriate attention.

Embassy Appeal Puts Due Process in Focus

The appeal to the United States Embassy places the case within a broader discussion about judicial accountability, due process, and public confidence in Liberia’s justice system.

Although the U.S. Embassy cannot substitute itself for Liberia’s courts, the family is asking the diplomatic mission to consider whether concerns involving the fairness of the proceedings may appropriately be brought to the attention of relevant human-rights institutions or other competent authorities.

The appeal also raises an important question about the availability of independent legal remedies when defendants believe that material evidence or defense arguments were not adequately considered.

For Bon Jallah and his family, the immediate concern is whether the verdict adequately reflects the totality of the evidence presented during the trial. Their request to the U.S. Ambassador is therefore not simply an appeal for diplomatic sympathy but a call for attention to questions they believe should be examined through established legal and accountability mechanisms.

World.title: Liberia: NPA Unveils Measures to Ease Port Congestion as Importers Protest Delays, Rising Fees
World.content:
Dukuly announces direct Maersk shipping to Monrovia, extended port operations, plans to clear stranded containers and $280 million investment initiative as businesses demand urgent relief from mounting costs and prolonged shipping delays.

MONROVIA — National Port Authority (NPA) Managing Director Sekou A. Dukuly has announced a series of measures to address congestion, prolonged cargo delays and rising port-related costs at the Freeport of Monrovia, following protests by Liberian businesswomen and importers demanding urgent government intervention.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh



Speaking at a press briefing at his office at the Freeport, Dukuly acknowledged that the port is operating below its required capacity, leaving hundreds of containers stranded and imposing additional financial burdens on importers.

He disclosed that approximately 700 containers have remained at the port for more than 30 days, describing the situation as unacceptable for a country whose economy depends heavily on maritime trade.

Among the immediate interventions, Dukuly announced that shipping giant Maersk has agreed to bring vessels directly to Monrovia, a move intended to reduce transit times and additional costs associated with transshipment through other West African ports.

Previously, some cargo shipments destined for Liberia were routed through regional ports before being transferred onto smaller vessels for delivery to Monrovia. The arrangement has contributed to prolonged shipping schedules and additional handling requirements.

The direct-shipping arrangement is expected to shorten delivery times and reduce logistical complications for importers. However, its actual impact on shipping costs and delivery schedules will depend on the frequency of direct services and effective implementation.

Dukuly also announced plans to clear approximately 700 containers that have remained at the port for extended periods, suspend ongoing berth repairs to allow two vessels to berth at a time, and extend working hours to improve cargo handling.

He said the NPA is exploring the possibility of granting additional free days to importers facing mounting demurrage and storage charges because of delays.

In a further proposal aimed at addressing the financial consequences of the congestion, Dukuly said the NPA could engage the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) and commercial banking institutions to provide short-term relief to affected businesses.

He proposed microeconomic support measures, including easing loan repayment obligations and extending repayment periods for importers whose capital remains tied up in goods they have been unable to retrieve from the port.

According to Dukuly, such engagement could help reduce the financial pressure on businesses while the NPA works to resolve the operational challenges.

The proposal comes amid complaints from importers who say they rely heavily on commercial bank loans, often secured against their homes and other personal properties, to finance their businesses. Prolonged shipping delays, combined with demurrage, storage fees and accumulating loan interest, have reportedly threatened their ability to sustain operations.

On infrastructure, Dukuly disclosed that capital dredging at the port is expected to begin within two to three weeks. The exercise is intended to improve navigational depth and allow larger vessels to access the port, potentially increasing its cargo-handling capacity.

He also said APM Terminals, the port’s terminal operator, has ordered additional equipment expected to arrive in Liberia soon to strengthen cargo-handling operations.

The NPA is further opening an unpaved section of the port yard to accommodate additional containers and create more space for incoming vessels.

Beyond these immediate interventions, Dukuly said the authority is working with the Liberia Revenue Authority, Ministry of Commerce, CTN, MedTech and other stakeholders to automate port operations.

The proposed system would allow Import Permit Declarations and other documentation processes to be completed online, reducing physical transactions, administrative bottlenecks and delays in cargo clearance.

In another major announcement, Dukuly disclosed that President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has established the Inter-Ministerial Concessions Committee, which he said has attracted approximately US$280 million in direct capital investment for the port.

The investment is expected to support efforts to modernize the Freeport of Monrovia and strengthen its competitiveness as a regional maritime and commercial gateway. However, details of the investment, including its financing structure, implementation timeline and specific projects, were not immediately provided.

Business Community Demands Government Intervention

The announcements follow growing frustration among Liberian importers, particularly women-owned businesses, over prolonged shipping delays, port congestion and escalating demurrage, storage and administrative charges.

On Tuesday, representatives of the China Business Women United with One Voice and the Consortium of Liberia Importers petitioned the National Legislature and the NPA, warning that the situation is threatening the survival of local businesses.

Reading the petition on behalf of the business community, advocate Sriya Musu Momolu said shipments originating from Asia and China are reportedly taking between six and seven months to reach the Freeport of Monrovia.

She explained that many importers depend on commercial bank loans, often secured with personal homes and other properties, to finance their businesses. Extended shipping timelines, she said, have left their capital tied up for months, making it difficult to repay loans, meet rental obligations and fulfill tax responsibilities.

The petition also highlighted problems associated with expired Delivery Orders, which require importers to pay renewal fees and additional administrative charges before retrieving their goods.

The businesswomen argued that importers should not be forced to shoulder demurrage and other penalties for delays beyond their control.

They called for a legislative inquiry into shipping companies over transit delays and surcharge structures. They also demanded that shipping lines and terminal operators waive reissuance fees and demurrage charges arising from expired Delivery Orders.

Other demands include mandatory shipping arrival timelines, streamlined container-clearance procedures, enforcement of the Liberianization Policy to protect local businesses from unfair foreign retail competition, and the development of a long-term national logistics policy.

Receiving the petition on behalf of the Legislature, Montserrado County District No. 8 Representative Prince Toles pledged to bring the concerns before his colleagues for consideration.

Toles, who identified himself as a fellow businessperson, described the grievances as concerning and emphasized the need for swift legislative and administrative intervention.

Pressure Mounts on Port Authorities

The protest and petition have placed renewed pressure on the NPA and other government institutions to demonstrate that the country’s principal commercial gateway can effectively handle the demands of importers and shipping companies.

The Freeport of Monrovia is central to Liberia’s import-dependent economy, serving as a major entry point for food, fuel, construction materials, machinery and other essential commodities.

Prolonged delays can increase the cost of doing business as importers incur additional storage, demurrage, transportation and administrative charges. Such expenses can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices in local markets.

While Dukuly’s proposed interventions could improve cargo movement and reduce delays, their effectiveness will depend on timely implementation, adequate equipment, improved coordination among government agencies and greater transparency in port operations.

For the protesting importers, the immediate concern remains the cost of retrieving goods already stranded at the port and the financial pressure accumulated during months of shipping delays.

World.title: REFLECTION ON THE WORLD BANK LIBERIA ECONOMIC UPDATE 2026: Beyond Growth—Addressing Structural Constraints to Job-Rich Growth in Liberia
World.content:
Liberia is growing, but too many Liberians are still not feeling that growth in their daily lives. The World Bank’s Liberia Economic Update 2026, under the theme “Beyond Growth: Addressing Structural Constraints to Job-Rich Growth,” tells a truth that is difficult to ignore: a country can post impressive economic numbers while ordinary people struggle with empty pockets, insecure work, and rising hardship. For Liberia, this is not a theoretical debate. It is the reality behind the headlines—seen in households where prices keep climbing, work remains scarce, and hope is often traded for survival.

By S Zohnjaty Joe Contributing author

According to the World Bank, the economy expanded by 5.1% in 2025, driven mainly by mining, including a 17% rise in that sector. Liberia exported about $1.3 billion in gold, $528 million in iron ore, and $115 million in rubber. On paper, it sounds like progress. But the same report shows the unsettling story behind the numbers: while the economy grows, too many people are left behind. Seventy-eight percent of Liberians are stuck in informal, unpaid, or self-employed work—jobs that rarely provide stability, protection, or decent income. Even more worrying, extreme poverty rose from 34.6% in 2024 to 36.1% in 2025, and government capital investment fell from 8.5% of GDP to 5.7%. This pattern—growth without inclusion—is what economists call jobless growth or enclave growth. In plain language, the mine may be producing and the exports may be rising, but the communities around those mines remain trapped in poverty. Gold may leave Buchanan, yet the road to Buchanan remains broken. That is what “growth without development” looks like in Liberia: statistics moving forward while people remain stuck.



A key issue behind this failure to translate mining wealth into national benefit is how much value Liberia actually keeps from its natural resources. The World Bank estimates that Liberia captures only 15–20% of the fiscal value from mining, far below 50–60% captured in countries such as Botswana, Ghana, and Zambia. This means that for every $100 worth of minerals shipped out of Liberia, the government retains only $15 to $20, while the rest escapes through arrangements that do not properly serve the country. The report also points to significant revenue being lost through incentives—citing roughly $240 million in tax expenditures in 2024 alone, including tax holidays, exemptions, and concessions that behave like sweetheart deals rather than national contracts. Liberia is not poor in resources. The problem is that the deals are not consistently designed to protect Liberia’s future.

There is also a troubling fiscal contradiction at the center of the challenge. The World Bank highlights that capital expenditure dropped from 8.5% to 5.7% of GDP. That decline matters because capital spending is the fuel for the kind of development that creates jobs: roads that connect markets, energy that powers businesses, schools that prepare workers, and public systems that help private enterprise thrive. When capital spending is reduced while other spending remains, a country ends up trying to manage today’s problems rather than building tomorrow’s opportunities. The report notes relative macroeconomic stability—such as inflation moving from 3.1% in February to 5.8% in April, then hovering around 5% by June, along with monetary policy adjustments where the policy rate reached 16% in July amid exchange rate pressures. But stability without investment can become a slow trap. It can keep the economy calm while keeping poverty loud.

The World Bank’s outlook is honest, but it is also a warning. It projects average growth of around 5.3% from 2026 to 2028, assuming no major changes. In reality, that is the ceiling of Liberia’s current growth model. If Liberia wants to truly grow—meaning grow in a way that delivers jobs, income, and resilience—then structural change has to begin now. The report’s recommendations are correct: protect macro stability, but do not do it by starving productive investment; diversify and improve implementation, including enforcing value addition rather than selling raw exports as if that were the end of the story; reform State-Owned Enterprises because fiscal leakage through SOEs can quietly drain public resources; and expand productive opportunities through human capital. With 78% of employment tied to informal work, Liberia cannot afford to delay skills and training. TVET, digital skills, and agribusiness development must be treated as job engines, not as side projects.

This report also has direct relevance for Liberia’s development agenda—especially for initiatives like the water transport project and broader efforts toward inclusive jobs. The message is clear: Liberia cannot rely on mining forever to feed employment. Water transport, particularly when structured through a PPP approach, can create formal work that mining alone cannot provide. It can support captains and crew, ticketing and operations staff, mechanics and maintenance workers, and logistics-linked roles that keep value moving through the economy. It can also reduce costs for farmers and traders by improving access and reliability, while supporting climate-resilient connectivity. But the water transport model will only succeed if Liberia refuses to repeat the mining mistake—allowing most of the value to slip away to private operators while government captures little. Any PPP structure, including models such as 70% operator and 30% maintenance fund, must be protected by transparent revenue tracking, clear reporting, and enforceable accountability. Without that discipline, even well-intended projects can turn into enclaves—systems that look profitable on paper but leave communities no better off.

Ultimately, the second World Bank document—Public Finance Review 2026: From Stabilization to Fiscal Transformation—names the moment accurately. Liberia has stabilized. Now the country must transform. Liberians do not need more growth reports as if reading numbers could fill empty plates. Liberia needs growth that returns value to the nation, expands productive sectors, and places jobs at the center of policy. That means renegotiating mining arrangements to close the fiscal leak, investing the country’s resources in capital projects that create employment, and turning informal survival work into formal, dignified employment.

The bottom line is simple and sharp: the economy may be growing, but children are still hungry. Unless Liberia fixes the fiscal leak—from low retention toward real value capture—and unless informal work is transformed into secure jobs, poverty will continue to rise even when GDP climbs. Growth without jobs is not growth worth celebrating.

World.title: Liberia: APM Terminals Moves to Ease Monrovia Port Congestion, Calls for Joint Action to Speed Up Cargo Clearance
World.content:
MONROVIA – APM Terminals Liberia, terminal operator at the Freeport of Monrovia, says it recognizes the pressure that current congestion of the port infrastructure and shipping delays are placing on importers, the business community and consumers.

In partnership with the National Port Authority and other port stakeholders, APM Terminals Liberia is implementing measures to increase terminal capacity instantly, improving the movement of containers and supporting a more efficient flow of cargo through Liberia’s main trade gateway.

“We acknowledge the congestion at the port and the impact it is having on our customers and businesses in Liberia. Our immediate focus is on improving the areas within our responsibility, particularly terminal capacity and the movement of containers through and out of the port.’’– Rachid Baho, Managing Director Some of the concrete measures taken from the terminal are to free up space by transferring hundreds of longstanding import containers from the full import area to another area of the Port to free up space to receive new import containers, removing buildings inside the terminal and converting the space to container stacking areas, as well as develop yard space, which is currently unpaved.



The impact of some of this work will have an effect within one week while others will deliver additional capacity in the coming months.

It is important to underline that for the long-term solutions – a collaborative reply to the issues from all stakeholders involved is needed, says Rachid Baho.

“Sustainable improvement requires coordinated action across the entire port community to solve the problem with containers not getting out of the terminal fast enough to create space for new cargo coming in,” he explains.

A GROWING PORT UNDER PRESSURE

Liberia’s container trade has grown significantly, with current volumes approaching 200,000 TEU annually – equal to about 30 per cent container volume growth within two years.

APM Terminals Liberia says that growth is positive for the economy and has to date invested USD 15 million in new container equipment, as e.g. reach stackers and other container handling equipment.

But growth needs to go hand in hand with a full ecosystem that is up to speed to handle the volumes in order not to create constraints to the supply chain.

The National Port Authority has publicly acknowledged the increasing pressure on the Freeport as the number and size of vessels serving Liberia grow.

NPA has announced plans for dredging and further expansion of the port’s capacity.

Against this backdrop, APM Terminals Liberia says improving the movement of containers out of the terminal after discharge is equally critical to restoring sustainable cargo flow.

“We have already committed to further investments than the ones already implemented this year – for instance in a third mobile harbor crane and additional terminal equipment to arrive in the new year. And we have a clear interest in always keeping the flow in the terminal fluent. However to put it simply, if you keep filling a container yard without making clear plans for how to empty is again – it is like filling a parking garage with cars and no one coming to drive away again: you will end up with no empty spaces left and new drivers coming will have to wait outside. We must solve the underlying issues together for the long-term.”

In other words, containers occupy valuable yard space until they are cleared and collected. If imports leave the terminal more slowly than new containers arrive, congestion builds and available capacity falls.

APM Terminals Liberia estimates that at least 250 import containers need to leave the terminal each day to maintain a sustainable flow.

However, only about 170 import containers are delivered on average daily, creating a huge imbalance in the terminals discharge capability vs number of containers taken by consignees daily.

The current dwell time going from 7-8 days in 2025 to 15-16 days in 2026 has effectively reduced the storage capacity in Freeport of Monrovia by almost 50%. Addressing all the touchpoints in the process of handling containers is therefore crucial for the future cargo flow – this includes vessel scheduling, terminal handling, customs and inspection, documentation, trucking and the timely collection of containers by importers.

APM Terminals Liberia therefore says it will continue working with the Government of Liberia, the National Port Authority, Liberia Revenue Authority Customs, shipping lines, Customs Brokers, Trickers Union, Consignees and other members of the port community to address the immediate situation.

BIG SURGE INTO WEST AFRICA CREATES DELAYS IN MONROVIA

To understand the full context of the issue, Liberia is currently handling, it is important to look at the journey each container takes before it reaches Freeport of Monrovia from, e.g. China.

Much of Liberia’s containerized cargo currently connects through major West African transshipment hubs that currently experience similar pressure with waiting time for vessels.

Congestion at those hubs can lead to missed connections, cargo accumulation and disruptions to vessel schedules before cargo reaches Liberia.

This distinction is important as public discussion around shipping delays continues.

Recent reports before the Legislature have referred to containers spending more than 30 days at sea before berthing in Monrovia.

Therefore, APM Terminals actively works with shipping lines to mitigate the issue of transshipment and has now confirmed a new direct service with A. P. Moller – Maersk to minimize the exposure of transshipment congested-delays.

“It will be a significant improvement for Monrovia that from January 2027, APM Terminals Liberia and Maersk has joined forces to make Monrovia the first port call for the W5A-service.’’

APM TERMINALS EXPANDING CAPACITY

Alongside efforts to improve container evacuation, APM Terminals Liberia is increasing capacity within the terminal. Measures underway include: • Creating additional container stacking capacity • Developing additional yard space • Adding a third Mobile Harbour Crane • Adding three Reach Stackers and two Empty Container Handlers; and • Adding five Terminal Trucks and two Spreaders These measures are intended to provide additional operating space and equipment capacity as Liberia’s container volumes continue to grow.

This will allow Liberia-bound cargo on the service to be discharged directly in Monrovia rather than being transshipped through Abidjan. I believe this will improve reliability and reduce the risk of delays happening elsewhere in the system,” says Rachid Baho.

BUILDING CAPACITY FOR LIBERIA’S GROWING TRADE

While the immediate priority is to improve cargo flow and ease congestion, the longer-term priority is ensuring that the Freeport has the marine infrastructure, terminal capacity, equipment and supporting processes required to accommodate Liberia’s future trade growth.

Planned direct service, additional equipment, expanded terminal capacity and the NPA’s wider port infrastructure initiatives are complementary steps toward building a more reliable and resilient gateway for Liberia.

APM Terminals Liberia remains committed to working with the Government through the National Port Authority, customers and the wider port community to address the present challenges and strengthen the Freeport of Monrovia as Liberia’s principal gateway to international trade.

World.title: 2026 Thanksgiving Message By The Executive Director Of The Office For The Establishment Of War And Economic Crimes Court For Liberia (Owecc-L)
World.content:
Fellow Liberians, Friends of Liberia, and All Well-Wishers:

On this National Thanksgiving Day, OWECC-L gives gratitude to the Almighty God for His enduring grace, peace, and protection over our beloved Republic.

This year’s Thanksgiving carries a uniquely sacred weight, underscored by the powerful spiritual devotion of our Liberian Women, who are currently engaged in a solemn “Three-day Fast and Prayer” for our Nation. Their intercession serves as a beautiful reminder of the foundational strength of our Mothers, Sisters, and Daughters, whose faith has historically anchored Liberia through its most challenging trials. We stand in solidarity with them, drawing inspiration from their spiritual fortitude as they cry out for justice, accountability, and the moral rebirth of our society.



Guided by this collective desire for healing, I appeal with a sense of national urgency to the Honorable Liberian Legislature to act swiftly and pass the War and Economic Crimes Court (WECC) and the National Anti-Corruption Court (NACC) Bills into law. The draft acts are before You, fully vetted and blessed by the traditional custodians of our land. The cries for justice from victims and survivors must no longer be delayed.

For the Executive, this pivotal historical moment requires a visible, uncompromising, and fortified demonstration of political will. We call upon the Executive to forcefully lead the implementation of these accountability mechanisms, ensuring that no internal obstruction or political hesitation delays the justice our citizens have long deserved.

True justice requires concrete resources, and our laws must be backed by financial commitment. I heavily emphasize the absolute necessity for the government to ensure the explicit inclusion of substantial, dedicated financial support for both courts within the 2027 National Budget. Providing this direct state funding is the ultimate test of our institutional integrity. It ensures that the Office for the Establishment of War and Economic Crimes Court (OWECC-L) can transition seamlessly into full operational courts. Allocating local revenue to these courts safeguards their legal independence, ensures proper case mapping, and guarantees that our structures are built to robust, unassailable standards.

As we fulfill our domestic responsibilities, we call for the intentional, tangible, and real support of our international partners. Liberia cannot walk this path toward transitional justice alone. We call upon ECOWAS, the African Union (AU), the European Union (EU), the United States Government, the United Nations (UN), and the entire global community to stand firmly with us. We require your technical expertise, security collaboration, and robust financial partnerships to bring these courts into full operation. This international solidarity is vital to erasing the culture of impunity, establishing deep-seated legal reforms, and showing that global commitment to human rights has a permanent home in Liberia.

This momentous season fills us with a renewed, unshakeable faith in the destiny of our Country. The synchronized alignment of the prayers of our Women, the imminent actions of our Government, and the willingness of our Global Allies signal that Liberia is undergoing a profound moral resurrection.

Let us carry this renewed faith forward into our daily lives, recognizing that true reconciliation walks hand-in-hand with accountability.

May the prayers of our Women (Our Grandma them, our Ma Them, our Sister Them; and our Daughter Them) continue to cover our land; May the steps we take toward justice be firm and unwavering; and

May God bless the Republic of Liberia.

Happy Thanksgiving to you all.

World.title: Govt. targets 2 million hectares of land for LIFE Project
World.content:
Government is targeting 2 million hectares of land for the Lobito Corridor Integrated Forest Economy (LIFE) Project.

Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame, says government is in a hurry to kick start the project in the first quarter of 2027.

Dr Siame disclosed this when a team from the World Bank Group paid a courtesy call on him at his office in Lusaka today, as part of the Bank’s appraisal mission covering Lusaka and Copperbelt Provinces.

The Minister called for the accelerated preparation of the project since discussions, design and investment plans have already been agreed.

He said the LIFE Project provides an opportunity to translate President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda into practical investments in the forest economy by expanding productive forestry, restoring degraded landscapes,

attracting private investment and strengthening local processing and value addition.

Dr Siame also encouraged the private companies, financial institutions, cooperatives, women and young entrepreneurs to identify investment opportunities and build partnerships, including out grower schemes to realise the project.

He is optimistic that the World Bank Group will soon approve the LIFE project to help spur economic growth in the country.

And World Bank Group Country Manager for Zambia, Martine Valcin, said the Bank is ready to help Zambia achieve her goal in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Ms Valcin said the LIFE Project would reward communities by protecting and restoring natural forests and attracting results-based climate finance.

The meeting was attended by Zambia Forestry and Forest Industries Corporation (ZAFFICO), senior government and bank officials on talks surrounding the forest ecosystem and economy.

World.title: CCPC calls for strong collaboration with the media
World.content:
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has called for stronger collaboration with the media to improve public understanding and reporting of competition and consumer protection matters.

CCPC Executive Director, Eunice Hamavhwa, says limited media coverage and occasional misinterpretation of the Commission’s regulatory decisions, highlight the need for greater awareness of its mandate and operations.

Ms Hamavhwa was speaking during a one day Media Training Workshop for journalists on the mandate of the CCPC in Lusaka.

“The Commission has organised a media training workshop to equip journalists with a better understanding of its legal framework, enforcement processes and broader responsibilities,” she said.

She noted that accurate and balanced reporting is essential in raising public awareness of consumer rights and promoting fair competition in the Zambian economy.

Ms Hamavhwa has also appealed to journalists to take greater interest in competition issues.

“You should take interest in cartels, abuse of market dominance, mergers and acquisitions, as well as unfair business practices that affect consumers,” Ms Hamavhwa said.

Ms Hamavhwa further said that the Commission would like to strengthen its working relationship with the media through increased engagement and information sharing.

World.title: Construction of bulking centre elates Luwingu farmers
World.content:
Small scale farmers in Chief Tungatis Chiefdom in Luwingu district in Northern Province says the construction of a bulking centre in the area has ensured a secure storage for their crops.

Fikonkonta Marketing Centre Secretary, Sylvester Kamfwa, says small scale farmers previously lacked a secure storage and central trading area.

He told the media in an interview in Luwingu district that the construction of fikonkonta marketing centre with support from World Vision Zambia has made it easy for the farmers to secure their farm produce.

“We used to have challenges with storage of crops, some farmers used to make post-harvest losses but now we have a secure storage facility,” Mr Kamfwa explained.

He added that the 10 000 capacity storage has made it easy for farmers to have a uniform price of crops which are on sale.

“Before the construction of this bulking centre, farmers would keep their produce in their homes and would sell their crops at different prices but now, we normally set prices for specific crops,” Mr Kamfwa added.

Meanwhile, Mercy Ngosa, a small-scale farmer, said the construction of the centre has motivated more women to venture into farming.

She said the use of scales to price products enables farmers to get an income which is equal to their input.

“As women, we feel motivated to work hard and produce enough because we now see the benefit that comes with farming, we have a storage facility making it easy to ensure our crops are safe,” she explained.

Ms Ngosa has, however, appealed to government to link the bulking centre with ready markets such as schools and hospitals.

World.title: Chilengi calls for prioritisation of community development in malaria elimination
World.content:
Minister of Health, Roma Chilengi, has called on governments to prioritise community development as a long-term strategy for eliminating malaria, noting that poverty and underdevelopment contribute to the persistence of the disease.

Professor Chilengi made the remarks during the High-Level Dialogue on Malaria Elimination in Botswana, which he attended on behalf of President Hakainde Hichilema.

Prof Chilengi said although enhanced surveillance, improved case management and targeted interventions remain important in controlling malaria, governments should also address the underlying developmental challenges that contribute to its transmission.

Speaking during the Ministerial Perspectives on Alignment, Delivery and Resilience, the Minister observed that countries which have successfully eliminated malaria share a common pattern of sustained development, stating that the disease is less prevalent in developed urban areas.

He said there is a historical correlation between the global distribution of malaria and poverty, adding that addressing development inequalities will significantly contribute to efforts to eliminate the disease.

Prof Chilengi has warned that environmental and financial challenges undermine malaria control efforts and lead to the disease re-emerging when countries experience disruptions to their interventions.

“When we are shaken, Malaria simply comes back again, but I think the one thing we must not lose sight of as governments is to focus our attention on developing our communities and our population and Malaria will go away,” he said.

The Minister further stressed the need to strengthen surveillance systems to ensure timely detection and response to malaria cases, particularly in areas where transmission persisted.

He has called for targeted interventions to interrupt transmission by identifying and treating infected individuals, thereby limiting the spread of the disease through mosquito vectors.

Prof Chilengi has advised countries to maintain their commitment to effective malaria control measures, placing greater emphasis on sustainable development as the foundation for lasting elimination.

This is in a statement issued to the media by the First Secretary for Press at the Zambia High Commission in Gaborone, Botswana, Julia Malunga.

World.title: Govt. to introduce environmental rating system
World.content:
Government says it will soon introduce an environmental rating system to recognise and reward companies that demonstrate good environmental stewardship.

Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame, says the initiative is aimed at encouraging companies to adopt responsible environmental practices through a positive incentive-based approach.

Dr Siame says the ratings will enable companies with good environmental records to earn recognition, which could enhance their corporate profiles and attract responsible investors.

The Minister disclosed this when officials from Konkola Copper Mines (KCM) called on him at his office in Lusaka this morning.

Dr Siame explained that the rating will also promote healthy competition among companies and encourage those performing poorly to improve their environmental management practices.

He commended KCM for its public commitment to responsible corporate citizenship and environmental protection, stressing that environmental pollution and land degradation should not be compromised.

Speaking earlier, KCM Board Chairperson, Moses Banda, disclosed that the company has committed U$D20 million towards Corporate Social Responsibility programmes aimed at benefiting communities in its areas of operation.

Dr Banda said the initiative is intended to enable the company and local communities to contribute to national development in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Meanwhile, Vedanta President for Strategy and Growth, Pushpender Singla, said the company has increased its investment portfolio in Zambia from U$D1.3 billion in 2024 to U$D2.5 billion this year.

He disclosed that KCM has increased copper production from 50, 000 metric tonnes in 2024 to 130,000 metric tonnes last year, with production expected to exceed 170,000 metric tonnes this year, through its 14,500 workforce.

Mr Singla attributed the growth in production to the growing mining sector which is also expected to create more opportunities for employment, suppliers and local businesses.

The Vadenta President revealed that his company will produce 300,000 metric tonnes of copper, representing 10 percent of the government’s three-million-metric-tonne national copper production target.

He said the mining firm is committed to invest in a country where policies are good.

World.title: Govt. seeks tangible results from German partnership
World.content:
Government has called on the German business delegation who visited the country to translate commitments made during its visit to Zambia into tangible investments, projects and job opportunities.

Minister of Technology and Science, Felix Mutati, says discussions held on digital transformation, artificial intelligence, skills development, innovation and investment had laid a strong foundation for cooperation between Zambia and Germany.

Mr Mutati made the remarks in a speech read on his behalf by Acting Permanent Secretary, Derick Saboi, during a farewell meeting with the delegation in Lusaka.

He noted that the partnership had the potential to create opportunities, strengthen institutions and accelerate economic transformation, noting that Zambia’s greatest resource was its people.

The Minister added that the focus should now shift from discussions to implementation, with commitments made during the visit translating into measurable results, including jobs, skills development and investments.

Mr Mutati further called for progress on agreed timelines, the establishment of permanent operational structures, expansion of training programmes and deployment of technological solutions.

He assured the delegation that Government was ready to facilitate collaboration between the public sector, academia, industry and German institutions, adding that Zambia was further committed to building a long-term partnership based on mutual trust and shared prosperity.

Mr Mutati further added that Government looked forward to key milestones, noting that the success of the visit would ultimately be measured by the results delivered.

Speaking at the same event, Head of the German Delegation, Michael Woitag, said the team had identified key projects for future cooperation, with the development of a full software Artificial Intelligence (AI) platform in Zambia being its key project.

Mr Woitag highlighted that the platform would be developed through joint ventures with Zambian companies to enable local people to safely use AI in software development and automate administrative and business processes.

He added that more German technology companies had expressed interest in investing in Zambia and employing local professionals to deliver digital solutions to European markets, creating employment opportunities and transferring valuable skills.

Mr Woitag noted that the delegation had already trained 50 Zambians in AI development and was committed to expanding the programme to help local talent gain more experience and grow.

He further said the delegation planned to establish a permanent contact office in Zambia to strengthen communication, build trust and ensure continued cooperation between German and Zambian companies.

Meanwhile, Representative of the State of Saxony in Berlin, Marcus Franke, said cooperation between German and Zambian companies offered great potential through technology transfer, job creation and business development.

Mr Franke further highlighted that Zambia’s skilled workforce and friendly people provided a strong foundation for mutually beneficial business partnerships.

He commended the government for facilitating the engagements, adding that the delegation had left with a positive impression of Zambia and was committed to promoting further business partnerships.

World.title: Don’t wait for medals to celebrate us – Judoka
World.content:
Elisha Zimba came home with Zambia’s first-ever judo medal from the Youth Olympic Games. What he did not come home with is a guarantee that the next Elisha Zimba will be found, funded and nurtured.

That was the blunt message as the Dakar 2026 bronze medallist in the men’s -55kg judo category touched down at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on Thursday to a thunderous welcome.

Receiving him were National Olympic Committee of Zambia (NOCZ) Board Member Mwape Zulu, National Sports Council of Zambia Chief Executive Officer Sombwa Musunsa, Acting OYDC Zambia Chief Executive Officer Benjamin Tembo, and Judo Association of Zambia General Secretary Mabvuto Ng’uni, among others.

Speaking on behalf of NOCZ President Alfred Foloko, Mr Zulu congratulated Zimba for making the nation proud, but turned the celebration into a challenge to the corporate world.

Invest in young talent now, he said, do not wait until they win medals to celebrate them.

Foloko noted that sustained investment would create opportunities for more Zambians to compete at major international events and return home with medals. Athletes, he emphasised, require support throughout their development journey, because considerable resources go into preparing them to compete at the highest level.

It is a point Judo Association of Zambia General Secretary Mabvuto Ng’uni underlined when he described Zimba’s bronze as record-breaking – the first time Zambia has won a judo medal at the Youth Olympic Games.

NOCZ Athletes Commission Chairperson Esther Siamfuko said her commission had rallied behind all Team Zambia athletes throughout the Games and was delighted to see Zimba return with bronze, describing it as an encouraging moment for Zambian sport and its young athletes.

National Sports Council CEO Sombwa Musunsa said Government was elated with Zimba’s achievement and reaffirmed the Council’s commitment to supporting young talents such as Zimba to develop into world-class athletes capable of representing Zambia at senior international competitions.

For now, Zimba’s bronze stands as both a triumph and a test: proof of what Zambian youth can do with limited support, and a question to corporate Zambia about what they could do with real backing.

Meanwhile, Team Zambia swimmer Sibongile Miti closed her Dakar 2026 campaign on Thursday, cheered on by her teammates.

Miti clocked 33.57 seconds in the women’s 50m backstroke Heat 2, before returning for the women’s 50m breaststroke Heat 4, where she recorded 35.56 seconds.

Team Zambia swimming Coach Ian Stephenson praised his swimmers for national records, personal bests and encouraging finishes.

“All in all, you can attest that they’re giving everything they’ve got and making Mother Zambia very proud,” he said.

Stephenson thanked NOCZ, particularly President Foloko and his team, for the support throughout the Games.

Attention now turns to Mulenga Cole, who will be Team Zambia’s final swimming competitor when he takes to the pool on Friday.

World.title: Higher copper prices present opportunity for restructured government ministries
World.content:
Ministry of Information and Media Director Spokesperson, Henry Kapata, says the World Bank’s projection that copper prices will average US$13,000 per tonne in 2027 presents an opportunity for Zambia.

Mr Kapata says the World Bank’s projection also puts the country’s production ambitions into perspective.

He says with a target of producing 3 million metric tonnes of copper annually by 2031, Zambia must expand its mining capacity, secure reliable electricity and strengthen its ability to turn mineral wealth into jobs, exports and revenue.

Mr Kapata has told the media business news that the World Bank has raised its 2027 copper price forecast by 18 per cent, reflecting expectations of sustained demand

driven by electricity networks, electric vehicles, data centres and other technologies.

Mr Kapata says Copper prices are projected to average US$13,200 per tonne in 2026 before settling at around US$13,000 per tonne in 2027.

For the Republic of Zambia, these projections come at an important time as President Hakainde Hichilema moves to restructure Government ministries to strengthen the implementation of national development priorities.

Mr Kapata noted that the restructuring creates an opportunity for more focused institutions to drive key sectors of the economy.

“The newly established Ministry of Electricity, Ministry of Petroleum, Ministry of Trade and Exports, and Ministry of Industry provide a more defined institutional framework for addressing some of the challenges affecting production, energy security, trade and industrial development, “he said.

Mr Kapata stated that the connection between copper production and electricity is particularly important.

He says achieving annual copper production of 3 million metric tonnes will require substantial investment in mining operations, processing facilities and supporting infrastructure saying these activities depend on reliable and affordable electricity.

Mr Kapata added that the creation of a dedicated Ministry of Electricity therefore provides an opportunity to give greater attention to power generation, transmission, distribution and regional electricity trade.

” As electricity generation expands towards the Government’s 10,000-megawatt target, the country will be better positioned to support mining and industrial activity while also exploring opportunities to export surplus power to regional markets,” says Mr Kapata.

Mr Kapata further stated that electricity can therefore, become an important economic sector in its own right, supporting domestic production, attracting investment and generating export earnings.

He explained that the benefits of higher copper prices also extend beyond the mining sector, increased global demand and favorable prices provide an opportunity to expand mineral production, strengthen exploration and develop local processing capacity.

World.title: MP demands fuel price cut, better salaries for civil servants
World.content:
MBIZO Member of Parliament Corban Madzivanyika has called for a fuel price cut, arguing that the current fuel costs are fueling the high cost of living and undermining industrial productivity.

Madzivanyika made the call during debate on President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Thursday, where he also raised concerns over unpaid Basic Education Assistance Module (BEAM) fees amounting to more than US$300 million, poor health infrastructure, and low civil servants’ salaries.

Madzivanyika said although fuel supplies had remained stable, as indicated by the President in his address, the commodity was increasingly unaffordable for ordinary Zimbabweans and businesses.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Kazakhstan leader bets big on ‘People’s Construction’
World.content:
ON October 28, 2026, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev delivered his annual State of the Nation Address, ‘Kazakhstan’s Current Priorities in a New Historical Cycle’.

It came in the year of the 35th anniversary of Kazakhstan’s independence and after the entry into force of the country’s new Constitution on July 1.

Against a backdrop of growing geopolitical uncertainty and rapid technological change, President Tokayev placed economic resilience, modern infrastructure and technological development at the centre of efforts to strengthen sovereignty and improve citizens’ well-being.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Lady Cheetahs target World Rugby Sevens Series qualification
World.content:
ZIMBABWE’S Lady Cheetahs are in Nairobi, Kenya, ready to begin their bid for qualification to the World Rugby Sevens Series when they compete in the 2026 Africa Sevens Series this weekend.

The Lady Cheetahs will be among 11 countries battling for continental honours at the Women’s Africa Cup, which doubles as the World Rugby SVNS 3 Africa qualifiers, at the RFUEA Grounds on Saturday and Sunday.

Zimbabwe head into the tournament in impressive form after an unbeaten run at the Rugby Africa Cup Sevens pre-qualifying tournament in Maseru, Lesotho, where they also kept clean sheets throughout their campaign.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Delta Beverages and Scottland join forces to ease Mabvuku’s water woes
World.content:
In a country where football sponsorship often begins and ends on the pitch, a significant partnership unfolded yesterday in Mabvuku.

Delta Beverages, through its flagship brand Castle Lager, officially handed over a newly drilled borehole to Premier Soccer League champions Scottland Football Club.

The gesture forms part of the corporate rewards package secured by the club following their 5–0 victory over Dynamos in the season-opening Castle Lager Challenge Cup at Rufaro Stadium in March.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: 2 people die in Harare-Chirundu road accident
World.content:
TWO people died on the spot while several others were injured in a head-on collision between a Rimbi bus and a haulage truck at the 194km peg along the Harare-Chirundu Highway this Friday morning.

National police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi confirmed the horror crash.

“The ZRP reports a fatal road traffic accident which occurred at the 194 kilometre peg along Harare-Chirundu Road near Tengwe turn-off this morning, November 6, 2026, in which two people were killed when a bus and a haulage truck collided,” Nyathi said.

World.title: Chatunga Mugabe, accomplices granted US$100 bail each
World.content:
CHATUNGA Bellarmine Mugabe and his four alleged accomplices in a robbery and malicious damage to property case that occurred in Harare early this week, have been released on US$100 bail each.

The five, represented by Tabison Bvekwa and Theophilus Mubhemi, appeared before magistrate Sheunesu Matova who remanded the matter to November 22 for a trial date.

The State, represented by Takudzwa Jambawo, said it had no compelling reasons to oppose bail before trial.

World.title: Bulawayo councillors divided over ward retention fund
World.content:
BULAWAYO councillors are divided following heated debate over the future of the ward retention facility. Some called for its cancellation due to implementation delays, while others demanded speedy delivery.

The debate followed the presentation of a third-quarter report on the facility to the general purposes committee, in line with the ward retention policy approved by council on December 3, 2025.
