World.title: A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval
World.content:
A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/Getty Images

A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.

Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later - barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia.

She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion, in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.

Sponsor Message

Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.

"The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.

Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.

The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.

A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.

Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.

Sponsor Message

Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.

The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.

Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.

Among their many concerns, critics said the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.

Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.

"Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."

Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.

Much of the night's testimony was heartfelt and personal: Many speakers had family members buried — or plans for their own future burials — at Arlington National Cemetery. Several implored the commissioners not to ruin their reputations by recording their support for the arch.

Sponsor Message

"[These are] warnings about the threat your own behavior poses to your political power, your moral authority, the legacy you leave to your descendants, and your eternal souls," said Stephen Eubank, some seven hours into the public testimony.

As the night wore on, a few speakers even questioned whether the commissioners — who were not shown on screen — were even listening. Many suggested the approval was a foregone conclusion, noting the political makeup of the commission and the fact that Trump-appointed Chair Mark Paoletta and several other members had expressed their support for the arch at the start of the meeting.

The commission started deliberating just before 10 p.m. The discussion lasted less than an hour.

The commissioners who spoke first were Trump allies and appointees. They thanked the speakers for taking the time to share their views, but — in brief comments — expressed their support for moving forward. They continued to cast the arch as a tribute to the nation and those who served, despite the broad pushback from individual veterans and veterans' groups.

The Trump allies dismissed concerns that the arch would violate D.C.'s restrictions on building heights as well as federal environmental and historic preservation laws. They maintained that Congress authorized the project when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle in 1925, which were never built.

And they pointed to recent claims by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the monument will enhance national security — even though officials at the meeting confirmed that no such analysis or details were included in the final submission. In fact, Interior Department official Greg Wischer said "specific national security functions have been filed under seal" in court but that the National Park Service "has not been privy to any national defense preparations."

The most vocal criticism of the arch came from D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, a Democrat who sits on the council. He asked questions about the arch's purpose — military and otherwise — earlier in the meeting and said, during deliberations, that he was dissatisfied with the government's contradictory answers.

Sponsor Message

"We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plan," Mendelson said. He introduced a motion to postpone the vote until those plans could be submitted, or until the commission's next meeting in early December. The motion failed by a vote of 4 to 8.

Vice Chair Stuart Levenbach, a Trump appointee, expressed concerns about delaying the vote because the "project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today," suggesting the government wants to "commence building very quickly."

Within minutes, the commission had given the arch its green light. The Trump administration notified the court within half an hour. By Friday, that light had turned red — at least temporarily.

"While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project," Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said in a statement.

Arch critics look to the courts and Congress for relief

Historic preservation groups wasted no time slamming both the process and the outcome.

Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, called the night's vote a "sham."

"It undermines the democratic process, violates federal statute, and insults our nation's veterans who have made the ultimate sacrifice," he said in a statement. "From the start, this Arch project has been driven by an artificial sense of urgency, while public opposition has been brushed aside."

Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager for the National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement that the organization is disappointed but not surprised. He vowed to "bring this to members of Congress, to ensure this arch is never built. Not here. Not ever."

Sponsor Message

Many Democratic lawmakers have vowed to stop — and investigate — the arch after they regain a Congressional majority in January.

Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen — the consumer rights nonprofit representing the veterans in their lawsuit — told NPR on Thursday that Congress doesn't need to act to stop the arch, since it never actively approved it. That decision, he said, will be up to the courts.

But, he added: "It would be fine if Congress takes additional measures to block construction, since we've seen this lawless administration circumvent the law and court orders so frequently."

Virginia Rep. Don Beyer has introduced a bill that would prohibit and defund the arch, and said Thursday he expects the number of co-sponsors to grow from 80 to at least 200 in the new year.

And Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners that companies and "officials working to advance a project not authorized by Congress will put themselves at legal risk."

He argued that the project violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws, which fall within the jurisdiction of the House committee he expects to soon lead.

"I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it, because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," Huffman said.

World.title: Carney's bet on economic growth — and the risks that come with it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mark Carney is making a bet.

He believes massive public investing now will position the Canadian economy to grow in spite of the trade war and the shifting winds of global geopolitics.

By the 2030-31 fiscal year, the federal government will shoulder $85.5 billion in annual public debt charges. By then, Carney hopes the bet will have paid off and the economy will have undergone a transformation.

"[Ottawa] is borrowing money for these major projects, hoping that it really jump-starts the economy," said Sahir Khan, executive vice-president of the Institute of Fiscal Studies and Democracy at the University of Ottawa.

Khan says the risk is the economy shifts and macro trends change and leave Canada holding a pile of debt that never actually catalyzed growth or investment or created actual jobs.

"There are no jobs created by MOUs and frameworks. They're done when the projects actually get financed, people get hired and we see economic activity," said Khan.

Why many experts are backing Carney's plan

Most experts, including Khan, believe the government's plan is a good idea. They say Canada has not taken steps to boost investment and productivity in years and it shows.

The economy was weak before the trade war began; in 2022, the Bank of Canada warned productivity was reaching emergency, " break glass" levels.

Carney says his plan will address productivity, bring in investment for major projects that will create revenue and build jobs. He says the cost of that is clear, but manageable.

WATCH | Spending is 'under control,' Carney says: ‘We’ve got spending under control’: Carney on federal budget | Duration closed caption 0:41 Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal government is balancing the operational budget a year early and has spending under control while shifting to invest to be ‘masters of our own destiny.’

The key plank to that is the so-called productivity mega-deduction . That alone is expected to encourage businesses to invest in their companies. It brings Canada's marginal effective tax rate to the lowest in any G7 country.

There's also a new Canada growth incentive , an exemption from capital gains that allows entrepreneurs to avoid taxes on up to $15 million in capital gains if those funds are reinvested in a Canadian business.

But those measures cost a lot of money. The productivity-mega deduction alone will cost some $36 billion over five years.

Carney told CBC News after the budget that his government is already taking measures to bring the deficit down.

"We've got spending under control, shifting to invest to be masters of our own destiny. Opportunity, affordability and sovereignty. Canada's moving forward is a fantastic day for the country," said Carney.

What are the risks of massive spending?

But the risk isn't just that these bets don't turn into shovels in the ground or actual jobs.

Adam Chambers, Conservative shadow critic for innovation, science and industry, worries what happens if some other global event crashes into the economy while we have taken on so much debt to deal with the current crisis.

"There's no question the probability of there being an event is rising. Certainly the debt markets would suggest that there is some volatility happening," he said.

The federal government has touted what it calls Canada's "fiscal capacity." Canada has not borrowed nearly as much as other advanced economies and, as a result, the borrowing costs here are lower than they are in many other jurisdictions.

But the list of unexpected events that have changed the economic landscape and made debt riskier is a long one.

"There's a bet being made that there will be no other significant negative shocks. But if the government is wrong, then the financial health of the country could deteriorate actually quite quickly," he told CBC News.

WATCH | Does Carney's budget meet the moment?: At Issue | Does Carney's budget meet the moment? | Duration closed caption 22:25 At Issue this week: Mark Carney's second budget lays out billions to build Canada's sovereignty and tackle the affordability crisis, but will it work? And what does the Democratic Blue-nami mean for Canada-U.S. trade talks?

Chambers says those rising debt service payments should give everyone pause.

By the end of the budget's projections, the deficit will be lower, the debt to GDP ratio will remain within the government's guardrails. But those debt service payments will be at $85.5 billion and sit as the second largest single expenditure in the budget.

And all that a full two years after the end of Donald Trump's term as president.

World.title: Federal budget maps out defence spending surge, but questions remain over NATO target
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The new federal budget sets Canada on a path to spend slightly more than four per cent of its gross domestic product on defence per year — roughly $157 billion — by the end of the decade.

The roadmap forecasts annual direct spending on the military will amount to $99.2 billion by 2030-31, with an additional $58.3 billion for defence infrastructure in the same year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has been under pressure to outline how the country will meet the NATO target of spending five per cent of GDP on defence (3.5 per cent on the military and 1.5 per cent on defence-related expenses) by 2035.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne's fiscal plan is heavy on details about how the Liberal government intends to build up the country's defence industry, but light on specific rearmament plans for the Canadian military.

The budget references the already planned purchase of up to 12 submarines, airborne early warning jets, armoured vehicles and drones, but doesn't address other urgent equipment shortfalls and operational pressures.

"We are investing in the capabilities we need to defend our country, particularly in our North and Arctic," Champagne said in his budget speech.

"We are strengthening our defence industry here at home, so that Canada makes more of what our Forces, and our allies, need to do the job. We are taking greater responsibility for our own security, just as we are for our economic future."

WATCH | Initial reaction as feds unveil budget: Cheers — and jeers — in the House as Champagne talks trust after budget release | Duration closed caption 2:00 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne drew applause and heckling from opposition members as he spoke on Thursday, promising a federal budget that will unlock Canada's 'full growth' potential.

Direct spending on the military in the ongoing budget year is expected to ring in at $75 billion (with an additional $50 billion for defence infrastructure). In the coming budget year (2027-28), it is expected to rise to $89 billion (and $52 billion).

Analysts are skeptical the federal government will remain on the path toward five per cent after 2029. That's the year NATO has set for a review of the commitment, which was insisted upon by the Trump administration.

Will Canada meet NATO's spending target?

When asked on a couple of occasions prior to the budget about the five per cent commitment, Carney reaffirmed Canada's commitment but hedged somewhat and pointed to the review year.

"I think there's some other indicators in here that the current government's commitment to national defence is not fiscally limitless," said Dave Perry, a defence analyst and president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

The commitment to five per cent of GDP, made at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, envisions a gradual rise and Perry said "Canada is basically living up to that mark exactly," but there's no plan for growth beyond 2030 when the fiscal lifting will be harder.

Sahir Khan, an executive vice-president at the University of Ottawa's Institute of Fiscal Studies and Democracy, said as the Trump administration winds down between now and 2029, there could be less pressure on allies to hold fast on the target.

"For those that were incredibly optimistic about where that defence envelope could go in the future, three-and-a-half, five per cent, I think we are going to find it will start to get tempered a bit," Khan said.

WATCH | How Carney is trying to increase defence investment: Will Carney's summit boost defence investment in Canada? | Duration closed caption 9:46 On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is on a path to spend four per cent of its GDP on defence by 2030. Could this investment summit help the country secure the capital it needs to raise its defence profile and capabilities, and meet new NATO spending targets? Power & Politics hears from David McGuinty, Canada's minister of national defence.

Khan said he believes that there will be less of an appetite among Canadians for higher defence spending in five years' time.

"As this starts to eat up more and more of the federal budget, it's going to mean rationing" of federal funds, Khan said. "If you ask Canadians after the Trump administration ends, you know, whether they want more in defence versus health care, the answer is going to be health care, right?"

The budget puts a figure on an important previously announced defence drone initiative, setting aside $2.3 billion over five years, starting next year, to accelerate "the discovery, acquisition and deployment of uncrewed and counter-uncrewed capabilities."

It also puts more money — $25 million — into military health services in order to support victims of the fire at the training range in Wainwright, Alta., and their families. And another $3 million will go directly to the Wainwright Military Family Resource Centre.

The federal government recently extended the deployment of Canadian troops in Latvia to 2031. The fiscal plan puts a figure of $7.1 billion on that NATO mission. The money, however, will come out of the Defence Department's annual budget.

In the past, during the Afghan war for example, the federal government would top up defence through supplementary appropriations.

Perry said, outside of the investments to build up the defence industrial base and create the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), there's little clarity about which specific direction the federal government intends to take the Canadian military.

He said he suspects the public might get a better glimpse when the revised defence policy is released sometime in the next few weeks.

WATCH | Finance minister defends spending plan: Finance minister defends billions in new spending in federal budget | Duration closed caption 12:06 The federal budget lays out the Carney government's plan to boost sovereignty and economic growth amid the U.S. trade war. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne joins Power & Politics to defend the government's proposed billions in new spending.

Feds 'very clear' on plan to reach spending targets

In a media availability, Champagne defended the level of detail in the budget when it came to military spending.

There was, the minister said, "more transparency than most G7 and countries."

The figures are all laid out.

"You can see the spending on a cash basis for every year until 2030," Champagne said. "So, we've been very clear how we're going to reach the four per cent target by 2030."

Khan said he believes the government has been forthright in this budget about its plans for defence and that he hopes it will set the bar for disclosure on other major initiatives where the government has been less than transparent.

He also cautioned that five years — in this fiscal and political environment — is a long time and there is truism about defence being the single largest discretionary line item in the federal budget.

The challenge, Khan said, will be for the Defence Department to spend the money it is being given.

"We saw that when we had an incredibly ambitious initial defence agenda under the Harper government, as the procurements started to get delayed, that became a source of funds to allow the government to get back to balance sooner," Khan said.

"The risk of not executing quickly is that the resources start to get very tempting for other purposes."

World.title: Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When wildfires were burning across Canada in July, and the smoke was blowing into the United States, Michigan's Mike Rogers was among those demanding punishment.

The now defeated Republican candidate for Senate, echoing U.S. President Donald Trump, said Canada should pay more, on top of the current tariffs, to cover the cost of that pollution.

"Canada must be held accountable for endangering Americans, and I will work with your administration to ensure they are!," he wrote on X, in a reply to Trump.

Rogers had, separately, enthused about the tariffs — telling Fox News they were "really positive" for the U.S. and that it was "absolutely unacceptable" for Canada to be selling cars into his border state.

Fast forward three months and Rogers — struggling in race for Senate — tried to cast himself as a friend of Canada.

While drinking a Labatt Blue and alluding to hockey, he called for an end to the tariffs in an ad posted four weeks ago.

"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," he said.

A man votes in the primary election at Northwestern High School in Detroit, on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)

It was one of many examples of Republicans trying to distance themselves from Trump’s trade war and anti-Canadian rhetoric.

Now, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal, the Democrats are hoping to use Republican discomfort with the cross-border trade war to end tariffs on Canada.

Democratic push to end trade war

“There is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada,” Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, told the WSJ on Wednesday.

Wyden and other Democrats believed they might be able to flip enough Republicans against Trump on the issue to override a veto, the Journal reported. That would likely require persuading about 30 to 35 Republican House members, and 11 to 13 Republican senators, the precise number depending on votes yet to be tallied from Tuesday's elections.

The new House and Senate will be seated on January 3, just two days after punishing 50 per cent tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel are scheduled to take effect.

Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers in Michigan, told the MS Now morning show on Thursday he was keen to work to lift the "stupid tariffs on Canada," and later told CNN that ending Trump's "vanity trade war" was a legislative priority for him in Washington.

“There is no economic reason why we are having a tariff war with our biggest trading partner. This has to end.”

That seems to be one of the lessons American politicians will take from the 2026 midterm elections, perhaps with lasting and positive effects for Canada.

From the early days of Trump’s second term, Americans have shown very little interest in picking fights with Canada. Although Trump's verbal attacks on Canada were a staple at rallies throughout October, the issue again failed to catch fire within the MAGA coalition.

Exit polls on Tuesday, according to CNN, found that two-thirds of American voters believed tariffs had hurt both the national and their local economies.

WATCH | Democrat sweep makes history: What the historic Democrat midterm surge means for Canada | Duration closed caption 7:36 Rob Russo, Canada correspondent for The Economist, had to reach back to 1954 for a comparable rebuke of a sitting U.S. president in midterm elections, when Republican Dwight D. Eisenhower lost control of both houses of U.S. Congress. Canada should now watch for any indication that President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans will try to nudge him to be more reasonable in trade talks, he says.

The tariffs were widely seen as having combined with the Iran war to create a double price shock.

Rural America has been hit especially hard by the spike in diesel, which contributed to higher costs for fertilizer. All of the eight main fertilizers used by U.S. farmers cost more than they did a year ago, according to one industry analysis.

Those numbers were key to the massive hemorrhaging of Republican votes in red states such as Kansas.

Trump backs down for Maine, Kansas

In two critical Senate races in Maine and Kansas, Republican candidates appealed directly to Trump to cancel or reconsider specific trade actions against Canada in order to avoid harming voters in their states (and therefore their campaigns).

In Maine, Susan Collins first asked him to drop tariffs on road salt, warning that they would dramatically increase costs for small municipalities, which might then have to raise property taxes. Trump complied.

Later, Trump lifted tariffs on about $5.1 billion US worth of goods to help her. (He replaced them with new tariffs on other goods, although for only about half the monetary value.)

Trump’s reversals weren’t enough to save Collins. Her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson gave his victory speech wearing a button that said "We can’t eat road salt!"

Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas speaks at a campaign event for Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Grosse Pointe Woods, Mich., on Oct. 28. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall asked Trump not to proceed with actions against Montreal-based Bombardier, which makes jets in Wichita. Again, Trump complied, but Marshall lost anyway.

Several Republicans mentioned tariffs in post-mortems of the midterm rout.

"Tragically, we alienated rural America,” said Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who was not up for re-election but saw his junior counterpart lose to Democrat James Talarico. The state's governor also lost to a Democrat.

"Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long.”

Cruz blamed the rout, in order, on the high cost of living, corruption, the cost of the war, sub-par candidates and the trade war with Canada.

The tariffs were, meanwhile, a topic of victory speeches in some of the biggest races.

"I will fight to end these chaotic tariffs," said senator-elect Josh Turek after his upset victory in Iowa.

WATCH | How Trump lost control of Congress: Midterms ‘bluenami’: The exact moment Trump lost control of Congress | About That | Duration closed caption 10:49 Democrats made historic gains in the U.S. midterm elections, winning majority control of both the House and Senate by flipping deep-red seats in several states including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. Andrew Chang breaks down shifts across key battlegrounds to explain how the 'bluenami' unfolded as traditional Republican strongholds fell. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Ohio senator-elect Sherrod Brown, famous for opposing NAFTA, said the same.

The success of the affordability message seemed to position Democrats as hard-core free-traders in a way they might not have otherwise been.

"The tariffs are ruining everything," became a kind of slogan for Talarico, who made a video at the Texas State Fair in which he blamed the price of fried Oreos and funnel cake on tariffs.

Tariffs were even an issue down in Mississippi, where underdog Scott Colom accused incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith of going along with them. (That race still hasn't been called.)

Canada is Mississippi's biggest export market, and Colom’s region is home to the state’s furniture industry, which normallly ships about $34 million US worth of kitchen cabinets, bedding and other furniture to Canada annually.

Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party on Tuesday, in Jackson, Miss. (Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today/The Associated Press)

Not only has the cost of framing a sofa or recliner increased because of tariffs on Canadian lumber, but the furniture now also faces a 50 per cent counter-tariff.

And while Mississippi has its own forestry industry, it depends on specialized logging machinery, much of it imported from Canada and also subject to tariffs.

Colom vowed to local media, if elected, that his first job would be to "get the tariff policy back to Congress."

The tariffs "are not working," he repeated in his election-night speech.

Canada’s softwood lumber industry might see some irony in the fact that its old nemesis, Wyden, is likely to lead the charge for free trade with Canada (he's expected to chair the Senate finance committee).

Wyden is a lumber hardliner who has butted heads with Canada for years, but more recently his positions have reflected a trend seen across the party. The success of the affordability message, linking high costs directly to tariffs and war, has strengthened a previously lukewarm commitment to free trade.

Wyden has opposed all of Trump’s tariffs on Canada, calling them a "shakedown” and a "reckless abuse.”

He says his fellow Democrats plan to "reassert congressional authority" over U.S. trade policy and roll back tariffs Trump instituted under various emergency authorities — good news for Canada.

But perhaps the best news for Canada from the midterms is that politicians in both parties appear to have concluded that tariffs on Canada cost votes, and that opposing them is good politics.

World.title: Elections Alberta reveals October referendum cost $84M, receives additional funds from legislature committee
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Elections Alberta is estimating the province’s Oct. 19 referendum cost just over $84 million to execute.

Chief electoral officer Gordon McClure and his senior staff revealed the cost at a multi-party MLA committee meeting on Thursday.

At the meeting, McClure requested an additional $49 million on top of the $34 million Elections Alberta already spent from its $51-million budget for 2026-27.

Costs included salaries and training for staff, rent for voting places, freight and postage costs, rental vehicles to transport ballot boxes to centralized counting facilities, and security.

The committee unanimously approved the request without a debate.

Last month, Albertans voted on 10 referendum questions including whether Alberta should remain in Canada or start work on a binding referendum on its future in the country.

The majority of Albertans — 75 per cent — voted to stay in Canada.

McClure said election workers counted 22 million ballots by hand, more than in the last federal election. Staffing costs for counting those ballots are estimated at $21 million.

Elections Alberta’s overall supplemental funding request on Thursday was $59 million — $49 million for the referendum, $9 million to cover preparations for the October 2027 provincial election and $993,742 to cover the cost of 23 additional full-time staff.

“I want to assure the committee that this request has been prepared carefully and will be managed responsibly,” McClure said.

Foot on the gas

Since January 2025, Elections Alberta has been tasked with managing 37 electoral events. They include MLA recall petitions, three citizen initiative petitions and a byelection — in addition to the referendum.

Thursday’s presentation revealed how the heavy workload of the referendum impacted staff.

Steve Kaye, Elections Alberta’s chief administrative officer, told the committee the referendum “was crushing” for most of the staff, noting some worked 16- to 20-hour days.

“We have had our foot on the gas for a long time,” he said. “People are tired.

“We have some concerns going forward about being able to hire some of the people that have worked for us in the past.

“We ran a marathon and included a triathlon and then [a] cross the English Channel swimming event. So it's, it's been quite a bit. Again, we're not complaining. This is our job and we'll do our job.”

Kaye said Elections Alberta is likely the leanest elections agency in the country. Elections Alberta has 54 employees. He said Quebec’s election agency has 300 full-time employees, which would be 224 if adjusted to Alberta’s population.

Last week, McClure sent a letter to every MLA asking that the 2027 provincial election either be held with the current election maps or be delayed so Elections Alberta can implement the new election boundaries that are expected to be approved by the legislature within the fall sitting.

His request was rejected outright by Justice Minister Mickey Amery.

World.title: Hidden cameras reveal accessibility barriers at leading restaurants
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Malfunctioning power door operators, inaccessible self-service kiosks and the inability to get a braille menu were among the issues people with disabilities faced while eating out as part of a Marketplace investigation into accessibility at fast-food and full-service restaurants in Ontario.

Marketplace put 10 popular restaurants to the test: five fast-food chains and five full-service restaurants.

The findings raise questions about the effectiveness of Ontario's decades-old accessibility legislation, the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA), and the province's overall approach to fulfilling the act's purpose: achieving accessibility for Ontarians with disabilities.

"There's so much more that can be done," said accessibility strategist Lorene Casiez, who manages Human Space, the accessible design practice of architectural firm BDP Quadrangle.

"There are a lot of better practices, a lot of lived experience … easy-to-do things to make the environment as usable as possible for everyone."

Robert Hampson, who is blind, visited five fast-food chains as part of a Marketplace investigation into restaurant accessibility. (Submitted by Robert Hampson)

Robert Hampson lost his vision at the age of four after undergoing surgery for a brain tumor.

"I remember as a very young kid bumping into things, walking over curbs, hitting my head, but I decided I could do anything I wanted," the Toronto resident said. "I just had to keep going and have no fear."

Watch the full investigation, "The Dining Divide," from Marketplace on YouTube, CBC-TV, or CBC Gem on Friday at 8 p.m.

Hampson said his confidence began to wane at a certain point, but it was restored when he decided to take on a mission.

"I need to educate people along the way," he said. "Every time I walk out the front door and step outside, I'm an advocate for people who are blind and people with disabilities."

Testing fast-food restaurants

Hampson, accompanied by a Marketplace producer, visited one Greater Toronto Area location for A&W, McDonald's, Thai Express, Tim Hortons and Wendy's to document his experience as a customer with a disability.

He started each trip with a simple question: Do you have a braille menu?

None of the locations he visited could provide one.

"I would have liked to have at least found one that had a braille menu," he said. "It's something that needs to be improved upon."

Two companies responded directly to the findings regarding braille menus. Tim Hortons said it doesn't offer them because of how frequently its menu changes. Wendy's told Marketplace braille menus are available across the country, but did not explain why Hampson wasn't offered one when he asked.

Accessibility strategist Lorene Casiez says Ontario’s accessibility laws fall short of what's needed for persons with disabilities. (Submitted by Lorene Casiez)

The AODA does not specifically require braille menus, but Casiez said having them on hand sends a positive signal to customers.

"If someone can't visually read, an alternate format might be braille. An alternative format might be an audible component," Casiez said.

"Thinking about different ways that people can understand the information is certainly a requirement in the AODA."

Beyond braille

Marketplace's fast-food restaurant test also included self-service kiosks, layout and washroom accessibility.

Hidden cameras documented Hampson's attempts to use self-service kiosks at McDonald's and Wendy's. Both had touchscreens and some accessibility features, but neither had a way for him to hear options.

At times, Hampson had difficulty navigating. He accidentally went through an emergency exit at Tim Hortons and was heading toward the drive-thru lane when a concerned motorist shouted toward him: "You're in the drive-thru."

WATCH | Testing self-service kiosk accessibility: Customer who is blind struggles with self-service kiosks | Duration closed caption 1:18 A Marketplace investigation found that self-service kiosks at McDonald’s and Wendy’s locations it visited were unusable for Robert Hampson, a blind customer.

He also got confused on the way to the washrooms at McDonald's and A&W. In the case of A&W, a producer intervened to help him.

On the bathroom door, there was no braille or tactile markings.

"I had no way of knowing, is that the women's? Is that the men's?" he said.

Casiez said a requirement for tactile signage on washroom doors has been in the Ontario Building Code for a long time.

"Not very expensive either, potentially."

Whether the A&W Hampson visited would have been required by the Ontario Building Code to have the signage is unclear.

When it comes to navigating restaurants independently, Hampson wants to see more consistency in how they're laid out. He's also in favour of markings on the ground he can feel with his white cane that can help him determine his location and direction.

In a statement, McDonald's Canada told Marketplace it's sorry to hear about the challenges Hampson experienced.

"This restaurant is independently owned and operated, and we have shared the observations provided to us with the franchisee for its review," the company said.

A Wendy's statement said the company is looking into what was documented during the visit and is working with the franchisee to "identify any opportunities to further support the customer experience."

"When this restaurant was built, it was built in accordance with all applicable standards at the time," said a statement from Tim Hortons. "We are working to identify design changes that could in the future better allow all guests to navigate the space independently."

A&W declined to comment on the investigation.

Taylor Lindsay-Noel and a Marketplace producer documented malfunctioning power door operators at chain restaurants in Toronto. (CBC)

Taking on full-service restaurants

Marketplace also visited one location in Toronto for full-service restaurants Boston Pizza, Earls, Milestones, Swiss Chalet and The Keg. At those locations, hidden cameras documented the experiences of two women who use wheelchairs.

Taylor Lindsay-Noel was one of the customers who, along with a Marketplace producer, dined at three of those establishments. She is a social media content creator who does accessibility-focused restaurant reviews.

"I want to show people that we live very full lives, but it also makes it hard for us to live our lives if places aren't accessible," she said.

The checklist included entrances, an area where Lindsay-Noel encountered challenges at Swiss Chalet and Boston Pizza. At Swiss Chalet, the power door operators malfunctioned on the way in and when she left.

The same was true of Boston Pizza, but on the way out there was a plant and a sign placed in front of the power door button.

"Even if it was working, I wouldn't have been able to hit it," she said.

Marketplace also documented that there were no power doors at the entrance to The Keg, which is required by the current building code. It's unclear which version of the building code applies to The Keg that Marketplace visited.

The full-service customers also asked employees if they were aware of the AODA, which is supposed to be covered in mandatory accessibility training. Of the five restaurants, only one frontline employee at The Keg said she was "a little bit" familiar with the legislation.

"It's part of who you're serving as your client base. So having an awareness of it is really important," said Casiez.

Government response

Marketplace shared the findings of its investigation with the office of Ontario's minister for seniors and accessibility, Raymond Cho, and requested an interview, but the request was declined.

Instead, his office sent a statement that said: "Individual businesses and organizations are responsible for ensuring they are in compliance with the AODA. The Ontario Building Code also sets out accessibility requirements for new construction and existing buildings undergoing extensive renovations."

A spokesperson for Cho said the ministry focuses its "compliance and enforcement efforts" on areas where it can have the greatest impact and added, "complaint trends are reviewed regularly to help determine which sectors should be prioritized for audits and inspections."

Under the AODA, businesses and non-profit organizations are required to file accessibility compliance reports every three years. The next deadline is Dec. 31.

Full-service restaurants make changes

Marketplace requested interviews with the full-service restaurant chains we documented in our investigation. None agreed to an on-camera interview.

Foodtastic, the parent company of Milestones, said in a statement that Milestones is committed to accessibility and added: "We have taken the opportunity to reiterate to our personnel the importance of being familiar with AODA rules, reminding all employees to ensure their training is up to date."

The company also confirmed it added braille and tactile washroom signs to the location in our test.

A statement from Earls said the location we visited "adheres to all municipal building codes and accessibility requirements." The response also affirmed the company's commitment to "a safe, inclusive and comfortable environment."

Boston Pizza, The Keg and Swiss Chalet provided no response to multiple requests for comment. But since sharing our findings with Swiss Chalet, new power door operators have been installed in the washrooms of the location Marketplace visited.

Swiss Chalet did not respond to Marketplace’s investigation, but has since installed power doors for the washrooms at the test location. (CBC)

Accessibility law 'pathetically weak,' advocate says

The AODA went into force in 2005. The regulations include standards for information and communications, customer service and design of public spaces.

"They're pathetically weak," said Toronto-based disability rights advocate David Lepofsky.

Lepofsky, who is blind, was at the forefront of efforts to create the AODA, but said it hasn't lived up to its potential.

"They deal with the public spaces in the built environment, but virtually nothing about the barriers inside buildings."

Lepofsky is pointing to the fact that many of the requirements for interior spaces are found in the Ontario Building Code, not the AODA. This includes details regarding doors, washrooms and signage.

But, according to Lepofsky, the Ontario Building Code has a crucial flaw: it only applies to new buildings or older buildings that have been extensively renovated.

"For the vast majority of our built environment, the building code's inadequate provisions won't even touch them."

WATCH | Power door problems at popular restaurants: Power doors absent or malfunctioning at popular restaurants | Duration closed caption 1:58 Diners Taylor Lindsay-Noel and Ruth Wallace encounter barriers at the entrances of leading restaurant chains.

Lepofsky said he wants standards that cover both old and new buildings "comprehensively."

He also wants to see better enforcement of the AODA.

"It's like a voluntary law because people who break the law, even though it has strong financial penalties built into it, sadly don't have to really worry about that at all."

That sentiment was echoed in the 2023 legislative review of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, which said "enforcement is non-existent under the AODA."

The review cited a "lack of resources" and "the size of the private sector that falls under the jurisdiction of this legislation."

Restaurants are also subject to Ontario's Human Rights Code, which says every person has the right to equal treatment "with respect to services, goods and facilities."

Disability rights advocate David Lepofsky says Ontario’s accessibility regulations are ‘pathetically weak.’ (Submitted by David Lepofsky)

For Hampson, the restaurant visits were sobering, but he hasn't lost hope.

"It's definitely disappointing and frustrating," he said.

"But I think change comes slowly and it has to be people like myself, other people who are blind, visually impaired and other people with disabilities just continuing to push and say if we're going to continue spending money here and coming to your businesses we need to see more things made accessible."

World.title: Worst of beef price hikes may be over, but don’t expect cheaper steak anytime soon
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After years of soaring beef prices, Canadians may finally be getting a break from steep price increases when buying their favourite cut of steak or roast at the grocery store.

Beef prices rose 8.7 per cent in September compared with a year earlier and have climbed 55.5 per cent over the past five years, according to Statistics Canada.

Prices remain at record highs, but industry experts say there are signs of stability, with grocery store price tags remaining relatively flat for much of 2026.

"The worst of the price jumps I would say are over," said Brenna Grant, executive director of Calgary-based beef statistics firm Canfax.

"We've had some really big price jumps in the last four years and any change going forward is going to be more moderate."

Brenna Grant, executive director of Canfax, says the worst of the beef price spikes may be over, but Canadians shouldn't expect prices to drop significantly. (Ina Sidhu/CBC)

Cattle supplies growing

Canada's cattle herd is growing after years of declining numbers.

Statistics Canada reported 12.1 million cattle and calves on Canadian farms as of July 1, 2026, up 3.2 per cent from a year earlier, the largest annual increase since 2004.

The industry has struggled with years of drought in Western Canada and the U.S. Midwest, rising feed costs and shrinking herds.

In southern Alberta, rancher Michael Munton is seeing a shift.

Munton operates Benchmark Angus near Warner, Alta., as well as a processing facility in Picture Butte, Alta.

"This summer prices were the highest that anyone has ever seen in the beef market and we're starting to see that come down," he said.

Munton said ranchers are working to expand their herds but face factors beyond their control.

"All of it is contingent on weather providing that we have good moisture this winter and in the spring, then we should be able to see some stability in that market," Munton said.

He said dry conditions could force producers to sell cattle and set back the recovery.

Cattle stand in a feedlot in southern Alberta. Canada’s cattle herd is growing after years of declining numbers, but experts warn it could take time before consumers see price relief at the grocery store. (Ina Sidhu/CBC)

Why beef could stay expensive in 2027

Experts say consumers shouldn't expect a significant drop in prices at the meat counter.

Kevin Grier, a livestock market analyst based in Guelph, Ont., said North American beef supplies remain tight, while demand has held up despite record prices.

"The only so-called hope of getting lower prices is if all of a sudden Canadian consumers decide that they don't want beef and then therefore the demand declines," he said.

Grier cautioned that North American cattle supplies could become even tighter in 2027 as ranchers hold back breeding animals. That means fewer cattle going to slaughter in the short term, even as producers work to increase supply over the longer term.

Whether that pushes beef prices up will depend on consumer demand, he said.

Stephen Deere is the owner of Modern Steak in Calgary. He says soaring beef prices are putting pressure on restaurant margins and changing how some customers order, with some opting to skip an appetizer or side dish to enjoy their favourite steak. (Ina Sidhu/CBC)

That appetite for beef is also holding up at restaurants.

At Modern Steak in Calgary, owner Stephen Deere said high beef prices are squeezing profits and have forced him to raise menu prices by as much as 10 per cent this year.

"No one wants to do it, it's the last resort," he said. "At the end of the day when you're a prime-grade steakhouse, it's prime-grade beef. There is no substitution for that."

Deere said diners aren't necessarily giving up their favourite steaks but finding other ways to keep bills down.

"I don't see too many people downsizing their regular order. Meaning if I order a rib eye I'm still ordering a rib eye," said Deere.

"What they're doing is they might have one less appetizer, one less side or one less drink."

Are high beef prices the new normal?

Michael Munton is the owner and operator of Benchmark Angus in southern Alberta. He says Canadian cattle herds are expanding after years of drought — but continued growth will depend on favourable weather conditions for grazing land. (Ina Sidhu/CBC News)

Even as cattle supplies recover, experts say beef prices are unlikely to return to what Canadians paid several years ago.

For ranchers, the economics of producing beef have changed dramatically.

"The cost of the infrastructure, the cost of the machinery, the cost of the equipment is astronomical. And the margins that we live on are very, very slim," Munton said.

Those rising costs extend throughout the entire supply chain, including fuel and transportation, according to Grant, and have changed the economics of producing beef.

"It's very rare that you actually see those retail prices come down in any significant way," Grant said.

"Any relief would be very modest and it may be on only some cuts."

World.title: Holocaust survivor, 90, dies nearly a year after being wounded in mass shooting at Australian Hanukkah event
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor has died almost a year after she was wounded during the massacre of 15 people at a Sydney Hanukkah celebration, officials said Friday.

Romanian-born Eva Geller died Thursday night in a Sydney hospital, Executive Council of Australian Jewry director Evan Zlatkis said.

She was one of around 40 people wounded when two gunmen allegedly inspired by the Islamic State group opened fire on a crowd at Bondi Beach on Dec. 14. Fifteen victims aged 10 to 87 died.

Rabbi Aron Moss said Geller had been "strong and pretty healthy right up until the Bondi attack where she was shot."

She had been admitted to the hospital several times in recent weeks due to surgery complications, Moss said.

"She's a proud mother, grandmother and great-grandmother. A beautiful, positive person who even in these difficult months maintained her positivity," Moss said on the family's behalf.

"She was told after being shot that she will never walk again by the doctors. But through sheer determination, she got back up and she did walk again," Moss added.

She walked with a cane following the leg wound, he said.

A life marked by unimaginable suffering, extraordinary strength and resilience. We mourn the passing of Eva Geller, Holocaust survivor and the 16th victim of the Bondi Beach terror attack. May Eva's memory be a blessing. 🕯️ Shabbat Shalom. https://t.co/YWeqsxnIOD —AIJAC_Update

State Premier Chris Minns offered his condolences to Geller's family.

"After everything Geller endured, the news of her death is heartbreaking," Minns said in a statement.

"Almost a year on, we are still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act. We will never forget Eva or any victim whose life was changed forever," Minns added.

Coroner expected to rule on cause of death

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the devastation of the Bondi attack continued to cause pain for families.

"Eva should have been able to celebrate Hanukkah in peace and safety and, instead, her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism," Albanese said in a statement.

The surviving gunman, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 15 counts of murder, 43 of attempted murder and one of committing a terrorist act. He has yet to enter a plea.

It was not yet clear whether Geller's death would change the charges the 25-year-old Akram faces.

WATCH | Bystander praised after overpowering, disarming armed man: Who is the Bondi Beach hero? | Duration 1:57 43-year-old shop owner Ahmed al-Ahmed is being hailed a hero after he was captured on video tackling and disarming a gunman during an attack at a Hanukkah celebration on Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia.

Police said in a statement they were awaiting advice from a state coroner, who would investigate the circumstances of her death.

Akram is next scheduled to appear in court on Feb. 24, when prosecutors expect to finalize what charges will go to the New South Wales state Supreme Court for trial.

Sajid Akram, his father and also a gunman in the attack, was shot dead by police at the scene on Dec. 14, 2025.

World.title: Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it’s Bridget! When I heard there was an internship where Canadian youth were learning about how climate change and brain health are connected, while also creating accessible resources to teach others, I knew I had to find out more.

This week:

Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain

The Big Picture: The Super El Niño

Hungry animals and local farmers want your leftover Halloween pumpkins

Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain

A screenshot from a virtual showcase held on Oct. 18, where students from around the country presented the neuroscience research projects they had been working on this summer. (Brain Climate Equity Collaborative)

Doctors know that climate impacts such as wildfire smoke and extreme heat lead to physical ailments like asthma and heat exhaustion. But more research has been coming out about how climate-related events are also harming the brain , and are linked to anxiety and higher rates of dementia and cognitive functioning issues.

Neuroscience graduate student Muskaan Laroyia researches how climate change affects neurological conditions — something she has discussed at length with others in the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine.

“There was a huge gap between how we perceive brain health, and the impact that the climate crisis is having on brain health,” said Laroyia.

Laroyia co-founded the Brain Climate Equity Collaborative to empower young people to do something about it, as they are most affected by eco-anxiety .

“Recent research has said that the best way to approach eco-anxiety, especially in youth, is not just to tell them all the negative things that are happening but to help them be a part of that change,” she said.

One of the ways Laroyia and her colleagues are addressing this is through their NeuroClimate Youth Internship , launched this year with the University of Calgary’s O'Brien Institute for Public Health. The goal is to help youth learn more about the link between climate change and brain health, and then help them turn that knowledge into action.

Safina Pamery’s group worked over the summer to create accessible resources about the impacts of climate on brain health. (Submitted by Safina Pamery)

From July to October, 30 high school students from across the country worked with researchers and clinicians to explore the intersections of climate change, brain health and health equity. The students attended expert lectures, including a talk from a neuroscientist from Stanford, and a panel with the creators of the University of Toronto’s MedComic Con talking about different ways to disseminate information creatively.

By the end of the internship, the students had produced accessible digital resources for health-care professionals and the public highlighting climate impacts on the brain and what to do about them.

They created websites, presentations and short stories covering everything from how wildfire smoke and air quality affect the brain to how to recognize eco-anxiety and respond to it in healthy ways.

The internship culminated in a virtual international showcase on Oct. 18, where the students presented their research projects and answered questions from researchers, clinicians and other attendees.

Khushi Laroyia led her group’s work on extreme heat and the neurological effects it can have. (Submitted by Khushi Laroyia)

Coincidentally, Laroyia's younger sister, Khushi Laroyia, was among the students chosen by an independent committee to participate in the program. Khushi Laroyia says she learned a lot about how much climate change can impact health equity in vulnerable communities, such as older adults, people with mental health conditions, and those without access to air conditioning and cool spaces.

“Before this internship, I never thought about how climate change doesn't just affect the environment — it affects people, it affects their brain, it affects their mental health,” she said.

“It really opened my eyes to things that I wouldn't ordinarily think about.”

Her group created a website with interactive guides, case studies and toolkits with resources to help people cope with eco-anxiety and figure out how to take action.

Making information accessible

Samarth Yandhe, 15, participated in the internship from Mississauga. Yandhe interviewed people in his community to find real-life examples of how people are struggling with smoke and was surprised to learn that people were not very informed about microscopic particles called PM2.5 that can affect brain function.

He turned research and statistics into short text blurbs that anyone could understand with no prior knowledge of the science.

Samarth Yandhe, 15, is one of the youngest internship participants. He now hopes to study neuroscience at university. (Submitted by Samarth Yandhe)

“Learning about this in more detail made me think about how I spend my day,” said Yandhe, who says the project has made him think differently about things like water usage and littering.

He now realizes that all environmental degradation can harm human health, including the brain, whereas actions to improve the environment, such as conserving water and picking up trash, can improve people's health.

“If I want to help our community and others, I have to start being the type of person who would change for others.”

This is exactly what the Brain Climate Equity Collaborative is meant to inspire — a new understanding of how climate and the brain are interconnected.

“Research is very siloed, it remains in journals, and what we're trying to do is bring that information out to the public,” said Daniela Oboh, the co-executive director of the Collaborative.

There are also plans underway for another internship cohort next year, and Laroyia and Oboh have already received interest from medical schools and community organizations.

And the students haven’t stopped at the presentations. They continue to share their work through ongoing community activities, lectures and articles.

“I'm so proud of these students,” said Oboh. “Our future is very, very bright.”

— Bridget Stringer-Holden

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : Sixty-five bats dropped dead inside a home custom-built to protect them. What went wrong? For bat moms looking for a place to raise their pups, it’s not the rent that’s through the roof, it’s the temperature. But bat people are busy building them safer homes, from tiny condos with emergency exits to mini bark roosts stuck to trees.

What On Earth? drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen . The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

Reader feedback

Last week, Emily Chung wrote about ways to make wind turbines less deadly to migratory bats. The article included an error: It said wind turbine curtailment happens between sunrise and sunset. In fact, it happens between sunset and sunrise. That has been corrected in the web version of the story.

Virginia Call wrote that regulations to protect bats from wind turbines are lacking in Manitoba compared to other provinces: "According to Craig Willis at U of Winnipeg , Alberta's guidelines should easily be adopted here in Manitoba. Thanks for this piece in time for Halloween, when bat-migration has just ended."

Kendyll Woodman wrote: "Thank you so much for the article on bats. I’ve loved bats since my childhood when my dad told me they eat mosquitoes. When I lived in Lesotho in Southern Africa my attic was filled with bats. Each evening around sunset I would watch as they flew away for their night time hunting. And speaking of extinction I highly recommend the novel Beasts of the Sea by Iida Turpeinen."

Gillian Arsenault and John Virag asked if vertical axis wind turbines, like some of the ones in our 2023 article on rooftop wind turbines (see animation below), might be safer for birds and bats. VAWT companies such as Freen and Wind Harvest and some researchers argue that they likely are, because the turbines spin more slowly, are more visible and cause less extreme pressure changes around them. However, Wind Harvest acknowledges that no large-scale studies have been done to verify this.

(IBIS Power/YouTube)

The Big Picture: The Super El Niño

(Climate Central)

At the beginning of the year, no one could have predicted just how strong an El Niño would develop. But by June, it became clear that not only would we be getting an El Niño, but it could be one for the record books .

In its June monthly update, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said that there was a chance that the El Niño “would rank among the largest El Niño events in the historical record going back to 1950.” And boy were they right.

Here’s what that really means: El Niño is part of a natural cycle where ocean temperatures in a particular region of the Pacific Ocean rise above average. Anything more than 2 C is considered a strong El Niño. Well, the temperature anomaly has risen to 3.5 C. That’s why some people are calling it a “super” El Niño.

As you can see above, the ocean temperature is a sweltering 30 C in the part of the central Pacific near the equator used to monitor El Niño events. And it hasn’t even peaked yet. That’s forecast to happen in either November or December. Why does this matter? It influences weather patterns around the world , with the largest impacts being droughts and heavy rainfall in regions mainly around the equator. For Canada, it means dry conditions in the already drought-stricken regions in the west and warmer temperatures across northern and central Canada. And an El Niño also helps to drive up the annual global temperature, which is already rising due to climate change.

— Nicole Mortillaro

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

The power-hungriness of AI now has companies retrofitting old jet engine turbines to provide more electricity to data centres. A solution that’s both polluting and costly.

In rural areas and colonias in Arizona, a state with a much higher maternal mortality rate than the national average, the dangers for pregnancies carried out near pesticide-sprayed fields is something state health plans don’t take into account, The Margin reports.

The gas-powered cars on Disneyland's Autopia ride have felt "stubbornly behind the times" considering the ride's location in Tomorrowland, says Rick Lye of Disney Fanatic. They're finally electrifying, but not with battery-electric technology. Lye explains what they're doing instead and why .

Some kinds of fishing are often allowed in marine protected areas. Greenpeace is trying to make that physically impossible. The group claimed it had "effectively closed 116 sq km (45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA) to bottom trawling” by doing this .

For more than a century, colonial policies disrupted and outlawed the practice of cultural burning in Canada, viewing fire as a threat and something to immediately suppress. Here's why Indigenous-led fire management is starting to be recognized as essential for Canada’s future, the Narwhal reports.

Hungry animals and local farmers want your leftover Halloween pumpkins

Justine Beaumont and her pig, Cupcake, pose alongside the pile of leftover pumpkins that people have donated to Beaumont Acres after Halloween on Nov. 2. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)

Some southwestern Ontario farms and municipalities are encouraging residents to keep pumpkins out of the trash as the Halloween season comes to an end.

The Great Pumpkin Rescue is an Oxford County-based volunteer group that shares ways people can repurpose their pumpkins, including through recipes, donations and composting.

“There are, quite frankly, benefits to the community when you find a locale [that's] going to take them,” said volunteer Bryan Smith. “Southwestern Ontario will grow as farmers grow more food and sell that locally, which is good for us more broadly … because it’s stimulating the local economy.”

The initiative to repurpose pumpkins started more than a decade ago at Northlane Farm in Thamesford, Ont., which to this day collects pumpkins for its farming operations.

Now, the Great Pumpkin Rescue group compiles an annual list of area farms that will take pumpkins, squash and gourds during the first week of November.

“There are quite a number of extremely happy goats, pigs and chickens who just love to eat them,” Smith said. “We want them to be turned into something that feeds farm animals.”

WATCH | Farm animals enjoy Halloween pumpkins: Hungry hogs want your Halloween leftovers | Duration 1:02 Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., is one of the several farms in southwestern Ontario accepting pumpkins, squash and gourds as the Halloween season comes to a close. CBC's Kendra Seguin speaks with owner Justine Beaumont about how pumpkins can support local farms and their animals.

Beaumont Acres, a sanctuary in London, Ont., has been accepting pumpkins from community members every fall since it opened six years ago. Founder Justine Beaumont estimates the farm has already received close to 100 pumpkins and gourds this year.

“Our animals love pumpkins and they’re also great for them. They are great for their gut health and great for their skin,” Beaumont said.

Beaumont Acres is home to nearly 30 rescue and retired working animals, including horses, pigs, ducks and a cow.

“Our cow, Trixie, loves pumpkins. She’ll come running across the field for them,” she said.

Trixie the cow is one of the many animals at Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., that enjoys eating pumpkins. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)

Beaumont said each animal likes a different part of the pumpkin: horses like the seeds, ducks and chickens like the gooey insides, and pigs will eat everything.

“Our pigs also love to play with the pumpkins. They find it very stimulating. They’ll roll them around and play with them like they’re a ball,” Beaumont said. “It’s a lot of fun to watch.”

No paint, no candles allowed

It’s important to assess the condition of pumpkins before deciding where to take them, Smith said, adding that any uncarved pumpkins can be used for homemade meals.

For residents planning to take pumpkins to local animal farms, Smith said it’s important to ensure they are clean and in good condition. Pumpkins should not have any paint, metal, toothpicks, candles, wax or other unsafe-to-eat substances on — or in — them, he said.

Beaumont said it’s fine if pumpkins come to her farm a bit squishy, but she is asking people to refrain from bringing anything with mould.

At Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., Cupcake the pig enjoys a gourd and piece of pumpkin that nearby residents donated to the farm. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)

Better options for mouldy and broken pumpkins include sending them to farms with a digester, Smith said, which breaks down organic materials to produce energy.

Put pumpkins in municipal green bins

It's not just farmers doing the work.

Some municipalities are making it easier for residents who want to give pumpkins a second life. Both Woodstock and Tillsonburg, Ont., are offering to collect pumpkins and redistribute them to people who want them for food or livestock.

Of course, another option is always to put the pumpkins in your green bin.

However, generally, if pumpkins are painted, they must go in the garbage.

— Kendra Seguin
