World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada tapped as LA Philharmonic’s first Latin music chair
World.content:
Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada will help shape the sound of the Los Angeles Philharmonic as its first creative chair for Latin music, expanding her relationship with the orchestra into a role championing Latin American artists and traditions.

The appointment, announced Wednesday, puts the 29-year-old Latin Grammy winner on an artistic leadership team preparing for music director Daniel Harding’s arrival in the 2027-28 season.

Described in 2024 as “the next Mexican global music star” by Mexico News Daily, Estrada will develop programming across Walt Disney Concert Hall, the Hollywood Bowl and The Ford, an intimate amphitheater in the Hollywood Hills.

Her appointment builds on three years of collaborations with the 107-year-old orchestra. She will also collaborate with guest artists and continue working with Youth Orchestra Los Angeles, the organization’s music education program.

“Latin music is not a single sound,” Estrada said in the Philharmonic’s announcement. “To me, it is the soul of an entire continent, an immense and profound richness woven together across generations, with the power to transcend any border.”

Estrada’s piercing lyricism and deeply soulful storytelling come through in her NPR Tiny Desk concerts in 2021 and 2025. Both performances offer English subtitles, allowing viewers who do not speak Spanish to follow her lyrics.

The first was taped at her family’s instrument workshop in Coatepec, Veracruz, during the COVID-19 pandemic and highlighted in the Mexico News Daily article “Regional Mexican music takes over NPR’s Tiny Desk.”

Estrada grew up in the coffee town of Coatepec surrounded by instruments and musicians in her parents’ workshop.

The second was a deeply affecting four-song set in the famously cramped NPR office space, encompassing heartbreak and a defiant message of hope for women facing violence in Mexico.

NPR’s Anamaria Sayre wrote that Estrada brings audiences to tears without extinguishing hope, adding that “her voice finds a way to bend wounds to her will and become whole.”

Her 2022 album, “Marchita,” helped establish her blend of indie folk, jazz and traditional Mexican influences. She won that year’s Latin Grammy for best new artist and received a Grammy nomination for best global music performance in 2024.

Her self-produced 2025 follow-up, “Vendrán Suaves Lluvias,” brought her six 2026 Latin Grammy nominations, including album of the year. The song “Dime” — described by KUTX in Austin, Texas, as “a deceptively lovely song about post-breakup wild rage” — is up for record and song of the year.

The 27th Latin Grammys will be held Nov. 12 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, with Estrada scheduled to perform and Puerto Rican actress Roselyn Sánchez hosting for the 10th time.

“Vendrán Suaves Lluvias” emerged from profound loss. Estrada told NPR that her best friend and his younger brother were murdered in Mexico City in 2022, leaving her to navigate grief while touring internationally.

The Philharmonic also named British composer and conductor Thomas Adès its creative chair for new music, succeeding John Adams, and Bronx-born jazz vocalist Samara Joy its creative chair for jazz, succeeding Herbie Hancock.

With reports from EFE and NPR

World.title: Mexico’s 2026 growth outlook improves in Banxico and Citi surveys
World.content:
Economic growth in Mexico in 2026 is expected to be higher than previously predicted, according to the median forecasts of economists and analysts surveyed by the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) and Citi.

Conducted in late October, Banxico’s most recent expectations survey yielded a median economic growth forecast of 1.5% in 2026, up from a prediction of 1.4% in September. Economists and analysts from 40 Mexican and foreign private sector economic research and consulting groups responded to the survey.

Economists consulted by Citi for its latest expectations survey are more optimistic about Mexico’s 2026 growth prospects. Their median forecast is 1.8% growth this year, up from 1.4% in the previous survey. Economists from 36 banks, brokerages and research organizations responded to Citi’s survey, whose results were published on Wednesday.

The range of 2026 growth estimates among the economists surveyed by Citi went from 0.9% to 2.1%.

According to preliminary data published by the national statistics agency INEGI last week, Mexico’s economy grew 1.9% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The economy contracted in sequential terms in the first quarter of the year, but expanded in both Q2 (+1.4% compared to Q1) and Q3 (+0.9% compared to Q2, per preliminary data).

President Claudia Sheinbaum said last week that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, was helping to drive growth. Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronic products in Mexico — many of which are exported to the United States — was providing momentum to the economy.

Growth outlooks for 2027

The median forecast of economists surveyed by Banxico is that Mexico’s economy will grow 1.83% in 2027. The prediction is up slightly from 1.80% in the central bank’s previous survey.

The median forecast of economists surveyed by Citi is that Mexico’s GDP will increase 1.9% next year, up from a 1.8% prediction in the bank’s previous survey.

Inflation predicted to approach 4% by end of year

The median forecasts for Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate at the end of 2026 were 3.88%, according to the Banxico survey, and 3.90%, per the Citi survey. The Banxico forecast rose by 0.01 percentage points while the Citi forecast was unchanged compared to the bank’s previous survey.

Inflation increased in September for a second consecutive month, reaching an annual headline rate of 3.45%. The headline rate spiked to 3.62% in the first half of October, according to INEGI’s most recent inflation data.

Despite the recent increase in inflation, the Banxico board decided on Thursday to lower the central bank’s benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%. Just six of the 36 respondents to Citi’s survey predicted that the bank would cut its key rate after its November monetary policy meeting.

What will the USD:MXN rate be at the end of 2026?

The median forecasts for the USD:MXN exchange rate at the end of 2026 were 18.39, according to the Banxico survey, and 18.50, per the Citi survey. The Banxico forecast increased from 17.50 in the previous survey, while the Citi prediction rose from 18.20.

The Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate on Thursday was 18.75. That rate represents a depreciation of 9.9% for the peso since Sept. 4, when it closed at 16.89 to the dollar — its strongest level in over two years.

The MND Peso Index™ determined that the peso was undervalued by 0.7% in early October when it was trading at just below 18 to the US dollar.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: United Airlines cancels all its remaining flights to Tulum starting in January
World.content:
United Airlines has announced it will cease operations at Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport in Tulum starting early next year, citing market conditions as the cause.

The announcement comes just two weeks after American Airlines revealed plans to halt its Miami-Tulum route, following similar moves by other domestic and international carriers including Aeroméxico, Volaris, Copa and Avianca.

The final flight for the connection from Newark is scheduled for Jan. 2, while service from Houston will conclude on Jan. 4. The withdrawal will not be immediate; rather, it will take effect after the year-end holiday period, in accordance with the published schedule.

According to United, affected passengers will be able to modify their bookings.

“Customers will have the option to change their booking to flights arriving at nearby airports, such as Cancún (CUN)—which is a 1.5 to 2-hour drive away and serves many of the same tourist areas as TQO—or, alternatively, they may request a refund,” United said in a statement sent to the newspaper El Financiero.

United’s departure marks the culmination of a gradual reduction in its operations in Tulum. Prior to announcing the cancellation of its connections from Newark and Houston, the airline had already withdrawn its services from Chicago and Los Angeles, thereby diminishing its presence at the Quintana Roo terminal.

Industry reports interpret the company’s “market conditions” rationale for eliminating the flights as Tulum’s lower-than-expected vacation demand.

Industry analysts cited by Aviación News blame the tourism decline on high hotel prices in the area and weaker-than-expected demand for leisure travel. Other contributing factors include the massive influx of sargassum and increased fees and other charges on foreign tourists.

The combination of factors has reportedly led airlines to reassess the profitability of their operations and shift capacity to other destinations with higher passenger volumes.

In this context, Cancún International Airport – located 130 kilometers north of Tulum – emerges as the primary beneficiary of the reorientation of supply.

In the meantime, Air Canada, WestJet, and Air Transat have announced that they will resume flights for the winter season. Viva Aerobus continues its operations at the terminal with no announced changes, and state-owned Mexicana de Aviación remains the only carrier offering an increased number of flights.

With reports from Reportur

World.title: Finance Ministry blocks accounts of former electoral institute chief and associates
World.content:
Guadalupe Taddei, former president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), and José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, a businessman whose companies received lucrative INE contracts, are reportedly among 25 people who have been added to the Finance Ministry’s Blocked Persons List.

The Finance Ministry’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) announced on Wednesday that 25 individuals and 15 companies “linked to electoral suppliers” had been added to the Blocked Persons List, meaning that financial institutions must freeze their bank accounts. It didn’t name the individuals or companies.

The UIF said in a statement that their inclusion on the list came after the detection of “financial transactions that involve elements of risk and warrant review by the appropriate authorities.”

“Inclusion on the Blocked Persons List is a preventive and precautionary administrative measure and does not imply a definitive determination of liability,” the UIF said. “Individuals included on the list are entitled to defense mechanisms and the right to a hearing provided for in applicable legislation.”

The UIF’s announcement of the additions to the Blocked Persons List came nine days after Taddei resigned as INE president amid allegations of corruption. Thirty other INE officials, including 17 who worked in Taddei’s office, have also recently resigned.

During Taddei’s 2023-2026 tenure at the helm of the electoral authority, companies linked to José Alfredo Hernández Casillas and his brother Raymundo Francisco Hernández Casillas received contracts to supply electoral materials to the INE. The ex-INE president reportedly had a close personal relationship with José Alfredo, with some media outlets speculating that they were romantic partners.

The Reforma newspaper reported that José Alfredo Hernández Casillas’ companies had obtained electoral authority contracts dating back to the time that Taddei presided over the electoral organization of Sonora between 2014 and 2021. Taddei’s “closeness” to Hernández allowed the latter to obtain contracts awarded by high-ranking INE officials, Reforma reported.

In an Oct. 25 statement announcing her resignation, Taddei said she was “aware of the allegations that have circulated in the media and on social media, … including rumors, fabrications, leaks and accounts whose authenticity, context and purpose — as in all cases — must be verified and corroborated.”

“… Each allegation must be examined with evidence and through institutional channels,” she said.

Taddei, Hernández Casillas brothers reported to be on the Blocked Persons List

The newspapers La Jornada and El Universal and various other media outlets reported that Taddei and José Alfredo Hernández Casillas are among the 25 people added to the Finance Ministry’s Blocked Persons List. La Jornada cited “a source with access to the list.”

El Universal reported that Raymundo Francisco Hernández Casillas was also added to the list.

The UIF said that in light of the “elements of risk” it detected in financial transactions, it filed a complaint with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) so that the FGR can conduct “the appropriate investigations and determine, in accordance with the law, any potential [criminal] liability.”

📢 #ComunicadoDePrensa La UIF realiza acciones preventivas sobre personas vinculadas con proveedores electorales. La Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, a través de la Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera (UIF), incorporó a la Lista de Personas Bloqueadas a 40 personas (25 físicas y 15 morales) vinculadas con proveedores electorales. https://t.co/DcPdyl2TU6 🌐 — Hacienda (@Hacienda_Mexico) November 5, 2026

The Federal Auditor’s Office has already launched its own investigation into allegations regarding the “improper use of public resources” by the INE.

At her morning press conference last Thursday, President Claudia Sheinbaum said that Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico” by allegedly acting corruptly during her leadership of the INE.

She also asserted that “two or three” companies that received contracts to supply materials such as ballot papers and ballot boxes to the INE — i.e. companies linked to the Hernández Casillas brothers — didn’t actually produce the materials themselves but rather acted as “intermediaries.”

At the same press conference, Pablo Gómez, head of the Presidential Commission for Electoral Reform and a former UIF chief, made similar remarks.

“The companies mentioned don’t have industrial plants. … They don’t make anything. … They’re intermediaries that win contracts and buy everything or go to printers and print everything,” he said.

In light of the alleged corruption in the awarding of INE contracts to companies linked to the Hernández Casillas brothers, Sheinbaum said last Thursday that “most electoral materials” should be made by Talleres Gráficos de México, a government-run printing agency.

To that end, Sheinbaum said today that her government would present a decree next week to strengthen the agency and its governance.

The president has sought to distance her government and the ruling Morena party from Taddei, who has family links to both. Sheinbaum has said that Taddei’s resignation and the scandal engulfing the INE won’t compromise Mexico’s 2027 elections, which are scheduled to take place on June 6.

With reports from La Jornada and El Universal

World.title: Mexico’s trade surplus with the US jumped 26% in the first nine months of 2026, reaching a record US $184 billion
World.content:
The U.S. trade deficit with Mexico grew at an annual rate of 26.1% during the first three-quarters of the year, reaching a record US $184.019 billion, according to U.S. Census Bureau data cited by El Economista.

The balance resulted from a 20.7% increase in U.S. imports of Mexican products compared to the first nine months of 2025, coming in at nearly US $481.6 billion, well above the nearly US $297.6 billion in U.S. exports to Mexico, a 17.6% year-on-year increase.

Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in September (US $62.2 billion) were also a record and mark the third consecutive month that the value of goods shipped from Mexico to the U.S. surpassed US $60 billion.

Mexico accounted for the largest U.S. goods trade deficit in September (US $28.15 billion, a 40% annual increase) and set a new monthly record, although the nine-month trade deficit with Mexico was the second largest for the United States behind only Vietnam (US $190.9 billion).

While the current U.S. administration has declared that one of its priorities is to reduce its trade deficit with the world (especially China), its trade deficit with Mexico has soared due to elevated purchases of computer equipment.

Meanwhile, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) reported this week that Mexican foreign trade increased 24.6% in the first half of the year, while also citing the expansion of manufacturing acquisitions by the United States, primarily information processing equipment, servers and electronic components for the construction of data centers and Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

U.S. demand for AI-related goods was so significant that it explains Mexico’s entire boom in 2025 and between 75-80% of that recorded thus far in 2026, the IDB said.

Mexico’s performance is part of a regional trend as exports of goods from Latin America and the Caribbean grew above the world average in the first half of 2026, with Mexico leading the way.

According to the IDB, exports from the region rose 19.5% year-on-year from January through June, above the 14.5% increase in global trade, primarily due to increased sales of AI infrastructure equipment in the United States.

The IDB noted that Mexico accounts for 93% of regional exports of data processing equipment, servers and electronic components for the construction of data centers and was responsible for 96% of its rebound last year.

With reports from El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How many people are emigrating from Mexico?
World.content:
In a previous “Mexico in Numbers” article, we reported on Intercensal Survey data that showed that almost 1.2 million foreign-born residents lived in Mexico in 2025.

Our focus today is on people who emigrated from Mexico to another country. Once again, the data comes from the 2025 Intercensal Survey results report, which was published by the national statistics agency INEGI in September. It looks at emigration from October 2020 to October 2025.

The emigrants counted by INEGI include Mexicans and people from other countries who were living in Mexico, but emigrated between October 2020 and October 2025. Migrants from many countries have spent time living in Mexico before moving on to another country, often the United States — though INEGI doesn’t specify destination countries of emigrants in the Intercensal Survey results report.

How many people emigrated from Mexico between 2020 and 2025?

INEGI reported that 1,259,978 (almost 1.26 million) people emigrated from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025.

That number represents an increase of 56.95% compared to the preceding five-year period, during which 802,807 people emigrated from Mexico.

Former U.S. President Joe Biden was in office for most of the October 2020 to October 2025 period. Current U.S. President Donald Trump was in office for most of the preceding five-year period. Biden’s border policies were generally more permissive than those of Trump, although he imposed stricter limits on asylum late in his four-year presidency, causing illegal crossings into the U.S. to fall.

How many emigrants returned to Mexico after leaving the country?

INEGI reported that 150,752 emigrants returned to Mexico after leaving the country between October 2020 and October 2025.

That figure represents just under 12% of all people who emigrated in the five-year period.

INEGI reported that 1,022,728 (1.02 million) people had not returned to Mexico after leaving the country between October 2020 and October 2025.

That figure represents 81.2% of all people who emigrated in the period.

INEGI noted in the Intercensal Survey results report that the number of emigrants who remained abroad and the number who returned to Mexico don’t add up to the total number of emigrants in the period between October 2020 and October 2025 because there is a third “not specified” category. A total of 86,498 emigrants fall into that category.

Which states were the largest sources of emigrants?

More than half of all emigrants were living in just 10 Mexican states before leaving the country between October 2020 and October 2025. Those states are:

Guanajuato: The source of 7.5% of all emigrants between October 2020 and October 2025

Michoacán: 6.8%

Veracruz: 6.4%

Puebla: 6.2%

México state: 6.1%

Oaxaca: 5.7%

Jalisco: 5.2%

Chiapas: 4.7%

Guerrero: 4.2%

Hidalgo: 3.7%

The 10 aforementioned states provided 56.5% of all emigrants from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025.

The five states that provided the lowest number of emigrants in the five-year period are Baja California Sur (0.3% of the total); Campeche (0.5%); Quintana Roo (0.6%); Colima (0.6%); and Tabasco (0.7%).

Men accounted for over 70% of emigrants between 2020 and 2025

INEGI reported that men accounted for 70.4% of emigrants from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025, while women accounted for 29.6%.

Over one in five emigrants — 22.5% — were aged between 20 and 24 when they left Mexico.

After the group aged 20-24, the next largest cohorts of emigrants were those aged:

25-29: 19.5% of all emigrants

15-19: 15%

30-34: 14.1%

Thus, 71.1% of all emigrants from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025 were aged between 15 and 34 when they left the country.

More Intercensal Survey coverage from MND

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: MND Local CDMX: A nighttime race, queer musical and medieval masquerade
World.content:
With Día de Muertos firmly in the rearview mirror, we have a couple of weeks before the Christmas season really kicks into high gear. But that doesn’t mean Mexico City is short on ways to keep busy in the meantime.

From a nighttime 10K run through UNAM and a musical celebration of queer identity to a medieval-inspired winter masquerade, the capital has a few quirky surprises up its sleeve this December.

Let’s get into it.

Mexico City’s Rave Run brings a nighttime 10K to UNAM

Runners looking for a different kind of nighttime outing can lace up for the Rave Run by Carrera Nocturna 2026, a 10-kilometer race taking place at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM).

Organized by Emoción Deportiva, the event is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 19, with the starting gun firing at 7 p.m. at Estadio Universitario in Ciudad Universitaria. The race will follow a circuit through the university campus, offering a unique opportunity to experience one of Mexico City’s most recognizable educational institutions after dark.

The competition, billed as a general 10K, is open to anyone 15 and older. Participants must complete the course within a maximum of 80 minutes, and the top three finishers in both the women’s and men’s divisions will receive awards — but don’t expect big cash prizes.

Registration is limited and costs 749 pesos, while late registration costs 849 pesos.

The entry fee includes a commemorative T-shirt, finisher’s medal, runner number, promotional item, race timing, finish-line photography, water and isotonic drinks along the course, medical assistance (hopefully that won’t be needed) and access to official results.

Date: Saturday, Dec. 19

Location: Estadio Olímpico Universitario

Cost: 749-849 pesos

For more information and to register your spot in the race, visit Emoción Deportiva.

Mexico City’s Gay Choir presents a musical journey of identity and self-actualization

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Teatros Ciudad de México (@teatroscdmx)



Mexico City’s premier queer choir, Coro Gay Ciudad de México, is gearing up for its rendition of “La Misteriosa Flama de la Reina Leona,” a coming-of-age musical journey that chronicles two characters as they navigate childhood, identity and self-acceptance.

The performance is slated to take place Tuesday, Dec. 15 at Teatro de la Ciudad Esperanza Iris in the capital’s Historic Center.

Described by the theater troupe as a “journey through shadows, memories and discoveries,” “La Misteriosa Flama de la Reina Leona” explores the search for a mysterious flame that, despite seeming lost, exists within us throughout our lives.

The production unfolds through two childhood stories: The first follows a girl trying to find her way in a world of giants, while the second centers on a boy who, while leading a parade, discovers the courage to realize the best version of himself. Together, the stories explore imagination, identity, fear and the possibility of growing up without abandoning one’s true self.

More than 100 singers and musicians bring the performance to life, allowing the power of music and storytelling to wade through the sometimes messy worlds of memory, reflection and resistance.

The performance is open to all ages, although children ages 3 and older require tickets. It’s also worth noting that Teatro de la Ciudad Esperanza Iris does not have an elevator.

Date: Tuesday, Dec. 15

Location: Donceles 36, Centro Histórico, Cuauhtémoc, 06010 Ciudad de México

Cost: 253-878 pesos

For more information or to purchase tickets, visit Ticketmaster. You can also check out the Coro Gay Choir on Instagram.

Tierra Mágica Navidad brings medieval fantasy to Mexico City

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival de Brujas MX (@festival_de_brujas_mx)

Our next event roundup will focus more heavily on Christmas-themed events, but for now, we’ll start with something truly unique and quirky. If your idea of Christmas involves a little more magic, a touch of medieval fantasy and perhaps a masquerade ball, Tierra Mágica Navidad might just be the event for you.

The family-friendly Christmas festival will take over Doméstico in Colonia Hipódromo on Dec. 12 and 13, transforming the venue into a fantasy-inspired celebration that blends traditional holiday festivities with the atmosphere of an enchanted medieval kingdom.

It’s like “Game of Thrones,” but Bran Stark is a young Santa and Westeros is Mexico City.

Visitors are invited to don their finest medieval or fantasy-inspired garb for a weekend of music, magical characters and festive entertainment. Don’t forget your mask, though, as one of the event’s flagship activities is a themed masquerade ball and mask competition, allowing attendees to show off their most imaginative creations.

The festivities will also include a Christmas-themed bazaar full of seasonal offerings. With its combination of holiday traditions, fantasy-inspired characters and immersive activities, Tierra Mágica Navidad sounds to us like an unusual alternative to the capital’s more traditional Christmas celebrations, and a great way to start the season.

Date: Dec. 12 and 13, 11 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Location: Av. Nuevo León 80, Hipódromo, Cuauhtémoc, Ciudad de México

Cost: Free

For more information and to register your free spot, visit Tierra Mágica Navidad on Boletia.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Navy seizes more than a tonne of cocaine off the coasts of Chiapas and Oaxaca
World.content:
The Navy seized more than a tonne of suspected cocaine in two separate operations off Mexico’s southwestern coast.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch on Thursday confirmed on social media that the actions occurred off the coasts of Chiapas and Oaxaca, adding that one person was arrested.

According to an official statement, the operations took place during maritime patrol and surveillance in the Pacific Ocean.

In the first operation, naval personnel seized 16 packages containing approximately 629 kilograms of “a substance with characteristics similar to cocaine,” while in a second operation they located another 16 packages with around 520 kilograms.

The Navy reported that the weight of 1,149 kilograms includes the packaging and the actual weight of the narcotics will be confirmed by prosecutors.

The statement said that the economic impact for criminal groups is an estimated 273 million pesos (US $14.5 million). “Each seized shipment is a direct blow to the finances of organized crime: reducing their resources to buy weapons, corrupt and generate violence, and fewer drugs on the streets to poison our youth,” García Harfuch said.

Despite the volume of drugs confiscated, authorities reported the arrest of only one person. “The detainee was informed of his rights and placed at the disposal of the Federal Attorney General’s Office,” the statement said.

The latest operation is part of a series of actions carried out in recent months in the Pacific maritime corridor, specifically off the coasts of Chiapas, Oaxaca, Guerrero and Michoacán. Before it, more than 97 tonnes of cocaine had been seized at sea since Claudia Sheinbaum became president in October 2024.

In October, more than 1.2 tonnes of cocaine were seized and six crew members detained in international waters 366 nautical miles south of Huatulco, Oaxaca, in a joint operation with the U.S. Coast Guard.

In August, more than 4 tonnes of cocaine were seized and 13 people arrested during several Pacific operations off Oaxaca and Chiapas.

The ongoing operations are part of permanent maritime and aerial surveillance actions against international drug trafficking, one of the main issues of cooperation and tension in security matters with the United States.

With reports from Proceso, El Financiero and Aristegui Noticias

South Africa — coalition maths · slow count Tanzania — verdict day · held breath DR Congo — Ebola toll · vaccine hope Kenya — rubble · border strain Nigeria — court fights · campaign nerves

Africa woke on Friday to three crowds waiting at once: South Africans for coalition deals, Tanzanians for a judge, and Congolese and Kenyans for a clinic to hold the line. The mood across the continent is patient but tight-jawed, the feeling of a region that has done its part and is waiting for institutions to do theirs.

The register is formal and a little defensive. Officials explain their process before anyone has asked.

The through-line is trust being tested in public. Counting rooms, courtrooms and treatment tents are all being asked to look fair at the same time.

Key Facts —South Africa count. . —Turnout. . —Tanzania. The High Court in Dar es Salaam is due to rule on opposition leader Tundu Lissu’s treason charge today. —Ebola. DR Congo had 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths as of 4 November. —Activity. South Africa’s October business-activity index (PMI) came in at 49, below the 50.2 forecast.

South Africa: A Count That Feels Like A Verdict

South Africa spent Thursday watching a ruling party it once treated as permanent slide to about a third of the vote. The mood is less triumph than exhaustion with a tinge of defiance. For a US reader, the point is that coalition bargaining, not the ballot box, will now decide who runs the big cities.

Tanzania: A Country Waits On Three Judges

Today is the day a three-judge bench of the High Court in Dar es Salaam is due to rule on Tundu Lissu, chairman of the opposition party Chadema. He is charged with treason over remarks he allegedly made on 3 April 2025 urging Tanzanians to prevent the 2025 election, and the penalty can be death.

The tone in the country is hushed and watchful, with people reading every procedural sign. Lissu, who has represented himself, said the case has no substantive basis, and on 21 August the court ruled he had a case to answer.

Whatever the bench decides, the reasoning will tell opposition parties how far a court will tolerate political speech. Our edition went to press before any judgment was reported, so the outcome is unknown at this writing.

DR Congo And Kenya: Fear Learns Procedure

In DR Congo the mood is dread with no end date. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths in DR Congo as of 4 November.

Kenya carries a quieter anxiety, with nine confirmed cases including two deaths as of 26 October, and Nigeria identified its first case on 20 October. In Nairobi, rescuers have so far recovered two bodies from the Eastleigh building that collapsed on Friday 23 October, a reminder that public trust is also tested by builders and inspectors.

Sudan And Abyei: Drones Over Daily Life

Nigeria: A Race Fought In Courtrooms

Nigeria’s pre-2027 mood is suspicion about who is protecting whom and who is allowed to run. Atiku Abubakar, the former vice-president running for the African Democratic Congress (ADC), said on Tuesday 3 November that the DSS, Nigeria’s domestic intelligence service, was recruiting protesters to disrupt a rally in Sokoto.

What This Means From Latin America

For Brazil and its BRICS partners, a South Africa governed by unstable city coalitions is a harder place to plan investment. Brazilian firms that treat Johannesburg as a gateway will want to see who holds the keys by the end of November.

Latin American health ministries and airlines that link the two continents will watch the Ebola numbers in Kenya and Nigeria. Governments that argue over how courts treat opposition leaders will recognise the debates in Dar es Salaam and Abuja.

The common thread is that distant crises travel through trade, travel and politics. A reader in the United States can see in Africa’s week a test of the same institutions that carry arguments at home.

The through-line from Latin America is a shared question about whether public trust can survive pressure. The answer will arrive slowly, and both regions will be watching.

Coalition bargaining will now decide who runs the big cities. The count was still under way when we wrote this.

The High Court in Dar es Salaam is due to rule on opposition leader Tundu Lissu’s treason charge. A conviction can carry the death penalty.

World.title: Kenya Jails Preacher Mackenzie for 200 Years
World.content:
The old Law Courts building on Nkrumah Road in Mombasa, now a gallery; the verdict was read at the city's current law courts. File photo, 2012. (Photo: Alex Wafula, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

KENYA · COURTS

Key Facts The sentence Kenya’s High Court, its senior trial court, in Mombasa jailed preacher Paul Mackenzie for 200 years on Friday 6 November 2026.

The crime He was convicted on 19 October 2026 of 191 murders, including 190 children, in Shakahola, a forest area in Kilifi County.

The limit Prosecutors asked for the death penalty, but the court did not impose it.

The others His 28 co-accused were sentenced alongside him; their terms are not yet fully reported.

A Kenyan court has sentenced Paul Mackenzie, a preacher who told followers to starve themselves to “meet Jesus”, to 200 years in prison. Justice Diana Kavedza of the High Court in Mombasa, Kenya’s main Indian Ocean port city, handed down the sentence on Friday 6 November 2026.

For US readers, the Paul Mackenzie sentence ends the first trial over a cult tragedy that shocked Kenya. Our earlier report on the guilty verdict explains how the case reached this point.

What Happened

Mackenzie, who led a church called Good News International Ministries, was convicted on Monday 19 October 2026 of 191 murders. The court found that he directed followers to fast to death, that children were targeted first, and that the fasting was enforced through religious indoctrination, intimidation and violence.

Mackenzie and 28 co-accused appeared in the Mombasa High Court on Friday morning to hear their sentences. The judge ordered a total of 200 years for Mackenzie, which is two 100-year terms served one after the other.

Prosecutors from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Kenya’s state prosecution service, had asked for the death penalty. The court did not impose it,.

The Paul Mackenzie Sentence Explained

A 200-year term is far longer than any lifetime, so the figure is largely symbolic. Whether Mackenzie can ever apply for early release is not stated in the public reports.

The two terms cover the starvation deaths and a smaller set of direct killings, according to the court’s reasoning as reported. Mackenzie’s 28 co-accused were sentenced in the same hearing, with each term reflecting the person’s role and level of involvement.

Their individual terms are not yet confirmed.

How Shakahola Became a Crime Scene

Shakahola is a stretch of bush in Kilifi County on Kenya’s coast, where Mackenzie’s followers settled and fasted. Investigators recovered more than 400 bodies from graves in the area.

The murder trial covered 191 of those deaths, and 190 of the victims were children. Other offences linked to Shakahola are handled separately from these convictions.

What It Means for You

The ruling is a criminal case, so it sets no new rules for visitors or investors in Kenya. Travellers to the coast should know that Shakahola is an inland forest area, not one of the beach resorts.

Readers in the United States who follow religious freedom and cult cases will see a Kenyan court rule on punishment for a religious leader. In this case the High Court treated forced religious fasting as murder, not as protected belief.

What Is Not Known

The individual sentences of the 28 co-accused are not yet confirmed in the public record we could check. It is also unclear whether Mackenzie or his co-accused will appeal, and whether any victims remain unaccounted for.

Where every victim lies is also not settled.

More: Kenya news in English, every day from The Rio Times. See also our guide to religion in Kenya.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Paul Mackenzie?

He is a Kenyan preacher who founded Good News International Ministries. The High Court in Mombasa convicted him on 19 October 2026 of 191 murders.

How Long Is the Sentence?

The court sentenced him to a total of 200 years in prison on Friday 6 November 2026. Prosecutors asked for the death penalty, which the judge did not impose.

Where Is Shakahola?

Shakahola is a forest area in Kilifi County on Kenya’s coast. Investigators recovered more than 400 bodies there.

What Happens to the Co-Accused?

Twenty-eight co-accused were sentenced in the same hearing, with terms based on their roles. Their individual terms are not yet fully reported.

Weather in Rio in November

Brazil’s national weather institute, INMET, and the city’s Alerta Rio service publish the official forecasts and storm alerts. No alert for the coming days was confirmed at the source on Tuesday 3 November 2026.

Afternoon storms are common in Rio as spring turns to summer, so plan beach hours for the morning. Forecasts change daily, so check both services before outdoor events.

This Week in Rio: 6 to 8 November

CASACOR Rio, an interior design show in its 35th year, fills the Aliança da Bahia building in Centro until Sunday 8 November. Tickets cost 120 reais (about US$22), or 60 reais (about US$11) half price; it opens Tuesday to Sunday, noon to 8pm.

The fifth Festival Gastronomia Sem Fronteiras fills the rooftop of the Fashion Mall shopping centre, Estrada da Gávea 899 in São Conrado, on Saturday 7 and Sunday 8 November, from 1pm to 11pm. Kitchens from Germany (Herr Pfeffer), Italy (Babbo), Portugal (Barsa), Japan (Jappa da Quitanda) and France (the Franco-Brazilian chefs’ association led by Frédéric Monnier) cook beside Rio’s São Miguel and QuiQui, with a market of producers from Rio de Janeiro state and cooking classes by the Senac RJ school.

The band Últimos and Rodrigo Santos play the Sesc stage on Saturday, and rock singer Paulo Ricardo closes the festival on Sunday with his voice-and-guitar show “Voz, Violão e Rock’n’Roll”. First-batch tickets cost 40 reais (about US$7), or 20 reais (about US$4) half price, and rise as batches sell; children up to 10 enter free, and food and drink are paid separately.

“Tom na Fazenda” (“Tom at the Farm”), an award-winning stage drama adapted from a play by Canadian writer Michel Marc Bouchard, plays the Teatro da Ilha on Ilha do Governador, the large island in Guanabara Bay that holds Rio’s international airport, on Friday 6 and Saturday 7 November at 8pm. It is the first time the touring production, starring Armando Babaioff and directed by Rodrigo Portella, stops on the island; the dialogue is in Portuguese, and ticket prices are available from the venue.

Jazz dos Muertos, a new weekly jazz series, opened at La Esquina in Lapa, the old-town nightlife district, on Thursday 5 November with Sergio Diab Stratoman’s “Western Latino” show, joined by guests Marcos Suzano and Humberto Barros. The Guilherme Dias Gomes Quartet plays on Friday 6 November at 8pm, and the series mixes Latin jazz, bossa nova, samba jazz and soul; ticket prices are available from the venue.

The Bossa Nova Sessions festival enters its final week at the Teatro Café Pequeno in Leblon and runs until Sunday 8 November. Cellist Aleska Chediak honours her father, the guitarist Almir Chediak, with her trio on Friday 6 November; ticket prices are available from the venue.

Pianist Osmar Milito, a jazz and bossa nova figure who died in 2024, is remembered in “Saudades de Osmar Milito” at Acaso Cultural in Botafogo on Sunday 8 November at 6.30pm. The Augusto Mattoso Trio, with Cliff Korman on piano and Xande Figueiredo on drums, plays his arrangements; ticket prices are available from the venue.

“Cordélia Brasil”, a tragicomedy by Antonio Bivár about a woman who carries the care of her household, runs at the Teatro Glauce Rocha in Centro on Thursdays at 7pm: 5, 12, 19 and 26 November. João Fonseca directs and Paula Goja plays the title role; the dialogue is in Portuguese, and ticket prices are available from the venue.

“Embarcação Perdue”, a stage comedy-drama about a mysterious expedition searching for what was lost in life, opened on Thursday 5 November at the Teatro Glaucio Gil in Copacabana. It runs Wednesday to Friday at 8pm until 27 November; the dialogue is in Portuguese, and ticket prices are available from the venue.

Bar Bukowski, a rock bar in Botafogo, holds a cliché-themed party on Friday 6 November from 7pm at Rua Álvaro Ramos 270. Singer Lunna Noug and the band Perdidos na Selva play rock classics, with two dance floors, DJs and karaoke; entry costs 39.90 reais (about US$7) at the door, including a free drink until 10pm.

Vasco da Gama host Palmeiras in the Copa do Brasil semi-final second leg on Sunday 8 November, planned for São Januário.

Concerts and Opera: 9 to 22 November

Turandot, Puccini’s last opera, plays the Theatro Municipal at 7pm on 13, 14, 18, 20 and 21 November. A school matinee is on 17 November at 2pm.

Individual Turandot tickets run from 20 reais (about US$4) in the gallery to 90 reais (about US$17) in the boxes. The Gilsons, a family trio, play Vivo Rio with Gilberto Gil as special guest on Friday 13 November at 9pm.

Half-price Gilsons seats start at 160 reais (about US$30) and full price at 320 reais (about US$59). The venue says last tickets remain.

Singer-songwriter Naiara Martins, a Jabuti Prize nominee (Brazil’s main book award), debuts her show “Terras do Sem-Fim” at the Dolores Club in Lapa on Thursday 12 November at 8.30pm. The programme blends bossa nova and samba with classics by Gilberto Gil, Baden Powell and Marcos Valle; ticket prices are available from the venue.

The Associação de Canto Coral, a Rio choral society, marks its 85th year with a concert of José Maurício Nunes Garcia’s Missa de Santa Cecília on 12 November and again on 22 November; the venue and times were not confirmed, so check with the society.

Country singer Simone Mendes brings her show “Intimidade” to Rio for the first time at Qualistage on Saturday 14 November at 10pm (doors open 8pm), with seated tables; tickets start at 130 reais (about US$24).

Mariah Carey brings her Christmas show to the Farmasi Arena’s outdoor area in Barra da Tijuca on Saturday 21 November. Standing-floor tickets cost 247.50 reais (about US$46) half price and 495 reais (about US$91) full price, with gates at 4pm.

Seal, with Seu Jorge opening, plays Qualistage in Barra on Thursday 26 November. Seated tickets start at 197.50 reais (about US$36) half price and 395 reais (about US$73) full price.

The 31st Rio Pride parade, the Parada do Orgulho LGBTI+, takes over the Copacabana seafront on Sunday 22 November. Organisers had not published a start time at the time of writing.

O Grande Encontro (“The Great Meeting”), a night of Umbanda music, fills Qualistage on Sunday 22 November. Umbanda is an Afro-Brazilian religion, and the singers Sandro Luiz and Tião Casemiro play with guests Leci Brandão and Luan Pureza as part of Black Consciousness celebrations; prices were not confirmed, so check the ticket seller.

Free Things to Do in Rio in November

The Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, a downtown arts centre, shows the Amazônicas exhibition free until Monday 16 November. It opens Wednesday to Monday, 9am to 8pm, and free tickets are online or at its box office.

The Theatro Municipal also runs a free midday opera series, Ópera do Meio-Dia. Its November dates were not confirmed on 3 November, so check the theatre.

Late November: Bethânia, Clássicos do Brasil and Sailing

The Festival Clássicos do Brasil fills the Marina da Glória on Saturday 28 November from 5pm and Sunday 29 November from 3pm. Saturday brings Maria Bethânia, Alceu Valença and Vanessa da Mata, and Sunday brings Alexandre Pires, Péricles and Ferrugem.

Tickets start at 120 reais (about US$22) on the festival’s own site. The festival returns on 5 and 6 December, and no line-up has been published for those dates.

Holidays, Money and Getting Around

Sunday 15 November, Proclamation of the Republic Day, falls on a weekend and gives no extra day off. Friday 20 November is Black Consciousness Day, a national holiday, and banks and public offices close.

The Banco Central do Brasil dollar rate was 5.4212 reais on Friday 30 October, so 100 reais is about US$18. Half-price tickets, the legal meia-entrada, go to students, people over 60 and others with ID.

What It Means for You

For US visitors, the busiest weekend is 20 to 22 November, when a holiday, Mariah Carey and Pride overlap. Book hotels early; the dollar has bought more reais since the 25 October runoff.

Buy tickets only from the venue or its named ticket seller. Carry photo ID, and keep a rain plan for afternoons.

What to Watch Next

Watch Friday 13 November for the Turandot premiere and the Gilsons concert, then Friday 20 November for the holiday. The Pride start time and the December Clássicos line-ups are still to be confirmed.

The central bank publishes a new dollar rate each business day, and this guide returns in December. Football dates for rounds 35 to 37, between 18 and 28 November, are not yet fixed.

What Is Not Known

Organisers had not published a Pride start time or the Ópera do Meio-Dia dates. The theatre site could not be opened on 3 November, so Turandot prices rest on published listings.

Gilberto Gil’s own site does not list the Vivo Rio date, which rests on the venue’s listing. The ticket seller shows 198 to 396 reais (about US$37 to US$73) with fees.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the holidays in Rio in November 2026?

Sunday 15 November (Proclamation of the Republic) and Friday 20 November (Black Consciousness Day) remain; Monday 2 November was All Souls’ Day. Banks and offices close on the 20th.

What are the best things to do in Rio in November?

The top picks are Turandot at the Theatro Municipal from 13 November and Gilberto Gil at Vivo Rio on 13 November. Pride on 22 November and the Clássicos do Brasil festival on 28 and 29 November follow.

What is free to do in Rio in November?

The Amazônicas exhibition at the Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil is free until 16 November. The Theatro Municipal also runs a free midday opera series; check its dates.

What is the weather in Rio in November?

Warm and humid, with afternoon storms common as spring turns to summer. Check INMET and Alerta Rio for the daily forecast and storm alerts.

Sources: Banco Central do Brasil (dollar rate, 30 October 2026); INMET, Brazil’s national weather institute (alerts); Riotur, Rio city tourism agency (Clássicos do Brasil); Vivo Rio concert hall (Gilsons with Gilberto Gil) (all accessed 3 November 2026).

World.title: Argentina Jobless Rate Rises to 7.9%
World.content:
The Casa Rosada, seat of Argentina's presidency, seen from Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires. File photo, 2018. (Photo: Rod85daido, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ARGENTINA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Argentina, a major South American economy, is led by libertarian President Javier Milei.

The rate Urban unemployment was 7.9% in April–June, from 7.6% a year earlier.

State jobs Federal payrolls fell to 266,205 people in September, down 6.1% in a year.

Next dates State headcount on Monday 30 November; the next jobless figure on Friday 18 December 2026.

Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 60.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Argentina’s jobless rate climbed to 7.9% in the second quarter of 2026, while the national government keeps shrinking its own payroll. INDEC, the country’s statistics office, counted about 1.2 million jobless people in the 31 urban areas it surveys between April and June.

For US readers, the numbers show a labour market under strain while President Javier Milei’s government trims its own payroll and relies on an International Monetary Fund (IMF) rescue programme. Investors who hold Argentine bonds or US-listed Argentine shares watch jobs because weak jobs can test public support for reforms.

What the Jobs Survey Shows

INDEC reported in September 2026 that 7.9% of people in the labour force in the 31 urban areas it surveys had no job but were looking for one. The rate was 7.6% in the second quarter of 2025, 6.6% in the third quarter, 7.5% in the fourth and 7.8% in the first quarter of 2026.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

INDEC calls the change from a year earlier statistically insignificant, which means it could be survey noise. In the interior cities, outside Greater Buenos Aires (the capital’s metropolitan area), unemployment rose 1.3 points in a year to 7.6%, a rise INDEC calls statistically significant, though the rate is still below Greater Buenos Aires at 8.2%.

The quality of work also slipped, as informal jobs, where workers pay no pension contributions or tax registration, made up 45.0% of employment, 1.0 point more than a year earlier. About 13.6 million people had a job in INDEC’s count.

How Many State Jobs Have Gone

INDEC published its monthly headcount of federal workers on Friday 30 October 2026. It counted 266,205 people at the end of September, 0.8% fewer than in August and 6.1% fewer than a year earlier.

The national public administration, meaning ministries and agencies, employed 179,396 people, which is 7.2% fewer than a year earlier. State-run companies and firms with state stakes employed 86,809, down 3.8%.

INDEC’s August count was 268,404 people. September’s loss of about 2,200 people shows the cuts continue, but slowly.

INDEC said 13 state bodies, 12 state companies and one agency, had not reported their staff numbers, so it carried forward their last figures for 7,598 people, or 2.9% of the total. That adds some uncertainty to the latest monthly figure.

Do the Cuts Explain the Jobless Rate?

Probably not much, and INDEC draws no link. The yearly loss of about 17,000 federal jobs is small next to 1.2 million jobless people, so the cuts alone cannot explain the rate.

Provincial and city governments are not in INDEC’s federal count, and private firms also shape the survey. INDEC says the employment rate (45.0%) did not change significantly, while the activity rate, the share of people working or looking for work, rose 0.8 points to 48.9%.

Milei’s Reforms and the IMF

Milei came to office in December 2023 promising to shrink the state and cut the budget deficit. IMF staff and Argentina reached a staff-level agreement on the third review of the four-year loan programme on Tuesday 27 October 2026, covering about US$900 million.

The IMF’s executive board is due to consider it in early December, and the deal keeps a 2026 primary surplus target of 1.4% of output, meaning the budget before interest must show a surplus. Staff-level agreements are not final until the board votes.

What It Means for You

If you own Argentine bonds, watch whether jobless numbers stay near 8% while inflation keeps falling, because that mix tests public patience. Our note on Argentina’s 1.9% September inflation shows the price side of the same story.

Travelers and expats are unlikely to see a direct effect, though strikes in the public sector can disrupt services such as airports and offices. US firms with Argentine staff should watch the 18 December figure for signs of easing hiring pressure.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how many jobs the provinces and cities have cut, because INDEC’s headcount covers only the federal government. It is also unclear how much of the 7.9% rate comes from people entering the job market rather than people losing jobs.

INDEC has not yet released the July to September survey, so any claim about a third-quarter trend is a guess. The next releases will show whether the pace of cuts and the jobless rate move together.

What to Watch

INDEC lists the October federal headcount for Monday 30 November 2026. It lists the July to September jobs survey for Friday 18 December 2026, when a financial-data calendar forecasts 7.8%.

Before that, INDEC publishes October inflation on Thursday 12 November 2026, with a financial-data calendar forecasting 2.2% after 1.9% in September. The IMF board decision is expected in early December.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Argentina’s Unemployment Rate?

INDEC measured 7.9% for April to June 2026, with about 1.2 million people jobless. The survey covers 31 urban areas and is published quarterly.

Is the Job Cut Causing Higher Unemployment?

INDEC does not draw that link, and it calls the yearly change in unemployment not statistically significant. The 17,000 federal jobs lost over the year are small next to 1.2 million jobless people.

When Is the Next Unemployment Figure?

INDEC lists the July to September survey for Friday 18 December 2026. A financial-data calendar forecasts 7.8%, against 7.9% now.

World.content:

EGYPT · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Egypt, the Arab world’s most populous nation, is a major wheat importer and Suez Canal host.

The figure Nationwide yearly inflation slowed to 12.0% in October 2026 from 12.8% in September.

City prices In cities, yearly inflation fell to 12.7% from 13.9%, while monthly prices rose 0.7%.

The squeeze Housing and utilities cost 24.1% more than a year ago, and transport 22.3% more.

Next step The central bank lifted its main bank-deposit rate to 20% on Thursday 29 October 2026.

Egypt’s yearly inflation slowed to 12.0% in October 2026, down from 12.8% in September, yet shoppers still paid more each month. CAPMAS, the national statistics agency, published the figures on Thursday 5 November 2026.

For US readers, the cooling matters because Egypt is a big importer of wheat and a gateway for Suez Canal trade. Lower inflation could open the door to cheaper money, but the central bank has just done the opposite, as our report on Egypt’s rate rise to 20% shows.

What Happened

CAPMAS said nationwide yearly inflation, covering cities and villages, eased to 12.0% in October from 12.8% in September. The consumer price index rose 0.6% from September to reach 296.1 points.

In urban areas, the rate fell to 12.7% from 13.9%, and prices rose 0.7% in the month against 1.3% in September. Urban inflation has now slowed for a second straight month.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where Prices Still Hurt

Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuel cost 24.1% more than a year earlier, the biggest rise among the main groups. Transport rose 22.3%, and education 20.0%.

Food prices rose 0.8% in the month because meat and poultry cost more. Fruit fell 2.9% and vegetables 2.6%.

Why the Central Bank Still Raised Rates

The Central Bank of Egypt raised its main bank-deposit rate, the overnight deposit rate, by 1 point to 20% on Thursday 29 October 2026, a week before this data. It said a regional conflict lasting longer than expected adds uncertainty and could push up energy and commodity prices, feeding imported inflation.

The move adds costs for the budget, as our note on the US$2.7 billion budget cost of the hike explains. Falling inflation gives the bank room to ease later, but only if prices keep cooling.

What It Means for You

If you hold Egyptian pound bonds, a 20% deposit rate against 12.0% inflation leaves a wide real return, which is the gain after prices. The central bank’s cushion of foreign currency reserves is covered in our separate report.

Rents, housing and transport are rising fastest for residents, which hits household budgets first. US companies selling to Egyptian customers should expect careful household spending while housing and fuel costs stay high.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the slowdown will last, because monthly prices are still rising at 0.6% and fuel or rent changes could lift them. The central bank has not said when it might cut rates again.

The official release does not tell us how much of the fall comes from last year’s high base, meaning last year’s price jumps dropping out of the comparison. CAPMAS will publish November’s figures in the coming weeks.

More: Egypt news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Egypt’s Inflation Rate?

Egypt’s statistics agency, CAPMAS, reported nationwide yearly inflation of 12.0% for October 2026. In cities the rate was 12.7%.

Why Is Egypt Inflation Falling?

Urban prices rose 0.7% in October against 1.3% in September, so monthly increases are smaller. Housing and transport remain the costliest items.

Did Egypt Raise Interest Rates?

Yes, the Central Bank of Egypt raised its overnight deposit rate by 1 point to 20% on Thursday 29 October 2026. It cited a prolonged regional conflict and higher energy and commodity prices.

What Does Egyptian Inflation Mean for US Investors?

Slower inflation reduces pressure on the Egyptian pound and bonds, but the rate hike shows the central bank is cautious. Egypt is also a key Suez Canal and wheat-trade country.

Sources: CAPMAS, Egypt’s Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics, consumer price index for October 2026, 5 November 2026; Central Bank of Egypt, Monetary Policy Committee statement, 29 October 2026.
