World.title: Bleeding billions
World.content:
In this file photo rescue crew and civilians are at a fatal crash scene in rural Jamaica.

THE Island Traffic Authority (ITA) has estimated the economic cost of road fatalities in Jamaica for 2025 was US$72 million (approximately $11.5 billion).

The estimate factors in the number of crash victims, their age at the time they died in a fatal crash, and their projected earnings if they had lived to retirement age.

According to the annual crash report, released this week by the ITA, the US$72 million was an increase of approximately US$4 million when compared to 2024 based on an increase in the number of lives lost last year.

“This underscores that road safety is not only a public health issue but also a critical economic concern,” the ITA said.

The report notes that 374 people lost their lives in 325 fatal crashes in 2025, a two per cent increase in fatalities and a three per cent increase in fatal crashes when compared to 2024.

Despite the increase, the ITA remains optimistic that things are trending in the right direction.

“Although the road-related deaths were slightly higher in 2025, it marks the second-consecutive year in which fatalities fell below the 400 mark,” said the authority

“The reduction signifies a noteworthy stride toward national and global road safety targets, and offers an opportunity for reflection, recalibration, and momentum-building,” the ITA added.

It noted that Jamaica‘s goal is to meet the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety (2020-2030) target, which is to reduce the tally of road fatalities that occurred in 2020 by half.

“Jamaica‘s current progress towards this target is a reduction of 14 per cent. To meet the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety (2020-2030) target Jamaica‘s road fatalities on average must be reduced by 8.3 per cent per annum,” said the ITA.

The report shows that St Catherine was the deadliest parish for road users in 2025 with 65 deaths.

St Ann came next with 36, followed by St Elizabeth with 34, St James 32, and Westmoreland 31.

St Andrew recorded 29 fatalities during the year, Clarendon had 26, Hanover and St Mary had 22 each.

They are followed by Trelawny and Manchester, which each recorded 20 deaths. The three safest parishes for road users last year were Portland with nine deaths, St Thomas with 11, and Kingston with 17.

As to what is driving the high number of crashes and fatalities, the ITA stated that “the majority of traffic crashes are rooted in driver behaviour, with excessive speed remaining the most dominant cause”.

Last year 114 fatal crashes were attributed to speeding — continuing a trend over the last six years. This was followed by failure to keep to the correct traffic lane with 68 crashes; pedestrians walking or standing in the road led to 26 crashes; turning to the right without due care saw 13 crashes; and overtaking improperly on the offside resulted in 31 crashes.

“These leading causes suggest a combination of aggressive driving and poor road discipline,” said the ITA, as it pointed out that the category “Others” represents the combined total of various other causes of road fatalities, accounting for 122 deaths in 2025.

The ITA said understanding the demographic composition and timing of fatal road crashes is crucial for developing targeted, equitable, and impactful road safety policies.

The data from 2020 to 2025 reveal persistent and concerning patterns regarding gender and age.

Worryingly, road traffic fatalities continue to be overwhelmingly male-dominated. In 2025, males accounted for 85 per cent of all traffic deaths (318 of 374), while females accounted for 15 per cent.

“The data reinforces that, while road safety strategies must address the general population, men — especially younger and middle-aged males — should be a primary focus for targeted road safety initiatives,” said ITA.

The data also pointed to age-based analysis which reveals another layer of vulnerability.

In 2025, the 25-29 and 30-34 age groups recorded 48 deaths each, accounting for 26 per cent of the total number of fatalities.

“Individuals aged 20-60 years constitute the core of Jamaica’s workforce [and accounted] for 223 fatalities in 2025, representing a substantial economic loss to the country in terms of productivity and labour force capacity,” the ITA noted.

Meanwhile, the elderly, aged 60 and above, recorded 71 deaths, an 82 per cent increase compared to 2024.

The ITA said understanding when fatal crashes are most likely to occur is critical for effective road safety planning.

It said the analysis of crash distribution across time — by month and day of the week — and road user category provide patterns that can point to potential behavioural and temporal risk factors.

Over the past five years, the first quarter of the year (January to March) has consistently recorded high fatality numbers. However, in 2025, the third quarter reported the highest number of fatalities (106 deaths).

The traditionally high-risk, mid-year months — July and August — saw a resurgence in 2025, with July recording the highest total crashes for the year (39 deaths). November recorded the least number of deaths in 2025 (24).

In terms of day of the week, the data show that weekends remain disproportionately dangerous.

The ITA said Saturdays and Sundays consistently record the highest number of crashes and fatalities. In 2025, Sundays recorded 58 crashes and 74 deaths, while Saturdays accounted for 52 crashes and 64 deaths.

“These figures reflect persistent risks associated with weekend travel, which is typically characterised by leisure driving, night-time events, increased alcohol consumption, and higher traffic volumes and more varied traffic patterns associated with non-work activities,” added the ITA.

Christmas Day emerged as the most dangerous holiday over the six-year period, recording the highest number of fatal crashes (17) and fatalities (19).

This is followed by New Year’s Day (13 deaths) and Independence Day (12 deaths).

“The data indicate that festive holidays tend to be associated with increased road traffic fatalities, likely due to higher traffic volumes, longer travel distances, and celebratory activities,” the ITA noted.

World.title: Detective recounts gun find
World.content:
The Supreme Court in downtown Kingston where 25 alleged members of the Tesha Miller-led faction of the Klansman Gang are being tried.

A Clarendon police detective testified Thursday that he discovered two firearms hidden in a vehicle driven by former Jamaica Urban Transit Company (JUTC) bus driver Charles McLeary, one of 25 men on trial for crimes allegedly committed by the reputed Tesha Miller faction of the Klansman Gang.

That motor vehicle, a 2011 Honda Stream, was one of two seized by investigators after the takedown of five alleged members of the gang on Friday, June 26, 2020.

According to prosecutors, the accused — Bjourn Thomas, Sharn Gilzene, Conroy Cadogan, McLeary, and Kemar Francis — “knowingly facilitated the commission of a serious offence to wit the murder of Jermaine Jones and Allen Cameron” in John’s Hall, Clarendon, that same day. They were taken into custody following a highway chase.

The detective sergeant, testifying during the ongoing trial which has been unfolding in the Home Circuit Division of the Supreme Court in downtown Kingston, told the court that he went to the May Pen Police Station on Sunday, June 28, where he was introduced to McLeary, who was then 40 years old and a resident of Portmore, St Catherine; and Thomas, who was unemployed and a resident of Spanish Town.

He said after being introduced to the two, he went to the two motor vehicles

— which had been sealed with evidence tape

— that were parked on the compound accompanied by three other cops and the two accused. According to the cop, who said he only searched one of the two cars, under the direct gaze of McLeary and the others, after partially detaching the glove compartment of the vehicle and looking further into the cavity of the dashboard in a section of the air conditioner’s air filter, he saw “what looked like the base of a magazine and a pistol with a grip”.

The sleuth said he “shouted out ‘Find!’” when he made the discovery and pointed to where he observed the objects. He said after ensuring that McLeary not only saw but verbalised what was found, two forensic scene of crime investigators who were present photographed the silver and black 9mm Beretta pistol with the magazine affixed and packaged it. He told the court, under further questioning by the prosecutor marshalling the evidence, that in continuing his search he checked the gear lever section of the car by removing an area closer to the flooring of the vehicle and observed what looked like the pistol grip of a firearm.

He said the weapon, which was removed, shown to McLeary, and photographed by the forensic crime scene experts, turned out to be a black Smith & Wesson Springfield .40 calibre pistol with a magazine affixed. That pistol, he said, along with ammunition, was also packaged. The cop said, a further search of the vehicle turned up a pair of shoes in the trunk which McLeary claimed as his.

Asked by the prosecutor eliciting the evidence if he would be able to identify McLeary again if he saw him, the detective sergeant answered confidently in the affirmative. He was only allowed to do so, however, after the docks were reshuffled in his absence following a request from McLeary’s attorney Javed Grant.

Interestingly, 15 of the 17 accused who were in the main dock held their heads down from the moment the lawman entered and throughout his entire testimony, only sitting upright after trial judge Justice Dale Palmer instructed that they do so for the identification.

The lawman, who returned to the courtroom following the reshuffle, despite several intense moments spent looking at the 25 accused row by row, incorrectly identified the accused Shawn Pottinger as McLeary, sending a ripple of murmurs across the room. The Crown, at that point, indicated that it had no further questions for the cop but would be recalling him in relation to items it intends to tender.

Following the failed identification, Grant, in cross-examining the cop, accused him of lying about his observation of the serial number on one of the pistols. According to the cop, he had not touched the firearm but based on his proximity to the scenes of crime officer who retrieved it, had been able to view the number.

“I am suggesting to you that you are lying when you say you observed the serial number while the forensic officers handled it,” Grant challenged.

“I totally reject that suggestion,” the cop shot back.

The 25 accused — the second faction of the gang to now be tried by the courts — are to answer to 16 offences allegedly committed over the span of five years between August 2017 and November 2022, according to the case being built by the Crown.

In the matter which began in February this year, the prosecution in unveiling what it said was the “anatomy” of the gang, said it would be leading evidence to show that members acted as drivers, among them Thomas and Francis, along with the accused Dwayne Frater, and Travis Drummond. It said it would establish that McLeary was linked by employment and by role in the criminal organisation.

World.title: Shenseea finds freedom in growth
World.content:
Shenseea’s latest EP, Catalyst, will be released on Friday, November 5.

“I feel like it’s better to be judged than not experience something at all,” said international recording artiste Shenseea.

For her, those words represent more than a change in perspective. They capture a personal turning point, one that required her to confront the things she had kept buried. It is this willingness to let go, to embrace the uncomfortable, and allow listeners access to a more unguarded side of her, that gives her latest EP, Catalyst, its emotional centre.

The eight-track project, which will be released today, Friday, November 6, finds the artiste reflecting on how far she has travelled, while making room for the woman she is still becoming.

Rather than abandoning the sounds and personality that first endeared her to audiences, Shenseea sees the release as an opportunity to reconnect with those foundations while moving confidently into another phase of her career.

At the heart of that journey is Vulnerability, a deeply personal offering that she describes as one of the most creatively fulfilling songs she has recorded.

“Vulnerability is the one song I really felt like I was putting it all out there on, for sure. It’s definitely in my top five of most creative songs ever, because it’s my most vulnerable song. Of all the records that I’ve put out, you’ve never heard me sing like that before, or say the stuff that I’m saying. It came straight from the heart,” she told the Jamaica Observer’s Splash.

For an artiste accustomed to commanding attention through her confident delivery and larger-than-life performances, allowing that level of emotional exposure was not necessarily an easy decision. However, she had reached a point at which keeping her thoughts and experiences to herself was beginning to take a toll on her creativity. There were things she wanted to communicate to her audience, experiences she wanted to put into context, and parts of her story she felt had remained misunderstood. Yet, in trying to keep those feelings contained, she was inadvertently creating a barrier between herself and the music.

“I had so much on my mind, so much I wanted to say to the people, letting them know what went down, giving them behind-the-scenes of why things are happening, and why I am how I am. I was holding it in and mi just couldn’t focus creatively. It was draining the life out of me. I couldn’t get to put it in my music and I couldn’t have fun with the music because I was so bothered personally,” she explained.

Eventually, she realised that the freedom she needed could only come from laying it all out on a track.

“I had to put it out there just to clear up myself and, honestly, ever since I released that track I feel so liberated and free,” she said.

The response from listeners further affirmed her decision, with many recognising the significance of seeing an otherwise guarded side of the artiste.

“I think people really took from it that, ‘Wow, she really let it all out,’ and that’s what it was made for,” she added.

That sense of liberation is central to the thinking behind Catalyst, whose title reflects Shenseea’s recognition that meaningful growth cannot be rushed.

Looking back at the earlier stages of her career, she acknowledges that her ambition sometimes made her eager to reach the destination without fully appreciating the experiences required to get there. Knowing the heights she wanted to achieve, she admits that she sometimes overlooked the importance of the journey itself.

“Earlier on in my career, there is a lesson I learnt. It’s that you cannot change from point A to Z without going through the rest of the alphabet, and I feel like I took that leap,” she said. “Being young and in the industry and knowing where I wanted to go, it was like I didn’t remember that I couldn’t do it all at once. That’s what helped me to make Catalyst, because I felt like I needed to take those steps that I felt like I stepped over.

“I felt like I missed some steps and Catalyst is me trying to make the smoothest transition into a new phase without changing me entirely,” she added.

It is a perspective that speaks to an artiste who is increasingly comfortable with the idea that evolution does not require abandoning one’s identity. Having explored different sounds and audiences throughout her career, Shenseea is now interested in bringing the different chapters of her musical journey into conversation with each other.

“The version of me that you’re getting on this EP is the Shenyeng Anthem mixed with Lighter Shenseea. Mi feel like it’s going to show where I’m coming from, you’ll feel the nostalgia. It’s also going to show where we are currently, and where we’re headed,” she said.

That connection to her beginnings is particularly important as she reflects on her personal growth; personally and artistically.

“Everything that I have said to myself that this is how I see myself in the future at this age, doing this, singing this, at this level, I am doing it right now,” she said. “So every other thing that I wanna accomplish is literally just for young Shenseea before the artistry begun. Just me listening to the music and deciding I wanted to become an international superstar. I am very proud of myself.”

The journey, however, has not been without its difficult moments. Shenseea acknowledged experiencing a period of depression that was unfamiliar to her and left her questioning herself in ways she had not previously experienced. With the help of God, and those around her, she said she was able to navigate that chapter and arrive at a place of greater contentment.

“This is how I felt when I just started out and this is why this project is so important to me. I feel like I’m starting over, but phase two,” she explained.

That renewed outlook has also influenced her relationship with music itself. While the pursuit of international recognition and industry accolades formed part of the ambition that propelled her forward, she is now placing greater emphasis on the simple pleasure of creating.

“I really had to bring back some stuff that makes me feel like I have to go hard, and that includes doing music for the love and not just for a submission or accolades. The music I am doing now is because I literally have fun doing them, I am in love with them, and I want to share them with the world,” she said.

The shift comes alongside another chapter in her professional journey, following a change in management as she continues to navigate the demands of an international career. For Shenseea, the transition is another reminder that growth sometimes requires accepting that certain people and circumstances are only meant to accompany you for a portion of the journey.

“I feel like nothing happens before its time, and one thing I had to sit with is that not everyone who started the journey with you, is meant to finish it with you,” she told Splash. “Stuff happens along the way and you can either decide to be like this is it, or you choose something or someone who will help you carry on your journey further. I feel like everything is just God. His timing is so impeccable, and I can’t argue with that. I have the drive in me to keep going and that’s what I’m going to do.”

Catalyst is now available for streaming across all digital platforms.

World.title: WE’VE GOT THIS!
World.content:
Head coach Sasher-Gaye Henry-Wright (second left) instructs Jamaica’s senior Sunshine Girls during a practice match against an All-Star Mixed Team at National Indoor Sports Centre on December 5, 2025. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

JAMAICA Netball Head Coach Sasher-Gaye Henry-Wright says the return of senior players, led by co-captain Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard, has lifted spirits in the camp as the Sunshine Girls prepare for the four-match Horizon Series against England Roses.

The series represents the final scheduled major assignment for the Sunshine Girls before the 2027 Netball World Cup.

The team leaves for England on November 14, ahead of the first two encounters at the Copper Box Arena in London on November 21 and 22. The series then returns home for the final two matches at the National Indoor Sports Centre (NISC) in St Andrew on December 5 and 6.

Contested in honour of netball icons Jamaica’s Molly Rhone and England’s Jean Hornsby, the Horizon Series has quickly developed into a keen rivalry since its inception in 2024.

The inaugural series produced a classic, with Jamaica claiming a 2-1 victory after one match was tied, underlining the evenly matched nature of the two sides.

Last year, England ran out 2-0 winners after both matches in Jamaica were cancelled due to the devastating passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, leaving unfinished business between the teams.

This year’s renewal carries added significance, coming on the back of a historic campaign for the Sunshine Girls, who captured a silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

And Henry-Wright says excitement is building.

“I mean, we’re excited that we have a lot of our senior players back. This is our last preparation. We’re actually picking up our preparation for World Cup next year. So it’s good to have most of your players in. It’s a great feeling,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“Training is going well, so far. We’re really trying to intensify as much as we can in terms of physical preparation and also in terms of tactical preparation. I mean, there are still areas that we really need to work on. You know, we still don’t have all the combinations, but, you know, sometimes when you don’t have it, it’s good that girls have to work without certain areas to keep a little bit more discipline.

“But we are quite excited that we have most of our players. So we have six players that are away that will join the squad, we have two in England and four in Australia and we have a week to prepare so it’s going to be hard work that is one disadvantage that we have to join so late but despite that we’re really trying to ramp up mental preparation, physical preparation and all the other preparations that we can,” Henry-Wright added.

The biggest boost, she said, is the return of Fowler-Nembhard from maternity leave.

“We’re just happy to have back Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard. I think you know she’s just coming out of maternity leave. You know nothing to prove and we’re just hoping that she will lead from the front as one of our captains. She’s always carrying the team, being disciplined leading from the front so the expectation is the same and I know she’s excited to rejoin so we just can’t wait to reunite with her,” Henry-Wright said.

Jamaica enter the series ranked number four in the world, one spot behind England at number three, and Henry-Wright expects a high-intensity battle for the trophy.

“We are very excited about our Commonwealth performance. It comes down to how hard we play and how steady and focused we keep so it’s a high intensity game. England is a very good component. They are number three in the world. We are ranked number four. They have the last tournament and they will be coming hard to maintain that. We also want to take back that trophy. It comes down to how disciplined our girls are, how well they will improve and take care of that ball. Try to get a lot of defensive plays so that they can keep attacking the game. We’re looking forward to a very intense and fierce competition from our rivals,” she said.

With six overseas-based players joining late, Henry-Wright admitted the short preparation window will be demanding, but said the squad is used to each other and will hit the ground running once together.

“I mean, we just have to start as we get there, you know, in terms of our preparation. As soon as we meet, we get together and we’ll start our preparation in terms of our court work and whatever team building and bonding activities we do, we’ll definitely do whatever mental preparation we need to do, we will definitely do to get them ready. And they are used to each other. I mean, they have not played. I mean, some of them might play with Janelle for the first time because I know Brie would be playing with her for the first time. So it’s going to be interesting and it’s something that will is going to be new to us so you know it’s just good that we can get that connection in the attack going,” Henry-Wright explained.

Despite the challenges, she insisted the mood in camp is high.

“The spirit is high, I think as we get closer I think the girls are even more excited and you know mean more you know going a little bit harder and harder for each training session I think we’re building nicely so it’s just the time that we will just meet together continue preparing ensuring that they stay healthy and, you know, giving all the good recoveries that we can and for them to really execute and keep practising and building for each training session,” she said.

World.title: 2026 Ford Ranger XL: Excellent value
World.content:
The 2026 Ranger XL goes straight for the heart of commercial buyers with features and a price tailored to meet their needs.(Photo: Rory Daley)

As the current darling of the lifestyle pickup crowd, Ford hopes to reassert its original image as the working man’s choice with the commercial buyer-friendly XL trim of the Ranger.



By focusing on necessities at this edge of the market, Ford is able to bring the Ranger in at a rather competitive price point.

EXTERIOR

It may be a starting point, but the Ranger XL does its best to avoid that United Nations poverty specification look. It’s not rolling around on steel wheels, as you do get rims. All the bumpers are body colour, but the niceties from the upper trims, such as the factory roll bar and tonneau cover, aren’t there, which is a potential positive for a section of the target demographic. Also gone are the C-shaped daytime running lights, for a more LED-powered standard setup.

INTERIOR

It’s the same with the interior. Those familiar with the higher trims of the Ranger will notice a difference. Those more interested in work than play won’t find fault with the durable cloth and hard-wearing plastics around the cabin. For passenger comfort, soft-touch elements grace the main contact points. Technology has always been part of the Ranger’s appeal, and even in XL trim it exceeds many class rivals.

Drivers have full digital instrumentation from an 8.8-inch screen and a 10-inch portrait infotainment screen. Everything is clear, with fast and easy connectivity via USB and Bluetooth.

Still in the Ranger XL’s corner is the spacious cabin and the low noise, making it more refined than class rivals on the road and comfortable for a wide range of functions. Ford didn’t drop the driver safety systems, and there are more than enough to ease the nerves of whoever is behind the wheel, from cameras and airbags to electronic intervention.

ON THE ROAD

There’s nothing missing here as well. The Ranger XL uses the 2-litre, bi-turbo diesel four-cylinder engine of its brothers, delivering powerful low and mid-range torque to handle its up to 2,925lb payload and 7,500 towing capacities. It’s relatively quiet, fading into the background often while operating with frugality.

The 10-speed transmission operates invisibly, continuing the Ford’s great on-road manners.

But the Ranger’s reputation was never built on being a soft-roader. It’s a top choice for when the going gets tough, and its off-road manners and abilities allow rookies and veterans alike to traverse tough terrain with little issue using its mechanical and electronic systems.

VERDICT

The XL trim shows off the breadth and flexibility of the Ford Ranger platform. Despite a bit of de-contenting to meet the needs of the commercial market, from individual business to fleets, it still retains the core abilities across all the trim levels. It’s still comfortable for everyday use, has the muscle for hard work, and is as agile off-road as a goat. However, Ford may have inadvertently created something that appeals even further to the lifestyle crowd. In XL form, the Ranger is a blank canvas, free to be customised as wanted and at the financial pace of its owner. Either way, the 2026 Ford Ranger XL cannot be ignored at this end of the segment, especially at its listed price point.

World.title: Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica to reopen in Runaway Bay on December 1
World.content:
Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica

Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica, formerly Bahia Principe Grand Jamaica, will reopen in Runaway Bay on December 1 following a comprehensive renovation carried out over approximately one year, the hotel chain announced in a press release Thursday.

The reopening brings 647 rooms back into operation and approximately 1,000 jobs on Jamaica’s north coast ahead of the winter tourism season, the release stated.

According to Bahia Principe, as part of the Explore sub-brand, the renovated property is designed for families and groups who travel together and want to enjoy their vacation at their own pace.

It said the renovations covered rooms, common areas, dining, leisure and entertainment spaces, “with a stronger connection to Jamaican culture and local identity.”

The hotel chain said the reopening of Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica reinforces a new chapter for Bahia Principe, marked by the evolution of its brand architecture, clearer positioning and a more premium hotel offering, segmented and connected to culture and destination. In this context, the release stated, the Explore and Escape sub-brands help organise Bahia Principe’s offering and make it easier for each guest to identify which hotel best fits their needs, motivations and travel style.

Explore is aimed at families, groups and travelers who want to combine relaxation, leisure,

entertainment and a connection with local culture, while Escape is geared toward an adult audience

seeking a more relaxed, sophisticated stay focused on disconnecting.

“This differentiation strengthens the identity of each property and builds a more coherent experience from the moment of choice, in line with a more current, experiential way of traveling that is tied to the surroundings,” the release stated, adding that the initiative is part of the 50 per cent joint venture between Hyatt and Piñero, which manages the Bahia Principe resorts and owns the brand.

Bahia Principe maintains its brand identity and hotel essence, and Hyatt integrates its resorts into the inclusive collection, strengthening its international reach and connecting them with the company’s global platform, the release stated.

Julio Pérez, CEO of Bahia Principe Hotels & Resorts, highlights that the reopening as a significant step in strengthening the company’s presence in Jamaica.

To mark the reopening of Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica, the brand has launched a promotional

campaign for the hotel, with exclusive discounts of up to 50 per cent.

World.title: Haunted House?
World.content:
GREEN... I think what we have happening too much is that where a decision is made and it does not find favour with the Opposition, they resort to some form of protest.

WHAT should be a place for elected representatives to challenge one another through debate has been interrupted, on several occasions over the past year, by protests, walkouts and heated exchanges, with Tuesday’s confrontation over the Cuba censure motion being the latest flashpoint.

However, Leader of Government Business Floyd Green and Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell have expressed contrasting views over what is driving the repeated breakdowns in order.

In separate interviews on Wednesday with the Jamaica Observer following Tuesday’s sitting, Green blamed what he described as a lack of discipline and leadership among Opposition members, while Paulwell argued that the management of Parliament, particularly the Speaker’s handling of proceedings, was increasingly putting the Opposition at a disadvantage.

Their contrasting accounts have brought into focus the growing strain between the two sides of the House and raised questions about whether the country’s Parliament can return to more orderly proceedings.

Green said members of Parliament were responsible for maintaining proper conduct, even when disagreeing with decisions made by the Speaker or other parliamentary authorities.

“I think what we have happening too much is that, where a decision is made and it does not find favour with the Opposition, they resort to some form of protest, and that is more than unfortunate, that is unparliamentary, quite frankly, and should not be the approach,” he told the Observer after speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday.

Green said he could not recall a previous period in Jamaica’s parliamentary history when an Opposition had responded to unfavourable decisions by attempting to halt proceedings.

He pointed to past Opposition responses, including walking out of the chamber or holding press conferences, as ways of expressing disagreement without stopping the business of Parliament.

He also rejected the suggestion that the problem was with the House itself, instead placing responsibility on the Opposition’s leadership to ensure its members followed parliamentary rules.

“It’s a challenge with the Opposition not appreciating that they too are bound by the principles of the House, and it’s unfortunate because every opposition wants to be Government, and when you set a precedent like this it just creates a very difficult situation,” he said.

Green said the way forward was for Opposition leader Mark Golding to exercise greater control over his members and encourage them to use other avenues when they felt aggrieved by a parliamentary decision.

He also suggested that Golding was sometimes contributing to the conduct he was criticising, making it difficult for him to correct the behaviour of his members and also blamed him for not allowing Paulwell to do his job as leader of opposition business effectively.

However, Paulwell rejected Green’s assessment, arguing that the repeated confrontations were rooted in how Parliament was being managed and the treatment of the Opposition.

He said the minority had been increasingly disadvantaged over the past year, particularly in its efforts to question decisions and hold the Government accountable.

“Well, I believe that the Parliament has declined into a state of disrepute, and it has to do with largely the management of the Parliament, all the affairs of the Parliament. I believe from our standpoint that we are seeing greater oppression of the minority in Parliament over the last year or so, when in fact there has always been a presumption that to enable greater accountability, and transparency, great leeway ought to be given to the minority in Parliament,” he said.

Paulwell said the interpretation of the standing orders, which govern how the House conducts its business could place Opposition members at a disadvantage depending on how the Speaker applies them.

He argued that the Speaker, who has the final authority to interpret the rules in the chamber, should remain above the political rivalry between Government and Opposition members.

“What I think has happened, and it might be due to the inexperience of the leader of government business, is that the Speaker is now embroiled in the cut and thrust of the democratic process that results from the two-party rivalry and competition,” he said.

“Now, the practice of the past, the leaders of Government business and Opposition business, they work things out, and it is true that he and I have a cordial relationship, and I believe that if he and I are allowed to manage the affairs of the Parliament, things wouldn’t go much further. But it cannot be that the Speaker, who is to be the final arbiter, the umpire, that person ought not to be engaged in the rivalry,” Paulwell added.

He said he had previously called for regular meetings involving himself, Green and Speaker Juliet Holness to settle disagreements away from the public proceedings of the House.

He also rejected Green’s suggestion that he was unable to maintain discipline among Opposition members, pointing to his own experience serving as both leader of Government business and leader of Opposition business.

“That is absolute nonsense, there are only a few persons on their side with the level of experience that I have, having served as leader of Government business for years, and also leader of Opposition business, and what has happened in the past is for the leader of opposition business and government business to work out the accommodation and the facilitation, and to make sure that there is greater harmony in the running of the Parliament,” he expressed.

Paulwell is therefore calling for a cooling-off period and renewed discussions involving the parliamentary business leaders, with the possibility of Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Golding also participating.

He said the matter could be addressed through renewed engagement between the country’s political leaders, including as part of the Vale Royal talks on constitutional reform.

World.title: Lower the temperature!
World.content:
HENRY-WILSON...I’m not sure if we are at a stage where, because of a person’s political persuasion, they can’t be civil towards other people

TWO former prominent Members of Parliament (MP) — Maxine Henry-Wilson of the People’s National Party (PNP) and Othneil Lawrence of the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) — are appealing to politicians currently serving in the nation’s Parliament to “lower the temperature”, and bring civility back to the legislature.

The two have called for a reset in the Parliament, while highlighting the approaches taken by former prime ministers PJ Patterson and Bruce Golding who were able to maintain order during some of the most robust debates in the country’s recent history when they served in the Parliament.

Their appeal follows Tuesday night’s dust-up in the House of Representatives that saw two senior MPs having to be separated by their colleagues after they appeared to come close to exchanging blows. The two are Mikael Phillips, PNP MP for Manchester North Western, and JLP’s Desmond McKenzie, MP for Kingston Western, who’s also minister of local government and community development.

The incident followed the adjournment of the parliamentary sitting after a tense and disruptive debate on a motion centred on the Government’s decision to abstain from a recent United Nations vote on the punishing United States economic embargo on Cuba. The MP for St Andrew Western Anthony Hylton who moved the motion, even called for the Government to be censured.

Both Henry-Wilson and Lawrence credited the prime ministers under who they served for keeping things in line when they threatened to go off the rails. Henry-Wilson served two terms as MP for St Andrew South Eastern during the Patterson era, while Lawrence served one-term under Golding from 2007-2011.

“One of the things that Patterson did was to try and bring down the tempo and the animosity between the two sides because there was a period when the animosity was really high, Henry-Wilson recalled.

“One of the things he did was to have social events where they [PNP and JLP members] interacted with each other. And, also downstairs, in the dining room, we actually ran jokes and we knew who and who were friends and so on,” she shared. The former minister of education and information minister, who was also the first female general secretary of a major political party in Jamaica, said the level of hostility and polarisation was abated by the deliberate social interactions.

“I’m not clear how that goes now, I’m not sure if we are at a stage where, because of a person’s political persuasion, they can’t be civil towards other people,” she said, while pointing out that, “We have to work in the best interest of the nation”.

“It’s a question of respect also, and a question of understanding that politics is about bargaining and compromise and negotiation and nobody ever gets everything they want,“ Henry-Wilson added. “It seems like some of that has gone and issues have become intensely personal. Why would you in Parliament talk about anybody’s mother? They’re not a part of the debate, the discussion or the cut-and-thrust. We can’t stoop to that level,” she remarked.

“We must understand what the parliamentary debate is about; it’s not about personal attacks. As Norman Manley said, “elevate the thing, take it up off the ground,” she added.

Henry-Wilson said it appeared MPs are not taking the time to learn about parliamentary rules.

“Some of the things that I hear people talking about, they contravene the parliamentary standing orders but whether you like the standing orders or not the fact of the matter is that it is there and you have to observe it”.

She opined that the breakdown in the Parliament also has to do with the exercise of leadership of the House of Representatives. She recommended that the Leader of Government Business in the House, Floyd Green, sit with the Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell and “come up with some kind of ground rules about how you interact with each other. I think it is important”.

For his part, Lawrence said he is “very disappointed seeing what has been taking place — not only yesterday [Tuesday] but previously”.

Although two senior multiple-term MPs were at the heart of Tuesday’s altercation, Lawrence seemed to point the finger of blame for disruptions in recent parliaments squarely at the feet of younger, inexperienced politicians. “I don’t know if proper training needs to apply,” he said.

A former minister of state, Lawrence said when he was elected, training sessions were organised for the incoming class of parliamentarians. “It guided us as to how we should conduct ourselves,” he said. “I served on about eight different committees including the Ethics Committee and that has guided me well,” he added.

“I’m wondering if we [serving politicians] are not cognisant of the fact that from the moment you walk through those doors [of the Parliament] each day, we must remember that the country is looking at us.“

He recalled experiencing robust debates involving members of both sides “and at the end of the day persons who just had a heated debate were seen sitting together having lunch”.

He told of a particularly heated exchange between the late Roger Clarke of the PNP and Robert Montague who serves in the current JLP cabinet. “It was really heated but I can tell you that at the end of the day, five minutes after that, Roger was downstairs giving joke”.

Like Henry-Wilson, Lawrence believes the leadership of the Parliament needs to take charge.

“I don’t know if they need to be a bit more firm but at the end of the day, they must understand that while we want to rule, we still must respect each other regardless of which side we sit on”.

He went further to suggest that politicians may be influenced by the crassness that is played out daily on social media. And going back to the younger parliamentarians, Lawrence opined that youthful exuberance was taking over.

“Because if you go back to the persons who are behaving a certain way, the younger ones are showing disrespect to the seniors and it’s a concern that’s creeping into the Parliament.“

He worried that with increasing conflicts in schools, with some turning physical with deadly consequences, it is becoming increasingly difficult to tell young people how to conduct themselves properly “when we’re not setting any example”.

“After [Tuesday’s] behaviour, how do we speak to students about proper behaviour? It cannot continue, we have to set a better example”.

Having sat through some of the most contentious debates, including during the global recession of 2008-2009 and the Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke extradition saga which ultimately ended Prime Minister Golding’s political career, Lawrence said he never saw the disrespect like what is being played out today.

“We debated robustly, we didn’t always see eye to eye but there was mutual respect. When I watched yesterday I cannot understand how they almost got physical. I’m saying, lower the temperature because the world is watching us”.

World.title: Mélenchon squares up to Brussels in election manifesto
World.content:
"We will immediately implement our program at the national level. This will therefore require a confrontation with European institutions," according to the manifesto from Mélenchon's France Unbowed. "This also means disobeying rules blocking [us] whenever necessary."

"Our logic is simple. As long as a deal on changing the treaties is not done, we negotiate with our partners and disobey [...] blocking rules in parallel. If we get to an agreement, it will be put to a referendum," the manifesto added.

The proposals, which echo Mélenchon's earlier statements, would likely face tough opposition from France's partners in the European Council, which is currently dominated by more conservative leaders.

The manifesto also said the European Central Bank should be "placed under democratic control and mobilized to fund the ecological and social transition." Mélenchon triggered a flurry of criticism earlier this year when he said he would “set fire” to a large chunk of France's public debt held by the ECB, setting off a nationwide debate on the subject.

France is among the countries hardest hit by a global surge in borrowing costs, with its fiscal situation also limiting the government's ability to soften the impact of higher fuel and food prices, part of a larger cost-of-living crisis on the continent.

With public debt amounting to 117.5% of GDP and a public deficit above 5%, fiscal issues have become a central concern for voters. Presidential candidates are pitching radically different solutions to the problem.

Le Pen has tried to rebrand herself as a responsible steward of the economy unafraid of cuts — despite critics saying her plan is "overly optimistic" and her flagship promises are yet to be funded. Centrist candidates, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, are pitching themselves as the voice of reason on economic and fiscal issues but are struggling to gain traction.

World.title: French far left enshrines leaving NATO in official presidential platform
World.content:
An increasing number of polls place Mélenchon in second place in next year’s high-stakes election to replace President Emmanuel Macron. The top two vote-getters go on to a second round, which could see Mélenchon facing off against far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who also pledges to take France out of NATO’s integrated command.

Unlike Le Pen’s far-right party, France Unbowed does not explicitly say it would stop providing assistance to Ukraine — but it does insist on the need for a diplomatic solution. Any peace agreement would need to lean on “collective security guarantees, between the belligerents and with the rest of Europe.”

France Unbowed wants more arms regulation, including of lethal autonomous weapons systems and nuclear weapons.

The far-left party is also pushing back against the “space arms race,” including by pledging to close NATO’s space center in Toulouse, but says France should have the means to guarantee its sovereignty. Unlike most other political parties, France Unbowed has strong interest in space policy, and argues in its presidential platform that France should acquire a space shuttle.

France Unbowed lawmakers have previously pushed for France to procure Dassault Aviation’s Vortex, a European reusable orbital spaceplane program spearheaded by the French aerospace manufacturer.

Overall, France should invest more in so-called critical enablers, meaning military equipment in areas such as communications, intelligence and logistics that are currently mostly provided by the U.S. via NATO. “They must be produced as a matter of priority,” the party wrote.

It also wants to nationalize some of the country’s main defense companies including ArianeGroup.

A more detailed platform specifically on defense will be released later, a France Unbowed lawmaker told POLITICO.

World.title: Belgian king refuses Bart De Wever’s resignation
World.content:
Since then, Philippe has met with the five party leaders who make up Belgium’s coalition government and concluded that there is still a possible path for them to agree under a De Wever premiership.

“Following his discussions with the leaders of the five majority parties, the King noted that each of them wishes to conclude the budget negotiations as quickly as possible … The King also received a formal commitment from the five party leaders that their respective parties are prepared to make concessions in order to reach an agreement within the government,” the palace’s statement said.

While the government is seeking to plug a €10 billion budget gap by 2029, coalition partners are at loggerheads over where to find the cash.



Flemish Socialist party Vooruit is pushing for the highest earners to contribute more, but French-speaking center-right Reformist Movement has ruled that out, and also opposed reforming the value-added tax.



De Wever, who had previously ruled out starting the new year with an emergency budget, this week confirmed that the country would have no choice but to fall back on it again.

Under that system, the government can spend one-twelfth of the preceding year’s budget per month. “This is a terrible failure on the part of the government,” De Wever told members of parliament while announcing he would submit his resignation.

The prime minister will meet the king again in 10 days on Nov. 16 to report on progress, the palace said.

World.title: Von der Leyen to visit Black Sea amid deadly drone attacks
World.content:
Romania has warned that the strikes are part of Moscow's escalating aggression against Ukraine, while Bulgaria has stopped short of formally blaming Moscow, referring instead to drones coming from "an eastern direction."

The security concerns reached Bulgaria's shores Friday, when a local resident discovered a drone washed up near the coastal town of Shabla. The aerial vehicle appeared to have been carried ashore by the sea, said the municipality's mayor, Mariyan Zhechev. The drone's origin and whether it was connected to the recent attacks on commercial shipping have not been established.

It is unclear whether von der Leyen will be accompanied by anyone else such as European Council President António Costa or EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. In Bucharest on Monday she will meet with Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Prime Minister Luca Niculescu. On Tuesday, she will meet Bulgarian Prime Minsiter Rumen Radev in Varna and visit the Nikola Vapsarov Naval Academy.

The plans come as NATO allies step up surveillance over the Black Sea following the attacks on commercial shipping. Italian, British and American reconnaissance aircraft were spotted conducting simultaneous missions over the region Tuesday, according to Bulgarian broadcaster bTV, while France has extended the deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft in Romania.

The deteriorating security situation is also prompting diplomatic efforts to protect commercial shipping. Speaking at Saturday's G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said India and Turkey had put forward proposals to help grain-carrying vessels navigate the Black Sea safely amid the continuing Russia-Ukraine war.

This article has been updated with details of Ursula von der Leyen's itinerary in Romania and Bulgaria.

World.title: EU accuses TikTok of designing algorithm that creates ‘rabbit holes’
World.content:
This is the fifth case of the EU executive accusing TikTok of breaching EU rules, even though it has issued no fines against the Chinese-owned platform.

In Friday's announcement, the Commission says the company didn't adequately consider the risk of sending users down "rabbit holes" through a "continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image."

The investigation focused on mental health impacts because "the evidence was strongest," when asked about how these rabbit holes contribute to radicalization, said another official.

The more users interact with content, even if it's potentially harmful, the more of that content they are recommended, the Commission said in its press release, which noted that the measures TikTok has put in place to curb the rabbit hole effect have not been effective.

TikTok should take into account "explicit" signals like buttons that say "I'm not interested" more than implicit ones, like engagement, said the first Commission official. Engagement metrics measure how much users interact with content, such as how much time they spend watching a video or the content they like. Talking about mitigation of these risks, the official said that remedies have to be effective and that TikTok's current measures are not.

"To say 'I'm not interested' has to have a meaning, an effective meaning, and not only should not only be an afterthought, and then you go back to the old recommender system," the official said.

World.title: Trump teases ‘beautiful’ deal covering ‘all of Europe’ after meeting Putin’s envoy
World.content:
An agreement is “going to involve more than Ukraine,” the U.S. president said after a meeting with Kirill Dmitriev.

U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated his promise of a “big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine after holding a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Thursday.

Dmitriev, who heads the U.S.-sanctioned Russian sovereign wealth fund, was attending a White House event hosted by First Lady Melania Trump where she delivered remarks about the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky that she helped negotiate. Although Russian and Ukrainian officials were present at the event, Trump told reporters Thursday evening he had only met Dmitriev.

“I can’t tell you what I discussed. But I’m just telling you, it’s going to be a big agreement,” he said. “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”

World.title: ‘I don’t trust them’: Lithuanian president warns Putin’s provocations will continue
World.content:
According to Nausėda, the Russians want to observe how the alliance responds to so-called hybrid attacks, which are suspected to have included drone incursions, cyberattacks and arson, among other things.

The hybrid war will therefore continue, not only on NATO’s eastern flank but also in Germany, Denmark and other countries, Nausėda explained. Russia is testing “how determined we are and whether we will respond collectively when certain red lines are crossed,” the Lithuanian president said.

Nausėda, an economist who has led Lithuania since 2019, also sees no serious willingness in Moscow to enter into negotiations to end its war against Ukraine before next spring.

Moscow will use the winter months to keep up the pressure on Ukraine through air strikes on cities, he said. “The Russians will only pretend to negotiate. I don’t trust them.”

Putin will make demands that are unacceptable to Ukraine from the outset, he added. “If Ukraine gets through this winter, and I am convinced that it will, the chances of serious talks will improve in 2027. I don’t expect them any earlier.”

Joe Stanley-Smith contributed to this report.
