It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

World.title: Trump’s final two years: Is the UK ready?
World.content:
After a Democratic wave in the U.S. midterms, Westminster is wondering whether Trump’s domestic setbacks could make him more unpredictable on the world stage — and how Britain should handle the final two years of his presidency.

Patrick Baker speaks to Simon McDonald, the former top civil servant at the Foreign Office, who takes us inside Britain’s diplomatic response to the 2018 midterms and explains what lessons can be learned from Trump’s first term.

Then Ed Roman, who recently left his role as director of communications at the British Embassy in Washington, reveals how diplomats are already preparing for the next U.S. president — and how to court Trump’s potential successors without upsetting the man currently in the Oval Office.

And POLITICO’s senior foreign and defence correspondent Esther Webber explains why she thinks Andy Burnham will take a different approach to the Trump White House than his predecessor.

World.title: UK: Thousands gather as London switches on its Christmas lights
World.content:
Around 300,000 energy-efficient LED lights brought the famous shopping street to life, with more than 30 angel-shaped decorations returning for their 11th year. Presenter Harriet Fisher switched on the display at 6.30 pm, coinciding with Britain's Bonfire Night celebrations.

 

With traffic banned for the evening for the first time since 2019, crowds filled the pedestrianised street to enjoy live bands, a Christmas choir, LED dancers, stilt walkers and playful Hamleys elves.

This year's decorations feature glowing words including "Joy", "Smile" and "Hope", as well as illuminated hearts, stars and new installations in Princes Arcade.

Nearby, visitors to St James's Market could also support food-rescue charity Felix through the returning Wishing Tree, where a tap triggers a £5 donation.

World.title: Could Thailand be your second home? Inside the membership that helps you stay for years
World.content:
Many of us have Thailand on our bucket list for travel, but some people take it one step further and make the Asian nation their home.

 

Enter: The Thailand Privilege Card. Starting at around €17,300 and going up to about €133,350, those keen to move to Thailand can do just that, while bypassing other visa considerations.

“We are right in the middle of Asia, so travelling to any part of Asia would be within two to four hours,” said Manatase Annawat, President of Thailand Privilege Card Co., speaking to Euronews Travel at World Travel Market in London. “So people can also use Thailand as a base to stay and then also travel to any parts of Asia easily.”.

Annawat says Thailand is also worth considering as a home destination for Europeans, as it has some of the best healthcare services in the world – “some hospitals are almost like a hotel” – famous hospitality and a staggering 20,000 restaurants which, he estimates, would take 10 years to experience in total.

There are also business opportunities, and the weather is famously appealing.

“We have 365 days of warm climate and also mountains, sea, sand, sun, everything,” said Annawat. “It’s a lifestyle that you have been dreaming of. It is a place to come, to visit, to stay longer and even retire in Thailand.”

Currently, most Thailand Privilege Card members live in the capital, Bangkok, but others live in the likes of peaceful Chiang Mai in the north, close to mountains, or Phuket in the south, known for its world-class beaches.

Thailand, Annawat explained, makes an especially great home for retirees, not least because money goes so much further in the Southeast Asian nation.

Annawat also emphasised that locals welcome foreigners who move to Thailand and don’t make them feel like outsiders. “We take good care of them,” he added.

While the shortest period for foreign residents using the Thailand Privilege Card is five years, membership packages also offer stays of 10, 15 and 20-plus years. Holders don’t have to stay in the country for the entire timeframe, but just having the membership ensures that getting into and out of Thailand is far easier.

Benefits of the card include VIP airport treatment, think fast-track immigration, airport lounge access, meet-and-greet services and limousine transfers, as well as lifestyle perks which range from access to golf courses and bookings at top restaurants, spas and wellness facilities.

Reliable service is on offer to those who hold the card Thailand Privilege Card

The card is, in theory, effectively offering a VIP pass to the country, allowing wealthy foreigners to enjoy longer stays with a range of perks that go well beyond a standard tourist visa.

For those keen to get peace of mind before signing up, the team behind the card also offer plenty of practical support, from help with opening bank accounts and obtaining driving licences to handling immigration reporting requirements.

“You know that whenever you come to Thailand and you need help or assistance, we have someone to assist you,” explained Annawat.

World.title: Scotland wants visitors to stay longer, slow down and experience authentic hospitality
World.content:
In Scotland, tourism is a “force for good”. That’s according to Jill Walker, the Director of Marketing at VisitScotland, as she told Euronews Travel about what’s coming up for the country in 2027.

 

Speaking at World Travel Market in London, Walker insisted that it’s imperative that tourism in Scotland benefits locals as well as those who visit.

For 2027, she’s particularly keen on highlighting immersive experiences, which can give people a proper sense of the real Scotland. For instance, in the market town of Wigtown in Dumfries and Galloway, there’s an Airbnb where visitors can stay in an actual, working bookstore and play shop while meeting locals.

While many tourism boards have a specific kind of tourist they want to attract, that’s not the case in Scotland.

“We don't have anybody that we wouldn't attract,” said Walker. “We're a very open and inclusive country and destination, and that will always continue.

“We've got destinations that are for families, we've got them for young professionals, we've got them for people who are from the older generation – the country is there for everybody.”

Her only caveats for visitors?

“We want people to come in the shoulder seasons and experience Scotland in a responsible way and, if they can stay a bit longer, if they could do a bit of slow travel, all the better.”

It’s a particularly exciting time for Dumfries and Galloway, which was recently named as one of National Geographic's Best of the World 2027, making it the only UK destination to feature in the top 25 global list.

Dumfries and Galloway was recently named as one of the best destinations in the world to visit in 2027 Hannah Smith/Unsplash

Walker says it’s an ideal choice for adventurous types and thrill seekers as it offers a vast number of outdoor thrills, from water sports and gorge scrambling to high-flying ziplines across scenic hills.

Scotland will also make history in 2027, as Edinburgh plays host to the Grand Départ of the Tour de France. The event will mark the northernmost start in Tour history.

In September and October 2027, the inaugural Rally Scotland will take place in Aberdeenshire, and will be the first time anywhere in the UK has hosted a round of the World Rally Championship since 2019.

For those less into sports, there’s plenty on offer to discover, too.

Perth Museum is a relatively new opening, while the Inverness Castle Experience officially opened to the public in February this year, following a multi-million transformation from a former prison and sheriff court into an interactive visitor attraction

Much of the tourist board’s focus, though, is on experiences, so visitors can really dig their teeth into the real Scotland.

That includes learning to shear sheep, staying in accommodation located right next to Highland "coo" (cow) pastures and cooking up Cullen Skink, a hearty Scottish delicacy soup made with smoked haddock and potatoes.

“We're always innovating in Scotland,” said Walker. “There's always lots to do and see, and it’s all very interactive, very hands-on, which is obviously important to see Scotland at its best.”

When it comes down to it, the tourist board says that Scotland is the ideal place to improve wellbeing for both the body and mind.

“That comes quite naturally to us because we are that hospitable kind of nation; we love hospitality, we're brought up to make sure people enjoy themselves,” said Walker.

“We've got that beautiful landscape, we've got that history, integrity and the food, and it's the way we live. It's not put on or contrived for people that are coming to visit.

“When people come to visit Scotland, they say that very thing. It all feels very grounded, very authentic and quite enriching.”

World.title: Pope Leo XIV departs for Uruguay as he begins tour of South America
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV set off for Uruguay on Friday as he begins a tour of South America that will also see him visit Argentina and Peru, where he worked for years as a missionary and then bishop.

 

Chicago-born Leo's flight took off from Rome’s Fiumicino International Airport shortly after 7 am on Friday, the Vatican said.

He is expected to land in the Uruguayan capital Montevideo at around 4:30 pm local time.

Leo has a packed three-day schedule in Uruguay that includes a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence.

“His stamina is fantastic. The way that he’s singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong,” Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said.

“His doctors are very confident and he’ll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen, but we don’t see that in his prognosis or even in the way that he’s acting,” she added.

In Uruguay, Leo will meet with President Yamandú Orsi before delivering a welcome address to government officials and diplomats. He will also preside over Vespers at the Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral. Visits to the cities of Paysandú and Florida are planned for the coming days.

Leo will then head on to Argentina, where he is due to visit Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján. In Peru, the pontiff is scheduled to appear in Chiclayo, Cusco, and Pucallpa.

The trip comes weeks after the 71-year-old underwent lung cancer surgery.

World.title: Cycling, castles and outdoor adventures: Wales gears up for a busy 2027
World.content:
Wales is still something of a “lesser-known destination”, but there's just “so much appeal and an incredible history and diversity that we offer”, says Lucy von Weber, the Head of Marketing for Visit Wales.

 

Speaking to Euronews Travel at World Travel Market in London, she discussed how the country is keen to attract visitors to explore its natural beauty, discover the many things to do, and to enjoy a very warm welcome from locals.

“It offers huge diversity with Cardiff in the south, three national parks, a beautiful, stunning landscape, lots of outdoor adventure activities like walking, cycling and more extreme ones like zipping,” said von Weber.

She also emphasised the fact that both English and Welsh are spoken here, making it a unique destination. “All of the signs are bilingual, and you just get a really strong sense that the tastes, the sounds and the locals that you're in somewhere very, very different.”

As well as a destination for thrill-seekers, von Weber says Wales is a great choice for those who prefer to “slow down a bit, go off the beaten track, and discover somewhere new and different, and really get to know the locals and the communities”.

In 2027, more people will likely discover the country as it plays host to a stage of the Tour de France's Grand Départ, which will run from Welshpool to Cardiff on 4 July. And It’s not just professional cyclists who can get the most out of Wales’ many bike trails.

The red dragon at Cardiff Castle Korng Sok/Unsplash

“We're hugely excited to be able to showcase Wales as a world-class cycling destination, not only for those who love to do the Tour de France climbs,” she said. “We have some beautiful, flat, easy off-road cycling routes that are really perfectly family-friendly.”

In fact, Wales is taking its hosting of the Tour de France so seriously that it’s named 2027 as a “Year of Cycling”.

The year-long programme will see a first-of-its-kind interactive mapping tool which showcases destinations, attractions and detours along Wales’ cycling routes.

Von Weber suggests combining a bike ride with a visit to one of the many castles or museums across Wales, or simply taking in stunning views and enjoying local food and drink, including favourites like Welsh rarebit – an elevated hot cheese sandwich – Cawl stew, or Welsh cakes, a sort of hybrid between a biscuit, a pancake, and a scone.

Next year, Wales will also play host to the Senior Open, a professional men’s golf tournament for players aged 50, which will be held at Royal Porthcawl Golf Club.

Meanwhile, Cardiff will be the temporary home of EuroGames, Europe’s largest LGBTQ+ multi-sport event. It will mark the first time the games have been hosted in the UK.

Conwy Castle in Wales K. Mitch Hodge/Unsplash

Despite much of Wales’ largest events taking place in the summer months, the tourist board is hoping to attract more visitors throughout the year.

“We have the castles, the museums, the attractions that are available all year round,” said von Weber.

“You can lean into all of the different seasons, from the daffodils in springtime, through to the bluebells in the woodlands in the summer, into the autumn colours and then in the winter, we've got great Christmas fairs and festivals that take place. You can just wrap up warm and enjoy the open fires and pub atmosphere, and things like that.”

For those who like to be a little more active than merely bask in a low-key atmosphere, the Tau'i Valley Trail in Carmarthenshire, a 21km-long flat route, is a good bet.

Surprisingly, there’s also a significant Hollywood influence in Wrexham, near the English border.

In 2021, actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney bought the town’s football club, Wrexham AFC.

The pair’s takeover, three successive promotions and hit documentary series “Welcome to Wrexham” have attracted football fans keen to see the club’s remarkable turnaround for themselves.

There’s a new reason to visit, too. The Football Museum of Wales and Wrexham Museum opened in September, bringing together the story of Welsh football and the city’s industrial and cultural heritage. Highlights include historic memorabilia, interactive displays and tributes to Welsh football legends.

World.title: Who is Ilija Srdanović? The doctor who took Serbia’s student movement to Macron and EU leaders
World.content:
Serbia’s Student List is winning recognition from EU institutions and governments, and one man has become the face of that outreach: a cardiologist and university professor who might become the country’s new leader.

 

Until two years ago, Ilija Srdanović was a little-known professor at the University of Novi Sad. Now he is the international face of the movement that has transformed Serbia’s political landscape, and the first number foreign leaders dial.

“I had a conversation with Ilija Srdanović, head of the Student List in Serbia,” French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X on Monday. “I reiterated to him France’s friendship toward Serbia and our determination to continue supporting it on its European path.”

Macron is only the latest leader to reach out since the 25 October elections. In them, the Student List, a force born of a grassroots protest movement, ousted Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) after 14 years of complete dominance. It won 140 of the 250 seats, enough to form a government alone.

European Council President António Costa, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos all rushed to congratulate the Student List. Almost all of them used the same number: Srdanović’s.

The 56-year-old cardiologist emerged as a leading figure of the student protests that followed the Novi Sad railway station disaster, which killed 16 people on 1 November 2024.

Born in Novi Sad and raised in Vrbas, he has worked at the Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases of Vojvodina in Sremska Kamenica since 1997 and teaches at the University of Novi Sad’s Faculty of Medicine.

The tragedy became the catalyst for mass protests, as it came to symbolise the corruption of public institutions and the concentration of power under SNS rule. Srdanović became an outspoken critic of Vučić, notably over the police’s violent repression of the protests and interference in academic autonomy.

“Those who are not aware that this unstoppable wave is present in society today and cannot understand it, unfortunately, are not worthy of the time they are in and do not serve this historical moment,” he told the Serbian daily Nova in September 2025.

Two months ago, he was named to head the Student List’s slate of 250 candidates, making him one of Serbia’s most recognisable public figures.

On foreign policy, Srdanović has publicly affirmed the Student List’s commitment to EU membership, and to anti-corruption, judicial independence and media freedom. “We remain committed to European integration,” he told Radio Free Europe in an interview published on 27 October.

However, the Student List grew out of a heterogeneous movement, with worldviews ranging from the radical left, such as sociologist Jovo Bakić, to more conservative figures. It was united not by a shared ideology but by a demand for change and opposition to SNS rule.

Its campaign was fought purely on domestic ground, with little attention paid to Serbia’s international orientation. So while Srdanović has already announced that better relations with neighbours will be a priority, there are points on which Serbia’s foreign policy is unlikely to change.

The most significant one for Brussels might be the lack of alignment with the EU on sanctions against Russia, as many Serbs still remember how Western sanctions against Slobodan Milošević’s regime hurt the population.

On Kosovo, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama told Euronews that the Student List was unwilling to discuss recognition, and that “the music in Belgrade will not change”. Srdanović has said dialogue with Pristina should continue, but has left open a review of agreements reached so far.

Srdanović is not the only prominent figure in the Student List, which has yet to agree on its leadership structure and the composition of the government. The movement’s elected lawmakers will vote on it.

Euronews can confirm that he was not part of the four-person delegation that met Commissioner Kos in Brussels on Monday, the first high-level meeting between the Student List and the EU executive. The meeting was not announced in advance, and the European Commission declined to name the attendees.

That reticence reflects the fact that the delegation’s members are not yet MPs and the old Vučić-led establishment formally remains in power. The Republic Electoral Commission only declared the final results on Thursday, setting in motion the deadlines for convening parliament and forming a government.

For two years, the student movement kept a collegial decision-making structure, with no clear leader and a cautious, strategic communication approach that avoided personalising the struggle.

Srdanović was not the obvious choice. Belgrade weekly Vreme reported that the top slot had been expected to go to Vladan Djokić, rector of the University of Belgrade, until a narrow majority of the movement’s plenum dropped him.

Other figures who might bid for the leadership are Dejan Šoškić, the former governor of Serbia’s National Bank, and Radomir Saičić, a university professor. Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović spoke to both, as well as to Srdanović.

In the Radio Free Europe interview, Srdanović said he would accept a nomination for prime minister, before adding that the list has no single leader and that candidates would be chosen collectively.

To get there, he will have to convince a grassroots movement without recognisable leaders that he is the right person to lead Serbia. It is not yet clear whether he will emerge as its political leader or remain, for now, its most internationally recognised face.

World.title: German carmakers drive surprise rise in industrial output
World.content:
A rebound in car production helped lift German industrial output more than expected in September, official data showed on Friday.

 

In September, industrial production rose by 0.7% month-on-month, following a revised 1% increase in August, and was 0.4% higher than a year earlier, according to Germany’s federal statistics agency, Destatis. Economists polled by Reuters had expected output to be flat on the month.

Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING, said supply chain disruptions linked to the Iran war and low river levels over the summer had so far done less damage to German industry than feared.

Car production jumped 17.1% from a month earlier after two weak months, when factory holidays and changes to production lines partly held back output.

The rebound comes as German carmakers face pressure from strong Chinese competition and rising costs.

Pharmaceutical output also rose 8% from August, helping lift September’s figures. But construction output fell 2.6%, and production of machinery and equipment dropped 6.5%, Destatis said.

Excluding energy and construction, industrial production rose 1.7% in September from the previous month. The economy ministry said that the rise made up for the sharp fall in output at mid-year.

Despite the September rebound, industrial output fell 0.4% in the third quarter compared with the second.

The data come as Germany’s economy struggles to regain momentum after a contraction in 2023 and stagnation in 2024, amid weak demand for its exports, Chinese competition and long-standing problems.

But the government expects the economy to grow by 1.3% in 2026, its fastest pace in several years, helped by public spending on defence and infrastructure.

Related German business confidence rises in October despite global economic risks

Brzeski said high energy prices and higher interest rates remained key risks. Still, Thursday’s rise in new orders and a slight fall in inventories pointed to modest growth in industrial output in the near term.

Brzeski said German industry had held up better than feared in the third quarter, even as the momentum it had gained in the second quarter faded. He described the rebound as gradual and said a strong recovery was still some way off.

I removed the duplicate sentences reporting the 17.1% car production jump and the 0.7% rise in overall industrial output, and moved the Reuters forecast next to the headline figure.

World.title: Trio suspected of attempting to smuggle 3,000 tarantulas into Germany
World.content:
Two German nationals and one Polish national have been detained after allegedly attempting to smuggle more than 3,000 tarantulas out of Peru.

 

During a check at an airport in Lima, customs officers discovered the spiders packed into socks and hidden in their luggage.

The men were reportedly detained whilst checking in for a flight to Germany. According to authorities, the arrests followed a tip-off from the public.

"We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones," Cora Suarez, a control technician with Peru's National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR), said.

One tarantula can sell for around €500 in Europe, Suarez said, adding that the spiders were found in varying stages of development, including eggs and hatchlings to adults.

SERFOR said the suspects were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and that they would face criminal proceedings.

In November 2023, Interpol said the black market for illegal wildlife products was worth up to $20 billion a year.

Interpol helps coordinate a global operation to target wildlife trafficking known as Operation Thunder, which it says involves police, customs, border control and forestry and wildlife officials from more than 130 countries and regions.

The operation led to 4,640 seizures in 2025, including tens of thousands of protected animals and plants, the agency said.

World.title: Iranians face looming war threat with no reliable info
World.content:
Ordinary people living in Iran have little idea of the course of the war and peace talks on the global stage. With few sources of information, they are forced to navigate conflicting rumors and fears of a nuclear attack.

"There is a constant sense of fear in the air. Every time I hear a loud noise, I flinch. Even when a door slams, I jump, thinking that bombs are falling," said a 37-year-old mother living in Tehran.

Unlike in the opening months of the war, her children are going to school.

"I don't work, but keeping the children at home out of fear is not a solution," she told DW. "They would go stir-crazy in our small apartment."

Iran's government takes aim at 'rumors'

Schools remain open across Iran despite the military standoff with the US and Israel. However, some parents whose children attend private schools have received messages from those schools explaining what to do in the event of a renewed war or other emergency.

Numerous parents have shared such messages on social media.

The country's Ministry of Education has tried to reassure the public.

Strike on Iran school: Did US commit a war crime? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"People should not pay attention to rumors spread with the aim of sowing fear and forcing schools to close," Ali Farhadi, a ministry spokesperson, said in a recent media interview.

He said the ministry will decide whether the schools stay open or close, and will do so in coordination with the security authorities. Should the security outlook change, the situation will be reassessed accordingly, the official said.

'Pickaxe Mountain' at the center of nuclear attack fears

Parallel to Farhadi's appeal to disregard rumors aimed at raising fear, state media themselves are discussing scenarios of a possible nuclear attack.

On November 2, Iranian state television broadcast an advisory on protective measures in case of a nuclear strike. People were advised to remain in a shelter for at least 24 hours in the event of such an emergency.

Specifically, many in Iran fear the US is preparing to use nuclear weapons against Iran's "Pickaxe Mountain" underground bunker located some 220 kilometers (140 miles) south of Tehran. US President Donald Trump has hinted at attacking the location, which is close to Iran's Natanz nuclear facility, but made no explicit mention of using nuclear weapons.

Iranian government denies that any work related to its nuclear program is being carried out at the mountain bunker.

The fighting between the US and Iran has mostly petered out in recent months as the Trump administration focused on the midterm election. But two days after the election, on November 5, the US news outlet Axios reported that the US military was making final preparations for a possible resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran.

Trump still has months before new Congress takes power

At the same time, there are also hopes that a Democrat-controlled Congress would force Trump to scale down his military ambitions.

"It is still difficult to make any concrete assessment of the implications of the US midterm election results for the war with Iran," writes Hamidreza Azizi, Senior Fellow and Iran expert at the International Crisis Group, in response to a request from DW.

Azizi says the Iranian leadership sees the election results as their own victory. The regime's resistance to the Trump administration has contributed to the Republican Party's loss in the US midterms, and some in Tehran are already seeking to frame the result as a sort of revenge for the US-Israeli assassination of senior Iranian leaders in the opening stages of the war.

Against this backdrop, Iran is likely to take an even harder line on its core demands.

At the same time, Azizi points out that Trump has at least two months before the new Congress officially takes office. He could decide to resume strikes on Iran in an attempt to offset a domestic political setback by targeting a foreign policy victory.

Republicans rebuke Trump on Iran war, economy after midterm wipeout To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reporters kept in the dark on peace talks

For now, Qatari mediators are trying to persuade Tehran and Washington to agree on a draft peace deal. The aim is to prevent another round of escalation and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks in the coming days.

But even well-connected journalists in Iran have little information on the substance of the talks, which are closed to the public.

In a post on X on October 31, Iranian journalist Hadi Mohammadi wrote: "Domestic media outlets are completely in the dark about negotiations that directly affect people's everyday lives. They have to wait for reports from Axios, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera and other international media outlets. In such an environment, developing our own narratives and doing journalism becomes pointless."

As the fog of war persists, many in Iran no longer have the energy to keep up with the media reporting. A 72-year-old retired woman from western Iran told DW she now deliberately avoids the news.

"I hardly have the strength to think about it anymore. I'm just glad that my three children have emigrated," she said.

Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: New bomb threats target Irish media, more flights
World.content:
Newsrooms have been evacuated across Ireland after another wave of bomb threats. Dublin is hosting a high-level EU meeting in several days.

Following days of bomb threats grounding flights across Europe, media institutions in Ireland were added to the list of targets on Friday.

Irish public broadcaster Raidio Teilifis Eirean (RTE) said that its buildings had been evacuated after receiving a bomb threat. Other media organizations were also taking security measures.

The threats come two days before Dublin, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, hosts a high-level meeting with other bloc members.

An RTE reporter said the group that claimed to be behind Friday's bomb threats was the same that had sent threats to airlines earlier in the week.

What did Irish officials say about bomb threats against media networks?

"We don't yet know whether it's an individual behind this effort, or some form of a co-ordinated effort," Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio.

He said it was a "serious and evolving situation."

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin called the developments "worrying," but said the Gardai (Irish police) and Defense Forces were looking into who was behind the threats.

He also urged any organization that receives a similar threat to take it seriously and report it to the police so they can have a "picture of what's happening."

"It just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause disruption, designed to cause fear and anxiety," RTE cited Martin as saying.

Asked about any possible connection with the European Union meetings coming up in Dublin, the prime minister, also known as the Taoiseach, said it was important to maintain the ability to let such meetings go ahead.

"We have the largest number of prime ministers ever at the one time in our country, and that does call for very significant security operations."

Further bomb threats made to flights

More than two dozen flights were affected by threats this week, with further incidents reported on Friday.

Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic responded to threats that ultimately proved to be false.

A flight operated by the Romanian carrier Tarom going from Prague to Bucharest received a threat, but landed at its intended destination before officials deemed it false.

Police in Copenhagen said they had been to the airport for the second day in a row "in connection with threats directed at air traffic" but that there had been no danger to passengers or disruption to flights.

While bomb threats are not uncommon, such a wave of threats being made in a short period of time is unusual, especially amid increasing geopolitical tensions with Russia and a wave of hybrid attacks that have brought disruption to Europe.

World.title: Tanzania: Opposition leader Tundu Lissu jailed for four years
World.content:
Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu has been sentenced to four years in prison after being cleared of treason. Lissu condemned his conviction for incitement, which had not been among the charges he faced.

Tundu Lissu, the leader of Tanzania's main opposition party, was sentenced to four years in prison on Friday for incitement to unrest after being cleared of treason.

While the verdict removed the threat of a death sentence, judges convicted Lissu of an offense that was not among the charges he faced.

What did the court decide?

Judges found that Chadema leader Lissu's statements about blocking the election were intended to disrupt the vote and encourage violence.

"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," the judge said.

Lissu disputed his conviction on a charge different from the treason accusation he had faced.

"I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles," he said, apparently referring to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Lissu was arrested in April 2025 over a speech in which prosecutors said he told supporters the opposition would "block the election" and "mobilize rebellion." He pleaded not guilty, arguing that his speech broke no law and that the prosecution was politically motivated. Lissu has already spent 19 months in jail.

The Tanzania voter boycott over opposition party exclusion To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"All this was political persecution. Excuses were created to imprison me," he told the court after the verdict.

How did the case fuel Tanzania's unrest?

Lissu's arrest, alleged abductions of government critics, and Chadema's exclusion from the October 2025 election helped drive protests across the country.

Hundreds died as police opened fire on protesters in several cities. Opposition figures and rights groups put the toll in the thousands.

A commission appointed by President Samia Suluhu Hassan reported in April that at least 518 people had been killed and blamed protesters for the violence. The government denied allegations that security forces used excessive force.

Security was tightened in the commercial capital, Dar es Salaam, and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict.

Why has the trial drawn international criticism?

British and European Union lawmakers described the case as politically motivated and called for Lissu's immediate release.

"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote to Hassan.

Meet Tundu Lissu: The leader of Tanzania's Chadema party To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lissu, 58, has been repeatedly arrested for opposing the government. In 2017, he survived an assassination attempt in which he was shot 16 times. He believes the attack was politically motivated.

World.title: 'No choice but to bear it': Delhi's unrelenting air pollution crisis
World.content:
Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a predictable crisis?

On a slightly chilly and distinctly smoggy morning in New Delhi, Khushboo Arora was looking for another air purifier for her mother, who has underlying health complications, before the city's air quality deteriorated further.

"Already, I am starting to get a recurring headache," she said. "These days when I wake up, I don't feel fresh. As the day progresses, I feel a heaviness in my head, itching in my eye and a constantly parched throat."

Not too long ago, the unpacking of woolens announced the advent of winter in Delhi. Now, it's the light hum of an air purifier in the corner.

Arora said she has already stopped doing yoga in the park and taking her morning walks. She has also filled her house with air-purifying plants and started spraying water mist inside the house to bring down the level of pollution.

"My parents look at me like I have gone mad. But I feel people are not realizing the gravity of the situation," she said.

A recurring crisis

Winters in Delhi increasingly follow a familiar pattern: Air quality deteriorates, residents struggle to breathe, emergency restrictions kick in and governments exchange blame. Then the season changes, only for the cycle to repeat the following year.

On Thursday, Delhi's air fell into the "Very unhealthy" category, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir, with an average PM2.5 concentration of 157.9 micrograms per cubic meter of air. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an annual safe limit of no more than 5 micrograms.

Studies have shown that exposure to PM2.5 — air particles with a diameter smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream — is associated with an increased incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC), like oral, nasal and throat cancers.

But despite years of attempted interventions, India's capital continues to struggle with the same pollution crisis.

The issue has persisted for years despite public outrage [FILE: November 6, 2025] Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

What is causing the air pollution?

Delhi is not dealing with an unknown problem. There is considerable scientific understanding of its causes.

A 2026 assessment by an expert panel reviewed by the Delhi government identified the major winter contributors of PM2.5 as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road and construction dust, biomass and waste burning, and pollution from neighboring regions.

Sunil Dahiya, founder of the environmental group EnviroCatalysts, said Delhi is part of a larger airshed. On most winter days, more pollution comes into Delhi than is generated inside it, according to the environmentalist.

"Analysis of the government's Decision Support System (DSS) data for winter 2025 found that around 65% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from outside the city and about 35% from sources within it," he told DW, adding that neighboring Noida and Gurugram, which comprise the National Capital Region (NCR), are some of the biggest contributors.

Coordinating action across the NCR, which spans Delhi and parts of three neighboring states, remains a major obstacle.

"This is a shared problem, and no single city can solve it alone," Dahiya said.

Why aren't anti-pollution policies working?

To understand why existing policies have not delivered sustained improvements, Dahiya highlighted the gap between scientific recommendations and state action.

"Scientists have said for over a decade that we need airshed-wide, year-round, source-specific action. What we mostly get is seasonal and reactive," he said.

According to the environmentalist, emergency restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels. Short-term measures such as water sprinklers and smog towers provide little relief, while bigger structural changes are slow to materialize. These include stricter enforcement of industrial emissions, cleaner fuels, expanded public transport, vehicle electrification and viable alternatives to crop burning for farmers.

Delhi has imposed restrictions on vehicles under a certain emission standard [FILE: December 19, 2025] Image: Sunil Ghosh/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

"The science is not the bottleneck. Implementation, regional coordination and political will are," said Dahiya. "Until targets are tied to emission reductions at each source, and someone is held accountable for meeting them, we will keep having the same conversation every November."

Bhavreen Kandhari, co-founder of Warrior Moms, agrees that official responses focus on reacting rather than preventing.

"They allow pollution to occur and then try to clean it up — producing nice photo opportunities of water sprinklers and smog guns, or talking about cloud seeding," Kandhari told DW. "Creating pollution only to clean it up later is a waste of public funds, time, and health."

Kandhari also added that incinerating waste instead of proper waste management has only exacerbated the situation.

The politics of pollution

Another obstacle to a lasting solution has been the political blame game that starts as soon as the air quality worsens.

On Thursday, Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said stubble-burning in the neighboring state of Punjab is contributing to the capital's rising pollution, according to public broadcaster All India Radio. He insisted that in Delhi, construction, vehicle and industrial sources were controlled.

Dahiya agreed that seasonal crop-burning fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana "is an episodic but sharp contributor" which "can tip 'very poor' air into 'severe'" for a few weeks. But it is not the lone contributor.

"Among sources within Delhi, vehicles alone contribute roughly 51-53% of local PM2.5. A large share of winter PM2.5 is also secondary particulate formed from gases like sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia," Dahiya said. "That points straight back to combustion in power plants, industry and transport."

"If stubble burning ended tomorrow, Delhi would still breathe unhealthy air for most of the year," he added.

DW reached out to several Delhi government officials for a response, but received no reply.

What needs to change?

Delhi is also home to millions of people who cannot afford air purifiers and have no escape from the toxic air.

Among them is Deepika, who works as domestic help in an affluent South Delhi neighborhood. She has been coughing for a week.

It is the same every year, she said.

"I have no choice but to bear it for the next few months."

Water sprinklers and smog towers provide some relief but experts say deeper reform is needed [FILE: December 16, 2025] Image: Arun Sankar/AFP

The people DW spoke to point to a common set of priorities: Addressing Delhi's pollution crisis requires year-round pollution control rather than seasonal restrictions, better coordination between governments and stronger enforcement of existing regulations and measurable targets. They say the city needs a sustained clean-air strategy more than another winter emergency plan.

Namrata Yadav is a Delhi resident and the mother of an eight-year-old boy. They both joined protests against air pollution in November. A year later, the problems persist.

"It is exhausting to repeat the same things year after year, only to be dismissed as paranoid or alarmist for demanding something as basic as clean air," she said.

Calling for lasting solutions driven by science, policy and accountability, Yadav said: "We have spent years learning how to live with pollution. It is time we demanded that those responsible learn how to end it."

World.title: Kenya cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to 200 years
World.content:
A court in Kenya has sentenced Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and an adult. He told them to starve themselves to death as part of his apocalyptic religious cult.

Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods.

A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.

Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.

Mombasa High Court Judge Diana Kavedza Mochache delivered the judgment against Mackenzie and his accomplices on October 19 Image: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.

However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.

What was the case about?

While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.

Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.

A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.

They included guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the dead in shallow graves. They all denied the charges, except for one who pleaded guilty and asked for leniency.

Among them was Mackenzie's assistant "pastor," Smart Mwakalama, who was sentenced to 160 years.

Judge Kavedza dismissed the argument from some of the accused that the fact they had lost their own children altered the nature of their involvement in the deaths of others.

More than 60 of the bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, but many of the remains were so decomposed that they could not be identified or claimed.
