Selected Network4 Go content free for One TV Family subscribers

Another key part of the agreement concerns streaming. From 1 December 2026, customers subscribed to One’s TV Family package will be able to access selected content from the Network4 Go streaming service without paying an additional fee.

The companies say the offer will include replays of sports broadcasts from Arena4, Match4 and Max4, around 1,800 hours of additional live sports events annually, Bundesliga match statistics, the 24-hour NFL Network channel, and approximately 600 hours of films and series.

Network4’s sports rights portfolio includes competitions such as the Premier League, Bundesliga, Serie A, NFL, MotoGP and UFC.

However, the announcement does not specify exactly which titles and features from the full Network4 Go catalogue will be available to One subscribers. The companies also said that the Network4 streaming app is expected to become part of One’s streaming line-up at a later date, although no timetable has been announced.

World.title: Hungary to launch new environmental watchdog in 2027, battery industry oversight among its key tasks
World.content:
Hungary will set up a new national environmental authority on 1 January 2027, under a government decree published in the official gazette Magyar Közlöny on Thursday.

The National Environmental Supervisory Authority will operate as a central budgetary body under the minister responsible for the living environment, headquartered in Budapest. It will be established by being spun off from the ministry and comprise a central organisation and territorial Environmental Supervisory Authorities, whose decisions may be appealed, where the law allows, to the central authority at second instance.

The new body will handle environmental, waste management, nature conservation, genetic technology, animal welfare, forestry, climate protection, and water management and water protection authority and administrative tasks nationwide, with the declared aim of creating a more unified professional practice and strengthening the protection of environmental values.

It receives a special mandate on batteries: permitting and supervision related to battery manufacturing, its associated activities and facilities, and the handling of battery waste may be transferred to the new authority’s nationwide competence, so that the professional expertise and authority action needed to police the industry are concentrated in a single organisation.

According to the decree’s justification, the qualitative and quantitative expansion of battery manufacturing and the battery waste it generates present new environmental protection tasks. On these, the authority is to cooperate with the other state bodies involved in overseeing the battery industry, including the metrology and technical safety, industrial safety, fire protection, market surveillance and consumer protection authorities.

The reorganisation will happen in two stages: the central authority and the Budapest Environmental Supervisory Authority are established on 1 January 2027, and the units of the government offices dealing with environmental, waste management, nature conservation, forestry, water management and related tasks will be merged into it on 1 July 2027. Staff employment relationships, property rights, movable and immovable assets, equipment and infrastructure tied to those tasks will transfer to the successor organisation.

World.title: Fidesz MP banned from Parliament for 3 sitting days over repeated disruptions
World.content:
Hungarian MP János Pócs has been banned from entering Parliament for three sitting days because of repeated disruptive behaviour, House Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer announced. The decision follows several verbal warnings and a written reprimand, which she said had failed to change the Fidesz politician’s conduct.

Forsthoffer said in a Facebook post that Pócs had repeatedly disregarded his parliamentary duties, broken the rules and disrupted the work of the National Assembly. He received the decision on Thursday morning and has eight days to appeal to Parliament’s Immunity Committee.

The ban means that Pócs cannot enter the Parliament building or its offices during the three sitting days. However, he may still take part in secret ballots in a room designated by the Speaker.

From shouting to filming with illuminated glasses

Forsthoffer said that MPs are both entitled and obliged to attend parliamentary sessions and votes, take an active part in the Assembly’s work and help ensure its effective operation – or at least refrain from disrupting it.

She listed several examples of Pócs’s behaviour, including shouting from the floor, filming during sessions, recording with illuminated glasses, playing bingo, displaying signs deemed offensive to the dignity of Parliament, deliberately reading books and newspapers as a provocation, drawing, straying from the subject under discussion and loudly talking to people in the gallery while repeatedly entering and leaving the chamber.

The latest incident took place on 3 November, when Pócs missed an electronic vote. According to Forsthoffer, he then caused an uproar by attempting, after some hesitation, to cast his vote verbally once the voting period had ended.

Pócs reportedly said he had not intended to mislead the chair but admitted that he had not known what was happening in the chamber at the time.

Forsthoffer argued that the incident was unacceptable, particularly from an experienced MP serving his fifth parliamentary term. She said Pócs should have followed the displays in the chamber and the information shown on his own voting device, as well as the words of the presiding officer, all of which made it clear that he had missed the deadline.

“He simply was not paying attention,” she wrote.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Previous warnings failed to change his conduct

The Speaker said the incident disrupted both the parliamentary session and the work of the person chairing it, and was not an isolated case.

She recalled that she had issued Pócs with a written warning on 20 October, expressing her trust that she would not have to impose sanctions on him again. He had also received numerous verbal warnings and had previously been deprived of the right to speak during sessions.

Forsthoffer said she chose a three-sitting-day ban in accordance with the principle of proportionality, noting that Pócs’s actions had not invalidated the Assembly’s decision.

Under the rules outlined by the Speaker, an MP banned by the Speaker cannot enter the Parliament building or its offices, while an MP excluded from a session may still enter Parliament but cannot participate in the sitting, except during votes. The maximum ban imposed by the Speaker is 15 calendar days or six sitting days.

World.title: Police chase ends in crash on M0 after driver enters motorway against traffic in Hungary – VIDEO
World.content:
A dramatic police chase ended in a crash on the M0 motorway near Gyál on Wednesday night after a driver fleeing officers entered the road in the wrong direction. Police fired shots at the car’s tyres during the pursuit, while two passengers were later taken to hospital.

According to the police, officers tried to stop the driver in Dány on the evening of 4 November after discovering that his vehicle did not have compulsory third-party motor insurance. The man ignored their instructions and drove off, prompting a pursuit through several settlements.

Police fired shots at the fleeing car

After repeated warnings failed to stop the driver, one of the officers fired shots at the vehicle’s tyres. No one was injured during the use of firearms, although the shots caused the tyres to deflate.

The driver nevertheless continued and entered the M0 motorway travelling against the direction of traffic. He eventually lost control of the vehicle and crashed into the safety barrier. Officers arrested him at the scene.

Two other people were travelling in the car. Ambulance crews took both passengers to hospital. Police have not released further details, citing the ongoing investigation.

Witnesses describe a near-disaster on the M0

Footage of the incident, which reportedly took place at around 10 pm near Gyál on the M3-bound side of the M0, was shared on TikTok. A witness quoted by BpiAutósok said that electronic signs above the motorway had already been warning drivers about a vehicle approaching in the wrong direction several kilometres earlier.

Another witness described how close the incident came to causing a serious collision. The driver of a lorry reportedly noticed the oncoming car just as he was allowing another vehicle to enter the outer lane. He swerved back and switched on his hazard lights.

Several motorists then braked sharply and tried to avoid the car. According to the witness, the tyres of some vehicles were smoking as drivers took evasive action. The commenter said it was only thanks to luck that a major pile-up did not occur.

Police have not confirmed these witness accounts in their statement and have declined to provide further information while the investigation is underway.

World.title: Rector of major Hungarian university resigns: Trust issues with governing board in the background
World.content:
Béla Merkely, rector of Budapest’s Semmelweis University, has announced that he will step down on 1 January 2027, citing a breakdown in trust with the board of trustees of the foundation that maintains the institution. He has led Hungary’s leading medical university since 2018, overseeing significant improvements in its international rankings.

Merkely announced his decision on Thursday after presenting the university Senate with an assessment of his eight and a half years in office. According to a statement published on the university’s website, the Senate unanimously approved the evaluation of his work.

Rector highlights university’s achievements

Merkely said the university had fulfilled its commitments in education, research and development, and patient care during his leadership. He also highlighted its work during the COVID-19 pandemic and said it had since become Hungary’s largest healthcare provider.

Among the achievements he listed were Semmelweis University’s rise to become one of the world’s top 250 universities and its position as the leading higher education institution in Central and Eastern Europe. Both Hungarian and international student numbers had also reached record levels, he said. The rector additionally pointed to changes in the university’s education system and major infrastructure developments.

If you missed it: Hungary’s Semmelweis University breaks into world’s top 250 after major leap in global rankings

Merkely has formally submitted his resignation to the foundation’s board of trustees. In his letter, he said he was stepping down with effect from 1 January 2027 because of trust-related difficulties with the board, in order to ensure the university’s continued development.

He added that he would continue to fulfil his duties until his departure and ensure a smooth and lawful transition. His resignation must be forwarded to the President of Hungary through the minister responsible for education and child affairs, in accordance with the relevant procedures.

Merkely’s current term was originally due to run until June 2028. He was re-elected in 2023 after winning the university’s rector election by a substantial margin.

Magyar and Orbán react to the resignation

The announcement prompted sharply contrasting reactions from Prime Minister Péter Magyar and former prime minister Viktor Orbán, who now leads the opposition Fidesz party.

Magyar welcomed the departure in a social media post, writing: “The cleansing fire is advancing step by step in higher education, too.”

Orbán, however, described Merkely’s departure as a major loss for Hungarian medicine, rejecting Magyar’s characterisation. “Driving Béla Merkely out is not a cleansing fire, but a huge loss for Hungarian medicine. Thank you for everything, Professor!” he wrote.

Merkely has also faced scrutiny over a potential conflict of interest. Earlier reports revealed that he had held an ownership stake in a company belonging to his son while it received public funding through tenders involving the university he led. An investigation was subsequently launched on suspicion of mismanagement, according to Hungarian media reports. Merkely later left the company.

World.title: Turkey Arrests Former Minister Over Stock Market Fraud Scandal
World.content:
A court in Istanbul on Friday ordered the arrest of Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a former minister and deputy chair of Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, over her alleged role in a major stock market financial fraud.

The Istanbul Prosecutor’s Office accused Kaya of “being a member of an organised crime group and violating stock market law”.

Her husband, Ilyas Kaya, and a former chair of the Capital Markets Board, Ibrahim Omer Gonul, were given a travel ban but not arrested.

Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, who was family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned in September as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling AKP after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

She is accused of illegally profiting through share-price manipulation after she received 2.17 billion Turkish lira (about 38.4 million euros) after reportedly investing 163 million lira (about 2.7 million euros) in an investment fund.

The couple deny wrongdoing. They have transferred some of the profits to an account designated by the banking regulators.

The AKP and the government welcomed the arrest order as proof of their good governance.

“We move forward by renewing ourselves! We are constantly reborn. We part ways with those who do wrong and those who succumb to their own desires, and we continue on our path stronger than before,” Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek wrote on X after Sayan Kaya’s arrest on Friday.

The investigation has already resulted in more than 100 detentions while Turkey’s Capital Markets Board has ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds managed by seven portfolio management companies.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. A Turkish television channel put the total number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya comes from a family with experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Serbia’s Anti-Terrorism Unit Chief Detained Over Alleged Abuse of Protesters
World.content:
A court in Belgrade on Friday ordered up to 30 days of detention for nine current and former employees of Serbia’s Interior Ministry, including the commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Igor Zmiric, over allegations of abusing and torturing students and others inside the government building following protests in August 2025.

According to the court, the nine suspects were remanded in custody over concerns that they could influence witnesses and obstruct criminal proceedings. The court also cited the seriousness of the alleged offence and the public concern it had caused, which could jeopardise the fair conduct of the proceedings.

The suspects are accused of jointly committing the criminal offence of abuse and torture.

According to the prosecution, the suspects used force and threats to inflict pain and suffering on students and other people in the government building’s garage between 10.30 p.m. on August 14 and 1 a.m. the following morning, with the aim of obtaining information, intimidating and unlawfully punishing them.

At the time of the offence, they were working as officers of the JZO, a police unit used to protect high-ranking state officials and major government buildings.

The suspects were arrested earlier this week. Among them is Milan Vukovic, a retired JZO officer who is now acting director of the detention facility where former JZO chief Marko Kricak is being held.

Kricak, who headed the unit at the time of the alleged abuse, has also been arrested, but in connection with a separate investigation into a murder in Belgrade.

During the mass anti-government protests of the past two years, some protesters have accused Kricak of using excessive force. Student Nikolina Sindjelic alleged that Kricak had threatened her with rape while she was detained in the garage beneath the government building in August 2025.

At least 15 people were detained in the garage beneath the government building on the night of August 14, 2025, amid anti-government protests, BIRN reported.

BIRN obtained testimonies given to prosecutors by four detainees and interviewed five others, who described being beaten, threatened with sexual violence and death, and having their personal belongings destroyed. Rights groups Amnesty International and Civil Rights Defenders warned that the alleged treatment could amount to torture and violate international law.

At the time, the Interior Ministry rejected the allegations, insisting that the officers had acted in accordance with the law. Then President Aleksandar Vucic later announced that the ministry’s internal affairs unit would investigate the allegations made by Sindjelic.

At the time of BIRN’s investigation, it was not clear whether the promised internal probe had been carried out.

World.title: Albania’s ‘Coordinator’? The Rapid Rise and Sudden Fall of Ergys Agasi
World.content:
On the afternoon of August 26, as the sun was setting over Durres beach, police in several unmarked vehicles pulled over a black Audi on the southern outskirts of the Albanian port city. Inside the car was Ergys Agasi, a businessman and former official at the environment ministry who had been on the run for the past eight months.

In video released by the police, 39-year-old Agasi is seen in a white T-shirt and shorts, hands cuffed behind his back, head bowed.

Albania’s Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, accuses Agasi of leading an organised criminal group that manipulated public tenders linked to the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, sometimes through violence.

Less than a month after his arrest, investigators moved against the head of the State Intelligence Service, SHISH, Vlora Hyseni, accusing her of aiding Agasi to evade arrest and providing him with classified information. Hyseni was placed under house arrest and dismissed from SHISH.

World.title: Serbian President’s Controversial Last-Minute Pardons Face Legal Challenges
World.content:
This Friday, a court in Belgrade was supposed to hear the verdict in the case against a man who rammed a car into a 20-year-old female student, Sonja Ponjavic, who was blocking a traffic intersection during an anti-government protest in the Serbian capital in January 2025.

The blockade was one of many rallies organised by students in memory of victims of the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster – an incident that transformed Serbian politics and ultimately led to the ousting of the government led by Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party at last month’s elections.

However, now the driver might not be punished for hitting the student because Vucic pardoned him in one of his last actions as President before stepping down to run for the premiership in the elections.

World.title: Transnistria’s Separatist Leader Decorated by Moscow, Denounced by Moldova
World.content:
In a ceremony at the Kremlin on Wednesday, Russian President Vladmir Putin formally pinned the Order of Honour award on the lapel of Vadim Krasnoselsky, the leader of Transnistria - a separatist region of Moldova where Moscow has maintained a military presence since the Soviet bloc disintegrated.

Putin said the decoration was awarded to recognise Krasnoselsky’s efforts to "strengthen ties" with Russia and amidst "pressure" from the West. Moldova is seeking to join the EU, but separatist Transnistria remains a potentially disruptive Russian lever of influence that Moscow wants to preserve.

“Despite difficult conditions and attempts at external pressure, the republic [Transnistria], under his leadership, is developing consistently. Its inhabitants, who are of various nationalities, defend their rights and interests together, uphold the historical truth and preserve the Russian language,” Putin explained.

Located on Moldova’s border with Ukraine, and home to 1,600 Russian troops, Transnistria is strategically important for the Russian leader. Speaking in Moscow, Krasnoselsky seemed happy to fall into line.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Frenzied Searching as Hungary Opens Communist Secret Service Files
World.content:
Poland’s constitutional crisis enters new phase; suspicious activity on Russian border

Poland’s top court, which rules on whether laws comply with the constitution and has been at the centre of the country’s decade-long rule-of-law dispute, began operating this week under new, contested leadership. The move has further escalated the confrontation between PM Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki. Tusk’s governing Civic Coalition (KO) argues the intervention to replace the Constitutional Tribunal’s leadership was necessary to restore the court’s functioning. On Monday, interim head justice Anna Korwin-Piotrowska said the Tribunal had a backlog of 1,171 cases, promising that they would now be expedited. The following day, she convened an assembly of eight judges despite a boycott by the court’s suspended president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski. The judges approved the Tribunal’s 2027 budget, initiated disciplinary proceedings against the suspended leadership, and declared a quorum had been reached, allowing them to take decisions. The presidential administration disputes that interpretation, insisting that ten judges are required. Nevertheless, on Thursday, parliamentary speaker Wlodzimierz Czarzasty forwarded the assembly’s budget resolution to a parliamentary committee. Meanwhile, prosecutors are investigating an alleged assault on two judges during a confrontation at the court on the night of October 30. Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek has also sought to lift the immunity of the suspended leadership over allegations including obstruction of judicial duties. The crisis spilled over into Tuesday’s National Security Council meeting, originally convened to discuss defence priorities and a US military presence. Nawrocki accused Tusk of responsibility for the turmoil. Tusk responded by offering private talks this week. On Thursday, Deputy PM Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said he would press on with plans for a constitutional reset. The model would retire all sitting Tribunal judges, replace them through a three-fifths parliamentary vote rather than a simple majority, and introduce a four-year cooling-off period for former politicians seeking judicial appointments. Parliamentary speaker Czarzasty said he doubts constitutional amendments could secure the necessary majority before the 2027 election. For now, the court is exercising authority without resolving the basic question of who legitimately controls it.

Tusk said on Tuesday that border guards had spotted suspicious activity along the country’s border with Russia overnight, prompting authorities to deploy additional security forces. Several people carrying flashlights were seen on the Russian side of the border, although no attempt to cross into Poland was reported. The PM said when NATO’s top military commander in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, visited Warsaw in October he had warned of a possible escalation this autumn. Meanwhile, allied intelligence has suggested that incidents, including “the incursion of armed individuals into Polish territory”, could occur in the first half of November. Police, border guards and counterterrorism units had been reinforced in the country’s northeast. Meanwhile, Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) detained six people suspected of working for Russian intelligence and illegally supplying military components to Moscow, authorities announced on Thursday. Four suspects, including a Russian woman and three Poles, have been charged with espionage and remanded in custody for three months. The remaining two face non-custodial restrictions. All six are suspected of involvement in an organised criminal group. According to the ABW, the group allegedly smuggled significant quantities of components used to manufacture ammunition and weapons systems, potentially strengthening Russia’s military capabilities. Investigators also suspect violations of export controls on strategically sensitive goods and technologies. The investigation remains ongoing. Between October 21 and November 2, security officers searched 21 locations across three northern and western Polish provinces.

World.title: Romania Restarts Nuclear Reactor as Danube River Levels Recover
World.content:
Romania on Thursday began to reconnect one of the two reactors at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant to the national grid after water levels in the Danube rose sufficiently to meet the conditions for safe operation, the state-owned operator Nuclearelectrica said.

The reactor, Unit 1, is expected to return to full capacity by November 7.

“Resuming the operation of Unit 1 is an important step towards ensuring the country’s energy security and the stability of the national power system,” Nuclearelectrica’s CEO Mihai Gioara said.

Romania has been facing its most difficult energy situation in decades after both Cernavoda reactors shut down this summer because of exceptionally low levels in the Danube, which threatened the supply of cooling water. Unit 1 was taken offline on July 28, followed by Unit 2 on August 13.

The shutdowns reduced Romania’s domestic electricity production and have increased its reliance on coal-fired power plants, hydropower and electricity imports, putting pressure on wholesale and consumer prices.

The two reactors normally generate around one-fifth of Romania’s electricity needs, making the prolonged shutdown a significant blow to energy security.

Unit 2 remains offline, its restart depending on a more sustained recovery in Danube water levels.

Romania therefore remains under pressure, and the government has extended a state of alert over energy security through November amid warnings that electricity reserves could become insufficient during peak-demand periods.

Authorities have ruled out consumption restrictions but warn that electricity bills could rise as Romania continues to rely on imports to cover part of its domestic demand.

World.title: Albania Fines 83 Protesters Under New Laws Targeting Anti-Govt Rallies
World.content:
Albanian police on Thursday said they issued 31 fines after a protest on Wednesday night – adding to a total of 83 over the past few days under new legislation intended to curb the unrest that has gripped the capital Tirana.

Police said they penalised “citizens who blocked the road and obstructed the movement of vehicles despite repeated calls from police officers over a loudspeaker”.

Each was issued an administrative fine of 5,000 Albanian lek (55 euros), police added.

The new legislation was introduced by embattled Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama after months of daily, peaceful anti-government protests turned violent last month. It went into force on October 28.

Rama described it as a “[legislative] package against violence and urban anarchy”. Among the measures are fines that can be imposed when protesters do not comply with police orders.

Rama also said fines would be levied for “participation in an unauthorised gathering and failure to comply with calls to disperse” as well as for people who conceal their identities using masks.

“Failure to comply with an order to disperse and the concealment of one’s identity shall be punishable by a fine of up to 5,000 euros for each participant,” he announced. Obstructing traffic carries a fine of 55 euros.

The police imposed the first 55-euro fines on 16 protesters on Tuesday, followed by another 36 on Wednesday and 31 more on Thursday.

“Yesterday I was exercising my democratic right to protest and arrived at a peaceful gathering in front of the prime minister’s office, as we have done for over 150 days,”

Mei Seva, a photographer and activist, told BIRN that she was fined on Wednesday after “exercising my democratic right to protest and arrived at a peaceful gathering in front of the prime minister’s office, as we have done for over 150 days”.

Seva said that as she went to get a snack nearby, a masked policeman without a visible badge number asked for her identity card.

“After taking a photo of my ID, they searched through photos on their phone until they found what they were looking for and proceeded to issue a 5,000 lek [55 euro] fine. When asked the reason, they told me it was because I had blocked the road,” she explained.

“This intimidation tactic is a desperate attempt by the government to hold on to power despite nearly five months of protests demanding their resignation,” she added.

On Tuesday, 15 civil society organisations urged parliament to block implementation of the legislation targeting public gatherings, describing it as unjustified and as a violation of constitutional rights and freedoms.

The legislative package includes amendments to the Law on Assemblies, the creation of a special electronic registry for people suspected of engaging in violence, and an act about compensation for damages caused during protests.

NGOs agree that violence must be condemned and investigated but have expressed concern that such measures could lead to the indiscriminate penalisation of all protesters.

“The violent actions of specific individuals cannot be used to broadly restrict citizens’ right to peaceful assembly, nor to impose collective responsibility upon protest participants or organisers,” the 15 NGOs’ statement said.

The demonstrations in Albania began on May 31 in opposition to a proposed luxury tourist resort in a protected environmental area in ​​Zvernec, a project linked to US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. They then widened to demanded the resignation of Rama’s government, who they accuse of corrupt governance and economic mismanagement.

In October, the protests took a violent turn, with daily clashes between police and young demonstrators. Rama has refused to step down.

World.title: Wanderlust: Croatian Islands Most Desirable Region in Europe
World.content:
November 6, 2026 – The season may be over, but the recognition keeps on coming. Croatian islands win big at the prestigious Wanderlist Reader Travel Awards.

Various studies cannot agree on how many there are exactly – some say 1185, others 1244, or even 1246 – but one thing is for sure – Croatian islands are gorgeous, a fact once more reinforced at the 2026 Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards in London earlier this week.

In the category Most Desirable Region (Europe), Croatian islands came away with the Gold Award, accompanied by this glowing tribute:

The rise of the Croatian Islands isn’t about riding a hot trend; it’s more a story of travellers simply discovering what’s there for themselves. With millions of visitors a year heading to Croatia’s Adriatic coast, those escaping its busier spots are realising how much more there is to see offshore. Beyond well-known Hvar, Brač and Korčula lie quiet, car-free communities such as Silba; incredible nature on Mljet, whose entire north-western end is a national park; pristine night skies on Lastovo, a candidate to become an official Dark Sky Park; and history aplenty in island-bound, UNESCO-listed Trogir. Even getting around invites reflection, with sailing trips from Vis aboard traditional sardine-fishing boats offering a recipe for slowing down.

Certain islands such as Hvar are no stranger to international recognition, having also been voted among the best islands in Europe in the 2026 Conde Nast Readers Traveler Awards, home to the first public theatre in all of Europe, and one where no island has more UNESCO heritage. But this was an award for all Croatia’s islands, 50 of which are inhabited, and which provide much of the country’s tourism draw.

While all the islands may look similar on the surface, there is an incredible diversity once you scratch the surface, which reveal some rather surprising facts, many of which I have summarised in this video below, 25 Things You Would Not Expect to FInd on a Croatian Island. These include the first place in the world to abolish slavery (Korcula), the birth of cricket in mainland Europe (Vis), and the birthplace of organise tourism in Europe (Hvar).

World.title: Eurowings to Keep Split Connected to Five German Cities This Winter
World.content:
November the 6th, 2026 – Eurowings will keep Split connected to give German cities this winter. The airline is otherwise one of the airport’s most important airlines.

Eurowings will keep Split connected with five German cities even during the winter months. As Slobodna Dalmacija reports, Eurowings is one of the most important airlines at Split Airport. According to the announced winter flight schedule for the 2026/2027 season, the German carrier plans a total of 130 rotations on the routes between Split and Germany, with an estimated capacity of more than 45,300 seats, reported the specialised portal Croatia aviation.

This is important news not only for Split Airport, but also for the entire Dalmatian tourism sector, which in recent years has been trying to reduce the pronounced seasonality and extend the period of operations outside the main summer months. Maintaining direct air links with Germany opens additional possibilities for the arrival of guests in the period when Split traditionally sinks into winter sleep, and the city centre becomes almost ghostly empty, with the exception during Advent. One of the main problems of the high seasonality of tourism is the lack of flights in the winter period, so this announcement from Eurowings also opens the possibility of the arrival of a larger number of guests from Germany, which is particularly dear to Croatians, from where a large number of tourists traditionally come to us, but still most often in the heart of the summer season. This is an opportunity to show them that we have something to offer even during winter.

stuttgart as the most important connection

Eurowings will during the winter operate on five routes from Germany, to Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Cologne, Berlin and Hamburg. Nevertheless, the traffic will not be evenly distributed throughout the entire winter period. The largest number of rotations is planned on the Split – Stuttgart route, 60 of them, which makes up 46.2 percent of the total number. Düsseldorf follows with 28 rotations and Cologne with 26. These three routes together make up as much as 88 percent of the total planned traffic.

The routes from Berlin and Hamburg will have a significantly shorter period of operation. From Berlin ten rotations are planned, and from Hamburg six are planned. What’s particularly significant is the fact that the route to Stuttgart will operate continuously throughout the entire winter, while Düsseldorf and Cologne will have certain interruptions. Thereby Split is ensured at least one stable direct connection with the German market even in the period of the lowest tourist demand. How significant the German market is for Split is shown by the data of Split Airport. During 2025, passengers from Germany achieved 796,707 passenger arrivals and departures, that is, they made up 20.5 percent of the total traffic of the airport. Eurowings was in the same year the third largest carrier in Split, with approximately 355 thousand passengers transported, almost 55 thousand more than the year before.

Germany is at the same time one of the most important source markets of Croatian tourism. According to data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, German tourists during 2025 achieved 21 million overnight stays in Croatia, that is, almost a quarter of all overnight stays of foreign guests.

For Dalmatia as whole, it’s particularly important that the interest of German guests does not have to stop with the end of summer. A city like Split has the potential to attract visitors throughout the whole year thanks to Diocletian’s Palace, cultural and historical contents, gastronomy, excursions, active holidays and the proximity of islands and other Dalmatian destinations.

a prerequisite for extending the season

The announced capacity of more than 45,000 seats doesn’t mean that so many passengers will actually arrive in Split, but it is an important prerequisite for maintaining tourist traffic outside the summer months. Direct flights, namely, reduce the time and costs of travel and facilitate the organisation of shorter holidays and weekend visits, which in the time of a hectic lifestyle is very important. This is also important for Split hoteliers, private renters, restaurants, tourist guides and excursion organisers. Every additional guest in the winter months contributes to the filling of accommodation capacities and the maintenance of business, which without such demand would be concentrated almost exclusively on a few summer months.

How pronounced this problem is is also shown by the Eurostat data according to which Croatia in 2025 was among the most seasonal tourist destinations of the European Union: as many as 54.5 percent of all overnight stays were achieved during July and August. Precisely because of that the development of air connections during winter has a wider meaning than the mere number of flights. Nevertheless, air routes by themselves cannot extend the season. Open hotels, year-round offer of restaurants and cultural contents, quality excursions and coordinated promotion of the destination on source markets are needed.

Eurowings’ winter schedule is therefore a positive signal for Split tourism, but also a reminder of how important it is to develop contents because of which guests will come to Split also in November, January or February, and not only during the months of July and August.

World.title: Croatian Defence Minister: Vučić Was Southeastern Europe’s Biggest Issue
World.content:
November the 6th, 2026 – Croatian Defence Minister Ivan Anušić has told Americans during his visit to the USA that Serbia under Aleksandar Vučić was southeastern Europe’s biggest issue.

Defence Minister Ivan Anušić stated during an official visit to the United States of America that Serbia under the leadership of Aleksandar Vučić was the biggest source of instability in southeastern Europe. Index reports that he added that the new Serbian authorities must very clearly distance themselves from the Greater Serbian policies of the 1990s. Anušić was recently at Harvard University upon the invitation of the former US ambassador to Croatia Nathalie Rayes. At the Belfer Centre for Science and International Affairs which took place there, he participated in a seminar on the security situation across southeastern Europe, where he commented on the recent elections in Serbia in which Vučić’s regime was finally overthrown.

serbia’s new leadership must make a clean break from the greater serbian policies of the 1990s

In his presentation, the defence minister emphasised that the new authorities in Belgrade, which are yet to be formed after the parliamentary elections held on 25 October, must renounce the previous political direction if they want peace and cooperation in the region. “Serbia under the leadership of Aleksandar Vučić was the biggest source of instability in southeastern Europe. In the interest of peace and stability, the new Serbian authorities must very clearly distance themselves from the Greater Serbian policies of Aleksandar Vučić, that is, from those of Slobodan Milošević from the 1990s,” Anušić stated, speaking about the political changes that in addition to Serbia also include the recent change of government in neighbouring Hungary.

security in bosnia and herzegovina is crucial

Speaking about Croatia’s specific role, Anušić pointed out that the country within the European Union and NATO is a guardian of stability that supports the Euro-Atlantic path of neighbouring countries. In doing so he particularly emphasised the importance of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the continuation of the American military presence in Kosovo as part of the KFOR mission.

“For Croatia the stability of southeastern Europe is of national interest, and especially the preservation of stability and peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is of key importance for the security of our entire neighbourhood,” the minister said. Anušić also commented on the ongoing war in Ukraine, emphasising the need for the continuation of military and political assistance to Kyiv and recalling that Ukraine with its defence is already almost in the fifth year keeping the conflict away from the borders of the rest of the continent.

World.title: Finance Minister Claims Inflation in Croatia Will Drop in 2027
World.content:
November the 6th, 2026 – Finance Minister Tomislav Ćorić has revealed that he expects inflation in Croatia will drop at the beginning of 2027.

Finance Minister Tomislav Ćorić has stated that he expects the inflation rate in Croatia to fall rapidly in 2027, adding that he believes it would already be below two percent now if the rise in energy prices were excluded from the calculation. Index reports that Minister Ćorić said the above at the traditional consultation “Economic Policy of Croatia in 2027” held in Opatija. “We absolutely expect a slowdown in inflation in 2027. Our projections clearly show that. Compared to the projected 4.5 percent average for this year, we expect a rapid drop during 2027,” the finance minister stated.

he hopes for calm regarding the strait of hormuz

Responding to journalists’ questions, Tomislav Ćorić expressed hope that on the global scene there will be forces, understanding and goodwill to calm the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and to re-establish the normal flow of oil and oil derivatives, which would then also affect the reduction of prices on world markets.

“Of course, we can’t have any influence over that; the influence of the European Union as a whole in that acute crisis is minimal. I believe that the coming period will bring calm, and whether the result of these elections that we had the opportunity to follow yesterday in the USA will also influence that, we will yet see,” Ćorić said. He recalled that the relevant data indicate that the energy crisis caused by the conflict between the USA and Iran affected the share of energy products in total inflation, because of which he assessed that the CBS estimate is expected.

CBS data shows that the estimated annual inflation rate for energy is 20.7 percent, while the rate for food, drinks and tobacco amounted to 0.2 percent back in October. “The energy products segment in the structure of inflation is very dominant. In the other product segments we do not have significant inflationary movements and that exclusively indicates the fact that the domestic components of inflation at this moment are under control. If there were not this shock that we have in the part of energy prices, inflation in the Republic of Croatia at this moment would actually be at a level below 2 percent,” the finance minister said.

He explained that the gradual de-escalation of the conflict that he expects over the coming months should consequently bring a reduction in energy prices. In turn, that should lead to a significant drop in inflation in Croatia at the beginning of 2027.

the government will continue to “protect” people from inflation

He stated that in 2027, the Croatian Government will take every possible measure to try to maintain the combination of economic growth and fiscal discipline. “That combination over the past decade has brought very good results for Croatia and we’ll continue going in the same direction,” he said, adding that economic growth next year in Croatia will be significantly above the European average. He emphasised that in the next multiannual European financial framework, the government’s primary focus will be on increasing the competitiveness and productivity of the Croatian economy. He also announced that the government will continue to “protect the public” from the consequences of inflation.

World.title: Croatia Deports 36 Egyptian Nationals on a Special Flight to Cairo
World.content:
November the 6th, 2026 – Croatia deports 36 Egyptian nationals on a special flight from Zagreb to Cairo. All of the individuals in question were in Croatia illegally, with some involved in criminal proceedings.

A special deportation flight left Zagreb for Cairo this week, carrying 36 Egyptian nationals who were illegally staying in the country. Index reports that among those deported were also individuals against whom criminal proceedings were conducted surrounding human smuggling, the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) reported.

The deportation was carried out with the escort of Croatian police officers, officials of the European agency Frontex and an official Arabic language interpreter. The total cost of the flight amounts to 77,350 euros. The money was secured from the European Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF), the MUP states. From the MUP they explain that they decided on a special flight because such a method of deportation is cheaper and enables a faster return of a larger number of people.

When deportations using regular passenger flights are carried out, due to security rules, for one person it is often necessary to ensure the escort of two or three police officers. If all 36 Egyptian citizens had been returned in that way, the cost would have amounted to around 144,000 euros, almost twice as much as for the organised flight.

The Croatian police have since stated that such a method of deportation enables a faster return of persons who are illegally staying in Croatia, lowers overall costs and ensures the more efficient use of police officers. The Police Directorate plans to organise special flights in the future as well, especially when a larger number of citizens of the same country need to be returned. Such flights will be organised when it is assessed that they are cheaper and simpler to implement than individual deportations by regular passenger flights.

From the MUP, they emphasise that all procedures are carried out with full respect for both legal and security rules. According to MUP’s data, this year, Croatia has returned a total of 6,885 people through official return and transfer procedures. At the same time, under the so-called Dublin procedure, by which it is determined which European country is responsible for examining the asylum application, it has officially accepted 1,005 migrants.

World.title: Hajduk’s Perfect Conference League Start Ends With 1-0 Loss to Lincoln
World.content:
Hajduk suffered their first European defeat of the season on Thursday night, beaten 1-0 by Gibraltar champions Lincoln Red Imps in the third round of the Conference League league phase. The only goal came in the 89th minute, when a header struck the post and rebounded into the net off Dennis Hadžikadunić.

It was a jarring result after Hajduk’s perfect start, with wins over Ajax and Thun. Lincoln, who had yet to take a point in the competition, won without registering a single shot on target.

Lineups

Lincoln Red Imps: Hankins; Nano, Rutjens, Cardozo, Eersteling; García, Mandi, Lopes, Torrilla, Toledano; Gómez

Hajduk: Silić; Hrgović, Hadžikadunić, Van Hoorenbeeck, Acapandié; Fayad, Del Moral; Šotiček, Dalisson, Bamba; Šego

Hajduk were without Adrion Pajaziti, Ivica Ivušić, Leander Dendoncker and Roko Brajković, while Lincoln had a full squad.

Match report

Hajduk quickly took control with a high press that forced plenty of errors from the hosts. The fast pitch caught Hajduk out at times. In the 10th minute, Bamba tried to send Šotiček through, but the pass ran away from the winger. Three minutes later, Bamba won the ball and charged towards goal, only for his attempted pass across to Šotiček to be blocked.

Dalisson went close in the 17th minute with a shot from around 20 meters that flew just past the bar. Lincoln’s first chance forward came in the 22nd minute, when Silić comfortably gathered Nano’s cross. Šego then tried one of his trademark free kicks from a tight angle in the 27th minute, but sent it over.

By the half-hour mark, the game was being played almost entirely in Lincoln’s half, and Rutjens was booked in the 30th minute. The hosts’ first real counter-attack came a minute later, but Acapandié reacted well to clear in his own box.

Hajduk’s best move of the half came in the 40th minute. Šego headed down a long ball, and Dalisson met it with a good volley, but again it went over. Just before the break, a run from Bamba through the Lincoln defense ended with a Fayad shot that was blocked. Hajduk dominated the half but went in at 0-0 without a single shot on target.

Neither side made changes at the break. Kike Gómez was booked in the 49th minute for another heavy challenge, and two minutes later, Lincoln right-back Eersteling landed awkwardly on his shoulder and needed treatment. He eventually made way for Álvarez.

Lincoln began to find openings. In the 53rd minute, Toledano was well placed around ten meters out, but Fayad nicked the ball off him before he could shoot. Šotiček was booked for diving in the 58th minute, and Bamba followed five minutes later for a foul on Gómez. In the 64th minute, Hajduk survived two dangerous moments. First, a Lincoln player missed the target from close range, then Silić came off his line in time to cut out a dangerous pass.

García made a double change in the 68th minute, bringing on Martin for Šego and Marešić for Van Hoorenbeeck. Dalisson tried his luck from distance again in the 72nd minute without hitting the target, and three minutes later, Hajduk wasted their clearest chance yet. Šotiček was left alone ten meters out after a rebound, with time to pick his spot, but failed to find the target.

Livaja replaced Dalisson in the 76th minute, and Hadžikadunić sent an overhead kick high over the crossbar two minutes later. In the 80th minute, Torrilla was booked for stopping Šotiček on a three-on-two counter, and Marešić put the resulting free kick over.

Hajduk’s only shot on target came in the 85th minute. Livaja chested down a ball from a corner and struck it at goal. García then sent on Huram and Šutalo for Šotiček and Bamba.

Then came the blow. In the 89th minute, Nano swung in a free kick, and Christian Rutjens rose highest in the Hajduk box. His header came back off the post, struck Hadžikadunić and went in. Six minutes of stoppage time were added, and Hajduk threw everything forward, but there was no way back.

It was Lincoln’s first win of the Conference League campaign, played in front of 1,309 spectators. Hajduk stay on six points, and in both previous seasons under the new format, seven points have been enough to finish in the top 24. They host Sint-Truiden on November 26 and Nordsjælland on December 10, before closing the league phase away to Midtjylland on December 17.

World.title: British Arrivals in Croatia Set to Increase in 2027 Following WTM London
World.content:
November the 5th, 2026 – British arrivals in Croatia are looking very likely to increase throughout 2027 as the country wows at the WTM in London.

The World Travel Market (WTM) is traditionally held in London at the beginning of November, and it’s one of the largest and most important tourism fairs in the world. Naturally, the Croatian National Tourist Board presented the overall Croatian tourism offer, and Slobodna Dalmacija reports that the delegation was led by the Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina and HTZ director Kristjan Staničić. The Croatian stand’s offer was presented by 32 co-exhibitors.

the uk is one of croatia’s most important source markets

“The signals from the British market are extremely positive for Croatia; the UK is one of the country’s most important source markets, from which we continuously achieve very good results, and British guests are among those with the highest average daily spending in Croatia.

Precisely for that reason, we’re using this appearance at the WTM also for a series of meetings with leading British tour operators, airlines and other partners, with special emphasis on strengthening air connectivity, further growth of tourist traffic and development of cooperation in 2027. Research of the British market shows that guests are paying more and more attention to the quality of the offer and value for money, and are looking for trips outside the main summer months, shorter city breaks and authentic experiences.

It’s exactly these trends that are fully in line with the direction in which we’re developing Croatian tourism – towards higher quality and competitiveness, a more diverse offer and more even tourist activity throughout the whole year. Our goal is to additionally strengthen Croatia’s position on the British market, but also to ensure that the further development of tourism brings greater value to our destinations, the economy and local communities,” Minister Glavina stated.

from huge airlines to travel agencies

During the first day of the fair meetings were held with representatives of partners and organisations such as Jet2.com & Jet2Holidays, EasyJet Holidays, British Airways, TravelZoo, Love Holidays, the British Association of Travel Agents (ABTA), CBS travel, Travel Weekly and others. Key topics were previous activities and results, and certain partners are also announcing additional expansions in their programmes towards Croatian destinations. The above is best confirmed by the latest ABTA trends research, according to which demand for travel on the British market is still strong despite the rise in the cost of living, geopolitical uncertainties, disruptions in air traffic and climate change.

As many as 88 percent of respondents went on at least one holiday during the previous 12 months, which is one percentage point more than the year before and equal to the result from 2019. An important indicator of the research is the position of Croatia, which is in 13th place on the list of world destinations that British travellers plan to visit in the next 12 months, which confirms the competitive position of our country on the important UK market.

research conducted by tomas

“The British market is extremely important for Croatian tourism given that it is a country that enters the top 10 markets from which Croatia achieves the highest tourist traffic, and the recently published results of the TOMAS research show that Brits are the second guests by spending.

On the UK market, we’re also observing an interesting change, which opens additional potentials for Croatia as well, and that is city break tourism, which has become the most popular form of holiday for British guests. Croatia is an interesting destination for them in that context due to its proximity, so we will carry out investments and activities with the aim of further strengthening air traffic towards Croatian destinations also during 2027, and the priority remains the further strengthening of the quality of the overall tourism offer,” director Staničić stated, adding that Croatia has a stable position on the market, which was also confirmed by numerous partners during the talks.

top destinations

Positive trends from the UK market are also indicated by the results of tourist traffic, that is, data from the eVisitor system, according to which from this market in our country during the first 10 months 841 thousand arrivals (+2%) and 4.1 million overnight stays (+1%) were achieved. In this, Britons achieved the most overnight stays in Dubrovnik-Neretva and Split-Dalmatia counties, and looking by destinations, in Dubrovnik, Split, Konavle, Župa Dubrovačka, Rovinj and Zadar.

“Our partners on the British market recognise Croatia not only as a summer destination, but as somewhere that carries high value, authenticity and exceptional diversity. We’re particularly pleased by the fact that British travel organisers are actively expanding their programmes, which directly affects the extension of the main part of the tourist year. British travellers today more than ever are looking for authentic experiences, top gastronomy, preserved nature and rich cultural heritage. Our focus on the promotion of sustainable tourism and the offer outside the summer season perfectly resonates with the trends on the UK market, where younger generations and experienced travellers are paying more and more attention to the ecological and social responsibility of the destination,” believes Bisera Fabrio, director of the HTZ Representative Office in London.

croatia’s incredible food and wine scene

The complete presentation of Croatian eno-gastronomy was complemented by a presentation and tasting of Croatian wines, held as part of the Croatian stand in cooperation between the Croatian National Tourist Board and the Croatian Chamber of Economy. Croatia presented itself within the exhibition stand with a recognisable visual identity, whose panels and video walls will be decorated with multimedia content connected with the new promotional video “Croatia – I hear it’s beautiful” with the one and only John Malkovich taking the main role.

World.title: Croatian-Made Circular Ice Rink Earns Popularity in London
World.content:
November the 5th, 2026 – A Croatian-made circular ice rink made by Wonderland Factory has earned enormous popularity in Leicester Square in the heart of London.

Interest in the new festive winter attraction exceeded expectations, and more than 90 percent of tickets for the season were sold out in the first 24 hours from the start of sales. Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni that the Croatian company Wonderland Factory, owner of the Ice Wonderland brand, realised the project of a circular ice rink with an area of 400 square metres on London’s Leicester Square, one of the most famous tourist locations in the British capital.

Interest in the new winter attraction exceeded expectations, and more than 90 percent of tickets for the season were sold out in the first 24 hours from the start of sales. It is expected that Leicester Square will be visited by more than 3.5 million tourists during the winter. “In recent years, we’ve realised a large number of projects in the UK, which is one of our main export markets. Leicester Square is a particularly interesting project, not only because of the unique and extremely popular location in the very centre of London, but also because of the complexity of the execution,” said Rahela Bošnjak, director of Wonderland Factory which stands behind the Ice Wonderland brand.

When it comes to the value of the projects, in Croatia it ranges up to 100,000 euros per location, for ice rinks with an area of 400 to 600 square metres.

On the British market, the amounts can reach even 300,000 euros, depending on the scope of the work and additional services, they said from the company. “We are currently also assembling an ice rink in Liverpool, and in Great Britain we have a series of other locations. Nevertheless, we most look forward to Croatia and the beautiful Advents of which Ice Wonderland will be a part. Since we started precisely in Croatia, so we’re always particularly happy to work in Croatia,” Bošnjak stated.

In order to maximally utilise the available space, the Ice Wonderland team designed the concept of a kind of “ice rink on a floor”. The entire construction and the ice rink surface are raised almost two metres above ground level, whereby space under the ice rink is ensured for the placement of the cooling system, technical equipment and all operational installations.

World.title: Estonian refugee couple still promoting their homeland's culture in Atlanta
World.content:
Estonian Honorary Consul in Atlanta Aadu Allpere and his wife Kristi Vuht-Allpere have spent years sharing their homeland's culture with Americans, calling it an "easy sell."

Tallinn-born Allpere and Pärnu native Vuht-Allpere are both part of the generation of refugees displaced by World War II and Estonia's occupation.

Allpere was nine when he arrived in the United States. He went on to study business and commerce at the University of Pennsylvania and spent 30 years at the Coca-Cola Company, including as president of its operations in Austria and five Eastern European countries. He now runs a healthcare center specializing in foot care.

In 1993, Allpere and his wife returned to Atlanta, Georgia, where his work with Coca-Cola first brought them several decades prior. He became Estonia's local honorary consul in town in 2011.

Both are avid classical music fans and regular season-ticket holders at the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra.

Late last month, they organized a reception with visiting Estonian conductor Kristiina Poska, along with an exhibition on Estonian musical culture in the lobby of the Atlanta Symphony Hall.

As soon as they had seen Poska's name on the upcoming season calendar, they knew they had to arrange something.

'Music is part of our soul'

"As Estonians, music is part of our soul," Allpere said. "Pair that with the fact that Estonian music is well known worldwide, and that makes it easier for us to promote and support it."

For both Allpere and Vuht-Allpere, who is active locally as a volunteer, cultural outreach is about more than their formal duties. Vuht-Allpere said they have made it a personal mission to introduce Americans to Estonia.

"We've taken Americans along with us to Estonia, where we've taken them everywhere, even to the Song Festival, which is an incredible experience for them," she said, noting that the more familiar people are with Estonia, the safer it is.

"We're from the refugee generation," she continued. "And as we know, when people know and understand something, they develop a connection to it."

Estonian conductor Kristiina Poska. Source: Anneli Ivaste

The couple has been cultivating those connections for years, both in Atlanta and in previous places they called home, including Chicago, New York and other parts of New England.

"We call everyone we know our 'friends of Estonia,'" Vuht-Allpere added. "We've been brainwashing them for years."

Estonians rarely tour in Atlanta

"It's really easy to sell people on Estonia," Allpere acknowledged. "Especially when it comes to culture, because Estonia offers so much to talk about."

They would nevertheless like to see more Estonian talent come perform in Atlanta. Vuht-Allpere said the Southern U.S. city sometimes feels overlooked when Estonian choirs and conductors tour cities like New York, Chicago and Los Angeles — all home to bigger diaspora communities.

"We're constantly talking about Arvo Pärt's music and asking whether it could be performed more in Atlanta," she said. "We keep putting the idea out there, hoping it will eventually happen. I know the music world is both big and small, but sometimes we really do feel left out. So having Kristiina Poska come here was a great boost for us, too."

Allpere also sees Georgia as an attractive destination for Estonian businesses, citing the busy Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the state's major seaport in Savannah and incentives for companies relocating to the U.S.

So far, however, he hasn't managed to attract any Estonian companies, "but there's always hope."

No Estonian businesses yet

The couple said Atlanta offers a good quality of life, pointing to how diverse and green the city is and perks like not having to worry about shoveling snow in the winter.

Life there and in the U.S. in general has its downsides, however, and not just when it comes to hot and humid Atlanta summers or a conspicuous lack of local sources for Estonian sült.

"Half our lives here are spent in the car," Allpere said. "You can't get around any other way."

U.S. cultural institutions also aren't taxpayer-supported the way they are in Estonia either, leaving museums and even some of the country's best major symphony orchestras scrambling for funding.

"The Atlanta Symphony Orchestra has been operating in the black for 12 years now, although it went through some very difficult periods," Vuht-Allpere noted. "Our volunteer committee has to raise more than $3.5 million annually from individuals and businesses."

The key, she said, is building relationships. "This year, we're even on track to exceed that goal," Vuht-Allpere said.

World.title: Taru Nature House picked Estonia's wooden building of the year
World.content:
Taru Nature House, designed by architects from the Kavakava architecture firm, has been named Estonia's Wooden Building of the Year.

According to jury chairman Lembit-Kaur Stöör, Taru (hive in Estonian and a play of the words tark and ruum, meaning smart space — ed.), located in Tallinn's Noblessner area, impressed with its cohesive design. The nearly zero-energy building is Estonia's largest public wooden building. Its architecture combines sustainable materials, large curved glued-laminated timber ceiling structures, a resulting sense of spaciousness and natural light. Taru will house the Estonian Museum of Natural History, the Environmental Board, the Estonian Environment Agency and several other government agencies.

"The building's overall composition, exterior and interior spaces, materials and structural design come together in harmony, creating something that is both emotionally engaging and intellectually stimulating," Stöör explained.

Henrik Välja, CEO of the Estonian Forest and Wood Industries Association (EMPL), which spearheads the competition, said the event's 24 years of consistent efforts have paid off. "We are approaching a point we dreamed of at the beginning of this journey but never truly dared to imagine we would reach," Välja said.

Erik Konze, the competition's organizer and EMPL's timber architecture consultant, added that he has spent years traveling across Europe on study trips to explore developments in leading architecture and timber construction.

"However, the entries in recent years' Wooden Building of the Year competitions confirm that we no longer need to look beyond Estonia to see world-class timber architecture," he said.

Competition is growing fiercer each year. Timber construction is becoming increasingly widespread, with the public sector continuing to lead the way.

"That is where the most interesting developments are taking place," Stöör said, adding that good architecture is essential for bringing communities together.

A total of 23 entries were submitted to the competition, organized for the 24th time by the Estonian Forest and Wood Industries Association. Entries were evaluated for their innovative, durable and creative uses of wood in structural elements as well as exterior and interior finishes.

World.title: Health system experts: Ownership changes won't solve family doctor shortage
World.content:
Changing who owns family medicine practices will not solve Estonia's shortage of family doctors, create more trained physicians, or ensure better access to care in the regions that need it most, write Kaija Kasekamp, Triin Habicht, and Ruth Kalda.

Estonia's family medicine system faces several challenges, including an aging physician workforce, limited recruitment of new doctors, and regional disparities in access to care.

As a solution, abandoning the patient list system and removing ownership restrictions in family medicine have been proposed. These two proposals are often discussed together, even though they are, in substance, two different issues. The patient list system concerns who is responsible for patients. Ownership determines who controls the organization providing the service and what objectives shape its management.

Patient lists provide accountability and continuity of care

The patient list system creates a clear link between a patient and a specific family doctor. This is an important strength of Estonia's primary health care system. A 2026 report by the WHO Regional Office for Europe found that an ongoing relationship with the same primary care physician or a small care team is associated with lower mortality, fewer emergency room visits, and fewer hospitalizations.

"Investors typically place money in a company on a temporary basis, seek to increase its value."

Continuity is especially important for people with chronic diseases, mental health conditions, and complex social needs. For patients with routine or acute concerns, rapid access to care may sometimes be more important than seeing their regular doctor. Family medicine centers can organize care in a way that provides quick access when needed while maintaining long-term doctor-patient relationships where they have the greatest impact.

In Estonia, the owner of a company providing family medicine services can be either a family physician or a local government. Proponents of removing that restriction argue that it would free family doctors from management responsibilities. Physicians should indeed be able to focus on clinical work. However, ownership and management are two different things. A physician owner does not have to manage the practice on a day-to-day basis. A manager can be hired, support services can be centralized, and a larger organization can be built without changing the ownership structure.

In health care, the owner's profile is particularly important because not every decision affecting service quality and the organization of care can be specified in advance through contracts. Service providers always retain a degree of discretion, and how that discretion is exercised, and what choices are made, is influenced by the owner's objectives.

A comparative study of five countries published in 2026 found clear differences between health care professional owners and financial investors. For a physician owner, the practice is often both a day-to-day workplace and a life's work. The company's profits may remain as the physician's income or be reinvested in the development of the practice.

Concerns over investor ownership

A financial investor has different objectives. Investors typically place money in a company on a temporary basis, seek to increase its value, and/or intend to sell their stake later at a profit. This can also affect how a family medicine center is managed, which costs are cut, how work is organized, and what services are offered to patients.

When discussing ownership, the focus is often primarily on profits and dividends, but in the case of a financial investor, that is too narrow a view.

Money can also flow to the owner or related companies through rent, loan interest, management fees, and other payments. For example, a health care provider may sell its real estate to an investor and then continue leasing it on a long-term basis. This may free up capital for investments, but at the same time creates an ongoing rental obligation. If that cost becomes substantial, less money remains available for employees and service development.

Private equity transactions have grown rapidly in health care, and investments are often made in outpatient services (OECD analysis). At the same time, little information is available about the actual owners, the transactions, and their impact. The situation is similar in Estonia. The Health Insurance Fund focuses primarily on purchasing and financing services, not on disclosing providers' capital structures, lease obligations, or payments to related parties.

Market concentration matters

Family medicine is not a typical service where, if one company leaves the market, another provider simply steps in to fill the gap. If a provider runs into difficulties or ceases operations, care must still be guaranteed.

"Family doctors must be, and already are, able to work as salaried employees if owning a company is not of interest to them."

According to the 2026 study referred to above, a private equity investor typically enters a company for a defined period, with the aim of increasing its value and selling its stake a few years later at a profit. This is the standard business model of such investors.

The need for family medicine services is not temporary. People need their family doctor both today and 10 years from now. For that reason, it is necessary to assess whether the owner's interests and time horizon support the long-term stability of the system.

For example, in the Netherlands, the large family medicine chain Co-Med encountered financial difficulties in 2024, raising questions about the sustainability of services and the need for oversight of investor-owned providers.

Another example comes from Lithuania, where InMedica grew from 18 primary care clinics to a network of more than 80 clinics in six years. During that period, the company completed 27 additional acquisitions, and more than 310,000 people, or over one-tenth of Lithuania's population, used its services. This is a typical growth strategy for private investors. In addition to family medicine, the company expanded into diagnostic and specialist care services, gaining increasing influence in the market. In 2021, Lithuania's Competition Council found it necessary to intervene and impose conditions on further market concentration, and in 2025 the network was sold to a Finnish group.

The Estonian market is small. What happens if a large share of the country's already scarce family doctors comes under the control of a single owner? The larger one company's role becomes, the more patients, the Health Insurance Fund, and the state depend on it. At a certain point, potential failures by such a company are no longer solely the owner's concern. International literature uses the term "too big to fail" to describe a company that becomes so important to the system that the public sector must intervene to ensure continued services if difficulties arise.

Significant market power can also affect negotiations with the Health Insurance Fund and create additional pressure for higher prices. Furthermore, as in the Lithuanian example, expanding the range of services offered also creates an economic incentive to direct patients to other services within the same company, which may not always serve the interests of patients or the public.

Private capital will not bring family doctors to underserved areas

Changing ownership will not solve the shortage of family doctors, create more trained family physicians, or ensure that access improves in the areas where it is most needed. Investors prefer areas with larger patient populations and stronger economic returns, primarily urban areas. That is understandable because investments are expected to generate returns.

Research also points to the risk that greater attention may be given to more profitable services and patient groups, while activities that are less profitable but socially necessary may receive less attention.

For that reason, removing ownership restrictions cannot be seen as a solution to regional shortages of family doctors. Improving access in less populous or more difficult-to-serve areas requires adequate funding, contract terms, and service obligations.

Family doctors must be, and already are, able to work as salaried employees if owning a company is not of interest to them. It is also worth discussing whether the circle of health care professionals eligible to own practices could be broader than it is today.

The role of local governments also deserves greater attention. The perspective of a local government differs from that of a financial investor. A municipality is interested in ensuring that family medicine services remain available in its area 10 or 20 years from now. At the same time, it is responsible for social services and much of the organization of local well-being.

If Estonia moves toward greater regional responsibility and closer integration of health and social services, the role of local governments in organizing family medicine may become more important, as has happened in other countries.

World.title: Tartu Mill industrial area could make way for new homes, offices
World.content:
The City of Tartu is planning a mixed-use redevelopment of a former industrial area near the main railway station, with offices, commercial space and apartments.

The city government has initiated a detailed plan for the four-hectare site at Lembitu 1b and Väike kaar 41 and 41b, behind the Lembitu Coop supermarket and adjacent to the railway. The area includes Tartu Mill's existing operations.

Deputy Mayor Kertu Vuks (Reform) said the goal is to gradually move industrial activity out of the area and make room for new development.

"Tartu Mill will continue operating, but we're planning a different kind of development around it, giving the former railway infrastructure and warehouse sites a new character," she added.

The current plan for the site would allow office and commercial buildings alongside apartment buildings, which could account for up to 40 percent of the development. Buildings would generally range from three to six stories, with up to 10 percent of the site allowed to have buildings as tall as eight stories.

A preliminary design is expected within six months.

A strategic environmental assessment will not be required, although noise mitigation measures will be necessary due to the site's proximity to the railway, Vuks added.

The Tartu Mill complex adjacent to Tartu's main railway yard. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

Several new developments

The proposal is the latest in a series of redevelopment plans for Central Tartu and surrounding areas.

New residential and commercial districts are also planned or already in the works for the sites of the current Zeppelin shopping center and a former district heating plant, while the adjacent Port Athena development is already well on its way toward completion.

Kaisa Hiire, Southern Estonian regional manager for Domus Kinnisvara, said the real estate market was ready for more centrally located housing, including not just small units suitable for students but also larger apartments that can accommodate families.

"Families also want to live somewhere they can utilize the surrounding infrastructure and services without hassle," she said, pointing to the convenience of walkable and bikeable shopping, cafes, libraries, schools and kindergartens.

Hiire nonetheless doesn't expect these newest developments to have a significant effect on average property prices across the Tartu region.

The Uus-Karlowa Quarter planned for the former site of Tartu's old district heating plant. Source: Kadarik Tüür Arhitektid/Merko
