World.title: Kazakhstan’s Cities Are Growing. Are Their Economies Keeping Pace?
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s accelerating urbanization is concentrating population growth in its largest cities, while smaller urban centers struggle to retain residents and attract investment. Experts say the challenge is to ensure that expanding cities create productive jobs and accessible public services rather than simply accommodate more people.

“Urbanization is taking place in every country, but in Kazakhstan it is happening at an accelerated pace. Astana and Almaty remain the main centers of attraction, as our experts have noted. (…) But urbanization is inevitable, and we must prepare for it,” said Zhuldyzai Iskakova, chairperson of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development (KIPD).

Iskakova spoke at a Nov. 6 meeting of the SARAP expert club, organized by KIPD, which brought together lawmakers, economists and urban planning specialists to examine urban growth following President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s State of the Nation Address and plans for nationwide infrastructure development.

Population growth and the economic divide

The growing concentration of Kazakhstan’s population in its largest cities is reflected in figures presented by Nurbolat Kurmetuly, director of the Center for Regional Studies and Quality of Life at the Economic Research Institute.

According to his findings, the combined population of Astana, Almaty and Shymkent increased by 721,800 between 2021 and 2025, including a positive net internal migration balance of 417,800 people. Astana alone recorded a positive net interregional migration balance of 87,500 in 2025, compared with a negative balance of 2,500 in 2015.

Shynar Tuleshova, head of the Demographic Research Department at the Center for Analysis and Forecasting of Demographic Processes under Kazakhstan’s Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, noted that migration to Astana currently exceeds that to Almaty, with approximately 100,000 newcomers registering in the capital annually.

“However, when we talk about migration, a person does not necessarily register as a city resident immediately after moving. Some register five or even 10 years later, while others continue living without registration. We can only see registered residents in official statistics, not those who remain unregistered,” she said.

Tuleshova added that migration to the Almaty Region has increased over the past two years, reflecting the metropolitan area’s expansion into surrounding settlements.

Population growth is also transforming surrounding settlements. In the Astana metropolitan area, the rural population of the suburban zone increased from 121,900 to 181,500 over five years, while employment remained concentrated in the capital. Kurmetuly noted a similar pattern around Shymkent, where employment increased primarily in the city itself and declined in some neighboring territories.

“In other words, cities are expanding outward rather than developing in depth. Population and housing are growing, but jobs, transport and social infrastructure are not keeping pace,” said Kurmetuly.

The geographical concentration of investment presents another challenge. According to Kurmetuly, more than 55% of Kazakhstan’s fixed assets are concentrated in the Atyrau Region, Astana and Almaty, while the southern macroregion, home to more than 30% of the country’s labor resources, accounts for less than 9%.

In 2025, approximately 1.29 trillion tenge (US$2.87 billion) was directed toward real estate activities in cities of regional significance, compared with 1.10 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion) in manufacturing.

“Housing construction is necessary, but it produces a quick, one-time effect. Sustainable income for cities comes from industries and services that sell their products beyond the local market, including manufacturing, engineering, logistics, IT and technical services. These are the sectors that create quality jobs,” said Kurmetuly.

“Astana, Almaty and Shymkent are our national engines. There is no need to restrain their growth. But a country the size of Kazakhstan cannot depend on just three cities. We need a network of strong regional centers,” he said.

Can smaller cities become centers of growth?

Kurultai deputy Yulia Kuchinskaya, a member of the Committee on International Affairs, Defense and Security, also emphasized the need to strengthen alternatives to Kazakhstan’s largest cities.

Kuchinskaya noted that the country’s 90 cities should be assessed according to their ability to create employment, attract residents and provide conditions for long-term economic development.

“Large-scale construction is a very good project, and a very important one. It can give an impetus to economic development, but we must all understand that construction will eventually end. What happens after construction? Where will people work, what will they do, and what will happen to the economy?” she said.

She also noted that infrastructure improvements do not necessarily prevent rural depopulation, and residents who want to relocate may face financial barriers, including difficulty selling their homes.

“There are many villages in Kazakhstan, at least in the northern regions, where all the infrastructure is in place. There are roads, water and lighting, but there are no people. New residents are not moving there,” she said.

This challenge also showed up in Kurmetuly’s findings. He noted that several regional capitals continue to lose residents despite their administrative status, with Semei’s population declining by 7.2% over five years.

To retain residents, he emphasized the need for economic specialization, permanent employment and stronger links with surrounding rural communities, including agricultural processing and logistics.

Human capital and regional competitiveness

According to Kurmetuly, Kazakhstan has approximately 670,000 students, more than half of whom study away from their home cities or regions. Three-quarters of doctoral students are concentrated in Almaty and Astana.

The distribution of educational opportunities also influences migration, as students who move to larger cities often remain after graduation to pursue careers and establish families.

“Moving away to study often becomes a permanent move. A person earns a degree, finds a job, starts a family and does not return. That is why human capital is not simply a social characteristic of a city,” said Kurmetuly.

“What matters is not how much money was invested, but how many permanent jobs were created with wages above the regional average. (…) Link education to the local economy. And track a simple indicator: how many graduates are working in their home region three years later,” he said.

Rethinking urban planning and mobility

Experts also examined how existing cities can manage growth through changes in urban planning.

Nurkozha Yersaiyn, senior urbanist at the Astana Urbanism Center, presented polycentric development as a way to reduce congestion and improve access to essential services.

“Polycentrism means that a city does not have a single center. It is a multicentered city, where all districts develop at the same pace. To put it more simply, everyone should have a recreational space within walking distance of their home,” he said.

Yersaiyn noted that placing commercial facilities and employment opportunities closer to residential neighborhoods could reduce the need for residents to travel across cities for everyday activities.

“Widening roads or increasing parking spaces will never solve traffic congestion. We can see this in the southern states of the United States. Building major highways will never solve congestion; on the contrary, they make cities less comfortable for people,” said Yersaiyn.

According to the principles used by the Astana Urbanism Center, every public space should offer at least seven reasons for people to visit, accommodating different groups and activities. Even a small park should serve older residents, children, couples and other visitors rather than a single recreational purpose.

“We want to live in a comfortable city. The needs of people with limited mobility are particularly important. This includes mothers with strollers and people with mobility impairments. If these groups are comfortable, the city becomes comfortable for everyone,” he added.

Public expectations also extend to existing infrastructure. According to KIPD’s third-quarter 2026 survey, satisfaction with road quality increased from 40% in 2022 to 57.8% in 2026. However, the institute’s 2024 research found that 46.2% of respondents identified environmental concerns as a priority, while 36.3% viewed dense urban development negatively.

According to Iskakova, such findings could help authorities prioritize infrastructure projects based on residents’ needs, particularly as the country prepares for further construction. The broader question is how to ensure that infrastructure investment generates lasting economic opportunities across the country.

World.title: Kazakhstan Hosts Aqaba Process Summit on Artificial Intelligence Security
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan hosts an international summit on artificial intelligence security in Astana on Nov. 6, bringing together regional leaders and senior officials to discuss emerging security challenges associated with the development of AI.

The summit was attended by Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, King Abdullah II of Jordan, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, reported the presidential press service.

Other participants included Speaker of Azerbaijan’s National Assembly Sahiba Gafarova, Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev and other officials.

The Aqaba Process is an international initiative launched by King Abdullah II in 2015 to counter terrorism and violent extremism.

The platform brings together heads of state, security service chiefs, military officials and representatives of international organizations to develop a shared understanding of security threats and coordinate practical responses.

World.title: Kazakhstan and Tajikistan Sign $135 Million in Business Agreements at Astana Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Tajikistan signed 11 agreements worth a combined $135.3 million during a bilateral business forum in Astana on Nov. 5, bringing together representatives of the two countries’ business communities to explore opportunities for trade, investment and industrial cooperation.

The forum was held ahead of the official visit of Tajik President Emomali Rahmon to Kazakhstan, who arrived in Astana later the same day. Discussions covered bilateral trade, industry, agriculture, the digital economy, information technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and renewable energy projects.

Kazakhstan’s Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Alibek Kuantyrov took part in the event, where renewable energy cooperation featured among the key areas of discussion.

Renewable energy cooperation

Tajikistan generates approximately 98% of its electricity from renewable sources, primarily hydropower plants, according to the information presented at the forum.

Kazakhstan is also expanding its renewable energy sector. The country’s power system comprises 254 energy-generating facilities, including 172 renewable energy installations, with a combined installed capacity of 27.1 gigawatts (GW). Renewable energy facilities account for 3.8 GW of that capacity.

In the first nine months of 2026, renewable energy sources accounted for 8.5% of Kazakhstan’s total electricity generation, exceeding the government’s target of 7%.

Solar power remains one of the country’s priorities. Projects are being developed through competitive auctions and intergovernmental agreements with international strategic investors. Kazakhstan has identified a pipeline of large-scale solar power projects with a combined capacity of 900 megawatts.

By the end of 2035, the country plans to commission at least 8.4 GW of new renewable energy capacity, including approximately 1.8 GW of solar power.

The forum took place alongside a series of high-level diplomatic engagements in Astana, including the Aqaba Process summit on artificial intelligence security on Nov. 6, attended by leaders and senior officials from Central Asia and other countries.

World.title: Turkish Artists Explore Tradition and Modernity Through Miniature Art in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Turkish artists Taner Alakuş and Yasemin Akyol presented their works at the “IZLEK” exhibition showcasing traditional miniature art through contemporary interpretations at the OzgeEpic center on Nov. 5 in Astana.

Supported by the Embassy of Türkiye in Kazakhstan, the exhibition highlights shared cultural heritage and the art’s role in bringing people and cultures closer.

The exhibition’s title, “IZLEK,” carries a special meaning for the artists. Akyol explained that the word has literary associations, and refers to a central theme. In contrast, its resemblance to the Kazakh word for “trace” inspired the artists to explore cultural connections through their work in Kazakhstan.

“We wanted to find our traces here by coming here,” she told The Astana Times, describing the exhibition as part of their shared artistic journey.

For Akyol, art is also a way to bring warmth and positive emotions to audiences. She said she incorporates humor and playful details into her works to make people smile and encourage their interest in art.

“Life is very difficult and exhausting. We want people to feel happy through the beauty of art. It is a way of sharing,” she said.

Preserving traditions through contemporary art

Alakuş, a Turkish miniature artist and academic who founded the Taner Alakuş Miniature Art Workshop in Istanbul, has practiced miniature art since 1983. He has created around 400 works, which have been exhibited in Türkiye, France, South Korea, China, Russia and other countries.

His work combines traditional techniques with contemporary artistic approaches.

“My intention has always been clear: to take our lines, our colors and every stroke we put on paper beyond these boundaries and bring them together in a universal language,” Alakuş said at the exhibition opening.

Both artists also emphasized the importance of maintaining cultural identity amid rapidly changing trends. Akyol noted that younger generations may have different interests and perspectives, but should remain connected to their cultural roots.

She pointed to similarities between Kazakh and Turkish traditions, including respect for ancestors, family values and food culture, saying these shared elements could help younger audiences connect with traditional art. She also stressed that introducing young people to traditional art requires access to education, training opportunities and support for emerging artists.

Art as a bridge between cultures

The artists see the exhibition as an opportunity to strengthen ties between the artistic communities of Kazakhstan and Türkiye.

Alakuş described art as a universal language that brings people together and expressed hope for further cooperation, including joint exhibitions with Kazakh artists.

“I believe this should be a first step. In the future, we could organize joint exhibitions with Kazakh artists and strengthen our exchange of ideas and culture,” he said.

Mustafa Kapucu, Türkiye’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, said the countries’ shared cultural heritage provides a foundation for closer artistic ties.

“Türkiye and Kazakhstan have very similar classical cultures and artistic traditions. At the same time, both countries have made significant progress in contemporary art,” he told The Astana Times .

Kapucu emphasized that cooperation should extend beyond relations between governments to direct connections between people through culture, tourism and education.

“Direct contacts like this exhibition help strengthen relations between our peoples. This, in turn, also contributes to our political relations and ties between our states,” he said.

The “IZLEK” exhibition reflects how traditional art can serve as a shared language, bringing together artists and audiences while creating opportunities for further cultural exchange between Kazakhstan and Türkiye.

The exhibition will remain open to visitors until Nov. 30.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans Capital Market Overhaul Under New Strategy Through 2030
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to modernize its capital market and expand access to stock market financing for businesses under a new development program through 2030 and a draft law designed to strengthen investor protection and align national regulations with international standards.

The program and draft law On the Capital Market were reviewed at a government meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin.

According to Nurzhan Tursunkhanov, deputy chairperson of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market, Kazakhstan’s securities market has nearly doubled over the past five years. The combined value of the stock and bond markets increased from 51.1 trillion tenge (US$112.6 billion) in 2021 to 99.8 trillion tenge (US$219.9 billion) in 2025.

The number of retail investor accounts exceeded 5 million in the first nine months of 2026. The stock market’s capitalization stands at 41.8 trillion tenge (US$92.1 billion), equivalent to 26% of gross domestic product, while the bond market is valued at 58 trillion tenge (US$127.8 billion), or 36% of GDP. However, much of the growth has been driven by share placements by quasi-state companies and the revaluation of issuers.

Government securities account for 59% of the bond market, while bonds issued by quasi-state entities make up 30%. Private businesses account for the remaining 11%.

Trading activity also remains relatively low. The turnover ratio for shares stands at 1.4%, compared with a target range of 5% to 10%. For bonds, it is approximately 9%, against a target of 20% to 25%.

Seven priorities for market development

The Capital Market Development Program to 2030 aims to address these gaps and expand opportunities for private-sector financing. It includes seven areas and 35 strategic initiatives covering pension assets, investment funds, debt securities, derivatives, initial public offerings (IPOs) and improved access to the equity market for small and medium-sized businesses.

The programme also focuses on increasing secondary-market liquidity, introducing new financial instruments and improving restructuring and regulatory mechanisms.

Among the proposed measures are securities lending and covered short-selling mechanisms, improvements to market-maker operations, support for independent investment research and broader access for international investors to Kazakh shares.

New legal framework

The draft law On the Capital Market is intended to provide the legal framework for implementing the program and replace the Law on the Securities Market, which has been in force since 2003.

The proposed legislation seeks to bring Kazakhstan’s regulatory framework closer to European Union standards and those of the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). It would also expand the scope of regulation to cover derivatives and digital financial assets.

To strengthen investor protection, the draft introduces uniform criteria for qualified investors and would require brokers to execute client orders on the most favourable terms available.

The legislation proposes a one-stop-shop mechanism, based at the Central Securities Depository, to simplify companies’ access to the stock market. It would also update requirements for securities prospectuses and improve self-regulation and settlement infrastructure.

The program and proposed law are expected to broaden businesses’ access to market-based financing, create more opportunities for citizens to invest their savings over the long term and strengthen investor rights.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Data Center Valley Targets 1 GW Capacity by 2029
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to increase the capacity of its Data Center Valley in the Pavlodar Region to 1 gigawatt by 2029, as construction advances on the first three facilities and the government seeks investors for the project’s next phase.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov chaired a meeting on Nov. 6 to review construction progress, investment attraction and plans to expand the project, which supports the country’s broader efforts to develop its digital economy.

According to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev, the project could generate up to $3.1 billion in annual export revenue. Total investment over the data centers’ expected 20-year operating lifespan is estimated at $115 billion.

The first phase provides the construction of three data centers with a combined capacity of 304 megawatts (MW). Kazakhtelecom Chairperson Bagdat Mussin reported that construction of the first facility, with a capacity of 68 MW, has moved beyond preparatory work. Construction teams are now laying foundations and building infrastructure facilities and an administrative building. The data center is scheduled to begin operations in the second quarter of 2027.

Work is also underway on the second facility, the 164-MW Firebird AI data center. Excavation has reached 70%, with further development planned to include expanded computing capacity and energy infrastructure. The facility is expected to be completed and launched in the third quarter of 2027.

The third data center, with a planned capacity of 72 MW, is scheduled to open in the fourth quarter of 2027.

Plans for the second phase

The project’s second phase is expected to bring additional computing capacity to the site. Preliminary agreements have been signed with Gaw Capital, Boosteroid and Firebird to deploy a combined 480 MW of capacity, with the potential to expand to 620 MW.

Negotiations are also underway with Aleria, Energy Capital Global and China Energy on an additional 240 MW, with a possible increase to 420 MW.

The expansion will require additional energy capacity and engineering infrastructure. The meeting also covered progress on the development of a third supercomputer cluster.

Bektenov stressed the project’s importance for economic development amid growing demand for computing infrastructure. He instructed the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and Kazakhtelecom to ensure that the data centers are completed and launched on schedule.

World.title: Erdogan to visit Baku after hijab dispute: what concessions has Ankara made, and what does Baku want?
World.content:
Turkey–Azerbaijan relations

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told journalists on 5 November that he planned to visit Azerbaijan on 8 November, Victory Day, provided no extraordinary circumstances arose. He also said he had spoken by phone with President Ilham Aliyev and sent Turkey’s intelligence chief and foreign minister to Baku.

“The unbreakable ties between our countries rest on a shared history, culture and destiny – and, God willing, a shared future.”

However, Erdoğan’s planned visit comes amid a two-month cooling of relations between the two countries. On 30 October, President Aliyev skipped the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States in Ankara, even though the meeting marked the transfer of the organisation’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan to Turkey.

We reported in October on Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan’s visit to Baku.

What steps has Ankara taken to resolve the disagreements, what does Baku want, and what does the current situation reveal about relations between the two countries?

How did the dispute erupt?

In September, new school uniform requirements came into force in Azerbaijan. Although the rules do not explicitly mention the hijab, schools began turning away pupils who wore one. Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan criticised bans on wearing the hijab in schools without naming any specific countries. In Baku, his remarks were seen as an indirect criticism of Azerbaijan.

The subsequent events unfolded as follows:

2 October. At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”.

At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”. 12 October. The Interior Ministry reported that police had detained 37 people during protests against the new school uniform requirements. On the same day, Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral wrote on X: “It is unacceptable to deny girls who wear the hijab the right to education in Azerbaijan! The hijab is not an obstacle, but a requirement of faith!”

The Interior Ministry reported that police had detained 37 people during protests against the new school uniform requirements. On the same day, Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral wrote on X: “It is unacceptable to deny girls who wear the hijab the right to education in Azerbaijan! The hijab is not an obstacle, but a requirement of faith!” 13 October. The New Azerbaijan Party described Saral’s remarks as “populist and irresponsible” and called on Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) to “abandon this harmful policy”.

The New Azerbaijan Party described Saral’s remarks as “populist and irresponsible” and called on Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) to “abandon this harmful policy”. 19 October. The Azerbaijan Press Council reported what it called a “biased campaign” in the Turkish media. In the council’s view, reports had taken the school uniform decision out of context and portrayed it as a “ban on wearing the hijab”.

The Azerbaijan Press Council reported what it called a “biased campaign” in the Turkish media. In the council’s view, reports had taken the school uniform decision out of context and portrayed it as a “ban on wearing the hijab”. 21 October. Azerbaijan banned 31 Turkish citizens from entering the country. The list included New Welfare Party leader Fatih Erbakan, MP Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu and several journalists. The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit.

The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit. 25 October. Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser.

Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser. 30 October. Aliyev did not attend the Ankara summit. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov represented the country at the meeting.

What concessions has Ankara made?

The most significant step was Erdoğan’s dismissal of Oktay Saral as his chief adviser. According to Middle East Eye, which cites its own sources, Baku made three demands of Ankara:

Dismiss Erdoğan’s adviser, prosecute commentators who insulted Aliyev, and block the social media accounts named on a list. The publication reports that Ankara has already blocked some of those accounts.

Saral himself, however, has not retracted his remarks. He said he left his post at the president’s request but stressed that he had said nothing that warranted an apology: “Azerbaijan is my homeland too.”

According to Middle East Eye, Turkish officials have described the disagreements as a “misunderstanding”. Speaking at the summit, Erdoğan made no direct reference to Azerbaijan but said:

“There is no room for division, hostility or discord in the family photograph of the Turkic world.”

On 3 November, while travelling to South Korea, Erdoğan also sent Aliyev Victory Day greetings as his plane passed through Azerbaijani airspace. He delivered the message over the radio through the aircraft’s pilot.

What does Baku want?

Baku has not officially explained why Aliyev skipped the summit. According to APA, the president was due to attend the closing ceremony of the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku that day.

Baku has also taken issue with other statements from Ankara. Middle East Eye reports that, at an event organised by a foundation in October, Erdoğan said Turkish children no longer had to go abroad to study because of restrictions linked to their clothing or political views. Azerbaijan also interpreted these remarks as another rebuke.

An Azerbaijani source cited by Middle East Eye summed up Baku’s position as follows: Turkey must recognise the principle of “one nation, two states”. In other words, Baku does not want Ankara to interfere in Azerbaijan’s domestic affairs.

Elman Fattah, head of the Khazar Centre for Research and Analysis, shares a similar view. In an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, he said: “This means rejecting Turkey’s right to veto.” Fattah believes Aliyev is “deliberately shifting the hidden tensions between the two countries into the religious sphere”.

Political analyst Asif Narimanli, meanwhile, argues that

“The tensions between Baku and Ankara have deeper roots.”

Speaking to TodayPress, he noted that Aliyev’s absence…на саммите дает основания для такого вывода.

What lies behind the disagreements?

One of the deeper sources of tension concerns Israel. In Turkey, Azerbaijan’s close ties with Israel have caused considerable discontent, particularly since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip. Middle East Eye reports that Erdoğan declined to attend the October summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) to avoid meeting Israeli President Isaac Herzog. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also boycotted Herzog’s address. Baku saw this as an unfriendly gesture towards Aliyev.

Another source of disagreement concerns Armenia. According to an analysis by OC Media, Ankara wants to normalise relations with Yerevan, while Baku insists that this process must remain linked to a peace settlement between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

At the same time, the two countries share significant interests. According to OC Media, on 30 September they signed defence contracts worth around $500 million in total. In early 2026, they also reached a 15-year agreement on gas supplies from the Absheron field to Turkey. Azerbaijan accounted for around 22% of all the gas Turkey imported in 2024. According to figures from Turkey’s Ministry of Trade, bilateral trade reached $4.3 billion in 2025.

What could the visit change?

Political analyst Elkhan Shahinoglu described Erdoğan’s decision to visit Baku as “the right one”. He said:

“If tensions arise between two allies for any reason, they should not delay resolving them.”

Shahinoglu recalled that Erdoğan also visited Baku and addressed the Milli Majlis in 2009, when Turkey was moving closer to Armenia. Relations between the two countries returned to normal afterwards.

There is another sign that tensions may be easing. According to the newspaper Karar, when Turkey considered nominating former Foreign Minister Feridun Sinirlioğlu for the post of UN secretary-general, Azerbaijan backed a candidate from the United Arab Emirates instead. However, in late October, Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry spokesman Aykhan Hajizada welcomed Turkey’s nomination of Sinirlioğlu.

The next test for relations will be the UN climate conference COP31, which will take place in Antalya this month. Middle East Eye reports that Ankara hopes Aliyev will attend the conference. Baku has yet to confirm his visit.

World.title: Abkhazia to raise electricity tariffs for businesses by 40% to pay for Russian power imports
World.content:
Electricity tariffs for commercial customers in Abkhazia will rise by 40%. However, the increase will apply only during the autumn-winter period, when the region imports electricity to cover its energy shortfall.

The Inguri hydroelectric power plant is Abkhazia’s only source of electricity. However, its output falls from around November until March or April as water levels in the Inguri River drop. Electricity consumption in the region, meanwhile, rises.

In 2025, a shortfall of 500 million kWh was covered by electricity imports from Russia. Russia provided some of this electricity to Abkhazia free of charge as humanitarian aid, but the authorities had to buy the rest at market prices.

This comes at a high cost for Abkhazia: Russian electricity is significantly more expensive than the domestic tariffs charged to consumers. The current rate is 2 roubles [$0.02] per kWh for households and 3 roubles [$0.03] for legal entities. Under the agreement with Russia, however, Abkhazia will have to pay 5.5 roubles [$0.06] per kWh for imported electricity.

This is why the authorities decided to raise tariffs for businesses.

“When we pay 5.5 roubles per kWh for imported electricity but sell it to households for 2 roubles, this is also an example of the state’s social responsibility towards its citizens.

“But for commercial enterprises and institutions – where businesses make money – the tariff should match the purchase price during periods when we import electricity,” Abkhaz President Badra Gunba said. He instructed the government to approve this as the republic’s new tariff policy.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: The evacuation from Oleshky: How Russia turned a humanitarian mission into a propaganda story
World.content:
The evacuation from Oleshky

The evacuation from Oleshky (Oleshky, formerly known as Oleshky/Aloshky) in Ukraine’s Kherson region, during which around 800 civilians were evacuated and aid was delivered to those who remained, was a rare example of Ukraine and Russia working together under international mediation. For Russian state media and Z-bloggers, it also became an opportunity to launch a new information campaign.

The Ukrainian side stressed the need to save lives and continue humanitarian missions. Russian media, meanwhile, portrayed the evacuation as an act of concern by Moscow for the residents of occupied territories, sought to discredit Ukraine and tried to intimidate those considering returning to territory under Kyiv’s control.

Four narratives stood out in the media coverage: Russia cast as a humanitarian intermediary; residents’ alleged unwillingness to return to Ukraine; attempts to frighten men with the prospect of forced mobilisation; and efforts to shift responsibility for threats to civilians onto Ukraine.

Some of these claims contradicted both the circumstances of the operation and statements by official representatives of the parties involved.

A report by Novosti Donbassa By Yulia Tararui.

A catastrophe whose causes the propaganda ignores

Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since February 2022. After Ukrainian forces liberated the right-bank part of the Kherson region in the autumn of that year, the city found itself on the front line.

The situation deteriorated dramatically in June 2023, when the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant was destroyed. Flooding, damaged infrastructure, disruptions to electricity and water supplies, and restrictions on movement made life extremely difficult for residents.

By 2026, the situation had become critical. Fighting, landmines and drone attacks had left the city in urgent need of food, medicine and other essentials, while opportunities to leave safely were almost nonexistent.

Russian publications described the hardships faced by residents in detail, but avoided the central fact: Oleshky had been under the control of Russian occupation authorities throughout this period.

Russian media circulated the account of a local woman who tried to leave in an ambulance but could not get even as far as the outskirts of the city because the road was mined.

Other reports described elderly residents cycling to Radensk during a ceasefire to buy food and medicine – a journey of around 20 kilometres each way.

These stories conveyed the scale of the catastrophe. But they also helped construct a narrative convenient for Moscow: the suffering was blamed on the proximity of the fighting, while the occupation administration’s responsibility for meeting residents’ basic needs was left out of the picture.

A joint operation turned into a story of Moscow’s concern

Agreements on a temporary ceasefire and the evacuation were reached with international mediation, including the active involvement of US First Lady Melania Trump.

According to figures she cited, around 750 people left the city. Reports mentioned 25 buses.

Residents were free to choose their destination: territory under Ukrainian control or Russia.

Those who chose Ukraine were evacuated via Belarus. The Russian side arranged an airlift from Anapa to Gomel using military transport aircraft.

Evacuees who chose Russia were taken to a temporary accommodation centre in Simferopol.

Food, water, medicine, fuel for generators and hospital equipment were brought into the city. A total of 105 pets were evacuated from Oleshky.

According to Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, the ceasefire lasted five days, 19 hours and 59 minutes. The operation also made it possible to arrange the repatriation of the bodies of fallen soldiers and civilians from morgues in Oleshky and other settlements.

The Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners said that both sides had fulfilled their obligations and thanked each other.

Russian media coverage, however, focused on Moscow’s role: the military aircraft, the transfer of evacuees to Simferopol, medical assistance and the work of Russian officials. In this way, the joint operation helped promote the image of a state that not only controls occupied territory but also looks after its residents.

The fact that an international operation was needed to evacuate people from a city that had been under Russian control for more than four years was barely examined in these reports.

The story of evacuees being mobilised: What a Z-Blogger claimed

One revealing episode involved Russian Z-blogger Sergei Kolyasnikov, better known as Zergulio. He circulated a claim that men who chose to travel to Ukraine were detained by staff from territorial recruitment and social support centres (TCCs and SPs, Ukraine’s equivalent of military enlistment offices) immediately after the evacuation and sent to the front.

The story drew on a familiar image of Ukraine, where men of conscription age are supposedly bound to become victims of forced mobilisation. But it had a problem with the timeline.

When the claim began circulating, evacuees heading towards Ukraine had, according to published reports, been flown to Gomel, the regional capital of Belarus. The allegation that they were detained by TCC staff after arriving in Ukraine did not match the known evacuation route.

The reports provided no publicly available evidence of mass detentions of evacuated men.

Lubinets stressed separately that no screening had taken place during the evacuation, including for people with problems concerning their documents. He said: “There was no screening whatsoever. Moreover, we had people who said they had problems with their documents – for example, they had lost them. There were no problems.”

He added: “There was not only no screening, there were no checks of phones or documents either.”

These remarks concerned the evacuation procedure and did not describe all subsequent actions by state authorities after people returned to Ukraine. But they offered no support for the blogger’s claim.

▇ Disinformation exploits people’s genuine fears of war and mobilisation, attaching them to a specific event.

Such a message could also have been aimed at residents of occupied territories, particularly men of conscription age and their relatives.

For people who have lived in information isolation for years, a story about evacuees being sent to the front could become a reason not to leave, even in the absence of evidence.

Why people chose to leave: An attempt to undermine their decisions

The Russian military blog Kotsnews claims that most men of conscription age refused to travel towards Ukraine. According to the blog, those who left were mainly elderly people, women and children, and they did so for personal reasons rather than out of political conviction.

The author of the post writes: “Not out of any great love for ‘independent Ukraine’, but to sort out their personal affairs. People in Oleshky have long felt no gratitude towards Ukraine.”

This explanation serves several purposes at once. It diminishes the significance of people’s decisions by portraying them as pragmatic choices – for example, a chance to reunite with relatives or move to Europe.

It creates the impression that residents of the occupied city no longer see their future as being tied to Ukraine. It also reinforces the narrative of inevitable mobilisation.

The result is a self-reinforcing argument: men do not want to go to Ukraine because they fear the TCCs, while those who do make the journey are supposedly immediately confronted with mobilisation. Russian commentators provide no reliable statistics on the evacuees’ reasons for leaving.

Lubinets said the parties had agreed not to disclose how many people chose Ukraine and how many chose Russia. According to him, honouring that agreement was necessary to ensure that humanitarian operations could continue.

Meanwhile, various figures circulated in the Russian information space. Russian Z-war correspondent Romanov initially reported that 17 buses had travelled to Ukraine and four to Russia, but later deleted the figures from his post.

Newsmax journalist Alex Salvi reported 11 buses heading to Ukraine and four to Russia.

Without official figures, these reports do not make it possible to establish how the evacuees were divided between the two destinations. But the very attempt to interpret their choices as an indication of political allegiance became part of the information war surrounding the operation.

Accusations of violating the ceasefire

At the same time, Russian officials accused Ukrainian forces of breaching the agreement. Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large, claimed that a Ukrainian drone had attacked a civilian vehicle leaving Oleshky.

According to Miroshnik, the vehicle was carrying civilians travelling to Radensk to buy food. Two people were injured. He alleged that attacks on civilians had resumed before the agreed ceasefire had expired.

These accusations contradicted statements that the terms of the agreement had been observed. After the operation, Lubinets said that both sides had fulfilled their commitments.

Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, gave a similar assessment. International media also reported that there had been no confirmed violations of the local ceasefire.

Miroshnik’s statement therefore remains an accusation made by the Russian side, not an established fact.

Such reports serve an obvious purpose. They portray Moscow as willing to take part in humanitarian initiatives while reinforcing the image of Ukraine as the side posing a threat to civilians.

Even during an operation that officials from both countries described in positive terms, the Russian information space continued to recycle familiar accusations.

The ceasefire ended, but the problem remains

Russia refused to extend the ceasefire. According to AFP, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry had proposed prolonging the agreement, but the Russian side rejected the offer.

The ceasefire ended on 1 November. The ombudsmen said they were considering organising further humanitarian missions.

The need for evacuation has not gone away. Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who has been helping residents of Oleshky since 2022, told the Agency that not everyone who wanted to leave had been evacuated.

According to her, some residents of the city’s suburbs were turned back at checkpoints, while no transport arrived for some people with limited mobility. The most vulnerable are elderly people, people with disabilities and those unable to reach an evacuation point on their own.

Lubinets said 22 ambulances had to be deployed. Some people were too unwell to withstand the planned journey.

In one case, medical staff initially approved a person for transport but, after examining them on site, decided they would not survive the journey. An alternative arrangement had to be made. Several families are now continuing their journey to Ukraine by road.

The ombudsman also said that the Ukrainian side had managed to deliver medical equipment and medicines to the hospital in Oleshky. But he acknowledged that it was still impossible to assess the quality of medical care there.

Russian reports focused on the number of vehicles involved, the aid delivered by Russia and the organisation of transport. The fate of those left behind amid the crisis received far less attention.

Why this poses a threat to future evacuations

Disinformation can put people’s safety at risk. If a resident of an occupied city believes that returning to Ukraine will mean being detained and sent to the front, they may refuse to evacuate even when a safe route is available.

Claims that large numbers of people are unwilling to return can make those who remain feel that choosing Ukraine is dangerous, unpopular or pointless. The reality is more complicated.

People choose where to go based on their health, whether they have relatives there, their documents, housing and access to assistance.

For an elderly person, for example, reuniting with children or grandchildren may be the priority. A person with a disability may need medical care. For a family with children, safety and the ability to continue their education may matter most.

None of these decisions, in itself, reveals a person’s political beliefs. Turning evacuation figures into a vote for either Ukraine or Russia is therefore a form of manipulation.

▇ Choosing an evacuation destination is not the same as voting for Ukraine or Russia.

The information war could also complicate future humanitarian missions, the need for which both sides acknowledge.

exchange

World.title: Russia declares Georgian opposition party Droa ‘undesirable organisation’
World.content:
Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office has designated the Georgian opposition party Droa an “undesirable organisation”, citing its “strongly anti-Russian stance”.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office press service, Droa representatives oppose the normalisation of political, economic, cultural and humanitarian relations between Georgia and Russia. They also call for the reinstatement of visa requirements for Russian citizens and an end to direct flights between the two countries.

The Prosecutor General’s Office also accuses the party of considering Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) territories occupied by Russia, and of accusing Moscow of violating international law and Georgia’s sovereignty.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, Droa’s activities are aimed at “exposing links between Georgia’s ruling elite and Russia”, dismantling the country’s one-party system and promoting faster integration with the European Union.

The Russian authorities also criticised the party’s leader, Elene Khoshtaria, who accuses the ruling Georgian Dream party of pursuing a pro-Russian course and attempting to isolate Georgia from the European integration process.

The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office also says Droa supports the Ukrainian authorities and advocates Georgia’s accession to the “Carpathian Eight”, a regional and economic cooperation format for countries in Central and South-Eastern Europe linked to the Carpathian region.

Droa’s response

Droa, in turn, says Russia’s accusations concern precisely the positions and activities that the party considers part of its efforts to defend Georgia’s national interests.

The party listed six reasons why it believes the Russian authorities designated it an “undesirable organisation: recognising Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as territories occupied by Russia; exposing secret links between Georgian Dream and Russia; working to end the one-party system in Georgia; supporting faster integration with the European Union; backing the Ukrainian authorities and cooperation between Georgia and Ukraine; and Elene Khoshtaria’s statements accusing Georgian Dream of pursuing a pro-Russian course and obstructing European integration.

“We are taking this opportunity, which we consider an honour, to reiterate: Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region are Georgia! Glory to the heroes! Ivanishvili’s regime is Russian! We will put an end to Ivanishvili’s Russian regime in Georgia! Georgia will become a member of the European Union and NATO!” the party said in a statement.

What is the “Carpathian Eight”?

The “Carpathian Eight” mentioned in this context is a new regional cooperation initiative unveiled by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit in western Ukraine on 18 September.

The initiative aims to deepen trade, energy, logistics and security cooperation among countries in Central and Eastern Europe. Its members are Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and the European Union.

At the summit, Zelensky said the Carpathian region could play an important role in supplying energy to the European Union rather than serving merely as a transit corridor. He added that stronger regional cooperation could also help reduce Europe’s dependence on Russian energy resources.

According to Zelensky, the new format will strengthen ties between the countries and provide an additional, robust framework for cooperation at EU level.

About the Droa party

Droa (“It’s Time!”) is a pro-Western, pro-European opposition party in Georgia. Former State Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Elene Khoshtaria founded it in 2021.

The party’s political agenda focuses on Georgia’s European and Euro-Atlantic integration, strengthening democratic institutions, fighting corruption and countering Russian influence.

Droa is a vocal critic of Georgian Dream’s policies and accuses the authorities of pursuing a pro-Russian course and obstructing the country’s European integration.

Droa emerged as a political movement in March 2021 and registered as a political party in August that year. Before founding it, Khoshtaria left European Georgia, which she had joined after the 2020 parliamentary elections. Earlier, she had been a member of another opposition party, the United National Movement.

From 2007 to 2012, under the previous government led by Mikheil Saakashvili, Khoshtaria served as First Deputy State Minister of Georgia for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration. From 2016 to 2022, under the current government, she was a member of parliament.

In the 2024 parliamentary elections, Droa ran as part of the opposition Coalition for Change, which also included the Akhali and Girchi – More Freedom parties.

Droa has actively participated in anti-government protests and criticised decisions by Georgian Dream, including the suspension of the country’s EU accession process.

Elene Khoshtaria is currently in prison. In September 2025, authorities arrested her for writing “Russian Dream” on an election campaign banner belonging to Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze. In March 2026, a court sentenced her to one year and six months in prison for damaging property belonging to another person.

Elene Khoshtaria

Партия Дроа

World.title: Election watchdogs warn that new amendments to Georgia’s Election Code will undermine trust in election results
World.content:
Three leading election watchdogs in Georgia – the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), Transparency International Georgia and the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED) – have criticised the amendments to the Election Code proposed by the authorities.

The organisations say the proposed legislation would significantly restrict the right to challenge election results in court, weaken oversight of the electoral process and further centralise the powers of the election administration.

They identify the proposed change to the procedure for challenging the CEC’s final results protocol as one of the most problematic amendments. Under the new rules, the protocol could only be challenged in court to correct mechanical and technical errors.

“Such a restriction at the stage of finalising election results rules out disputes over systemic violations and their cumulative impact on the outcome,” the organisations warn.

They explain that the systemic nature and scale of electoral violations can only become apparent through a joint analysis of data from different polling stations and the electoral process as a whole. Therefore, the possibility of challenging results at individual polling stations cannot replace full judicial scrutiny of the final election results.

The organisations also criticise the abolition of mandatory recounts at five polling stations, selected at random by district election commissions. In their view, this change will reduce the transparency of the electoral process and further undermine public trust in the official results.

Another controversial amendment concerns the registration of election observer organisations. Under the proposed rules, the authority to make decisions on registration would rest solely with the chair of the election commission. The organisations warn that this approach increases the risk of subjective and politically motivated decisions, as other commission members, including representatives appointed by political parties, would no longer have a say in the process.

The watchdogs also raise concerns about shorter deadlines for registering election observers and media representatives ahead of the second round of voting. They believe this could hamper the work of electoral stakeholders, observers and journalists.

The organisations have also criticised changes to the rules governing the allocation of free airtime for election campaign advertising. They say the proposed restrictions could further widen the gap between the ruling party and opposition parties, undermining political pluralism.

GYLA, Transparency International Georgia and ISFED note that the authorities did not hold public discussions or consult interested parties before drafting the legislative initiative. According to the organisations, this runs counter to electoral standards set by the Venice Commission.

The watchdogs also view the initiative in the context of the legislative practices that have taken hold in Georgia in recent years. They say legislation is increasingly tailored to serve the interests of the ruling group, while mechanisms for public oversight are steadily weakening.

“Without effective oversight and accountability, the state loses public trust and, instead of protecting the common interest, becomes a system that serves narrow group interests,” the organisations say.

What exactly will change in the Election Code?

The ruling Georgian Dream party has introduced amendments to the Election Code in parliament. Under the proposed changes:

● District election commissions will no longer compile final election results: Precinct election commissions will send their final results protocols directly to the Central Election Commission (CEC), which will compile the definitive results.

● The grounds for challenging the CEC’s final results protocol will be restricted: A challenge will only be admissible if the protocol incorrectly or incompletely records data from precinct election commissions or final court rulings on electoral violations. Courts will reject claims based on any other grounds.

● Mandatory random recounts at five polling stations will be abolished: Previously, district election commissions had to recount the votes at five randomly selected polling stations within six days of the election.

● The deadline for finalising election results will be shortened: The CEC will have a maximum of 15 days to finalise the results of all elections. Previously, the deadline for parliamentary elections and elections in Tbilisi was 26 days.

● The deadline for financial reporting by the winning party will be shortened: A party that, according to preliminary results, receives the legally required number of votes will have to submit a report on its election campaign spending to the State Audit Office within five days. Previously, the deadline was 12 days.

● The consequences of financial violations by electoral contestants will change: If the State Audit Office identifies a serious violation that could have affected the election results, the CEC will be able to apply to the court and finalise the results without counting the votes cast for the party concerned.

● Broadcasters and newspapers will be prohibited from reallocating unused party advertising time: If an electoral contestant does not use its allocated advertising time, the broadcaster or newspaper will no longer be allowed to give that time to another party.

● Requirements for political advertising will be tightened: The name and number of the electoral contestant must appear on screen during the final second of an advert. Broadcasters will be prohibited from airing adverts that fail to meet this requirement.

Amendments to Georgia’s Election Code

World.title: Birth rate hits lowest level since 1950: why has number of newborns in Azerbaijan fallen by 42% in 10 years?
World.content:
Declining birth rates in Azerbaijan

In 2025, 95,875 children were born in Azerbaijan. According to the State Statistics Committee, this was the lowest annual figure since 1950. By comparison, 166,210 children were born in the country in 2015. This means the number of newborns fell by 42% over the decade.

The decline in births has continued this year. In the first half of 2026, the number of births fell by 10.6% compared with the same period last year. Between January and August, 56,404 children were born, while the birth rate dropped from 9.3 to 8.2 per 1,000 people.

However, opinions differ on how serious the situation is. Bahar Muradova, chair of the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs, said the situation had not yet reached a critical level. Economist Natig Jafarli, by contrast, believes that “the country is heading towards a demographic catastrophe”. The key question is:

Is this a temporary decline, or are families genuinely choosing to have fewer children while the government fails to take the necessary steps to reverse the trend?

What do the statistics show?

Indicator 2015 2025 Number of births 166 210 95 875 Average number of children per woman 2,1 1,4 Urban areas 2,0 1,2 Rural areas 2,2 1,6 Natural population increase 111 513 36 041 Registered marriages 68 773 48 546 Divorces 12 764 20 675 Population aged 20–29 1.84 million 1.34 million

Source: State Statistics Committee

Azerbaijan’s population is still growing. As of 1 July 2026, it stood at 10,273,000. However, the rate of growth is slowing. To maintain a stable population in the long term, each woman needs to have an average of 2.1 children. Azerbaijan’s figure has remained below this level since 2016.

According to calculations by the State Statistics Committee, in 2025 the female population’s replacement rate stood at around 61% of the level needed to replace generations. Between January and August 2026, natural population growth amounted to just 16,213 people.

The decline in birth rates is also uneven. In urban areas, women have an average of 1.2 children, compared with 1.6 in rural areas. In the first half of 2026, the overall birth rate stood at 8.0 per 1,000 people. In the Mountainous Shirvan economic region, it reached 10.1, while in the Lankaran-Astara economic region it stood at 9.9.

A temporary decline or a long-term trend?

Two distinct demographic processes lie behind the falling birth rate.

The first stems from the consequences of the 1990s. In 1991, 190,353 children were born in Azerbaijan. By 2001, that figure had fallen to just 110,356. The smaller generation born during the years of war and economic crisis has now reached the age when people typically start families and have children. Over the past decade, the population aged 20–29 has fallen by around 27%. This factor alone would have been enough to reduce the number of births.

However, the impact of this demographic wave may begin to ease. Birth rates started rising again in the mid-2000s, and today the number of teenagers aged 15–19 is significantly higher than the number of young people aged 20–24: 817,000 compared with 672,000. In the coming years, more people will reach the age at which they typically start families.

The second process cannot be explained by demographic fluctuations alone: the average number of children per woman has fallen from 2.1 to 1.4. In other words, not only are there fewer potential parents, but they are also having fewer children. If the next generation maintains the current birth rate, the number of newborns may not increase significantly.

Marriage statistics also point to this trend. In 2013, Azerbaijan recorded 86,852 marriages, compared with just 48,546 in 2025. In the first half of this year, the number of marriages fell by a further 22.5%. Meanwhile, the average age at which women marry for the first time has changed little over the past decade, rising from 23.6 to 24.1. This suggests that the main change is not that people are marrying later, but that fewer marriages are taking place. It is worth noting that these statistics cover only officially registered marriages.

“A change in mindset” or housing problems?

Bahar Muradova, chair of the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs, believes the decline in births has more to do with changing attitudes. She expressed confidence that the situation in Azerbaijan would not reach a critical level and compared the trend with developments in developed countries.

The statistics partly support this comparison. According to Eurostat, the average fertility rate in the European Union stood at 1.34 children per woman in 2024. However, Azerbaijan’s figure fell from 2.1 to 1.4 in just ten years. The country’s birth rate has therefore reached a level comparable to that of the EU, although household incomes remain significantly lower than in Europe.

Economist Natig Jafarli, by contrast, links the problem to economic factors. He identifies limited access to housing and high property prices as major causes. He also points to growing emigration among young people of reproductive age.

It is difficult to assess the impact of migration on birth rates. According to official statistics, 2,000 people left Azerbaijan to take up permanent residence abroad in 2025, while 3,400 moved to the country. However, these figures cover only registered cases of permanent relocation and do not capture the scale of emigration Jafarli describes.

Access to kindergartens is another problem. According to a report by the Cabinet of Ministers, only 38.7% of children aged one to five have access to pre-school education. The government’s target for 2026 is 50%.

What measures is the government proposing?

According to the State Social Protection Fund, mothers who are not in employment receive a one-off payment of 600 manats following the birth of a child. Between January and October this year, the fund awarded this benefit to 72,655 recipients.

Working parents who take parental leave receive a monthly allowance of 44 manats until the child reaches 18 months, and 28 manats from 18 months to three years. Women who give birth to and raise five or more children receive 140 manats per child. A total of 2,939 women receive this benefit.

Azerbaijan does not provide a universal monthly child benefit. Sociologist Uzeyir Shafiyev says the authorities abolished such payments in 2006 after introducing targeted social assistance. He proposes reinstating child benefits and revising the criteria for recognising families as large.

“It would make sense to lower the minimum number of children required for a family to qualify for large-family status from five to three,” the sociologist says.

Akif Nasirli, head of the Centre for Liberal Economists, also sees child benefits as a long-term investment in improving the demographic situation.

However, MPs have differing views on the issue. Gunay Agamali, an MP and chair of the Ana Vatan party, argues that child benefits could encourage a sense of entitlement among parents:

“When deciding to have a child, families should not expect the state to be obliged to provide them with something in return.”

Expert Ilgar Huseynli disagrees: “There is no reason to associate this with laziness.”

MP Razi Nurullayev also believes it is wrong to reduce the problem of falling birth rates solely to child benefits. He proposes a comprehensive programme that would include preferential mortgages and better access to kindergartens.

The government has yet to announce any plans to reinstate child benefits.

When will the effects become tangible?

The effects of falling birth rates are already being felt in the education system. In March, Ali Ahmadov, First Deputy Speaker of the Milli Majlis, told parliament that 1.5–1.6 million pupils attended schools in 2015. However, if the current trend continues, that figure could fall to one million within a few years. This would put around 50,000 teachers’ jobs at risk. At the start of the 2024–2025 academic year, Azerbaijan had 146,381 teachers. In other words, roughly one in three could be affected.

In the longer term, falling birth rates could also affect the labour market and pension system. The number of children under five fell from 851,000 in 2015 to 539,000 at the beginning of 2026. Jafarli believes that “pension funding will become one of the main items of state budget expenditure”. He warns: “If we do not take action today, it will be too late tomorrow.”

If the birth rate recorded between January and August continues through the end of the year, around 85,000 children will be born in Azerbaijan in 2026. By comparison, 90,280 children were born in 1950, which until recently was the lowest annual figure in the State Statistics Committee’s records.

Declining birth rates in Azerbaijan

World.title: Abkhazia’s ‘MP budgets’: why do ‘servants of the people’ receive $100,000 in public funds every year?
World.content:
A debate has erupted in Abkhazia over so-called “MP budgets”. Each of the 35 MPs receives 10 million roubles (around $100,000) from the state budget every year. For the past three years, parliament and the government have agreed to allocate this money to local infrastructure and maintenance projects in the constituencies where the MPs were elected.

The MPs themselves say the funds allow them to address problems in their constituencies quickly, such as repairing water pipes, paving rural roads and building playgrounds.

Those who oppose the scheme, however, describe it as outright corruption.

According to Daut Khutaba, head of parliament’s committee on legislation, MPs have reached an agreement with the government. Each MP can now decide how to spend up to 10 million roubles on construction and repair work in their constituency, consulting local voters or town and village administrations.

“Thanks to this agreement, over the past three years I have secured the construction of more than 2.5 kilometres of fencing in the Pitsunda Nature Reserve, at a cost of around 20 million roubles, as well as the laying of more than a kilometre of roads,” says Khutaba, who represents the Pitsunda constituency.

Abkhaz journalist Inal Khashig believes that giving individual MPs a separate budget for municipal spending will eventually turn parliament into a closed club and undermine the rotation of elected representatives:

“Under this system, any MP running in the next election has a significant advantage over other candidates. In voters’ eyes, they have already ‘invested’ in their constituency by repairing water pipes, laying gravel on rural roads or replacing light bulbs in street lamps.

“At first glance, this may seem like a worthy initiative: listening to voters and quickly addressing local infrastructure problems. But ultimately, this small handout – or, more accurately, an undisguised form of electoral bribery – will effectively give incumbent MPs a lifetime position, unless, of course, they decide not to stand for re-election.”

According to well-known blogger and civic activist Tengiz Jopua, the “MP budget” effectively violates the fundamental principles of parliamentarism and a democratic state governed by the rule of law.

“In a civilised country, the same rules apply to everyone. There are dedicated institutions people must approach, along with established procedures for submitting applications, reviewing them and allocating funds.

“The money allocated to [MPs] comes from the state budget. It is our money – taxpayers’ money – and belongs to the people as a whole, not to the state, prime ministers, presidents or MPs. That is why I believe this way of distributing public funds is wrong,” Jopua said, expressing his firm opposition to the scheme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘Factual inaccuracies and misjudgements’ – Georgian Foreign Ministry responds to European Commission report
World.content:
In response to the European Commission’s critical enlargement report, Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said the document contained factual inaccuracies and flawed assessments. It argued that these reinforced anti-Georgian narratives and narrowed the scope for constructive engagement between the European Union and Georgia.

The Foreign Ministry says the report wrongly describes the Georgian authorities’ actions as “state capture”. It argues that governing the country is the duty of a government elected by an overwhelming majority in a democratic society.

“It is concerning that the European Commission’s report, through factual inaccuracies and flawed assessments, reinforces anti-Georgian narratives. This, in turn, narrows the scope for constructive engagement and dialogue between the European Union and Georgia,” the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry claims that the European Union held no meetings with Georgia at any level during the reporting period, despite the Association Agreement providing for them. It says this resulted from the suspension of dialogue with the Georgian side following the European Council’s conclusions of 27 June 2024. According to the ministry, this has limited the European Commission’s ability to assess Georgia’s progress objectively.

The ministry also argues that the report’s selective analysis of legal issues encourages their politicisation, undermines the rule of law and amounts to an attempt to interfere in the country’s internal affairs.

It further says that describing Georgian politicians’ responses to actions targeting Georgia as “hostile rhetoric” infringes on freedom of speech and damages the partnership between Georgia and the European Union.

“Although the enlargement report on Georgia has largely served to voice biased assessments and reinforce political speculation, the Georgian side will examine the European Commission’s report in detail and submit substantiated comments to the Commission,” the statement said.

The Foreign Ministry insists that Georgia’s leadership remains ready to engage in open and constructive dialogue with the European Union, based on mutual respect.

What does the European Commission’s 2026 report say?

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, the state of democracy in Georgia has deteriorated further. The document sets out several key criticisms of the country’s government:

● Democratic backsliding and concentration of power: The European Commission says democratic institutions are weakening, political and civil liberties are being restricted, and the government is increasingly concentrating power in its own hands.

● Attempt to ban opposition parties: The Commission believes the proposal to ban five opposition parties threatens the country’s democratic foundations and raises further concerns about the use of the judiciary for political purposes.

● Electoral environment: The authorities have failed to carry out fundamental electoral reform. According to the report, the 2025 municipal elections took place in a polarised and repressive environment, marked by voter intimidation, pressure and legislative changes that gave the ruling party an advantage.

● Restrictions on civil society: The European Commission is concerned about the use of criminal proceedings and charges such as sabotage and assisting hostile activities by foreign organisations against civil society representatives. In the Commission’s assessment, this runs counter to democratic pluralism.

● Judicial independence: For the third consecutive year, the European Commission has recorded a deterioration in the judiciary. According to the report, judicial independence and impartiality have been undermined, while legal changes have increased the risk of state capture of the system. The Commission also criticised the harsh sentences imposed on demonstrators.

● Corruption and de-oligarchisation: The Commission says there has been no progress in tackling corruption. Georgia has had no anti-corruption strategy since 2020, and the authorities have taken no steps towards de-oligarchisation. The report also points to the role of oligarchic influence in facilitating state capture.

● Failure to meet visa-free travel requirements: Georgia has made virtually no progress on the European Commission’s previous recommendations, which concerned the protection of fundamental rights, combating discrimination and fighting corruption. As a result, the Commission has activated the revised visa suspension mechanism.

● Relations with Russia and sanctions: Georgia’s alignment with the EU’s foreign policy has fallen from 40% to 38%. The country has not joined most of the sanctions imposed by the EU on Russia, Belarus and Iran. The report also notes an increase in the number of direct flights to Russia.

● EU financial assistance: In response to democratic backsliding, the EU suspended €121.3 million in bilateral funding for the Georgian government in 2024. Georgia’s participation in new EU programmes under the Association Agreement has also been suspended.

● Anaklia port project: The European Commission notes that the project has become fully state-owned, construction work was suspended for several months, and budget funding for the project fell by 60% during the reporting period.
