World.title: New wave of bomb threats hits European flights, media outlets
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeAviation New wave of bomb threats hits European flights, media outlets Updated November 6, 2026 — 11:19pm ,first published November 5, 2026 — 7:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Bomb threats were issued to media outlets across Europe on Friday, as passenger flights around the continent received a wave of similar threats for the third time this week. Irish national broadcaster RTE and the Independent newspaper evacuated their respective office after receiving threats on Friday morning local time. Hours later, British broadcaster Sky said it had received a security threat also. Members of the Irish Armed Response Unit outside the RTE offices in Donnybroook, Dublin. RTE News The bomb threat emailed to Irish broadcaster RTE claimed to be from the same group behind a wave of bomb threats issued to passenger flights around Europe this week, an RTE reporter said on air, reading excerpts from the email. The excerpts read on air did not name the group.



Meanwhile, hoax threats are again disrupting dozens of passenger flights across Europe on Friday, after similar threats on Thursday led to unplanned landings by some planes and prompted fighter jets to escort or intercept others, a dramatic escalation after an initial wave on Tuesday. No explosive devices have been found and all planes have landed safely. Danish police said on Friday they were investigating threats directed at air traffic at Copenhagen airport, but that their immediate assessment was that there had been no danger to passengers. The airport said it was “operating normally”. Czech police said they had registered bomb threats to flights departing from and arriving in Prague. An airport spokesperson said they concerned four inbound and five outbound flights, but that no explosive devices had been found and no flights had been cancelled or diverted as a result. Loading



Shortly afterwards, an Italian airport authority source said a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome had been diverted to Venice and landed there safely. The French prime minister’s office said four new bomb threats had been made to aircraft flying over French territory, and that all had landed safely. A bomb alert on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon prompted a security operation when it landed, CNN Portugal reported. On Thursday, more than a dozen bomb threats forced unplanned landings by some planes and prompted fighter jets to escort or intercept others, in a dramatic escalation after an initial wave during the week. The highly unusual spate of bomb threats affected nearly 30 flights by the end of Thursday (Friday AEDT), after at least seven flights and a cruise ship also received hoax threats on Tuesday.



No government has said who was behind the threats, and no claim of responsibility has been verified. Security experts said it could be individuals acting on personal grievances or copycats, but also that it had the hallmarks of a more co-ordinated “hybrid attack”. “When it comes to a situation like this or even other sabotage attacks, it’s really hard to prove there’s a certain country behind it. But it does fit in the modus operandi,” said Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami. Many European officials have accused Russia of masterminding sabotage and hybrid attacks since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. These are often inexpensive to carry out, easily deniable and not expected to trigger an armed response. Planes on the tarmac after multiple flights bound for Prague received bomb threats on Thursday. Getty Images Denmark, Poland and Romania, all affected by the disruptions, have previously accused Moscow directly of being behind hybrid attacks, while Germany blamed Russia for an August attack on Leipzig Airport.



Britain, which has in the past blamed Russia, linked Iran to a suspected plot against a US air base. Both Russia and Iran have denied those accusations. An airport source in Italy told Reuters that an email with the subject line “Threat report” had been sent to several addresses for airlines, airport operators and airport service providers at Rome’s Fiumicino and Milan’s Malpensa airports. The email, which claimed it was from “fighters of the Male State”, said devices had been placed on inbound flights from Helsinki and Dublin, and they would explode in 60 minutes. “Today your sky will be red,” it said. Reuters could not independently confirm who had sent the email, and there was no immediate indication of who was behind the other threats across Europe.



The path of flight EI402 going from Dublin to Rome, after it was diverted following a bomb threat. FlightRadar24 Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up an anti-feminist movement called the Male State in 2016 that was later banned in Russia, said that the group no longer existed and was not involved in any way. “Anyone currently orchestrating provocations within European Union countries under the banner of this ‘brand’ is acting in their own self-interest – essentially flying someone else’s flag,” he wrote on his popular Telegram channel. In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said he had sent fighter jets to intercept an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome and escort it to an air force base at Evreux after the pilot did not co-operate with authorities as expected. Lecornu’s office gave no reason for the pilot’s behaviour. Bulgaria’s Air Force said its fighter jets had escorted three airliners to the ground. One Ryanair flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second city. Romania’s intelligence agency said a KLM flight to Tel Aviv with a layover in Bucharest had received a bomb threat.



Passengers wait at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague after bomb hoaxes caused travel disruptions across Europe. Getty Images Spanish police said three emailed threats came in within 20 minutes involving two Air Europa departures from Madrid to Paris and four inbound Iberia flights from Rome and Milan. Several aircraft were halted or returned to their stands in Madrid, and passengers disembarked as the aircraft were inspected. In Warsaw, a LOT flight to Paris was stopped as it taxied toward take-off, and passengers were transferred to another plane, while Danish police said they searched two planes in Copenhagen. Other flights that received threats, including EasyJet, Finnair, LOT, Wizz Air, Ryanair and Air Serbia services to Prague, Sofia, Vienna, Brussels, Bucharest, Rome and Milan, landed as scheduled, some after military escorts. Elena Pala, a passenger on a Wizz Air flight from Milan, described what happened when the plane landed in Bucharest, Romania.



“First, they took us a long way from the terminal … far away on the runway. The plane was surrounded by fire trucks, ambulances and anti-terrorist units,” she told Digi TV. “I asked what was happening. They said it was an emergency issue. That is all they said,” Pala added. Joji Waites, director of flight safety for the British Airline Pilots’ Association, said airlines did not act on threats unless assessors rated them credible. Departing passengers were philosophical. “We still have to get around. So, well, we just have to deal with it as best we can,” said Spaniard Lucia Parga. Another traveller, Gabriele Franzese, added: “You can’t worry too much about every piece of news. If the plane crashes, so be it. If it’s meant to happen, it’ll happen anyway.”



Eliran Almog, chief executive of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation, said the hoaxes could both disrupt operations and let the perpetrators observe how airlines, airports, and authorities respond. “These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe,” Almog said. “Different essential services are experiencing disruption that carries economic costs and can undermine public confidence.” This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries for the second time, also affecting French blood banks. World.title: Don’t blame Chalmers, some things are beyond his control
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Don’t blame Chalmers, some things are beyond his control November 6, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Columnist Niki Savva’s relatively positive comments about Jim Chalmers (Comment, 5/11) are apposite, but I would go further and make some different historical comparisons. He’s been one of our wisest and most courageous treasurers. He has started to undo the profound damage caused by Paul Keating retreating for party political reasons from a ban on negative gearing and by Peter Costello weakening an already very mild capital gains tax. He’s addressing the huge tax loophole for discretionary trusts that his predecessors either refused to acknowledge or left in place. Chalmers has reportedly tried to tax gas exports but been overridden from above in the same way as prime minister Bob Hawke protected an utterly anomalous tax favour for the gold industry. The treasurer is now being blamed for economic difficulties that are almost entirely due to circumstances beyond his decisive control, although he should have reversed his predecessors’ entrenchment of the Reserve Bank’s control over interest rates.

Julian Disney, Geelong GST as lever a sound idea

Your correspondent’s idea of using the GST as a lever to control inflation (Letters, 5/11) is not crazy and should be considered. In fact, eminent economists, professors David Gruen and Ross Garnaut have suggested that very idea with the creation of a central fiscal authority to lift the GST (and other taxes) in times of inflation. The independent authority would work in tandem with the RBA and its interest rate lever, with consumers sharing the burden of inflation measures with borrowers. It is much fairer too, because as consumers we can put off buying a lot of stuff we don’t need when the GST rises, whereas borrowers have no control over their monthly mortgage repayments.

Xavier Duff, West Brunswick Caught in a dilemma

I feel for the Reserve Bank board and governor Michele Bullock in particular, as they are copping flack simply for doing their job. I feel for the borrowers paying increased mortgage repayments but the central bank, like others globally, really has no other weapon for lowering inflation. The only other institutions that can curb inflation are governments by increasing taxes – and look what happens when they even attempt to do just that.

Phil Labrum, Trentham



Raising GST, and rates, are both regressive

Your correspondent (Letters, 5/11) suggests raising the GST as an alternative to raising interest rates. Unfortunately, both methods are regressive, as they affect the lower socioeconomic group far more than the wealthy. The poor are already struggling, while a couple of percentage points makes no noticeable difference to the rich. Nobody actually needs millions of dollars. While the homeless are offered tents, how about a wealth tax as a starting point in reducing needless spending?

Keith Fletcher, Glenlyon THE FORUM Jobs first for Werribee

The last thing we need in Werribee is more housing, at least until the infrastructure catches up (″⁣The sites the Coalition would sell″⁣, 6/11). What we really need are the jobs that were proposed for this large vacant tract, a plan that has now been abandoned for the site.

What happened to decentralisation which was also a previous promise by government. In reality, those running the state (read Melbourne) are keeping the jobs in town while hoping that the workers will find their way into town on already saturated roads and public transport.

John Marks, Werribee Social housing missing

Interesting plan from the Coalition to sell state-owned land, but I see no mention of social housing anywhere.

Yes, it’s good to use land that is lying fallow, but there are still so many people who cannot afford and have no access to housing. What is the plan for them – get a job?

David Jeffery, East Geelong Voters’ needs first

Your correspondent (Letters, 6/11) calls for independent bodies to be established at federal and state level to be responsible for costing and implementation of infrastructure projects. There is no doubt that the decisions in Victoria on the Suburban Rail Loop, Airport Rail, the public housing towers, train services to Melton and Tarneit, road gridlock in Beveridge and many others seem to be based on politics.

I could not agree more that we need to have decisions based on evidence of need plus objectivity in determining relative priorities. Such bodies already exist in Infrastructure Australia and Infrastructure Victoria with both being responsible for providing independent advice to government. The challenge then is how to ensure that governments make decisions for the benefit of the people rather than perceived electoral advantage. Hopefully, all candidates for the upcoming election take note of the US election results and see the value of keeping the needs of the voters in the centre of their decision making.

Pauline Brown, Woodend



Not Israel’s fault

Interesting how your correspondent (Letters, 6/11) identifies Donald Trump as the one cutting aid to Israel while claiming that it’s the state of Israel that has the anti-Palestine policies.

The reality, however, is that until some 20 years ago consecutive Israeli governments have made all the efforts for a two-state solution, but the Palestinians rejected them. This is all well-documented in history books.

What is of concern is that your correspondent makes out that it’s all Israel’s fault when in reality the Palestinian authorities have set many obstacles along the way. It’s this type of misinformation that makes it all the harder for Jewish Australians to be treated like all other Australians.

Henry Herzog, St Kilda East Slim pickings

With an overwhelming body of evidence on One Nation’s inability to articulate any of their costings, the Premier, Ben Carroll, desperately trying to navigate the smouldering plane wreckage of Jacinta Allan’s time as leader and Jess Wilson walking out on press conferences and also having troubles answering critical questions on her team’s state financial resurrection, what quality of candidates are we left with? Slim pickings this time around.

David West, Essendon Trump’s sense of self

Numerous commentators are describing the outcome of the American midterm elections as a defeat for the president’s Republican Party. That supposes that Donald Trump is interested in political parties. I do not think he is. The usual work of political parties, developing policies, and when in government, working through ways to implement them, has no interest for him. His is a cultish view of political parties as simply a prop to his sense of self, with all its strange vagaries. The American electorate has now seen through that. Can the Republican Party rebuild itself as a recognisable political party? Are there lessons for Australian political parties to take note of? And if there are, do they have the strength of character to look and learn? Time alone will tell.

David Ben-Tovim, Carlton Dealing with Congress

Donald Trump is erratic, but he also has very strong survival instincts. While many are concerned about a conflict-driven, strong-arm approach to the remainder of his presidency, I can also envisage him taking a more conciliatory “keep your friends close but keep your enemies closer″⁣ approach to Congress so as not to act as a catalyst in relation to any investigations that may be being considered.

Claire Merry, Wantirna Plan B please

If inflation doesn’t come down in the next 12 months, will the Reserve Bank just keep putting interest rates up ad nauseum? What is its plan B?

Robert Scheffer, Bayswater North



Getting balance right

Many of your recent correspondents have bemoaned the actions of the RBA and the government in trying to control inflation. Booms and busts have occurred throughout history, well before the Tulipmania of the 1630s. Governments have struggled to find ways of taming these excesses and have identified only a few levers to achieve this. Governments use taxes and spending, while banks use increases and decreases in interest rates. We should not lambast these institutions when they use the limited means available to them. Getting the balance right for all of us is a constant, legitimate struggle. Let them get on with the job.

Graeme Rose, Wangaratta History repeats

The Second World War exposed humanity’s darkest side. Hitler exploited economic hardship, fear and racial prejudice, manipulating the German media and public opinion to turn the Jewish minority into scapegoats for the nation’s problems. The consequences were catastrophic.

In the aftermath, the United Nations was established with the hope of preventing such horrors from ever happening again.

Yet today, we are seeing familiar patterns emerging across the world. Political leaders are exploiting economic uncertainty, social division and public frustration, using fear and misinformation to undermine trust in established institutions and blame vulnerable minorities, particularly immigrants, for society’s problems. Social media has provided a powerful new platform for these tactics.

Are we witnessing history repeating itself? I sincerely hope not.

Civil societies must recognise these dangers and work together. We must challenge prejudice, expose misinformation and resist those who seek to gain power by dividing communities and turning people against one another.The lessons of history are there for all of us to learn, but only if we are prepared to listen. Humanity has no real external enemies. Its greatest enemy is the one within, and its name is ignorance.

Rod Horton, Sale Follow this lead

Thank you to Alexandra and Julian Burt, beneficiaries of mining interests, for their donation (″⁣Billionaire couple make $120m donation to nature″⁣, 5/11). We hope this will inspire other corporations and high net-worth individuals who have benefited from exploiting Australia’s natural resources, to make similar contributions. The environmental problems of feral plants and animals, high intensity bushfires, land clearance and the decline of plant and animal species deserve the attention of all of us, especially the rich.

Andrew Isles, Prahran Clarification

Some recent letters suggested the government was directly responsible for decisions on rates. These decisions are made independently by the RBA, but government policy can affect those decisions. Photo: Matt Golding



AND ANOTHER THING The US

Donald Trump should join the Democrats because the Republicans are losers.

David Mandara, Hepburn Springs Donald Trump and his ilk should remember the old saying “you reap what you sow”. Sowing division and hate has been rejected by the American people thankfully.

Randall Bradshaw, Fitzroy How long can a US president rule by decree? If I were a US citizen I would very quickly be cheesed off.

John Walsh, Watsonia California Governor Gavin Newsom, in his final acts in the position, has commuted the death penalties of more than 500 prisoners to life imprisonment. It is a shining example for the other states that still perform the barbaric practice of the death penalty.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris



Furthermore

If One Nation ″⁣has the guts to say what you’re thinking″⁣, it’s probably time to stop thinking that.

Steve Melzer, Hughesdale The advertising jingle goes ″⁣there’s no other store like David Jones″⁣. Not any more.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill David Jones has now sunk to Davy Jones’ Locker.

Bryan Fraser, St Kilda West With a cost-of-living crisis, how do people find $500 million to spend on Halloween decorations? It’s to be hoped they’re kept for future years and not just sent to landfill.

Lorraine Bates, Balwyn Ross Gittins suggests ″⁣higher interest rates make it more attractive to save″⁣ (Comment, 4/11). Just how do you save anything when rates eat even more of your income?

Bryan Lewis, St Helena



When you spend a dollar, you vote for the world you want to live in. When you buy a Chinese electric car, you are supporting a political system that imprisons a peaceful democrat.

Adam Thomson, Collingwood Finally

As I get older, are my declining intellectual powers correlated to my increasingly bad handwriting (Letters, 6/11)? Jan Newmarch, Oakleigh

World.title: Former Cronulla Sharks star knocked out in first round
World.content:
Nelson Asofa-Solomona claims a racial taunt prompted him to lash out at a spectator in the moments after his devastating first-round knockout win over Paul Gallen.

Asofa-Solomona landed a straight right and two uppercuts that left Gallen sprawled on the canvas for several minutes, raising serious concerns about his health. The former NSW skipper eventually recovered sufficiently to congratulate Asofa-Solomona on the victory, but was rushed to hospital shortly afterwards.

Loading

Just moments after inflicting the final blow, the former Melbourne Storm forward leapt out of the ring to lash out at a spectator. He appeared poised to unleash a roundhouse right before pulling the punch.

“I looked into the crowd, and someone was making an ape gesture,” Asofa-Solomona said.

“I stood on the ropes, and it looked like someone threw something at me, so I just lost my temper. As I said, if I could have my time back, I would handle it differently, because that behavior isn’t acceptable. At the same time, what that person did with that gesture isn’t acceptable either.

“I think it was a mix of everything. The adrenaline was there, but I also don’t tolerate that kind of nonsense. Once I saw it, I just saw red. But like I said, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t do that again.”

Paul Gallen is knocked out by Nelson Asofa-Solomona. Getty Images

Gallen, at the age of 45, was no match for the bigger and younger man. “Big Nelson” was 15 years younger and 33 kilograms heavier, with a decided reach advantage that he exploited during the opening exchanges.

With the final seconds of the opening round ticking down, Asofa-Solomona landed a series of sickening blows. Two straight right hands, followed by four uppercuts all hit flush, with the last punches landing as Gallen was canvas bound.

“It’s pretty emotional,” Asofa-Solomona said. “I guess the build-up and everything - words were said.

“He’s the crossover heavyweight king. I remember watching him as a young kid growing up. Even when we were playing against each other, I admired what he did, because it’s not a road that everyone walks, you know? It’s a scary one.

“You get a lot of your ego from footy, and you have this character you want to uphold. When you step into the ring, you feel a bit exposed in there.”

Asofa-Solomona said that he was concerned about the welfare of Gallen after seeing him lie motionless on the canvas.

“Yeah, for sure,” he said. “Once things settled down, it kind of hit me what had just happened. Anyone who has been in that position knows that when things get heated, situations can quickly turn for the worse.

“I’m happy I got the win, but if I could have my time back regarding what happened at the end, I would change it.”

World.title: Hot seats in spotlight as Victorian voters eye burning issues
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaHot seats Hot seats in spotlight as Victorian voters eye burning issues Katy Hall November 6, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For many Victorians, there is no one singular burning issue that crystallises the mood heading into this year’s state election. Rather, as the inimitable Dennis Denuto famously said in The Castle, it’s the vibe. Premier Ben Carroll, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering. After 12 years in government and three Labor premiers, there is a distinct mood for change in the air. But what direction that change will take is still very much up for debate. Whether it’s potholes, data centres, hospital waiting times, housing affordability and accessibility, allegations of corruption on government Big Build sites or just a general frustration of unmet promises, there’s a veritable cornucopia of issues for voters to choose from this time around. Whatever happens on November 28, the outcome is likely to be historic. If Labor manages to hold on, their consecutive fourth-term win will be a first for the party, and something the state hasn’t seen in more than 50 years. If the Liberals take office, Jess Wilson will become the first female-elected premier of Victoria – and one of the youngest at just 36 years old. And then there is One Nation, whose rising popularity remains the biggest unknown.



With so many variables at play, we’ve embedded four of our journalists into electorates across the state to hit the streets, speak with locals, scrutinise candidates and their campaigns, and provide a real-time vibe check. Victorian affairs editor Annika Smethurst is in Hawthorn, a seat once considered a jewel in the Liberal Party’s crown. But much like the federal electorate of Kooyong (which Hawthorn sits within), any guaranteed safety the Liberals once enjoyed in Melbourne’s eastern suburbs is long gone. Related Article Victorian election Wilson’s ‘Jess Express’ campaign bus crashes into small business after just two hours on the road The threat of the so-called teal independents isn’t the only thing that makes Hawthorn especially noteworthy this year, though. The past four years of John Pesutto’s political life could hardly be described as smooth. After winning the seat back in 2022, his most recent term in parliament has included a stint as the opposition leader, a drawn out legal battle with a former colleague that came with a bill of more than $2.6 million, and a move to the backbench.



For most, this would be enough to call it a day. And yet, in a sit down interview with Smethurst we’ll be publishing next week, the 56-year-old says he is optimistic about his chances of returning to Spring Street, and possibly earning a cabinet position. Another seat where the national mood could inform what happens at a state level is Shepparton, which neighbours Farrer – the federal electorate One Nation claimed from the Liberals in a shock byelection victory earlier this year. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election We asked Ben Carroll’s loved ones to sing his praises. They gave us the same backhanded compliment Much like Hawthorn for the Liberals, Shepparton has long been considered a safe seat for the Nationals, having only been held by people outside the party twice in its 59 years. With One Nation representing a tide of change for disillusioned voters and breathing down the Nationals’ neck, senior city reporter Angelica Snowden is busy pounding the region’s pavements to get a sense of where things are headed, and the major issues keeping voters up at night.



In Ringwood, sports affairs reporter Bridget McArthur has been getting well acquainted with the EastLink, and taking the temperature in a seat Labor picked up as part of the “Danslide” election in 2018, but could be lost thanks to a controversial outgoing member and undelivered election promises. Following in the footsteps of Will Fowles, the Labor member who turned independent after being kicked out of the party by Daniel Andrews in 2023, the party’s candidate for Ringwood this year, Rachel Halse, will have a tough job trying to retain the margin Labor once enjoyed. But as an emergency nurse running in a seat where health and aged care are among the biggest employers, it would be a mistake to count anything – or anyone – out yet. In Sydenham, the sparks are well and truly flying. Investigative reporter Liam Mannix describes the electorate as “a genuine three-horse race” between Labor, the Liberals and One Nation. And with the retirement of Natalie Hutchins, Labor’s sitting member, this will be a race of untested candidates, which is always a guarantee for compelling viewing. Traditionally seen as a central brick in Labor’s “Red Wall”, Sydenham locals in a recent focus group made it clear that like other seats across the state, theirs is ripe for turning. For those outside of these electorates, fear not. We will be travelling across the state to cover the big issues, while the Spring Street bureau will be on the campaign trail to offer extensive and in-depth stories from the road. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

Located in the tightly held Toxteth Estate on a tree-lined street, this c. 1880 freestanding Victorian blends its distinctive period design with contemporary updates. Period features include its facade, high ceilings, parquet floors, formal lounge and dining rooms and fireplaces. An indoor-outdoor flow links the two private courtyards to the open-plan family rooms and kitchen, which has stone benchtops and a walk-in pantry. Part of a landmark Victorian Italianate row dating back to c. 1887, this Balmain terrace showcases quality craftsmanship. Natural light fills the interior through a series of skylights; it features herringbone floors, detailed skirtings/architraves, underfloor heating and heated towel rails in the bathrooms. World.title: Labor flags corruption risks for widening police DV powers
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Labor flags corruption risks for widening police DV powers Matt Dennien November 6, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queensland’s Labor opposition has raised major concerns with a government push to expand police on-the-spot domestic violence order powers, urging greater safeguards as an LNP-controlled committee rubber-stamped the bill for passage through parliament. In a statement of reservation attached to the committee report, released on Friday, Labor MPs highlighted a submission from the Crime and Corruption Commission warning of the inherent risk of such powers and unwinding of a key oversight measure. A separate government-controlled committee has also greenlit another bill which would place significant new limits on who can lodge objections to mining lease applications, and whether those objections will be heard by the state’s Land Court. The Victims’ Commissioner has also urged a long-awaited Police Integrity Unit be “established as soon as possible to enhance victim and community confidence”. Michelle Smith The Crisafulli government introduced the bill to expand the police powers in September, citing criticism from police that an initial scheme established late last year, and due for review within two years but not yet subject to one, was too onerous to be of use.



Most existing restrictions around use of the “police protection directions” would be removed, and directions will be able to be issued for up to three years, rather than one. Previous powers acting as a stop-gap until a matter could be urgently heard in court will be repealed. Issuing a direction will be a requirement when releasing a person from custody, unless that person is deemed to be most in need of protection, and any direction “in error” will be able to be scrubbed from a person’s domestic violence history. “There is no clear rationale for the change in policy position from 2025 ...” Crime and Corruption Commission submission Police will still have to file a direction with a court in certain circumstances, such as when there are related proceedings under way. The bill will also increase penalties for repeat breaches of domestic violence orders, and expand a statewide electronic monitoring trial. The corruption watchdog’s submission to education, arts and communities committee consideration of the bill noted the proposed removal of exclusions barring police from issuing a direction when another officer is involved as either the alleged perpetrator or victim.



This had been done, according to explanatory notes at the time, “to ensure DFV [domestic and family violence] matters involving police are heard by a court and are not handled internally,” the watchdog noted. Related Article Queensland government Police handed new powers to issue on-the-spot domestic violence orders “The Bill removes the protection this exclusion provides,” acting chair Kathryn McMillan wrote. “There is no clear rationale for the change in policy position from 2025, nor provision for additional safeguards to manage the potential risks that may arise in circumstances where a police officer is involved in a DFV matter.” McMillan said there were inherent corruption risks associated with discretionary police powers around issuing such directions when an officer is involved, and said dumping safeguards appeared at odds with calls from the 2022 Richards Inquiry – including for a new police integrity unit.



Labor MPs noted a submission from the Victims’ Commissioner also highlighted that outstanding work, and urged that the unit be “established as soon as possible to enhance victim and community confidence in police integrity”. Related Article Queensland government ‘Fossil fuel free-for-all’: Queensland to block ‘activists’ from objecting to mining leases “The Attorney-General [Deb Frecklington] has now had more than two years, and the government is still only considering the recommendation,” the Labor MPs wrote, noting they supported reforms giving police better support to protect victims survivors and the community. “Again, these steps need to be based in the evidence, and they must be carefully balanced with the inherent risks that are associated with responding to domestic and family violence and they need to have victim survivors front and centre. “This bill, without additional safeguards, does not appear to meet that threshold.”



The committee recommended the bill pass as drafted. The committee leading consideration of the government’s mining objection overhaul suggested one change to allow objections from neighbouring councils. Labor MPs, along with Traeger MP Robbie Katter, also issued statements of reservation in the report on that bill, citing the removal of pathways for community involvement in decision-making. Parliament returns for its next three-day sitting week on November 17. The government, with its majority, does not require votes of the Opposition or crossbench to pass laws. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: What you can and can't do on election day
World.content:
Explainer - Take down those signs, pause that Instagram post - here's what you need to know about restrictions on election day.

New Zealand has mandatory rules about how much campaigning is allowed, and you could possibly be hit with a fine of up to $20,000 if you ignore them.

What can't I do?

Once it's election day on Saturday, 7 November, you are no longer allowed to do any campaigning or anything that would influence voters. This includes signs, demonstrations and posts on social media.

"I think there is a good argument for giving voters a bit of peace and quiet on election day," said Mona Krewel, a senior lecturer on comparative politics at Victoria University of Wellington Te Herenga Waka who has been tracking the role of social media in previous elections.

"At this point, the campaign has been going on for long enough, and all parties have had a fair opportunity to inform voters about their policies and candidates," she said.

Download the Electoral Commission's full guide to rules on election day here.

What are the penalties?

According to the Electoral Act 1993, interfering with or influencing voters can lead to a fine of up to $20,000.

Is there any campaigning allowed at a polling place?

On election day, it's strictly forbidden to do anything anywhere that might influence voters until the polls close at 7pm.

During early voting, any campaigning or advertising is prohibited at voting places or within 10 metres of their entrance.

Can I keep that election hoarding up on my front fence?

No. All election signs and hoardings must be removed by midnight Friday before election day. Vehicles with election signs, bumper stickers and other political advertising must be out of public view as well.

Political parties and MPs can leave fixed signage at their offices and headquarters if they were up before election day and aren't explicitly part of the campaign.

Can I post a selfie online with my ballot telling everyone to vote like me?

Heck no. On election day from midnight to 7pm, you can't post or share any content on social media about your vote.

"Don't post anything to social media or a website on election day that could influence voters," the Electoral Commission warns.

There is no exemption for "the expression of personal political views online" according to the Electoral Commission, so in other words, no matter how you feel really, really strongly about your personal party vote, keep it to yourself for a few hours.

People can get caught out by the rules around social media posts.

Several sports stars including Israel Dagg and the late Jonah Lomu were called out over tweets seen as endorsing the National Party in 2014. In 2017, broadcaster Sean Plunket was referred to police over posts that were seen as endorsing TOP (the former name of Opportunity) on election day.

And in 2023, the Electoral Commission said it reported 20 people referred to police over social media posts on election day.

Social media posts on election day can violate the rules. ROBIN UTRECHT / ANP MAG / ANP via AFP

Do I have to take down everything I've ever written in the past about the election?

No. You're not required to remove existing material on websites or social media as long as you don't update it on election day or advertise it, or repost old material on election day, and as long as it's only available to people who choose to access it.

Even things like having your profile picture promoting a party or candidate could be considered an offence, so check your socials carefully.

"The Electoral Commission does not ask people to completely remove stuff from social media or websites on election day, as long as people are not actively being pushed towards that content and only see it when they decide to access it voluntarily," Krewel said.

"Asking for everything to be removed entirely is probably also unrealistic these days."

There is an argument that restrictions laid out in the Electoral Act 1993 aren't quite fit for purpose in 2026, and that plenty of influencing still goes on during early voting.

"With advance voting becoming increasingly popular and many New Zealanders casting their ballots well before election day, the regulation is becoming somewhat outdated," Krewel noted.

"We essentially have a situation where some voters are still exposed to active campaigning right up until the moment they cast their vote, while those who vote on election day get a campaign-free environment. So the original rationale for the restriction is becoming less convincing as voting habits change."

Many people probably aren't even aware of the restrictions on election day posting, Krewel said.

"Most people probably know the basics, but I doubt that many are aware that something as seemingly harmless as posting 'Vote for the Greens!' on their personal social media account on election day could constitute a breach of electoral law."

Krewel said the restrictions "strike a fair balance" as people can still seek out previous information online on voting day if they wish, but they also give voters a break from a feed full of election hype on the day itself.

Can I just take a cool TikTok of the people who are voting?

Absolutely not. The Electoral Commission asks people to respect the privacy of others.

Publishing photos or videos of someone filling out their ballot is a potential offence.

Some permissions can be granted by electorate managers for photo ops, like a candidate casting their vote or media coverage of voting.

Enforcement of the social media rules are difficult, though, Krewel said.

"The Electoral Commission does not actively monitor everyone's conduct on election day, and realistically, it couldn't possibly police everything people post online. Instead, it largely relies on complaints and responds when potential breaches are brought to its attention."

There are rules about conduct around voting places, too. RNZ/Nosiphi Mapukata

Can I give away free sausages outside polling places to everyone voting?

Nah, mate.

Last year, the government moved to strengthen the offence of "treating" by creating a 100-metre buffer around polling stations where free food, drink and entertainment are not allowed.

Any place acting as a voting place that would ordinarily be providing food is allowed to - such as refreshments at a tangi or tea and coffee in a school staffroom.

Can I poll people leaving about who they voted for?

Nope. You can't do that on election day or during advance voting.

"Our processes ensure people have a positive experience, and that their privacy and other rights are protected," the Electoral Commission notes.

Aggressive behaviour will not be tolerated at the polls. RNZ / Nick Monro

Can I just hang out at the voting place for a while afterwards to soak up the vibes?

"Once you have voted, we ask that you don't linger and leave the voting place straight away," the Electoral Commission advises.

The Electoral Commission has also warned people that aggressive behaviour won't be tolerated - a concern particularly high this year.

"Members of the public who are disruptive or causing a disturbance will be told to leave the voting place. Failure to comply with this direction is an offence and may be referred to police."

Can I stand out in front of the polling place with a megaphone telling everyone to vote for my candidate?

That's a definite no, for all the reasons mentioned above.

Can I at least wear my red for Labour badge or blue for National rosette?

According to the Electoral Commission, you may wear a party lapel badge or rosette with party colours, a party name and branding, but not a candidate name. Any lapel badge or rosette you wear must include a promoter statement. You can also wear party colours, but only on people or vehicles.

Can I remind people to vote or help them get to the polls?

You are allowed to contact people to offer help or a reminder, but must not influence how they vote.

If you need help to vote, the Electoral Commission also offers several special services for those with disabilities or in need of support.

Dogs are OK - outside, at least. RNZ / Rhonwyn Newson

Last question - can I bring my dog?

Of course, although they can't vote if they're not enrolled, and it's strictly up to the polling place's rules itself if they're allowed inside.

Who do I complain to if someone is breaking those rules?

You can start with the Electoral Commission. If they believe an offence has been committed, they'll refer people to the police. They can't enforce the law or prosecute offenders themselves.

Krewel said she didn't see the election day restrictions as any real kind of freedom of speech issue.

"People have plenty of time to express their political opinions throughout the election campaign and can freely do so again immediately after election day," she said.

World.title: How your votes are counted on election day
World.content:
Explainer: Election day is Saturday and close to 4 million enrolled Kiwis will have their say on picking the next government.

Who's going to count all those votes, how do they do it and why does it take so long to get a final result?

Here's what you need to know.

What happens when the votes are counted?

All votes are counted by hand and not by machines.

A preliminary count is done on election day and then the official count begins afterwards, with the final results expected by Friday, 27 November.

Several things are counted - advance votes cast before election day, ordinary votes cast on election day and special votes.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dKa9ieYTwVw

Before voting closes on Saturday, early ordinary votes made during advance voting are taken to electorate headquarters and the count begins. Those results won't be released until 7pm.

Votes made on election day itself are counted after polls close at 7pm and released as preliminary results.

Candidates and parties are also allowed to appoint scrutineers, who can witness the early and election day vote counts.

Most votes are counted on election day and on election night. Supplied / Electoral Commission

Why do official results take so long?

Early votes and votes on election day are counted quickly, and make up the preliminary results. The Electoral Commission's target is to have 50 percent of the results available by 10pm and 95 percent by 11.30pm on election day.

Then there are the special votes, which require extra checking and time to process. Special votes are by anyone not on the electoral roll or unpublished roll, living overseas or voting away from a polling place, because they can't get to one.

They have a stricter checking procedure and any overseas votes can also take longer to process.

In 2023, it took three weeks to count special votes to confirm the election results.

Special votes have to be returned to the electorate they were cast for before they're counted. Every special vote declaration is checked to make sure the voter is enrolled and eligible to vote.

The Electoral Commission expects as many as 700,000 special votes this year.

The commission has already said that it expects to take about 20 days to do the required checks and deliver final election results.

Once the count is complete for each voting place during the official count, the totals are recorded on a certificate signed by the returning officer and a Justice of the Peace.

For the official count, the commission will also "scrutinise the roll" - comparing every copy of the electorate roll in each electorate to identify any voters who may have voted more than once. If any person suspected of double-voting is found, there's an investigation and any voter found to have voted more than once is not included in the final official count.

The official count is entered into New Zealand's Election Management System, which was developed in the country and "regularly undergoes independent security testing and certification", according to the commission.

Finally, the official count is declared by the Chief Electoral Officer.

Who does all this checking?

Those who count the votes are Electoral Commission staff and not volunteers.

The commission said all staff were fully trained, including on how to count the votes.

What happens to my voting paper?

After the count, the voting papers are sealed in envelopes and then put in boxes closed with tamper-proof seals. They're held in secure storage for six months after the election, in case ballots are needed for a legal challenge.

After six months, those papers are taken out of storage, shredded and destroyed. Official representatives from Parliament and the Electoral Commission will witness the destruction.

Voting papers are held in secure storage for six months after the election. Supplied / Electoral Commission

Who can be a scrutineer?

Electorate candidates can appoint scrutineers to observe vote counting - but candidates themselves and MPs cannot be scrutineers, and list-only candidates can't appoint them.

When it comes to special votes, they can observe the checking of special vote declarations, and the official count of overseas, remote and dictation votes in Wellington, and checking of special vote declarations in any designated enrolment office of the Electoral Commission.

Party secretaries of registered parties contesting the party vote can also appoint scrutineers to observe parts of the counting process under certain circumstances.

According to the Electoral Commission's handbook for scrutineers, those chosen are allowed in a designated area within voting places. They are not allowed to obstruct voters or staff, and while they can photograph certain records, they cannot touch any voting materials or photograph voters.

Election staff check a voter roll during a simulation exercise. Supplied / Electoral Commission

Can you get a recount?

If you're an electorate candidate, you can apply to a District Court judge for a recount. You must apply within three working days of the official results being declared and include a deposit of $1022.22 with the application.

The judge must then start the recount within three working days.

There is no threshold laid out in section 180 of the Electoral Act 1993 that requires how close the vote has to be for a candidate to apply for a recount, so theoretically, any losing candidate could apply for one.

If there's a tie in the electorate, a recount is automatic.

There were three judicial recounts in the 2023 election - for close races in Nelson, Mt Albert and the Māori electorate Tamaki Makarau. None of those recounts changed who won the seat.

For the party vote, only the party secretary can apply for a recount. That can either be for a specific electorate or for every electorate.

A recount for every electorate requires a $92,000 deposit to be paid.

An election petition can also be filed as a formal legal challenge to a result and it's the next step if someone wants to challenge an outcome beyond the recount process.

One such petition was filed in 1999 in the Coromandel electorate by National incumbent Murray McLean over Green candidate Jeanette Fitzsimons' 250-vote victory. The court upheld Fitzsimons' win.

What if there are mistakes in the election?

The Electoral Commission says it runs parliamentary elections "that are free and fair", and their goal is to "provide an effective and impartial electoral system that New Zealanders can understand and trust".

Following the voting process, probes can be made, if issues are reported.

After the 2023 election, the auditor-general launched an investigation, after more than two dozen voting places made errors when confirming the final election result. The errors did not result in any major changes to the overall results or allocation of seats once amended.

In the final report, that investigation found the final check of the official election result was done in a few hours under extreme pressure.

The auditor-general identified several factors he thought had contributed to a situation where mistakes could be made and go undetected, including an increase in late enrolments and special votes.

Enrolments this year ended on 25 October, instead of carrying on to election day, as in 2023.

World.title: What are special votes and why they could change the election results?
World.content:
Explainer - Election Day is coming up fast, but don't expect complete clarity on 7 November, thanks to special votes.

Special votes, which are counted slower, have shifted preliminary election results the last several times. And they may well do it again in 2026.

Here's what you need to know about what makes a vote special, why they take longer to sort and why some may end up getting discarded.

What are special votes?

Special votes are made by anyone who isn't on their electoral roll at their voting place, on the unpublished roll, lives overseas or votes away from a polling place because they can't get to one.

When you cast a special vote, you must also sign a declaration form that must be witnessed by another person. (If you vote at a voting place, that witness can be an Electoral Commission volunteer or staff member.)

And if you have yet to enrol for this year's election - remember the absolute latest you can do that is by midnight on Sunday, 25 October - you will be casting a special vote.

The printed roll for this year's election closed on 4 October, which was Writ Day. Any voter who enrols after that must cast a special vote.

"The number of special votes, and the proportion they make up of the overall vote, have increased in recent elections," an Electoral Commission spokesperson told RNZ.

"Over 600,000 special votes were issued in 2023 - meaning 21 percent of voters cast a special vote."

Richard Shaw, professor of politics at Massey University, noted that in the last election many people enrolled during the early voting period - which will no longer be allowed due to the government changing the deadline so you must be enrolled 13 days before the election.

In 2023, "450,000 people enrolled or updated their enrolment during the voting period; 110,000 did so on Election Day itself," Shaw said.

Despite the changes to enrolment, the Electoral Commission expects as many as 700,000 special votes this year.

The number of special votes has been steadily rising in recent elections, up from 13.5 percent of the overall total in 2014.

Have special votes made a difference in past elections?

They have. In the last three general elections, the final results including special votes have seen National lose two party seats and some electorates have changed sides from the preliminary tally.

It means that even after Election Day on 7 November and preliminary results come in, we may not know the final, final results for a couple of weeks.

Special votes generally tend to benefit the left-leaning parties.

Shaw said that tends to reflect the demographics of those who cast them: "typically younger; typically more mobile (eg renters); typically a little less attached to institutional politics".

"Those groups don't always break left, but they tend to. Or they tend not to engage at all."

In 2017, 2020 and 2023, National lost two seats with special votes, while Labour gained one in 2017 and 2020, Te Pāti Māori gained one in 2020 and two in 2023, and the Greens gained one party seat in 2017 and 2023.

The Electoral Commission is predicting it will take up to 20 days to total special votes. The commission said it has found ways to improve the speed of its checks, but it's still a lengthy process.

"Our forecasts indicate we could receive around 700,000 special votes, which take up to ten times longer to check and count," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

"If our forecast is right, then we will need 20 days to do all the required checks and deliver final results."

This year's election does away with being able to enrol to vote and cast a ballot all the way up to Election Day.

That change is likely to affect special votes, Shaw said.

"There will almost certainly be a higher rate of rejection of special votes this time round."

"At this point, of course, we have no way of knowing how many people are going to show up and cast a special which won't be counted ... some specials will be tallied, of course, because they are overseas votes or people out of their electorate or whatever, but plenty won't."

Voting papers being printed in Petone, Wellington weeks ahead of the election. Samuel Rillstone/RNZ

Why do they take longer to count?

They have a stricter checking procedure, and any overseas votes can also take longer to process. In 2023 it took three weeks for special votes to be counted to confirm the election results.

By law, 10 days are allowed for votes to be returned from overseas.

Special votes have to be returned to the electorate they were cast for before they're counted. Every special vote declaration is checked to make sure the voter is enrolled and eligible to vote.

"We check the voter was enrolled in the electorate where they voted, and check that the special declaration form has been completed and witnessed," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

"Special votes that are allowed can only be counted after these checks have been done. Votes are tallied and quality assurance checks are made before we release the results."

Shaw said overseas votes, once they're counted, could also affect how the election shakes out.

"The overseas voting population is interesting this year: there are more of them than previously (and at least some of them are presumably people who have left the country while they might rather have remained, had the economic conditions been better), so that might count against the incumbent administration too."

The government pushed for this year's changes to enrolment deadlines and one of the reasons it gave was to speed up vote counting.

"I just think three weeks is way too long to count special votes, I think that needs to be sped up," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said in 2023.

However, when those enrolment changes were still being considered last year as part of the Electoral Amendment Bill, Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said it ultimately wouldn't make results arrive any faster.

"We're forecasting that there'll still be around 700,000 special votes we've got to run through all these integrity checks," he said then.

Some special votes in the election may be disqualified. RNZ / Nick Monro

Why can special votes be tossed out?

In the 2023 general election, 15,555 special votes were disqualified.

"Reasons special votes are disallowed include if the voter is not enrolled, the vote received was late, or the declaration was not signed by an authorised witness or not signed by voter," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

The Electoral Commission has a full breakdown of why special votes were disallowed broken down by electorate on their website.

By far the biggest reason was that voters were not actually enrolled at all, with 10,566 discounted for that reason. Far behind was having a declaration not being signed by an authorised witness, with 2384 rejections.

In last year's Auckland local body elections, nearly half of the special votes were disqualified.

Auckland Council said 4162 special votes were deemed invalid, due to incorrect or missing declaration details, or outdated enrolment details. Special votes were only 1.68 percent of the total vote cast, it said.

Similar high rates of disqualification were seen in Kaipara's local council election.

However, it's important to note that local body elections are not run by the Electoral Commission, but by local councils, and can have different rules and procedures.

In a council post-mortem on the Auckland local elections, it was found that "in most cases the reason for the declaration not being in order was the required 'occupation' field left blank, leading to special votes being disallowed on what could be perceived as a technicality."

That occupation requirement is no longer needed in parliamentary elections.

"For the general election, the required fields on special voting declaration forms are your name, the grounds (reason) for casting a special vote, and your signature," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

"Some special voting declaration forms may still include an occupation field. This field is no longer required and can be left blank. We are gradually phasing out older versions of the form that include this field."

The Auckland Council's report said that in the future "a similar amendment should be made to remove the requirement to include occupation from the special voting declaration for local elections".

"Why should providing your occupation determine whether your vote is counted?" City Vision candidate Raphaela Rose asked The Spinoff in a report on the invalidated local body votes.

Only 29 percent of those eligible voted in Auckland in 2025, and Auckland has moved to remove postal voting at the next local body elections and require in-person voting.

Shaw said the changes to voter enrolment this year are a bit of an X-factor in trying to figure out how important special votes will be in November's election.

"One possibility, given the new policy settings, is that special votes are less, not more, important as far as the final outcome is concerned, in the sense that there may well be fewer of them that count this time round.

World.title: What you need to know about how MMP works
World.content:
* This article has been updated to correct the number of seats that typically make up Parliament.

Explainer - Our MMP electoral system is marking its 30th anniversary this year, but it can still be tricky to explain exactly how it all works.

If you're confused about all the recent talk about overhangs and party votes and just want to know what you're deciding on at the ballot box, here's what you need to know about voting and MMP.

What is MMP?

MMP stands for Mixed Member Proportional representation, the electoral system used in New Zealand.

A majority of New Zealanders voted for it - twice, first in a non-binding referendum in 1992, and again in a binding referendum at the election the following year. It was introduced at the next election, in 1996.

National's leader Christopher Luxon has proposed another referendum over MMP, to be held after the 7 November election.

MMP aims to ensure that people will be represented in Parliament both by a person in their local area (electorate) and by a group (a political party).

How does it work?

New Zealanders have two votes - one for a local representative, and one for a political party. You just pick the person in your electorate you think best advances your interests, and the political party that best represents your interests.

Simple, right?

The complexity comes in when trying to calculate how these votes translate into the seats available for members of Parliament (MPs).

There are (typically) 120 seats:

71 are electorate seats and are won by candidates standing in specific areas

are electorate seats and are won by candidates standing in specific areas 49 are list seats and are allocated depending on the proportion of party votes won, taking into account the number of electorate seats each party has won

Basically, it all means that the proportion of party votes should be about the same as the proportion of seats in the Parliament. Electorate MPs will belong to one party or another unless they're running as an independent, but voters do not need to vote for an electorate representative that matches their party vote.

You must be registered - or enrolled - to be able to vote, and unlike in previous elections this year you will not be able to enrol on the day, or in the two weeks before election day.

In 2026, this means voters must be enrolled before 25 October.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins and National leader Christopher Luxon. RNZ/ Nick Monro / Marika Khabazi

Other things to consider

A party has to win at least 5 percent of votes or an electorate seat to win a seat in Parliament.

If they win an electorate seat, the party gets allocated a percentage of list seats based on their party vote - known as the "coat tail" rule.

If a party wins more electorates than its share of party votes allows for, extra seats can be added to the Parliament to make up for the "overhang" and ensure the proportions remain closer to the party vote than they would otherwise.

For instance, this meant there were 121 MPs in 2005, 122 MPs in 2008, and 121 in 2011, and 123 - a record number of MPs - after the election in 2023. It's possible there could be even more this year due to some calls for "strategic voting".

MMP determines the shape of Parliament. Gerry Brownlee has been Speaker in its most recent term. VNP/Phil Smith

So who wins the election?

In contrast to some countries overseas - the United States for example - the election in New Zealand is not voting for the country's leader. People vote only for the parties and electorates.

But someone has to be in charge. Someone has to make sure the organisations doing all the management of the country - funding hospitals and schools, repairing roads and infrastructure, managing prisons - all that administrative stuff, and more, is being done properly.

This responsibility - and the power it entails - belongs to the government.

Who gets to become the government is basically whichever party can get a majority - more than 50 percent - of the seats, based on their party vote. If none of the parties has enough to reach more than 50 percent, they must negotiate with each other about their plans until a combination of the parties has at least half the seats.

This can result in a coalition - where the bigger party and smaller party form a government together and come up with a complete policy plan - or a confidence and supply agreement, where the smaller parties agree to support the main governing party on specific policies.

Under confidence and supply, the smaller party does not need to support policies that fall outside the agreement.

With 50 percent of the seats in Parliament, the governing party or coalition can decide what to change about how the country works and enact these decisions in Parliament. We currently have a coalition government between National, New Zealand First and ACT.

The governing parties have most of the power. The parties that are not governing are known as the opposition, and it is their job to criticise and poke holes in the plans the government is putting forward.

National leader Christopher Luxon has said another referendum on MMP is needed. RNZ/Nick Monro

Will MMP ever change?

Not everyone likes MMP, and National's leader Christopher Luxon is campaigning on holding a referendum on it - to test whether the public still supports the model.

This would be the fourth public vote on changing the electoral system. A consultative referendum in 1992 indicated public appetite to change the system from the previous First Past the Post approach, and a binding referendum a year later in 1993 confirmed that, prompting the shift to MMP.

At the 2011 election, another referendum asked whether voters wanted to keep MMP or replace it, and what system would be preferred if it was changed. Almost 58 percent of voters wanted to keep it, an increase of 3.91 percentage points over the 1993 result.

First Past the Post was the most popular alternative, with 46.7 percent of people selecting that over preferential voting (12.5 percent), single transferable vote (16.7 percent), and supplementary member systems (24.4 percent).

The result triggered an Electoral Commission review of how well MMP was working, which recommended several changes that have largely not been taken up.

Another review in 2022 and 2023 by the Ministry of Justice heard from more than 1700 groups or individuals and also recommended multiple changes.

World.title: Hato Pāora College hostel closes after damning Education Review Office report
World.content:
A Manawatū school hostel's licence to operate has been suspended by education authorities, because "it is contrary to the boarders' interests for the hostel to remain open".

The suspension took effect at 5pm Friday for the hostel at Hato Pāora College, near Feilding.

The state-integrated Catholic Māori boys' school has a roll of more than 100 students.

The Education Review Office is responsible for school hostels and in a statement confirmed the suspension.

"The decision to suspend the Hato Pāora College hostel licence is on the basis that it is contrary to the boarders' interests for the hostel to remain open," ERO said.

"The decision is based on information obtained through carrying out ERO's statutory functions in relation to school hostels."

The ERO said that included information obtained during an inspection of the hostel on Wednesday and Thursday.

"The statutory functions as director of regulation include helping to ensure the safety of students who board at hostels, including by making decisions on the suspension of hostel licences," it said of its oversight role.

Lexi Manuel, who has a son at the college, told RNZ she was disappointed ERO had suspended the licence.

"It feels as though this decision may have been made in haste, without fully considering all of the positive changes that have occurred and the significant efforts being made to provide a safe, supportive, and high-quality environment for the students," she said.

The suspension had a "significant impact" on her son's education at a crucial time of the year, just ahead of exams.

"He has come home to find himself without a school to finish the year. As a whānau this has created a lot of uncertainty."

Manuel said school principal Kahurangi Falaoa had brought positive change, and that the new hostels were welcoming, modern and safe.

"My experience has been the staff are exceptional and consistently demonstrate that they have the boys' best interests at heart," she said.

"My son's experience at Hato Pāora has been mana-enhancing. He has developed a strong sense of identity, made meaningful connections, and built lasting relationships.

"The support and aroha he has received have been genuine and instrumental in his growth and development. I am deeply grateful for the positive impact that Hato Pāora has had on his life."

Previous ERO report found no problems

A previous ERO report for the hostel in March 2025 found a clear management structure there, and thorough systems and processes in place for its operation.

"Boarder wellbeing is well monitored," that report said. "The hostel manager meets the hostel staff at the conclusion of every shift, where any matters pertaining to the wellbeing of boarders are discussed.

"The principal and hostel manager work closely together for the benefit of the boarders to ensure both education and wellbeing outcomes are positive. The principal is well informed about operational and student-related matters, and acts on these when appropriate.

"Boarding life supports students' learning. Boarders spoken to reported that hostel staff were caring and supportive.

"Whānau report that there is good communication between parents, caregivers, hostel and the school."

The hostel was expected to be upgraded last year, the report said.

World.title: Lightning strikes cause fires in Auckland during severe storm, rain passes over Far North
World.content:
Lightning strikes caused three fires in Auckland Friday afternoon, as violent thunderstorms moved across the region.

A red alert went out for Kaipara, Auckland City, Waitākere, Franklin, Rodney and Albany about 3pm and lifted just after 4pm.

On Friday night, MetService issued severe thunderstorm watches for large parts of the North Island, warning of localised downpours and possible flash flooding.

The watch for northern areas, including Northland, Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty, was in place from midnight until midday Saturday.

A separate watch covers southern areas, including Wellington, Wairarapa and Manawatū, until Saturday evening.

MetService said rainfall rates could reach 40 millimetres an hour, increasing the risk of surface flooding, slips and hazardous driving conditions.

MetService said 1170 lightning strikes were detected on Friday before 5.30pm, including 280 over Auckland.

Embedded content removed for printing https://twitter.com/MetService/status/2118560448786448761

Fire and Emergency shift manager Colin Underdown said fire crews responded to about 30 jobs, including lightning-related blazes in Westhaven, Westmere and Albany.

Voting booths at the PAK'nSAVE Māngere supermarket carpark and at Old Flat Bush School Hall in Takanini closed early because of the weather.

There were also a small number of properties affected by surface flooding.

Lines company Vector reported a handful of power outages, mainly in the north and west of the region.

Delays and cancelations on the east-west and Onehunga-west rail lines from a storm-related power outage between Sunnyvale and Mangawhau was likely to cause further travel disruption.

The barrier arms at Rossgrove Terrace level crossing were down after a power cut caused a signaling fault.

An Auckland Airport spokesperson says a lightning alert was in place for around 20 minutes this afternoon, which meant a small number of aircraft were unable to refuel, in line with standard safety procedures.

There were no resulting impacts to flight schedules, they say.

Metservice has now cancelled the severe weather warning for the Auckland region though a thunderstorm watch remains in place until 11am Saturday.

Heavy rain in Northland

A band of heavy rain passing over the top of the Far North has so far caused no significant flooding, Kaitāia's fire chief says.

In fact, Craig Rogers said every farmer in the district and every homeowner relying on rainwater tanks would be delighted with the downpour after an unusually dry spring so far.

"We've had a good bit of warm rain, with thunder mixed in. It's not enough but the farmers will be happy."

Rogers said the rain peaked around 1pm and had now eased to showers.

The rain was light enough now that he was able to go back to his golf after taking shelter at the proverbial 19th hole.

"We just sat it out," he said.

Around 2pm the MetService rain radar showed the band of heavy rain making its way south over Northland with particularly intense falls over Doubtless Bay, inland from the Bay of Islands and over the Kaipara Harbour.

Northland Regional Council rainfall data shows the heaviest rain so far, 30mm per hour, was recorded near Pawarenga in North Hokianga in the hour to 1pm.

Further south, Hakaru, near Kaiwaka, and the often dry Pouto Peninsula, both in the Kaipara District, were also experiencing heavy rain.

Regional council records show the last significant rain in the Kaitāia area was in mid-September.

World.title: Political donations tracker: The wealthy donors dominating large donations
World.content:
More than $8 million in large donations has been given this election year, with almost 40 percent coming from just 10 donors.

Throughout the campaign, RNZ has been tracking the money flowing to the parties and where it has come from.

Some of the country's wealthiest individuals are linked to the biggest donation totals.



Nick Mowbray donated $475,000 and Rank Group, owned by Graeme Hart, donated $800,000, according to Electoral Commission disclosures.

Their donations went to parties in the current coalition government, taking the total given to coalition parties to more than $6m, roughly three quarters of the large donation total. Parties not in the coalition received $2.3m.



Tech entrepreneur Brian Cartmell was the only big donor who gave to parties both in the coalition and outside of it, supporting ACT, NZ First and Opportunity.

But Opportunity’s biggest donor was board member Alan Wilderland, who has given around $221,000 to the party, both individually and through a company.



Despite being a large donor he says he supports Opportunity’s policy of a $30,000 cap on donations. The party says this would be among its “bottom lines” in any talks to form a government.

“To change the game, you have to play the game first,” Wilderland told RNZ.

The Green party also has a policy calling for a $30,000 cap.



The cap was a recommendation made in an independent review of the electoral system. A survey found 43 percent of people think big donors have undue influence on politics.

The review's recommendation was not implemented by the current government.



Academic Max Rashbrooke, who is also in favour of capping donations to improve trust in the political system, told RNZ there’s no incentive to change the status quo.

"That's why it stays as it is - not because the public likes it, but because politicians don't really want to change."

Here’s where things stand, as of 6 November, across all parties for declared donations of over $20,000.

To date $8,422,281.22 has been donated. Large donations made anonymously, classed as “protected from disclosure” add a further $629,322 to the total.

When the donations made to the parties in the governing coalition are combined, the spread looks as below.

Who are this election's big donors?

The following donors have given $100,000 or more so far in 2026.

Not all donors are individuals. Companies, trusts and unions also give to political parties. The chart below shows the split between organisational and individual giving over $20,000 for each party.

In the 2023 election, unions gave $335,000 to Labour. National received no donations from unions, but did receive more than $1m from businesses.
