Exploring the data in the below chart shows where donors have focused on a single party or donated to more than one party.

Each line represents a donor with wider lines indicating larger amounts.

How the money grew

Donations of $20,000 and more made from the start of the year are captured on the below chart.

If someone makes numerous donations under $20,000, once the cumulative total tops $20,000 it must be declared.

How much bigger could the donation pot grow?

The below chart shows the 2023 annual total of donations over $20,000, compared to the current 2026 total.

Some who donated in 2023 haven't given more than $20,000 so far in 2026 to the same party. The table below identifies who these donors are.

Each row represents a party. A donor may appear more than once if they gave to multiple parties in 2023.

The following donors haven't donated before 2026.

How we analysed the data

All original data comes from the Electoral Commission website. RNZ's analysis normalises names which may appear more than once, but with different treatment. For example a John Smith and J Smith with the same address are updated to both be John Smith. In some instances where people have given individually as well as jointly their names are collated. If Joan Smith had the same address as John Smith and had donated individually, as well as made a joint donation with John Smith, the name is updated to John and / or Joan Smith.

Donation dates are taken from the "date received by party" information. In some cases one donation entry will consist of several donations made over time. The date received is the date on the donation return and should be the date the total donated by the donor tipped over $20,000.

World.title: Ex-CFMEU boss admits to illegal tirade against AFL umpiring boss
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka is unapologetic for breaking workplace laws, with his barrister saying he did not "deliberately" wage a public campaign against an ex-building regulator and AFL umpiring chief.

Mr Setka, the former powerful Victorian secretary of the CFMEU, faces a fine of up to $18,730, but could be hit with a much heftier legal bill because the union has refused to indemnify his court costs.

The Federal Court on Friday heard Mr Setka admitted breaching the Fair Work Act by trying to coerce the AFL into sacking its head of umpiring Stephen McBurney in mid-2024.

Mr McBurney was the Australian Building and Construction Commissioner and participated in more than 50 court cases against the union between 2018 and 2023.

Mr Setka's barrister Margo Harris said her client should not receive a severe penalty.

She said he was now retired, in the middle of a divorce, and spent most of his time looking after his elderly mother.

"He doesn't express any remorse but he has made an admission that what he did was wrong," Ms Harris said.

Mr Setka was not in court for Friday's hearing.

Former union boss admits to breaching law

The development comes three days before the start of hearings in Victoria's Royal Commission into the state government's "Big Build" construction projects, which have been dogged by claims of widespread corruption and crime.

Mr Setka, who left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Mr McBurney, is also facing separate criminal charges over alleged harassment of the union's administrators.

In the Fair Work case, Mr Setka was still union boss when he made social media posts and gave media interviews over a two-week period, threatening that the CFMEU would disrupt or delay AFL building projects if it did not get rid of Mr McBurney, the court heard.

"This is going to cost the AFL a lot of f**king money. I hope it's worth it," Mr Setka said.

"Projects without our full co-operation are going to be a f**king misery for them. They will regret the day they ever employed him."

John Setka left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Stephen McBurney. (ABC News)

The Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) prosecuted Mr Setka and the CFMEU, alleging the demands to sack Mr McBurney were made because of his lawful work as ABCC commissioner.

On Friday, barristers for Mr Setka and the CFMEU admitted to the breaches.

Ms Harris said there was no evidence Mr Setka "actively sought" media attention, even though he made statements to newspapers, and appeared in radio and television interviews where he said the AFL should sack Mr McBurney.

Ms Harris also said Mr Setka did not "deliberately" engage in a media campaign against Mr McBurney, prompting Federal Court judge John Snaden to clarify what she meant.

"When I say deliberate, there's a range of deliberateness. It's not a question of being pregnant or not pregnant," she replied.

"It comes in the stream of the interview. There's a question asked of him, he answers it."

However, FWO barrister Marc Felman said Mr Setka was not forced to give interviews.

"There can be no question that this is a media campaign," he said.

During one press conference, Mr Setka said of Mr McBurney: "He's a zealot. He hates unions. He hates workers in general."

He also put up a social media post depicting Mr McBurney in a mock poster containing the words: "(Not) Wanted Dead or Alive".

Penalty to be set for Setka and CFMEU despite claims of new regime

Mr Felman said Mr Setka's breaches of the Fair Work Act were "very, very serious".

He said Mr Setka wasn't the first person to call for the sacking of an AFL umpire, but it became illegal because the demands were connected to Mr McBurney's lawful work in an old job.

Mr McBurney, who has umpired four grand finals, was backed by the AFL at the time and remains the league's head of officiating.

Stephen McBurney adjudicated 401 AFL games and is still employed as the league's head of officiating. (AFLUA Hall of Fame)

The CFMEU, which has since been taken over by administrators, could be fined up to $93,900.

Barrister Andrew White, for the CFMEU, called for the penalty to be moderated because the union's new regime no longer saw breaking the law as "the cost of doing business".

He said the cultural shift had occurred following hundreds of Setka-era officials being removed or leaving their jobs.

"A new culture of lawful but robust unionism is taking hold," he said.

Justice Snaden will set the penalty for Mr Setka and the CFMEU at a later date.

World.title: Baseballer loses sight in one eye in 'horrific freak accident'
World.content:
Adelaide's baseball community is rallying around a "tough cookie" player who lost sight in one eye after a "horrific freak accident" during a weekend game.

Veteran member of the Adelaide Angels Baseball Club, Tyler Forney, was struck in the eye by a foul ball off his own bat, during a double-header against Woodville on Saturday.

Close friend and long-time teammate Chris Congdon said Mr Forney was in the batter's box during the second game when the incident happened.

"His ball ricocheted off his bat and basically collected his right eye," Mr Congdon said.

"[It] resulted in him getting taken off to hospital by ambulance in a bad way and having significant eye surgery that evening.

"However, he's permanently lost vision in his right eye as a result of that.

"Anyone I've spoken to around the club that was there was just really mortified by the accident … it's a really horrific freak accident."

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was an integral member of the club since joining back in 2016, after moving from Arizona in the United States.

He said Mr Forney had a gifted athletic ability which he had honed while playing college baseball.

"He's a really really tough cookie, Ty — I'm sure he played through a broken hand for parts of last season," Mr Congdon said.

"He was a walking highlight reel, he would make plays at shortstop that just no one else could make.

"He just stuck with us and [he's] a massive reason why the last five years we've had huge success."

'So grateful' for support

A GoFundMe page has since raised more than $16,200 by Friday afternoon to cover Mr Forney's medical fees.

"He [Mr Forney] did not realise how much of an impact that he has had on people — not only in our club, but the wider baseball community," Mr Congdon said.

" He's a very humble person, but this has really, really taken him taken by surprise and he's just so grateful. "

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was being supported by his partner, two children and three stepchildren as he recovers.

He said while Mr Forney's playing career may have come to an end, the club is already talking about ways to transition him to a coaching role.

"He's the sort of person that is quite private and reserved, but when he speaks and he does, everybody listens, so I think he wouldn't have thought about coaching," he said.

"He had so much left to do as a player and still so valuable as a player."

World.title: Man sues former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May
World.content:
A man is suing former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May over an alleged brawl on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula.

The two players were previously charged over an alleged streetside altercation with another group in the coastal town of Sorrento on Boxing Day in 2024, but the charges were dropped in May 2026.

Mr Prestia, a former Richmond premiership player, had been charged with recklessly causing serious injury and affray, while Mr May, an ex-Demons player who retired this year, was charged with affray.

The incident left two men in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Previously, both Mr Prestia and Mr May strenuously denied their involvement in the alleged incident.

A personal injury claim is now underway in the Supreme Court over the alleged assault.

It is understood medical costs are among the damages being sought by a single plaintiff, who claims he was assaulted.

His name has been restricted by the court.

Court documents containing the exact details of the claim are yet to be released.

At a directions hearing in the Supreme Court on Friday, lawyers confirmed two more defendants were being added to the civil case alongside Mr May and Mr Prestia.

Their criminal matters remain before the court which means civil action is unlikely to commence before their cases are finalised.

Mr Prestia played 254 games for Richmond and Gold Coast and is a three-time premiership player.

It was recently announced he would join Hawthorn's coaching line-up for the 2027 season as an AFL development coach.

Mr May played 251 AFL games for Melbourne and Gold Coast and was a member of the Demons' 2021 premiership-winning squad.

He retired suddenly on the eve of the 2026 season.

Mr Prestia's employer and Mr May have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Aussie Calleja ready for winner-takes-all world championship weekend
World.content:
The biggest weekend in karting is here, with nearly 200 drivers descending on south-east Italy for the FIA Karting World Championship.

This weekend's event is the grand final of international karting, with drivers from around the world qualifying throughout the year for a chance to become world champion.

The OK (Original Kart) and OK-Junior world championships will be decided this weekend at the World Circuit La Conca in Muro Leccese, Italy.

F1 records broken by Kimi Antonelli in 2026 Kimi Antonelli sets numerous benchmarks that are likely to stand for some time.

There will be three Australians among the 194 competitors set to enter this weekend's racing.

William Calleja, Jenson Burns and Chris Lowe will all compete in the OK class, while Australian-born female racer Ava Jean Lawrence is in the OK-Junior event.

Calleja enters this weekend's world championship with a genuine chance of winning after a terrific season in the European Karting Championship.

The teenager from Victoria finished fourth in the championship, dominating the final round of the season in Kristiansand, Sweden, where he was fastest in qualifying and went on to win the final.

"It's great to have an FIA win under my belt, and I go into this very important race with winning experience in my hands," the Victorian said.

"The level of competition is the highest in the world in this category of motorsport, so winning any race at this level is a high achievement. I'm feeling good and looking forward to showing my best at La Conca."

The weekend's racing begins on Friday. Drivers go through qualifying sessions and heats in a bid to make it to Sunday's final race, which decides the world champion.

"It's a very mentally challenging race, and it will require proper preparation," Calleja said.

"I need to block out external noise and keep my eyes on the job ahead of me, not focusing too much on the end result but performing well in each stage throughout the weekend is what matters."

Burns, 16, from the Gold Coast in Queensland, placed 26th in the OK-N karting class at the FIA World Cup last month.

Lowe, from Melbourne, won a Victorian state title at his home track, Oakleigh, last year.

Meanwhile, Ava Jean Lawrence will compete in the junior class this weekend.

Despite racing under an Emirati licence, Lawrence is very much an Australian driver on the rise. She was signed to the Aston Martin F1 Academy program earlier this year.

World.title: Lynn's secret drugs ban revealed on BBL eve
World.content:
Big Bash League record-setter Chris Lynn's one-month suspension for a positive drugs test has been revealed, two months after he served the ban.

The revelation comes just days after the former Brisbane and Adelaide BBL big-hitter was linked with a move to the Melbourne Renegades for the season, which begins next month.

The 36-year-old was handed the suspension in August, after he tested positive on the day of England's T20 Blast finals in July, having helped Northamptonshire to the title.

After tests revealed an adverse analytical finding for cocaine's metabolite benzoylecgonine, Lynn admitted to using the drug days earlier.

The findings noted Lynn did not have a therapeutic use exemption for cocaine and that the cricketer had successfully argued his drug use amounted to an out-of-competition violation unrelated to sporting performance.

He was given a one-month ban, backdated to the period of between July 31 and August 30.

Lynn was set to play in Sri Lanka after the T20 Blast, but after one appearance he was ruled out with an unspecified leg injury on July 29.

Any further punishment would be at his BBL club's discretion, with Lynn available given he has served his penalty and is not on a Cricket Australia contract.

Lynn is the BBL's leading run-scorer and six-hitter, and has also played four one-day internationals and 18 T20 internationals for Australia.

He has also played for at least 25 different T20 franchises around the globe.

AAP

World.title: How a toy giraffe helped the AFLW Bulldogs rise back into finals
World.content:
Each week, Western Bulldogs fan-favourite Elaine Grigg looks forward to the side's player meetings.

It has been a good year for the Dogs, with eight wins from 12 games, finishing seventh on the ladder and back playing finals since 2022.

But reviewing the side's victories isn't the only reason Grigg likes getting together.

"This year, we've had a little mascot. Its name is Sawya, and it's a pet giraffe," Grigg told ABC Sport.

"Every week we spin a wheel, and someone has to take Sawya during the week … You have to make a video of what you do with it. So every Monday you present that, and it has been a really good laugh every week."

The "little mascot" a player takes home every week. (Supplied: Elaine Grigg)

Grigg, who joined the club as a high-profile draftee in 2023, said it has been a great way to get to know teammates and who they are off the field.

When she took Sawya, she said it was mostly work (as a student support officer at a school) and recovery, including a lot of time in the sauna. However, it has given away some teammates' hobbies, such as goalsneak Sarah Hartwig's creative side.

"That really surprised me," Grigg said. "How many different things she can do … She sews, she bakes, she does all these different things. I'm like, 'Twiggy, you need to start a business.' She makes all these different clothes as well."

More than bonding for the fun of it, Grigg said it's part of the Bulldogs's focus on building team connection, which has helped them immensely on the field.

Elaine Grigg is quickly becoming one of the personalities of AFLW. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

In 2023, the club hit rock bottom with a last-place finish, resulting in a review of its program and the appointment of a new coach, Tamara Hyett.

From there, it was a slow and steady climb back up the ladder. In both 2024 and 2025, the Dogs finished 12th.

This year, however, they fired back with a 26-point win over fellow finals team Gold Coast.

The Bulldogs' great AFLW turnaround The team's turnaround from rock bottom to the AFLW finals seems rapid but has been many years in the making. This is how they did it.

Many AFLW pundits and commentators have remarked on the side's new feel, particularly the excitement and "fun" factor.

"We know we need to lock in when we're at the club (and) when we're out on the footy field. But then it's the balance of having fun and also when it's time to be serious, to be serious as well," Grigg said.

"The connections that we have with everyone, it actually helps on the footy field."

The Western Bulldogs with their "little mascot" in Sawya. (Supplied: Elaine Grigg)

The side also dances before every game, with a new player picked each week to lead.

"That came about in our off-season trip. We were having a pool party and that dance, we did it, and that's carried on to our pre-game," she said, citing teammate Ellie Blackburn as the main instigator.

"It just shows how much fun we can have as a group, even before a game, to just let loose and be really connected with each other … It's something you look forward to and brings us closer as a group."

There was a lot of excitement around Elaine Grigg when she was drafted to the Bulldogs in 2023. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

On the field, Grigg said one of her favourite moments this year was Emma McDonald kicking a fourth-quarter haul against Sydney in round four, handing the Swans their first loss of the season.

"She went on a rampage to kick her three goals and to get us up and about," Grigg said.

"But it was her first one (liked the most). It was a team goal."

Grigg will hope for a similar finish this Sunday, when the Bulldogs face the Swans in an elimination final at Henson Park.

World.title: The anthem mix-up that became an enduring myth in the Alan Jones legend
World.content:
The engines screamed in anticipation as the grid for the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix waited for the signal to burst into action.

On pole was the indomitable hometown hero Niki Lauda, almost exactly a year on from the horrific crash in Germany that would leave his face permanently scarred.

A spot behind him was the glamorous and charismatic Brit James Hunt, a man that Lauda described as the only person he ever envied.

Niki Lauda and James Hunt were the stars of the F1 circuit in the 1970s. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

In third there was the American motorsport legend Mario Andretti, who ended his career with an incomparable resume that included an F1 championship, four IndyCar titles, and a Daytona 500 victory.

And 11 places back from there, waiting in a car that had never won a race, sat the understated and comparably unfashionable Alan Jones, the 30-year-old Victorian who had only joined the F1 season four months earlier to replace Welshman Tom Pryce after his horrific death at the South African Grand Prix.

Alan Jones (left) trains with Frank Williams, owner and founder of F1 team Williams. Jones's physique was often questioned through his career. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

Jones, who died on Thursday aged 80, didn't have the glitz of Hunt or the unwavering focus of Lauda. He would variously be described as overweight, laconic and underprepared throughout his career.

But what he did have was raw talent.

On that overcast August day, the underdog Aussie who used to sell Holdens for his dad at a car dealership in suburban Melbourne would shock the Formula One world with his daring and deftness.

Niki Lauda chats with Alan Jones in the pit lane ahead of the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAT)

With rain clearing as the race started, the grid was split between those racing on wet weather tyres and those on slicks. Lauda fell behind quickly in his Ferrari as it struggled in the slippery conditions, as Andretti overtook both the Austrian and Hunt following a small collision between the two.

Fans and pundits kept one eye on the superstar American, and another on the Swedish driver Gunnar Nilsson, who had made a stunning run from 16th into second on the back of wet weather tyres.

Quietly, Jones had moved up from his 11th spot into fourth, weaving in and out of the pack on slicks in a daring decision that other drivers had battled with.

Alan Jones in action driving his Shadow car at the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

As the sun came out, Nilsson was forced to pit to replace his shredded rubber, while Andretti's Lotus engine exploded both his car and his chances of victory, leaving Hunt to take the lead with Jones hot on his tail.

Lauda, now on fresh tyres and with greater control, hammered through the field to sit in third.

Hunt and Lauda, the protagonists of the 2013 Hollywood blockbuster Rush, were split only by the chubby-cheeked Aussie who let his racing do the talking.

Then, in a moment that would change Jones's life forever, Hunt's McLaren blew up in a burst of sparks and flames, his car slowing to a stop on the side of the track as marshals enveloped the vehicle in the thick dust of their fire extinguishers.

Shadow team members run onto the track and jump in celebration as Alan Jones claimed their first, and only, F1 grand prix victory. (Getty Images: LAT)

From the cloud, Jones would emerge as the race leader, holding off Lauda to claim the first of his 12 grand prix victories, and the only race win his team, Shadow, would ever claim in its eight-year F1 history.

Jones's team would run out onto the road to celebrate as the track announcer told the crowd, with uncertainty, that it was Australia's first F1 victory in seven years.

"The first Grand Prix win for Alan Jones, and the first Grand Prix win for the hard-working Shadow team," he said over the PA system.

"And, we think, the first Grand Prix win for Australia in seven years."

Jones would be surrounded by well-wishers in pit lane. With then-wife Beverley in one arm, and a bottle of champagne in the other, he laid a big kiss on Bev before popping the champers at the encouragement of his better half.

Alan Jones smiles as he speaks with fellow driver Hans-Joachim Stuck after the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

Taking a big swig of booze before being ushered to the podium and draped in a golden wreath, the band played in the background, leading to one of the more enduring, and ultimately false, stories that Jones would tell of his win.

"[The win] was a bit of a surprise to everybody," Jones would later tell Wide World of Sports co-host Daryl Eastlake.

"In fact they had trouble finding the Australian national anthem, so some drunk played Happy Birthday on a trumpet.

"That'll give you an idea how prepared they were for me to win."

Australian racing icon and F1 world champion Alan Jones dies Alan Jones dies a few days after turning 80, after a short illness. He won the 1980 Formula 1 world championship and 12 grands prix.

Audio from the day shows the story is not entirely true.

Trumpeters were blasting away somewhere in the distance playing La Cucaracha, among other songs, before launching into Advance Australia Fair as Jones accepted his trophy.

The Australian national anthem of God Save the Queen, which had been reinstated as the country's tune in 1976 after Gough Whitlam had introduced Advance Australia Fair in 1974, was not played.

It's possible that in the excitement and colour of it all that Jones had mistaken Advance Australia Fair for Happy Birthday to You. It's possible that he had blanked out the anthem all together and could only remember the joyous refrains of various other trumpeted songs before he took his place on top of the podium. It's also possible that he didn't even recognise the new anthem, which had already become the old anthem, before becoming the new anthem again.

What is unequivocal though is that in the coming years, F1 organisers came to know our national anthem well as Jones left his indelible mark.

In the golden age of F1, Australia's contribution to it was a bloke who looked more like a bank teller than a movie star.

And it's that understated legacy that has, and always will, fill Australian motorsport fans with pride.

World.title: Socceroos still waiting for World Cup payment from FA
World.content:
Socceroos players who competed at this year's World Cup are yet to be paid their match fees, three months after the tournament's conclusion.

Just days after it was revealed that both male and female national team players were taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) in a dispute over their revenue-sharing agreement, members of the Socceroos World Cup squad in North America are also chasing match payments from the FA.

The payments were due within a fortnight of the players' departure from camp.

Socceroos, Matildas take FA to court The players' union is expected to argue the revenue share agreement between the governing body and national teams players is not being serviced properly.

Australia was knocked out of the tournament at the round-of-32 stage in a loss to Egypt on July 3.

FA, which recorded a $23 million loss over the last two financial years, said tax complications in the US were the cause of the delay.

The body said it was working with the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), to "resolve the outstanding matters as quickly as possible".

"Football Australia is ready to make the match payments related to the FIFA World Cup," FA said in a statement.

"Before those payments can be processed, however, we require final specialist advice on the North American taxation obligations applicable to the payments, as well as some further player distribution information being provided through the PFA.

"Recognising the complexity of North American taxation requirements, FIFA facilitated access to specialist tax support for all participating member associations to help them understand and meet their respective obligations.

"We have been actively engaging with those specialist advisers since the World Cup to confirm the applicable tax and withholding treatment."

If a player sees game time or is an unused substitute for the national team, they earn about $6,000 in match fees.

The Socceroos played two friendlies against Mexico and Switzerland before three World Cup group games and the Egypt shootout defeat, meaning players named for all six games are heading into camp this week out of pocket to the tune of roughly $36,000.

There were no known payment issues for the four friendlies which took place in the US in the October and November windows last year.

Australia played Canada, the US, Venezuela and Colombia in North America in the back half of 2025 in the build-up towards the World Cup.

"It is clearly an unacceptable situation that three months after the conclusion of the World Cup the Socceroos match fees remain unpaid," PFA chief executive Beau Busch said.

"Any matter related to international tax was foreseeable and should have been addressed long before a ball was kicked at the tournament."

Members of the squad who faced Brazil in two friendlies in Queensland in September earlier this year are understood to have been paid in full.

The FA's delay in paying World Cup match fees has done little to quell discontent from Socceroos players heading into November's friendly window in the Middle East.

Some players have expressed concerns about travelling to the region — Australia will face Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman — in light of the wider conflict.

The purpose of those friendlies in the current climate has been brought into question since the Asian Football Confederation opted to delay the Asian Cup.

AAP

Tech.title: How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
Tech.content:
Note: Some spoilers for Control Resonant’s “Recursions and Iterations” mission follow.

One of Control Resonant’s most memorable missions involves time travel — kind of. There are certainly multiple timelines intersecting, or maybe overlapping, or maybe running in parallel. As protagonist Dylan Faden, you meet some of the researchers who are trapped in and investigating these timeline anomalies. Dylan’s first encounter with the researchers is somehow not the researchers’ first time meeting Dylan. But before we can learn much more, time glitches out, and they all turn up dead.

That seems to be the end result in every timeline Dylan comes across, even toward the end of the mission. What does it all mean for this timeline, the one we’re playing? Did the act of tracking down the researchers change our timeline? Are we in a different timeline entirely?

I wasn’t sure what to make of it when I finished the mission, and I’m not alone — even the developers at Remedy had trouble keeping track of it all. “I don’t actually remember where we landed on with the writing,” says lead level designer Anne-Marie Grönroos, turning the question over to senior level designer Admir Burnic. “Like, are the researchers even there after the mission is done? Are they still living their life?”

Image: Remedy Entertainment

Burnic isn’t sure, and I tell them I’m not entirely sure, either. But that’s not really the point of the mission. Like many of Remedy’s best sequences, the “Recursions and Iterations” mission is more about the unease of knowing something is wrong but not exactly what it is, the subtle horror of realizing generally what’s been happening but not necessarily why. Maybe the narrative team did establish a canon ending for the researchers and all three of us just missed it, or maybe it was ambiguous on purpose.

“It’s funny, when you’re dealing with this sort of time-travel stuff, timelines, whatever, there’s always this aspect to it where it’s almost illogical,” Burnic says. “So anything kind of goes. I mean, it could be intentional. It could also not be intentional.”

Prepare for (being inspired by) Titanfall. Toward the end of “Recursions and Iterations,” there’s a mind-bending combat sequence in which a bunch of Dylans, presumably from the other timelines, glitch in to join the fight. Burnic says this was a somewhat late addition inspired by “Effect and Cause,” a mission from Titanfall 2. There’s this time-travel mission in Titanfall 2. I was really inspired by that. I wanted to do something along those lines, but I was looking for “What’s the Remedy version of it?” And at some point I had this idea of glitches of Dylan showing up executing enemies. I remember it was fairly late in production, so it was a bit risky. I knew I can’t just go and pitch this. I have other stuff to do at the same time. So I was finding something that was relatively easy to do, a way to reuse Dylan’s animations that we already have. So I remember just going to one of our animators and going, “Hey, can you just throw me some of these animations? I have an idea.”

Either way, the storyline was a consistent standout for Remedy’s playtesters, Grönroos and Burnic tell me. What they had to fine-tune — and very intentionally so — was the language and narrative of the physical space. In the final version of the mission, Dylan has to travel between three different research stations in the labyrinthine Underpass, an expanse of floating concrete islands, to search for the researchers. Ambiguity here was going to be a problem.

“In the beginning, it was, like, identical stations, and we would more rely on the narrative content inside of stations to [tell you] what happened there,” Burnic says. In the final version, the stations share the same layout but are in visibly different states of disarray and disrepair. “We found a sort of language we could use. Station A was, ‘They were here for two weeks,’ station B [was], ‘They were here for three months,’ and I think the last one was the extreme one, which was like, ‘Oh, this was 10 years into this.’”

The team used that concept as a guide to visually differentiate each station from the others. “And that came very much from a need,” Grönroos explains. “When we had people playtesting that mission before, they didn’t even know how many stations there were. Like, there were people who thought there’s one station, maybe there’s six stations, who knows, because they look so identical and the environment is not that easy to tell apart, either.”

Concept art of the Underpass in all its brutalist glory. Image: Remedy Entertainment

There were, aptly, a lot of iterations of this, and art was just part of it. One of the biggest changes was mechanical: You need the Reach ability, which allows Dylan to essentially grapple over long distances, to access the Underpass area to begin with. This wasn’t an explicit requirement early on, but it makes the floating islands of the Underpass much easier to navigate. And “it was the navigation issues that were keeping this mission down” during development, Grönroos says.

But Dylan’s abilities presented their own problems. “If I remember correctly, we wanted to have certain beats, certain narrative moments, being represented to you first, and I think one of the biggest difficulties for me especially was that Dylan as a character is so powerful. The gaps he can close with his powers is quite insane, right? And it was so easy to break [the flow],” Burnic says.

“I remember at some point kind of realizing that, however you twist and turn it, you can never really guarantee that a player sees this, and trying to guarantee it will be a bad design because it will be too hand-holdy,” he adds. “It was more like these narrative moments were pieces of the puzzle, almost. So it doesn’t matter which one you get to first, but hopefully the player will be able to put them together once they have all the pieces.”

With a supremely powerful character like Dylan, Burnic says, “you need to lean into it and just design in a way where you can trust the player.” And with multiple timelines involved, seeing certain things out of the intended order wasn’t going to break the overall story of the mission.

I certainly got turned around a few times in the Underpass and doubled back to look for collectibles I might’ve missed. But I didn’t struggle too much, and I understood the story Remedy was trying to tell — maybe not every single detail possible, but the most important beats, and definitely the unsettling, otherworldly mood it created.

That was ultimately the “fragile balance” they had to strike, Grönroos says: trying “to have enough guidance that you understand what you are doing and where you’re supposed to be going” without holding the player’s hand.

“It’s in the DNA of the whole game, really.”

Tech.title: I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
Tech.content:
When I first read Allison and Nilay’s Verge review of the iPhone Duo, I was immediately struck by one of their complaints: that the cover display is too small. That’s not how the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels, I thought. Had they got it wrong?

After a week and a half using the Duo, I know exactly what they mean — and it’s not the screen’s fault at all. Apps that feel comfortable on Samsung’s short foldable and the similarly sized Xiaomi 18 Fold are often cramped and compact on the Duo’s cover screen, robbed of screen space by a right-hand rail that most apps don’t make use of anyway.

That’s just one of the ways that Apple’s first foldable feels fundamentally different from the Android alternatives. I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable that was released this year, from Samsung and Google to Honor and Oppo, and I’ve been surprised to realize that the Duo holds its own against them all on hardware, but is let down by iOS itself. For now at least, Android is slicker for folding phones — though I don’t know how long that will last.

Size, shape, and build quality

The iPhone Duo feels great. Mostly. Its curved frame and Ceramic Shield back have that ineffable Apple feeling, a sense of polish that helps justify the $2,000 price tag. The hinge in particular is satisfyingly smooth, closing and opening with a comforting magnetic click. Compared with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Xiaomi 18 Fold, the Duo just feels better.

But part of that is down to the Duo’s big drawback: its weight. At first it feels encouraging, the reassuring heft of all that glass and metal. Then I started using the phone, and I realized it’s just plain heavy. It weighs more than all of its rivals — even ones with larger screens — and any attempt to use the Duo one-handed makes that obvious quickly. It’s a little thicker than some other foldables, too, though in practice that bothers me far less.

Honor’s Magic V6 (right) is the thinnest foldable around, but not by enough to really matter.

The squat shape won’t be for everyone. The Duo is even shorter and wider than the Z Fold 8, though almost identical in dimensions to Xiaomi’s 18 Fold. I’m a fan of this design, which is both cute and comfortable when folded shut and gives you a natural choice of portrait or landscape orientations when open. The major downsides are that the short cover screen makes some apps awkward to use, and it’s wide when you need to stretch across to the other side — a problem worsened by some of Apple’s software choices. More on that later.

And while the Duo’s IP68 rating is an obvious advantage over much of the competition (only Google and Honor can match it), we’ve not seen many recent Android foldables struggle with hinge and display damage quite like the Duo. It’s still not clear how widespread Duo screen failures really are — they don’t seem to be as ubiquitous as Samsung’s first-generation failures back in 2019 — but non-impact damage like this is almost unheard of in modern Android foldables. It’s a reminder that the Duo is still a first-gen product while some Android rivals are into their eighth iteration.

The crease and screen

The screen is the Duo’s smartest hardware trick, and easily my favorite thing about the phone compared with other foldable phones. No rival offers anything like the “nano-texture” (read: matte) finish on the inner screen, which is easy on the eyes in more ways than one.

The Duo’s crease (right) is about as hard to spot as the Oppo Find N6’s.

Crucially, it also helps mask the phone’s crease, which isn’t quite invisible but is well-hidden. The Duo’s crease is somewhere in the middle of the Android pack: subtler than Google’s and Honor’s, more obvious than Samsung’s. Oppo’s near-invisible crease remains the best, but not by much. The Duo’s matte screen means it’s harder than most to see (though visible from an angle), but it’s still easy enough to feel, and a couple of friends have immediately remarked on it when trying the phone. Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem. The Duo’s crease is easy to ignore.

I’d actually say the Duo’s under-display camera is more of an annoyance. It’s not only inside an extra-pixelated circle of screen, but that’s the only patch without the matte coating, which makes it a little more distracting. I can mostly tune it out, but not entirely. I’d probably prefer a regular selfie camera tucked right into the corner, as on the Xiaomi 18 Fold and a few others, but I suspect opinions will differ here.

Finally, the Duo benefits from stylus support, letting you use a USB-C Apple Pencil on the central screen. This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option. I don’t have an Apple Pencil, so I haven’t been able to test it myself, but my colleague Allison is clearly a fan.

Cameras and battery life

Despite being the same size, Xiaomi’s 18 Fold (right) fits in a triple rear camera.

The iPhone Duo’s cameras, like those on most foldables, are fairly basic, with a pair of 48-megapixel rear lenses, one main and one ultrawide. It’s a setup comparable to the Z Fold 8, and both phones’ cameras are good, but not great. Most other Android foldables (including Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra) instead offer triple rear cameras, netting you a big boost in photographic flexibility. They often use larger sensors than either Apple or Samsung, so their main cameras are better, too. Still, Vivo is the only manufacturer getting close to slab flagship quality in its foldable cameras, and its hardware lags behind in a few other respects that would prevent it from being my foldable recommendation overall.

As for selfies, the front-screen camera is pretty basic, but you can take better shots using the rear cameras by opening the phone up and flipping it round. That under-display camera is worse than a regular selfie camera, but good enough so long as you only use it for video calls.

As for battery, Nilay and Allison had different experiences in our Duo review. I’ve mostly found the battery long-lasting, easily running a full day of mixed use. It’s got a higher capacity than either of Samsung’s foldables, so that’s no real surprise. It still pales in comparison to the two-day battery of Honor’s Magic V6, but once you’re past lasting a day, I think you get diminishing returns anyway.

Software support and multitasking

On hardware alone, the Duo holds its own.

So far, the Duo looks like a competitive foldable, albeit a little middle-of-the-pack. It beats its rivals in some hardware areas, falls behind in others, and has one truly unique selling point in the matte foldable display.

Unusually for Apple, the software is what lets it down.

The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo. In the best case, that means apps that don’t make full use of the Duo’s new right-hand rail, showing an empty black bar instead of app controls. Worse are the ones that don’t even scale to the larger screen — apps like Bluesky or Duolingo can use the whole display on other foldables, but appear in thin strips with huge black bars on the Duo.

This will improve with time. I’ve seen Google Maps, Google Translate, and Instagram update in the last few days alone, and no doubt more will follow. Some are already better on the Duo: Slack uses a helpful desktop-style two-column layout, while on Android foldables you just get the mobile UI but bigger. But for now at least, most apps run better on my Android foldables than on my Duo.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold (right) makes full use of its cover screen, though different app scaling can affect how useful that is.

OS-level improvements are harder to predict. At first I loved the idea of Apple moving key controls to the right-hand edge, but it takes up so much space that it leaves the Duo’s cover screen feeling smaller than it needs to: You get all the awkward stretching of a wide phone without the expansive screen space. Samsung and Xiaomi’s wide foldables may be about the same size, but in use they feel much bigger. I wonder how many software developers will follow Google’s lead in app optimization — it essentially ignored the right rail entirely while updating Google Maps, instead just spreading the map to the edge of the screen. It feels bigger and better than most other Duo apps as a result.

And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones. Sometimes, moving backward in an app requires a button in the right rail, sometimes one in the top-left corner, sometimes a swipe from the left-hand edge of the screen. It’s annoyingly inconsistent, and more often than not requires stretching across the phone’s width, whether it’s open or closed. Being able to swipe back from either side of the screen gives Android foldables a huge advantage in one-handed use.

Xiaomi’s 18 Fold (right) has substantially more flexible multitasking than the Duo.

As for multitasking, the Duo is well behind the competition. You can run two apps at once in split-screen, but only in landscape mode, and each must take up exactly half the display. Compare this to Oppo, which allows you to fluidly move between multiple split-screen apps and floating windows; or Xiaomi, which allows up to six apps to run side by side in split-screen, and Apple’s implementation feels downright basic. These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day.

The bottom line

Apple hasn’t waded into the foldable market and fixed all its flaws. If anything, “crackgate” is proof that it’s still playing catch-up with the Android alternatives, which have a few years of fine-tuning behind them. Many are still lighter, and thinner, and have subtler creases than the Duo, or bigger batteries and better cameras. In broad strokes, though, this hardware is up to scratch — and, crucially, on par with its most direct worldwide rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

For now, though, Android has the software edge. Google has worked hard to make its OS adaptable to various screen sizes so most apps take full advantage of the bigger inner screen while individual OEMs have designed ambitious multitasking tools. That isn’t yet true for iOS, and some of Apple’s own software tweaks in the OS make things more awkward still. It’s those that I’m worried about long term. The best thing about foldables is their flexibility — something Apple itself often lacks. If the Duo is going to catch up to Android, Apple might have to adapt.
